method: 7-stage multi-agent pipeline, <=10 concurrent; 97 deep-reads vs primary sources; 39 skeptical verifications (30 confirmed, 9 corrected)

papers.title: TPP: Transparent Page Placement for CXL-Enabled Tiered-Memory
papers.venue: ASPLOS 2023 (28th ACM ASPLOS, Volume 3; DOI 10.1145/3582016.3582063)
papers.numCXLDevices: functional-validation testbed: unspecified number of pre-production FPGA CXL 1.1 expansion cards (count never stated); performance-evaluation testbed: 0 (dual-socket NUMA emulation, one CPU-less memory node)
papers.mainProblem: Datacenter memory is a dominant cost (Meta production data) and DRAM cannot scale with compute; CXL enables a second, slower memory tier, but default Linux memory management (allocation, reclaim, NUMA balancing) is oblivious to tiered memory — hot pages get trapped on the slow CXL node and applications lose performance, while manual/application-level placement is impractical at fleet scale.
papers.mainIdea: TPP: an OS-kernel-transparent page placement mechanism for CXL memory exposed as a CPU-less NUMA node, with three components — (a) lightweight reclamation that demotes cold pages to the CXL node, (b) decoupled allocation vs. reclamation watermarks to keep free-page headroom on the fast node, (c) reactive hot-page promotion from CXL back to local DRAM — plus page-type-aware allocation (e.g., steering cold file-backed pages to CXL). Preceded by Chameleon, a PEBS-based user-space tool to characterize production applications' page temperature. Most TPP patches merged in Linux v5.18.
papers.hardwareEnv: Functional validation: "a number of pre-production x86 CPUs with FPGA-based CXL-Memory expansion card that support CXL 1.1 specification" (CPU model, DRAM size, card capacity/link width all undisclosed); the FPGA cards have "around 250ns higher latency than our eventual target" so they are used only for functional validation. Performance evaluation: dual-socket x86 systems configured "to mimic our target CXL-enabled system's characteristics (one memory node with all active CPU cores and one CPU-less memory node) according to the guidance of our CPU vendors" — i.e., remote-socket CPUs disabled, remote memory acts as the CXL tier. TPP implemented on Linux kernel v5.12. Local:CXL capacity ratios of 2:1 and 1:4 tested. Paper states "CXL adds around 50-100 nanoseconds of extra latency over normal DRAM access" as the design assumption.
papers.evalSetup: Production Meta datacenter applications: Web1, Web2, Cache1, Cache2, Data Warehouse, Ads characterized with Chameleon (PEBS-based); performance evaluation focuses on Web1, Cache1, Cache2, Data Warehouse run under two local:CXL capacity ratios (2:1 and 1:4). Baseline runs disable the memory node and CPU cores on one socket. Metrics: application throughput relative to all-local-DRAM ideal, fraction of hot pages trapped on CXL node, migration overheads.
papers.baselines: Default Linux (v5.12 memory management), Linux NUMA Balancing (AutoNUMA), AutoTiering, TMO (Meta's Transparent Memory Offloading) mentioned in characterization context; ideal = 100% local DRAM.
papers.keyFindings: TPP achieves near-ideal performance: e.g., Web1 (2:1) 99.5% of all-DRAM throughput vs 83.5% for default Linux; Cache1 (2:1) 99.9% vs 97.0%; Cache1 (1:4) 99.5% vs 86.0%. Overall "TPP improves default Linux's performance by up to 18%" and "outperforms NUMA Balancing and AutoTiering by 5–17%". Default Linux traps hot pages on the CXL node (e.g., for Cache1 at 1:4 only 8% of hot pages escape; Cache2 at 1:4 loses 18% throughput with only 14% of anon pages local). Most TPP patches merged into Linux v5.18.
papers.limitations: (1) Performance numbers come from dual-socket NUMA emulation, not real CXL silicon — the FPGA CXL 1.1 cards were used only for functional validation and admittedly have ~250ns extra latency vs the target part. (2) CXL is modeled as a single CPU-less NUMA node; no multi-device topology, no per-device management, no CXL bandwidth-contention modeling (a remote socket has full inter-socket bandwidth, unlike a x8 CXL link). (3) Testbed details (CPU model, DRAM/CXL capacities, device count) undisclosed. (4) Single-application runs; authors themselves flag that multi-tenant/QoS-aware management is unsolved ("Integrating a well-designed QoS-aware memory management mechanism over TPP can address this problem"). (5) Page-granularity only; latency-centric hotness (PEBS/fault-based), not bandwidth-sensitivity driven.
papers.openQuestions: Explicitly punted in "Discussion and Future Research": tiered memory for multi-tenant clouds (QoS-aware management on top of TPP), allocation policy when CXL is used for bandwidth expansion rather than capacity, and hardware support for placement (memory-side caches, prefetchers, hardware-assisted page migration — "Hardware support for data movement between memory tiers can help reduce page migration overheads"). Untested: behavior on real CXL ASICs with constrained per-device bandwidth, multiple independent CXL devices, cross-device interference, tail-latency effects under co-location.
evidenceQuotes: We deploy a number of pre-production x86 CPUs with FPGA-based CXL-Memory expansion card that support CXL 1.1 specification. Memory attached to the expansion card shows up to the OS as a CPU-less NUMA node.
Although our current FPGA-based CXL cards have around 250ns higher latency than our eventual target, we use them for the functional validation.

For performance evaluation, we primarily use dual-socket systems and configure them to mimic our target CXL-enabled system's characteristics (one memory node with all active CPU cores and one CPU-less memory node) according to the guidance of our CPU vendors.
For baseline, we disable the memory node and CPU cores on a socket while enabling sufficient memory on another socket.
We integrate TPP on Linux kernel v5.12.

TPP has three prime components: (a) a lightweight reclamation mechanism to demote colder pages to the slow tier node; (b) decoupling the allocation and reclamation logic for multi-NUMA systems to maintain a headroom of free pages on fast tier node; and (c) a reactive page promotion mechanism.
Most of the TPP patches have been merged in the Linux v5.18 release while the remaining ones are just pending for more discussion.
We use two memory configurations where the ratio of local node and CXL-Memory capacity is (a) 2:1 (§6.1.1) and (b) 1:4 (§6.1.2).
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: TPP is the canonical kernel-tiering baseline and the direct intellectual ancestor of Memstrata-style work, but its performance evaluation is NUMA emulation and it collapses all CXL capacity into ONE CPU-less NUMA node — it has no concept of per-device placement, per-device bandwidth limits, or CXL-to-CXL interference. The requester's measurements (per-region ~35.5 GiB/s saturating at 4 threads; 2.0-2.13x victim slowdown under a CXL co-runner) are exactly the phenomena TPP's latency/hotness-driven model cannot see, and TPP's own future-work section concedes multi-tenant QoS and bandwidth-expansion allocation are unsolved. For the 4x CZ120 testbed, TPP serves two roles: (1) a must-have baseline (Linux v5.18+ demotion/promotion is essentially TPP) for both ObjPlace and any per-device scheduler, and (2) positioning ammunition — a top-venue paper whose single-node, emulated-latency assumptions can be empirically falsified on real multi-device silicon.

papers.title: Memtis: Efficient Memory Tiering with Dynamic Page Classification and Page Size Determination
papers.venue: SOSP (ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles)
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no physical CXL devices; main capacity tier is 6x128GB Intel Optane DCPMM per socket; CXL evaluated only as a remote-NUMA-emulated tier at 177ns)
papers.mainProblem: Existing tiered-memory systems make suboptimal page placement because they use heuristics and static hotness thresholds that ignore the overall access distribution, migrate pages on the critical path, and mishandle huge pages whose subpage accesses are skewed, wasting fast-tier DRAM.
papers.mainIdea: A Linux-kernel tiering system that uses PEBS sampling to build exponential access-count histograms, dynamically adapts hot/warm/cold thresholds to exactly fill fast-tier capacity, migrates pages only in background threads, and performs skewness-aware huge-page splitting (eHR vs rHR benefit estimation) to promote only hot subpages.
papers.hardwareEnv: Dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 5218R @2.1GHz (20 cores/socket), 6x16GB DDR4 + 6x128GB Optane DCPMM per socket; single socket used; DRAM+NVM (300ns) and DRAM+emulated-CXL (remote NUMA socket throttled to 177ns) configs; Linux v5.15.19; no physical CXL devices.
papers.evalSetup: Eight memory-intensive benchmarks (Graph500, PageRank, XSBench, Liblinear, Silo/YCSB-C, Btree, 603.bwaves, 654.roms), 20 threads, fast:capacity ratios 1:2/1:8/1:16 plus 2:1, normalized to all-NVM+THP; scalability to 690GB RSS; CXL section re-runs vs TPP on the emulated node; single app at a time.
papers.baselines: AutoNUMA, AutoTiering, Tiering-0.8, TPP, Nimble, HeMem (and HeMem+ variant); TPP specifically for the emulated-CXL and 2:1 configurations; TMTS discussed qualitatively.
papers.keyFindings: Best in 23/24 cases; +33.6% geomean over second-best (up to 169% over state of the art); huge-page split gives up to +19.9% perf and -45.4% memory bloat; <3% CPU and <=0.195% memory overhead; beats TPP by up to 102.9% on emulated CXL.
papers.limitations: No real CXL hardware (remote-NUMA emulation at one fixed 177ns point); latency-only model ignores bandwidth contention; one capacity node, no multi-device or multi-tenant runs; PEBS cannot classify rarely-accessed pages (authors' admission); Intel-only tracking.
papers.openQuestions: Real-ASIC behavior with device bandwidth limits; CXL switches/pooling (explicitly excluded); multi-tenant QoS/interference; >2 tiers; page-table-scan hybrid tracking; AMD IBS port.
evidenceQuotes: We evaluated Memtis on a dual-socket server equipped with Intel Xeon Gold 5218R @2.1 GHz processors (20 cores), where each socket has 6×16GB DDR4 DRAM and 6×128GB Intel Optane DCPMM. To demonstrate Memtis's generality and robustness, we use two different tiered memory settings: 1) DRAM + NVM (Optane DCPMM, load: 300ns) and 2) DRAM + emulated CXL memory (cross-NUMA DRAM with increased latency, load: 177ns).

We emulated CXL memory using a remote NUMA node and decreased the cross-NUMA interconnect frequency. We set the access latency of emulated CXL memory to 177ns since previous studies report that CXL adds 70-90ns to local memory access [42]. Note that we only consider directly-attached CXL memory supported by CXL 1.1 since we expect accessing memory via CXL switches has a much higher latency, similar to or even more than NVM access latency.
As of this writing, there is no publicly available CXL memory hardware.
Similar to prior works [49, 68, 84], we use a single socket for our evaluations to avoid NUMA effects, which are out of scope of this paper.
Memtis performs the best in almost all cases (23/24), and its geomean performance is 33.6% higher than the second-best system.

However, Memtis outperforms TPP in all evaluated benchmarks by up to 32.8%, 102.9%, 39.2%, 27.1%, 16.4%, 12.4%, 32.3%, and 23.2% for Graph500, PageRank, XSBench, Liblinear, Silo, Btree, 603.bwaves, and 654.roms, respectively. Thus, due to its generality, we believe Memtis will be beneficial when CXL memory is finally available.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Memtis is the canonical SOSP'23 page-granularity tiering baseline, but its evaluation predates real CXL silicon: the capacity tier is Optane or a remote NUMA socket throttled to one fixed 177ns latency, with zero physical CXL devices, one flat capacity node, and single-application runs. It is purely latency/hotness-driven — it has no concept of per-device bandwidth ceilings, CXL-to-CXL co-runner interference, or multi-tenant QoS, which are exactly the phenomena the requester measured on the 4x CZ120 box (35.5 GiB/s per-region saturation at 4 threads; 2.0-2.13x victim slowdown). This makes Memtis a strong contrast/baseline for ObjPlace (page vs. object granularity, hotness vs. bandwidth-sensitivity signals) and leaves the per-device-independent-resource direction entirely open. Practical caveat for reproduction on the AMD EPYC 9745 host: Memtis's tracking is built on Intel PEBS; an IBS port would be needed.
couldNotVerify: Exact mechanism/frequency value used to throttle the cross-NUMA interconnect for CXL emulation (paper states only that the frequency was decreased to reach 177ns)
CXL link width/bandwidth characteristics of the emulated tier (never stated; emulation targets latency only)

papers.title: Direct Access, High-Performance Memory Disaggregation with DirectCXL
papers.venue: USENIX ATC (2022 USENIX Annual Technical Conference), pp. 287-294 (short paper)
papers.numCXLDevices: 4 (custom FPGA CXL memory add-in-cards, each with 8 DDR4 DIMMs; 32 DRAM modules total), connected to 4 FPGA RISC-V hosts via a custom CXL 2.0 switch
papers.mainProblem: Pre-CXL memory disaggregation (page-based swap and object-based KVS systems) requires RDMA-style networks with redundant data copies between host and remote memory plus software-fabric intervention (page-fault handling, kswapd, KV hashing), making remote memory latency orders of magnitude worse than local DRAM. No real CXL product, platform, or OS support existed to integrate CXL memory into a disaggregation/pooling network.
papers.mainIdea: Build the first real end-to-end CXL 2.0 memory disaggregation system, DirectCXL: passive FPGA-based CXL memory devices (CXL controller + DRAM controllers, no remote compute), in-house RISC-V host processors whose LLC implements a CXL root port, a custom CXL switch with a fabric manager that creates 1:1 virtual hierarchies from each host to a CXL device, and a Linux "CXL software runtime" that splits HDM into cxl-namespaces exposed to applications via mmap — so applications access disaggregated memory with sheer load/store instructions and zero data copies.
papers.hardwareEnv: Fully custom FPGA testbed (no commercial CXL silicon or commercial CPU): 4 in-house RISC-V host processors, each 4 out-of-order cores at 100 MHz implemented on a high-performance datacenter accelerator card, LLC implements CXL RP; 4 custom add-in-card CXL memory blades, each a 16nm FPGA with a from-scratch CXL controller + 8 DRAM controllers and 8 DDR4 DIMMs (64GB) — 32 DRAM modules total; custom CXL 2.0 switch with fabric manager on another accelerator card; PCIe backplane (FlexBus); CXL/PCIe IPs (RP, EP, Switch) at 250 MHz; hosts run Linux 5.13 (RISC-V Linux 5.13.19). RDMA baseline hardware: Mellanox ConnectX-3 VPI 56Gbps InfiniBand RNIC with OFED v4.9.
papers.evalSetup: Host and memory node configured 1:1 for the RDMA-vs-CXL analysis. In-house microbenchmark issuing groups of random RISC-V load/store instructions with varying payload (64B-4KB) and working-set sizes (1K-1G), measured via register-level cycle instrumentation; latency breakdowns (Library/Copy/Network/Memory for RDMA; CPU cache/PCIe/Memory for CXL), latency CDFs, and a speed-scaling estimation to a 1.2GHz CPU / 1GHz CXL-IP clock domain. Real workloads: Facebook DLRM (68GB embedding tables), MemDB in-memory KV database from HERD (16GB, 2M KV pairs, 8M random Gets), and 4 Ligra graph workloads (MIS, BFS, CC, BC; 28GB), with tables/data in remote memory and code/static data in host-local memory.
papers.baselines: Local (host-local DRAM only, CXL nodes disabled); RDMA raw one-sided transfers (ConnectX-3 56Gbps InfiniBand); Swap = FastSwap (page-based disaggregation over RDMA); KVS = HERD (object-based disaggregation over RDMA) — all ported to the same RISC-V Linux 5.13.19 FPGA testbed.
papers.keyFindings: First work to bring CXL 2.0 into a real (FPGA-prototyped) system. 64B load: DirectCXL 328 cycles vs RDMA 2705 cycles (8.3x faster); vs RDMA's best-case 2027 cycles, DirectCXL is 6.2x faster on average; InfiniBand network alone is 78.7% of RDMA latency. DirectCXL best-case latency equals Local (4-24 cycles) when served from CPU caches; its tail is 2.8x worse than Local but the CDF shape tracks Local, while RDMA is 36.8x worse than Local on average. PCIe + CXL IPs account for 77.8% of DirectCXL latency (pure FlexBus 28%), so faster IP clocks help: scaled estimate is 426 ns for a 64B load at 1.2GHz CPU / 1GHz CXL IPs (Table 2: L1/L2 25ns, CXL IPs 239ns, FlexBus 57ns, DRAM controller 105ns). Real workloads: DirectCXL 3x better than Swap and 2.2x better than KVS on average; graph workloads 2.2x better than Swap (Swap moves 4KB pages to read 8B pointers); Swap spends 51.8% of execution in kswapd+FastSwap driver.
papers.limitations: Authors' own: cycle counts come from a 100 MHz softcore CPU with 250 MHz CXL/PCIe IPs, so absolute latency on production silicon is only estimated (426 ns projection); future work explicitly defers efficient kernel CXL memory management and an SoC silicon implementation. Methodology-evident: everything is in-house FPGA IP (no commercial CXL device, CPU, or switch), and the host is a 4-core RISC-V softcore, so cache hierarchy/MSHR behavior (16 concurrent misses) is unrepresentative of server CPUs; all performance experiments use a 1:1 host-to-device virtual hierarchy, so despite having 4 devices and 4 hosts there are no multi-host or cross-device contention/interference measurements; virtual hierarchies deliberately prohibit HDM sharing between hosts; no NUMA integration, tiering, or placement policy (HDM exposed only via mmap'd cxl-namespaces); no multi-tenant runs, no bandwidth-saturation study, no tail-latency QoS mechanisms; small workload footprints relative to modern servers.
papers.openQuestions: Contention and QoS when multiple hosts share the CXL switch or when a device's logical devices serve multiple hosts (the architecture supports it, but it is never evaluated); performance of the design at production clock speeds and on real CXL silicon; kernel-level CXL memory management (they punt to future work) and integration with virtual memory/NUMA tiering rather than mmap namespaces; coherent memory sharing across hosts (explicitly disallowed in their virtual hierarchy design); scaling beyond n=m=4 with cascaded switches; bandwidth behavior (the paper is almost entirely latency-focused).
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: DirectCXL is the canonical "real CXL beats RDMA" citation but is architecturally distant from the requester's box: a 100 MHz RISC-V softcore with FPGA CXL devices behind a switch, versus a production EPYC 9745 with 4 direct-attached CZ120 ASICs, so its latency numbers (328 cycles / est. 426 ns) are not comparable to the requester's 277 ns load-to-use measurement. Its most relevant aspect for the per-device-scheduling direction is that its switch fabric manager treats each CXL device as an independently assignable, whole-device resource (1:1 virtual hierarchies, no HDM sharing) — device-granularity partitioning with zero evaluation of cross-device interference, multi-tenant contention, bandwidth saturation, or tail QoS. That gap is exactly what the requester's ObjPlace follow-on could fill with measured CXL-to-CXL co-runner interference on real silicon; DirectCXL serves as positioning/related work (pooling feasibility), not as a competing baseline.
evidenceQuotes: In this work, we prototype DIRECTCXL using many customized memory add-in-cards, 16nm FPGA-based processor nodes, a switch, and a PCIe backplane.

Specifically, each CXL device prototype is built on our customized add-in-card (AIC) CXL memory blade that employs 16nm FPGA and 8 different DDR4 DRAM modules (64GB). In the FPGA, we fabricate a CXL controller and eight DRAM controllers, each managing the CXL endpoint and internal DRAM channels.

As yet there is no processor architecture supporting CXL, we also build our own in-house host processor using RISC-V ISAs, which employs four out-of-order cores whose last-level cache (LLC) implements CXL RP.
We expose four CXL devices (32 DRAM modules) to the four hosts through our PCIe backplane.
There are n numbers of compute hosts connected to m number of CXL devices through a CXL switch; in our prototype, n and m are four, but those numbers can scale by having more CXL switches.
Note that each CXL virtual hierarchy only offers the path from one to another to ensure that no host is sharing an HDM.
Our in-house softcore processors work at 100MHz while CXL and PCIe IPs (RP, EP, and Switch) operate at 250MHz.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that brings CXL 2.0 into a real system and analyzes the performance characteristics of CXL-enabled disaggregated memory design.
In contrast, DirectCXL only takes 328 cycles for memory load request, which is 8.3× faster than RDMA.
For real-world applications, D IRECT CXL exhibits 3× better performance than RDMA-based memory disaggregation, on average.
In this subsection, we compare the performance of RDMA and CXL technologies when the host and memory nodes are configured through a 1:1 connection.
The authors are extending the kernel for efficient CXL memory management and consider having an SoC silicon as future work of DirectCXL.
couldNotVerify: Exact per-DIMM capacity is ambiguous in the text: '8 different DDR4 DRAM modules (64GB)' most plausibly means 64GB per add-in-card, but per-module size is not stated.

Figure-only details (exact CDF tail values, some breakdown percentages in Figures 7/9/10) were read from surrounding prose, not from the figures themselves, since figure text extracted imperfectly from the PDF.

papers.title: LegoOS: A Disseminated, Distributed OS for Hardware Resource Disaggregation
papers.venue: OSDI (13th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation), Carlsbad CA; Best Paper award
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no CXL hardware at all; disaggregation is emulated on 10 commodity x86 servers connected by 40 Gbps Mellanox ConnectX-3 InfiniBand RDMA)
papers.mainProblem: The monolithic-server model makes datacenter resource utilization, elasticity, hardware heterogeneity, and failure isolation poor (Google/Alibaba traces show only ~50% CPU/memory utilization; motherboard/memory/CPU/power failures kill whole servers). Hardware resource disaggregation (network-attached CPU/memory/storage components) promises to fix this, but no existing OS (monolithic, microkernel, multi-kernel, or distributed OS) can manage a set of non-coherent, network-attached, independently failing hardware components.
papers.mainIdea: The "splitkernel" OS architecture: disseminate OS functionality into loosely-coupled monitors, each running on and managing one hardware component (pComponent=CPU, mComponent=DRAM, sComponent=storage), communicating only via network messaging (customized RDMA-based RPC), with no cross-component coherence and only occasional global resource/failure management. LegoOS is the first splitkernel: it exposes vNodes (VM-like abstraction) with Linux ABI compatibility; moves ALL memory hardware/software (page tables, TLBs, virtual memory) to mComponents, leaving pComponents with only virtually-indexed caches plus a small software-managed DRAM "ExCache" (extended cache below LLC); uses two-level distributed virtual memory management (coarse 1GB vRegions owned by mComponents, home-mComponent + GMM/GPM/GSM global managers, delayed physical allocation until first write); and provides best-effort in-memory replication (primary mComponent + append-only log on a secondary + backup file on sComponent) for memory failure.
papers.hardwareEnv: Cluster of 10 machines, each with 2x Intel Xeon E5-2620 2.40GHz, 128 GB DRAM, and one 40 Gbps Mellanox ConnectX-3 InfiniBand adapter, connected by a Mellanox 40 Gbps IB switch; comparison Linux is v4.9.47. NO real disaggregated hardware and NO CXL: pComponents emulated by limiting a server's usable DRAM and configuring it as software-managed ExCache (paged, 4KB lines); mComponents/sComponents emulated by limiting a server to 2 (up to 2-5) usable cores. Storage microbenchmark uses a Samsung PM1725s NVMe SSD. LegoOS itself is 206K SLOC C on x86-64 (56K for drivers), supporting 113 Linux syscalls. Fetching an ExCache line from an mComponent takes ~6.5 us.
papers.evalSetup: Micro- and macro-benchmarks plus two unmodified applications. Microbenchmarks: network latency (LegoOS-RPC-over-IB vs LegoOS-socket-over-IB vs Linux IPoIB, 128B-4KB messages); memory throughput (per-thread 1M sequential 4KB loads with a huge empty 32GB ExCache so every access is a cold miss to the mComponent, varying 1-8 worker threads and 1-2 mComponents); storage throughput (single-thread 4KB seq/random read/write over a 25GB file on the NVMe SSD, fsync after each write). PARSEC: BlackScholes, Freqmine, StreamCluster (1 pComponent w/ 128MB ExCache, 1 mComponent, 1 sComponent; 1 and 4 workload threads). Applications: unmodified TensorFlow (Cifar-10, 256MB 64-way ExCache, 0.9GB working set) and Phoenix MapReduce (Wikipedia dataset, 512MB ExCache, 1.7GB working set), 4 threads, ExCache set to ~25% of working set; sweeps of ExCache size, eviction policy (FIFO vs LRU, bitmap vs free-list, piggyback flush+fetch), 1-4 mComponents, replication on/off; a multi-application run of TensorFlow+Phoenix in 2P1M and 1P2M configurations; and an analytical failure study computing MTTF from published per-device replacement statistics.
papers.baselines: Monolithic Linux server v4.9.47 with all working set in memory; Linux with swap to local high-end NVMe SSD; Linux with swap to local ramdisk; InfiniSwap (RDMA remote-memory swapping); Linux IPoIB for network microbenchmarks; single-node Linux for memory/storage microbenchmarks.
papers.keyFindings: (1) With ExCache = ~25% of working set, LegoOS is only 1.68x (TensorFlow) and 1.34x (Phoenix) slower than a monolithic Linux server holding the entire working set (abstract states 1.3x-1.7x across workloads). (2) Against Linux with the same memory size swapping to SSD/ramdisk or InfiniSwap network swap, LegoOS is 0.8x-3.2x (mostly faster, even beating ramdisk swap). (3) Analytical MTTF: LegoOS 6.8-8.7 years vs 5.8 years for an equivalent monolithic cluster, a 17%-49% improvement, while improving resource packing (on-demand allocation from separate CPU/memory pools). (4) LegoOS RPC-over-IB latency far below Linux IPoIB; network stack + RPC optimizations gave up to 50% improvement; piggybacking dirty-flush with miss-fetch and p-local zero-fill lines add up to 5%. (5) Going from 1 to 4 mComponents LOWERS performance by up to 6% (piggyback optimization only works when flush and fetch target the same mComponent); memory replication costs 2%-23%. (6) FIFO beats LRU for ExCache eviction (LRU suffers lock contention); associativity benefit plateaus beyond 512-way. (7) In the 2P1M multi-app run, both applications suffer because their requests saturate the single mComponent's worker threads.
papers.limitations: Authors' own: no real disaggregation hardware exists, so everything is emulated on commodity servers over InfiniBand ("Since there is no real resource disaggregation hardware, we emulate..."); memory monitor is purely software and its worker-thread count bottlenecks throughput (they suggest future FPGA/many-core mComponents); no writable shared memory across processes (MAP_SHARED apps must be adapted); only mComponent failure is handled — pComponent failure and storage replication are left to future work; secondary-mComponent failure just restarts replication; no memory data migration, so their load-balancing mechanism shows little benefit; large-scale resource management declared out of scope; MTTF analysis excludes transient failures and is analytical, not fault-injection. Evident from methodology: microsecond-scale RDMA emulation (6.5 us ExCache miss) does not model real memory-bus-attached disaggregated memory; small scale (10 machines, max 4 mComponents); only two real applications (TensorFlow on Cifar-10, Phoenix), 4 threads each; only one two-application co-run experiment, no multi-tenant isolation/QoS or tail-latency evaluation; ExCache line fixed at 4KB pages due to x86 paging constraints.
papers.openQuestions: Handling pComponent failure; storage (sComponent) reliability inside LegoOS; memory migration between mComponents and real load-balancing policies; hardware implementations of memory monitors (ASIC/FPGA/cheap cores) and how much parallelism real mComponents need; scaling global resource management to the envisioned hundreds-to-thousands of components; supporting other hardware (GPU, NVM, DPU) as components; multi-tenant sharing of components (each component can host multiple vNodes, but isolation/interference between them is never evaluated); performance under real (non-emulated) disaggregated memory latencies.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Foundational positioning/related-work material, not a source of transferable numbers: LegoOS's "memory components" are RDMA-emulated servers with ~6.5 us access, two orders of magnitude slower than the requester's 277 ns CZ120 loads, and there is no CXL, no bandwidth-interference, and no tail-latency study. Its conceptual contribution IS directly aligned with the candidate direction: each mComponent is an independently managed, independently failing device with its own monitor, per-device load-aware placement (GMM picks the least-loaded mComponent), per-device replication, and per-vRegion ownership — a 2018 precedent for treating each of the 4 CZ120s as an independently schedulable resource with per-device failure domains. Two evaluation findings are worth citing when arguing per-device management matters: spreading across more mComponents can HURT (up to 6% from lost locality/piggybacking), and co-running two apps on one mComponent saturates it — an early, coarse observation of per-memory-device contention that the requester's CXL-to-CXL interference work can sharpen with real hardware. Use it to frame the lineage (splitkernel -> CXL pooling) and to contrast message-passing disaggregation against load/store CXL, where OS-level per-device scheduling remains unexplored.
evidenceQuotes: Since there is no real resource disaggregation hardware, we emulate disaggregated hardware components using commodity servers by limiting their internal hardware usages. For example, to emulate controllers for mComponents and sComponents, we limit the usable cores of a server to two. To emulate pComponents, we limit the amount of usable main memory of a server and configure it as LegoOS software-managed ExCache.

We ran all experiments on a cluster of 10 machines, each with two Intel Xeon CPU E5-2620 2.40GHz processors, 128 GB DRAM, and one 40 Gbps Mellanox ConnectX-3 InfiniBand network adapter; a Mellanox 40 Gbps InfiniBand switch connects all of the machines. The Linux version we used for comparison is v4.9.47.

We use regular machines to emulate mComponents by limiting usable cores to a small number (2 to 5 depending on configuration). We dedicate one core to busy poll network requests and the rest for performing memory functionalities.

We implemented LegoOS on x86-64 and evaluated it by emulating hardware components using commodity servers. Our evaluation results show that LegoOS' performance is comparable to monolithic Linux servers, while largely improving resource packing and reducing failure rate over monolithic clusters.
With around 25% working set, LegoOS only has a slowdown of 1.68x and 1.34x for TensorFlow and Phoenix compared to a monolithic Linux server that can fit all working sets in its main memory.
Surprisingly, using more mComponents lowers application performance by up to 6%. This performance drop is due to the effect of ExCache piggyback optimization.
With better resource utilization and simplified hardware components (e.g., no motherboard), LegoOS improves MTTF by 17% to 49% compared to an equivalent monolithic server cluster.

papers.title: Demystifying CXL Memory with Genuine CXL-Ready Systems and Devices
papers.venue: MICRO 2023 (56th IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture), DOI 10.1145/3613424.3614256
papers.numCXLDevices: 3 physical devices characterized (CXL-A: ASIC hard-IP DDR5-4800; CXL-B: ASIC hard-IP 2x DDR4-2400; CXL-C: FPGA soft-IP DDR4-3200), but only 1 device attached to the server at any time ("our system can accommodate only one CXL memory device"); application/Caption experiments use CXL-A only
papers.mainProblem: Because commercial CXL hardware was scarce, nearly all prior CXL-memory research emulated CXL using DDR memory on a remote NUMA node of a multi-socket system; it was unknown whether this emulation faithfully reflects true CXL memory behavior, how real CXL devices differ across vendors/controller designs, how CXL memory interacts with the CPU cache hierarchy, and how real CXL affects latency-sensitive and bandwidth-intensive applications.
papers.mainIdea: First comprehensive characterization of a genuine CXL-ready system: a 4th-gen Intel Xeon (Sapphire Rapids) host with three real CXL 1.1 memory devices from different manufacturers, measured with Intel MLC plus a custom microbenchmark ("memo") for per-instruction-type latency/bandwidth (ld, nt-ld, st, nt-st), compared head-to-head against remote-NUMA-emulated CXL; in-depth analysis of the CPU/CXL interplay (SNC mode, LLC isolation breaking, on-chip coherence structure for cache-less CXL devices); application studies (Redis/YCSB, DeathStarBench, FIO, DLRM, SPEC CPU2017); and Caption, a CXL-memory-aware dynamic page-allocation policy that monitors CPU counters (L1 miss latency, DDR read latency, IPC via Intel PCM), estimates memory-subsystem performance with a linear model, and greedily tunes the DDR:CXL page-allocation ratio to use CXL as a bandwidth expander.
papers.hardwareEnv: Dual-socket server: 2x Intel Xeon 6430 (Sapphire Rapids) @2.1 GHz, 32 cores and 60 MB LLC per CPU, Hyper-Threading disabled; Socket 0: 8x DDR5-4800 128 GB DIMMs across 8 channels; Socket 1: 1x DDR5-4800 DIMM used as emulated CXL memory (remote NUMA); Ubuntu 22.04.2 LTS, Linux kernel v6.2. Three anonymized CXL 1.1 memory devices, one attached at a time: CXL-A (ASIC hard IP, DDR5-4800, 38.4 GB/s per channel max), CXL-B (ASIC hard IP, 2x DDR4-2400, 19.2 GB/s per channel), CXL-C (FPGA soft IP, DDR4-3200, 25.6 GB/s per channel). Device vendors, capacities, and CXL link widths are not disclosed. SNC (sub-NUMA clustering) mode used for application experiments (2 local DDR5 channels + 1 CXL channel per SNC node).
papers.evalSetup: Microbenchmarks: Intel MLC (pointer-chasing latency, bandwidth at various read:write ratios) and custom "memo" tool measuring random-parallel latency and sequential bandwidth per instruction type (temporal/non-temporal loads and stores, AVX-512), rdtsc-timed, median of 10,000 repetitions. Latency-sensitive apps: Redis with YCSB (uniform keys), DeathStarBench social-network microservices (compose posts, read user timelines, mixed) in Docker, FIO with 4 GB page cache (Zipfian). Throughput apps: DLRM embedding reduction (MERCI setup), SPECrate CPU2017 top-MPKI benchmarks (fotonik3d, mcf, roms, cactuBSSN) run as multiple instances or mixes. Page placement varied via numactl and a recent Linux weighted-interleave kernel patch (percentage of pages to CXL: 0/25/50/75/100%). Caption evaluated co-running SPEC-Mix, Redis+DLRM, DLRM.
papers.baselines: Emulated CXL memory (remote NUMA socket with one DDR5-4800 DIMM, "DDR5-R"); local DDR5 ("DDR5-L"/DDR 100%); static page-allocation ratios via numactl/weighted interleaving (25/50/75/100% to CXL); TPP (transparent page placement, OSDI'24-era Meta tiering patch) for Redis tail latency; default Linux NUMA page-allocation policy (for Caption's +24% claim).
papers.keyFindings: (1) True CXL != remote-NUMA emulation: true CXL gives up to 26% lower latency and 3-66% higher bandwidth efficiency than emulated CXL depending on instruction type and device, because CXL devices have no caches/cores so the CPU uses a fast on-chip coherence structure. (2) Huge cross-device variance: CXL-A shows only 35% longer ld latency than DDR5-R while CXL-B and CXL-C are ~2x and ~3x longer; bandwidth efficiency (fraction of theoretical max, All Read) is 70% (DDR5-R), 46% (CXL-A), 47% (CXL-B), 20% (CXL-C, FPGA). (3) CXL access breaks LLC isolation in SNC mode, giving CXL-bound accesses an effective 2-4x larger LLC (41 ns vs 76.8 ns for a 32 MB buffer). (4) Allocating pages to CXL raises p99 latency of us-scale apps (Redis) by 10-82%; TPP is 174% worse in p99 than statically allocating 25% to CXL due to migration overhead; ms-scale microservices (DSB) are largely insensitive. (5) Naive 50% CXL allocation can reduce throughput vs 100% DDR despite higher aggregate bandwidth; for DLRM at 32 threads, tuning to 63% pages on CXL yields 88% higher throughput than DDR-only. (6) Caption improves co-running SPEC CPU2017 throughput by up to 24% vs the default OS policy (19%/18%/8%/20% vs best static for fotonik3d/mcf/roms/cactuBSSN), converging to 29-41% of pages on CXL.
papers.limitations: Only ONE CXL device can be attached to the system at a time (stated explicitly), so no multi-device, pooling, cross-device interference, or per-device management is evaluated; application and Caption experiments use CXL-A only. Devices are anonymized (no vendor, capacity, or link-width disclosure), limiting reproducibility. Intel SPR only — SNC/LLC-eviction findings are Intel-cache-hierarchy specific and may not transfer to AMD. CXL 1.1 memory expansion only (no CXL 2.0 switching/pooling). Caption's linear estimation model was fitted exclusively on DLRM counters (authors admit this and note it "has the potential for further improvement by fitting counter values from a more diverse range of applications"); Caption targets bandwidth expansion only and is "albeit not perfect" — for Redis it is 8.6% below the best (100% DDR) allocation; desired latency counters were inaccessible ("we currently cannot access the corresponding counters"). No multi-tenant isolation or QoS mechanisms; tail-latency problems are diagnosed but not solved.
papers.openQuestions: Explicitly punted: multi-device configurations — "As future platforms accommodate more CXL memory devices, we may connect up to four CXL memory devices to a single CPU socket with eight DDR5 memory channels" (exactly the requester's 4-device regime, untested here); further enhancement of Caption is left as future work (they emphasize the need for a dynamic policy over its specific design). Untested: CXL-to-CXL device interference, per-device differentiated placement, tail-aware/QoS policies for latency-sensitive apps on CXL (they only show TPP and static splits both hurt), CXL 2.0 pooling/switching, behavior on AMD hosts, and richer performance estimators (ML models, eBPF/PMU counters are mentioned as optional improvements).
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: This is the canonical real-vs-emulated CXL characterization and validates the requester's methodology of measuring on genuine silicon (their 1.53x load-to-use ratio is close to this paper's CXL-A at 35% longer ld latency; their ~35.5 GiB/s per-region bandwidth echoes the paper's finding that devices deliver only 20-47% of theoretical channel bandwidth). Critically, this paper never had more than one CXL device attached and explicitly names 4-devices-per-socket as a future configuration — the requester's 4x CZ120 testbed realizes exactly that, so per-device placement, CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference, and multi-device QoS are genuinely beyond this paper's scope and citable as open. Caption (counter-driven dynamic DDR:CXL page-ratio tuning, bandwidth-expander framing) is the closest prior policy to ObjPlace and should be treated as a page-granularity, single-device baseline/contrast; the paper's tail-latency findings (10-82% p99 inflation, TPP 174% worse) directly motivate the tail-aware direction. Caveat: its cache-hierarchy/SNC insights are Intel-SPR-specific and may not transfer to the requester's AMD Turin host.
evidenceQuotes: We take three CXL memory devices ('CXL memory devices' in Table 1), each featuring different CXL IPs (ASIC-based hard IP and FPGA-based soft IP) and DRAM technologies (DDR5-4800, DDR4-2400, and DDR4-3200).

Table 1: System configurations — CXL memory devices: CXL-A | Hard IP | DDR5-4800 | 38.4 GB/s per channel; CXL-B | Hard IP | 2x DDR4-2400 | 19.2 GB/s per channel; CXL-C | Soft IP | DDR4-3200 | 25.6 GB/s per channel

Note that we enable the SNC mode to use only two local DDR5 memory channels along with one CXL memory channel. This is because our system can accommodate only one CXL memory device, and it needs to make a meaningful contribution to the total bandwidth of the system.

The server consists of two Intel Sapphire Rapids (SPR) CPU sockets. One socket is populated with eight 4800 MT/s DDR5 DRAM DIMMs (128 GB) across eight memory channels. The other socket is populated with only one 4800 MT/s DDR5 DRAM DIMM to emulate the bandwidth and capacity of CXL memory.

As future platforms accommodate more CXL memory devices, we may connect up to four CXL memory devices to a single CPU socket with eight DDR5 memory channels, providing the same DDR5 to CXL channel ratio as our setup.
(C2) True CXL memory can give up to 26% lower latency and 3−66% higher bandwidth efficiency than emulated CXL memory, depending on memory access instruction types and CXL memory devices.
Figure 3 shows that CXL-A exhibits only 35% longer ld latency than DDR5-R, while CXL-B and CXL-C present almost 2x and 3x longer ld latency, respectively.
Ubuntu 22.04.2 LTS (Linux kernel v6.2) ... 2x Intel Xeon 6430 CPUs @2.1 GHz, 32 cores and 60 MB LLC per CPU, Hyper-Threading disabled

papers.title: AIFM: High-Performance, Application-Integrated Far Memory
papers.venue: USENIX OSDI (14th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation)
papers.mainProblem: Datacenter memory is inelastic and stranded: servers run at ~60% memory utilization while jobs elsewhere are killed under memory pressure. Existing far-memory/swap systems (e.g., Fastswap) are kernel-integrated and page-granular, so they suffer up to 128x read/write amplification for small objects, page-granular (not object-granular) hotness tracking, kernel-crossing/page-fault overheads, and cores that spin uselessly waiting for remote data.
papers.mainIdea: Application-integrated far memory: expose application-level semantics to a high-performance userspace runtime. Developers use remoteable smart pointers and remoteable data structures (array, hashtable, vector, etc.); the runtime (built on Shenango green threads + DPDK kernel-bypass TCP) handles object-granularity swap-in/out, semantic prefetching, non-temporal access hints, a pauseless memory evacuator, and switches to other green threads while waiting on remote fetches. It also supports offloading light computation to the remote memory server ("active remote components"). Hot-path dereference costs are close to a plain C++ unique_ptr.
papers.hardwareEnv: Two CloudLab xl170 nodes (one compute node, one remote memory node): 10-core Intel Xeon E5-2640 v4 @ 2.40 GHz, 64 GB RAM, 25 Gbit/s Mellanox ConnectX-4 Lx MT27710 NIC each. Hyper-threads enabled; C-states, DVFS, transparent huge pages, and speculation mitigations disabled. Ubuntu 18.04.3, kernel v5.0.0, DPDK 18.11.0 (Fastswap experiments use kernel v4.11, the latest it supports). Far memory is a TCP/DPDK remote memory server; a secondary SPDK NVMe SSD backend exists but evaluation focuses on the remote-memory backend. No CXL hardware of any kind — the word CXL does not appear in the paper (2020, pre-CXL-hardware).
papers.evalSetup: Four workloads plus microbenchmarks, all on the 2-node compute/memory-server pair: (1) synthetic web-service frontend combining a remoteable hashtable (128M KV pairs, 10 GB) and an 8KB-object array (16 GB), 26 GB working set, Zipf-distributed closed-loop requests with AES-CBC encryption + Snappy compression; (2) C++ DataFrame library (24.3k LOC, 1,192 lines modified + 233 lines of remote-device code) running the Kaggle NYC taxi trip analysis (16 GB dataset, 31 GB working set), sweeping local memory 1-31 GB; (3) memcached-style hashtable GETs with Facebook USR key/value sizes, Zipf skew s=0 to 1.35, 5 GB local cap vs 10 GB data; (4) Snappy compression/decompression of a 16 GB array (30 x 0.5 GB files), streaming access; plus hot-path (pointer dereference cycles) and cold-path (64B/4KB miss latency in cycles) microbenchmarks.
papers.baselines: Fastswap (state-of-the-art kernel-integrated, page-granular far memory over RDMA); an idealized all-in-local-memory baseline; plain C++ unique_ptr for hot-path dereference microbenchmarks.
papers.keyFindings: AIFM outperforms Fastswap by up to 61x (hashtable at Zipf s=0.8); 6.8x higher throughput for 64B objects and 1.81x for 4KB objects. Web frontend: 20x Fastswap max throughput (370k vs 19k req/s) and 84% of all-local performance with 5x less local memory; non-temporal hints are decisive (temporal variant stalls at 140k req/s). DataFrame/NYC-taxi: 78% of in-memory throughput with only 3.2% (1 GB) local memory, >95% from ~20%; Fastswap gets only 20% at 1 GB. Snappy: near-local performance independent of local memory size due to userspace prefetching. Cold path 90th-pct latency: AIFM 18,582 cycles for 64B reads vs Fastswap 23,712 (AIFM overheads 888 vs Fastswap 7,191 cycles, ~10x lower); for 4KB reads AIFM is ~10% slower since its TCP transfer is slower than Fastswap's RDMA. Hot path: 4x latency / 2x throughput overhead vs raw pointer for L1-resident objects.
papers.limitations: Authors' own admissions: no TCP offloading or RDMA support (higher CPU overhead); a compute server connects to exactly one remote memory server; remote memory cannot be shared by different clients; local/remote memory sizes are fixed at runtime; prototype limited to unshared far-memory objects on a single memory server. Evident from methodology: no CXL or load/store-addressable far memory at all — far memory is microsecond-scale TCP to another server, so its cost model (kernel-crossing and amplification avoidance, green-thread context switching to hide ~18k-cycle misses) does not transfer directly to ~277 ns CXL loads; requires nontrivial application porting (5 person-days, 1,192 LOC for DataFrame); single-application runs only, no multi-tenant or interference experiments; small 10-core/64 GB testbed; bandwidth contention on the memory path is never studied.
papers.openQuestions: Explicitly punted: multi-server far memory, dynamic sizing of local/remote memory, sharing remote memory among clients, RDMA/offloaded-TCP backends. Untested and open: how AIFM-style object-granular, semantics-driven placement behaves when far memory is directly load/store-accessible (CXL) rather than runtime-mediated; object placement across multiple independent far-memory devices; QoS/isolation when several tenants share the far-memory tier; interaction of its evacuator/prefetcher with bandwidth saturation rather than latency.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: AIFM is the canonical object-granularity far-memory runtime and thus the closest published ancestor to ObjPlace's object-level DRAM/CXL placement — its remoteable-pointer API, per-data-structure memory partitioning, object-granular CLOCK hotness tracking, non-temporal/semantic hints, and pauseless evacuator are directly reusable design vocabulary, and a paper on per-device CXL placement must cite and differentiate from it. However, its far tier is a single TCP-connected remote server at microsecond latency: all of its headline wins come from avoiding page-fault amplification and hiding ~18k-cycle misses via green threads, mechanisms that are moot for 277 ns load/store CXL. It offers no evidence on bandwidth contention, per-device scheduling, or multi-tenant isolation — exactly the gaps the 4x CZ120 direction targets — and its explicit single-memory-server limitation means "multiple independently managed far-memory devices" is literally its stated future work.
evidenceQuotes: We run experiments on two xl170 nodes on CloudLab [25] with 10-core Intel Xeon E5-2640 v4 CPUs (2.40 GHz), 64GB RAM, and a 25 Gbits/s Mellanox ConnectX-4 Lx MT27710 NIC.
We use Ubuntu 18.04.3 (kernel v5.0.0) and DPDK 18.11.0, except for experiments with Fastswap, which use Linux kernel v4.11, the latest version Fastswap supports.
We integrated two far memory backends into AIFM: a remote memory server based on a DPDK-based TCP stack, and an NVMe SSD using an SPDK-based storage stack.
TCP/IP is the dominant protocol for accessing data remotely, and AIFM currently uses TCP/IP.

Our prototype is limited to unshared far memory objects on a single memory server. Future work may add multi-server support, devise strategies for dynamic sizing of remote memory, or investigate sharing.

The current implementation has some limitations. First, we do not support TCP offloading or RDMA, which would reduce CPU overhead of our runtime. Second, a local compute server connects to a single remote memory server, and the remote memory cannot be shared by different clients. Finally, the local and remote memory size cannot be changed at runtime.
AIFM outperforms Fastswap, a state-of-the-art kernel-integrated, pagingbased far memory system [6] by up to 61×.

papers.title: Clio: A Hardware-Software Co-Designed Disaggregated Memory System
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no CXL devices; testbed has 4 Xilinx ZCU106 FPGA-based memory nodes attached over Ethernet)
papers.mainProblem: Memory disaggregation research had taken two extremes: server-based memory nodes (high monetary cost, poor tail latency, poor scalability) or raw passive memory devices with no processing power (PDM model — performance, security, and management problems, requires memory pinning). Neither meets the combined goals of low cost, 100 Gbps throughput, microsecond-level average AND tail latency, TBs of memory, and thousands of concurrent clients.
papers.mainIdea: A hardware-software co-designed "middle ground": a hardware-based memory node (CBoard, prototyped on FPGA, anticipated as ASIC) that virtualizes, protects, and manages disaggregated memory in hardware. Key elements: a hardware virtual memory system with bounded-time page-fault handling on the data path (asymmetric design keeping most state at compute nodes), a connectionless co-designed network stack terminating at the memory node (no RDMA QPs/MRs), and a framework for offloading computation to memory nodes. Compute-node library (CLib) is kernel-bypass userspace issuing raw Ethernet.
papers.hardwareEnv: Local cluster: 4 compute nodes (Dell PowerEdge R740, Intel "Xeon Gold 5128" CPU as printed in the paper, 40 Gbps Nvidia ConnectX-3 NIC; two CNs also have Nvidia BlueField SmartNICs) + 4 memory nodes = Xilinx ZCU106 Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC FPGA boards ($2495 each: 504K LUTs, 4.75 MB BRAM, quad-core ARM Cortex-A53, two 10 Gbps SFP+ ports, 2 GB on-board DRAM), all connected via an Nvidia 40 Gbps VPI switch. FPGA modules run at 250 MHz, 512-bit datapath. Additional RDMA results from CloudLab with ConnectX-5. No CXL hardware anywhere; CXL appears only as a related-work citation ("coherent interconnect proposals" not yet built). Kernel version not stated. End-to-end line rate limited to 9.4 Gbps by the board's 10 Gbps port; 100+ Gbps numbers measured via on-board traffic generation; ASIC latencies are projections (scaled to 2 GHz).
papers.evalSetup: Microbenchmarks: read/write latency CDFs (16 B), throughput vs client threads, scalability vs number of processes (up to ~1000, connectionless vs RDMA QPs), PTE/MR scalability mapping up to 4 TB of virtual address space onto 2 GB physical memory, TLB hit/miss/page-fault latency breakdown, allocation/free latency and retry rate. Applications: image compression/decompression (1000 256x256-pixel images per client, scaling clients), radix tree search (pointer-chasing offload, 10K-1M entries), Clio-KV key-value store under YCSB workloads A/B/C (100K 1 KB entries, Zipf theta=0.99, 2 CNs x 8 threads, also scaled across 1-4 MNs), Clio-MV multi-version object store (1-4 CNs, 50/50 read-write, uniform and Zipf), and a select-aggregate data analytics offload. Plus energy measurement (CPU/ARM/FPGA cycles x Watts, omitting DRAM and NICs), CapEx estimation, and FPGA resource utilization vs StRoM-RoCEv2 and Tonic-SACK.
papers.baselines: Native one-sided RDMA (ConnectX-3 local, ConnectX-5 on CloudLab); Clover (adapted as passive disaggregated memory); HERD on CPU and on BlueField (HERD-BF); LegoOS; FPGA-resource comparison vs StRoM-RoCEv2 and Tonic-SACK.
papers.keyFindings: FPGA prototype achieves ~100 Gbps per memory node (110+ Gbps on-board for large requests, 128 Gbps max datapath at II=1) and end-to-end latency of 2.5 us median / 3.2 us 99th percentile with far smaller tail than RDMA. Clio is connectionless and scales flat to ~1000 processes and 4 TB VA, while RDMA degrades beyond 2^8 MRs (local) / 2^12 (CloudLab) and fails beyond 2^18 MRs; RDMA remote page fault costs 16.8 ms (ConnectX-4) vs Clio's small TLB-miss cost only. LegoOS peaks at 77 Gbps vs Clio's 110 Gbps and has ~2x Clio's latency at small sizes. Energy: 1.1-3.4x savings vs CPU-based and SmartNIC-based systems (HERD 1.6-3x more energy; HERD-BF worst); 2.7x faster than software SmartNIC solutions. CapEx: 1 TB server-based MN costs 1.1-1.5x and consumes 1.9-2.7x power vs CBoard. Clio's whole design uses 31% LUT / 31% BRAM of a small FPGA (VirtMem only 5.5%/3%), less than StRoM's or Tonic's network stacks alone.
papers.limitations: Authors' own admissions: prototype board has only 2 GB memory and 10 Gbps ports (end-to-end tests capped at 9.4 Gbps line rate; 100 Gbps results come from on-board traffic generation, ASIC latency is a projection); no built-in failure handling (replication APIs left to future work); TLB shared across processes and no per-connection bandwidth limits, so side-channel/DoS isolation is unaddressed; security depends on trusted CN attaching authentic PIDs; CN-side software stack became the bottleneck; energy accounting omits DRAM and NICs; analytics offload is slower than RDMA at high select ratios (FPGA compute slower than CPU). Evident from methodology: 4 TB scalability is emulated via VA mapping onto 2 GB physical memory; microsecond-scale network-attached latency regime, not nanosecond load/store; no cross-tenant interference or QoS experiments despite multi-client scaling; pre-CXL (CXL cited only as an unbuilt "coherent interconnect proposal").
papers.openQuestions: How to extend RDMA-style security defenses (forged-request attacks) to disaggregated memory; isolation vs cost/performance tradeoffs for shared TLB and per-connection bandwidth limits (explicit future work); failure-handling primitives (replicated writes) as API extensions; real ASIC CBoard implementation; offloading the CN-side software stack to a custom NIC; better on-board memory controller. Untested: multi-tenant performance isolation/QoS between clients sharing one CBoard, coherent load/store access semantics (CXL-style), and behavior with real TB-scale physical memory.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Clio is pre-CXL, Ethernet-attached far memory at 2.5 us median latency — an order of magnitude slower regime than the requester's 277 ns CXL load-to-use, so its mechanisms (RPC-style rread/rwrite, hardware page tables on the memory node) do not transfer directly. Its main value to the 4x CZ120 work is as related-work lineage and as precedent for two candidate-direction ideas: (1) Clio-KV explicitly scales throughput across 1-4 independent memory nodes (Fig. 15), the network-attached analog of treating each CXL device as an independently schedulable resource; (2) it argues that per-memory-node processing is where protection/management belongs, yet openly leaves multi-client performance isolation (shared TLB, no bandwidth limits) to future work — exactly the CXL-to-CXL interference / tail-aware QoS gap the requester's measurements (2.0-2.13x victim slowdown) expose on real passive CXL devices that have no such processing. Cite it to position passive CXL expanders as the "no processing power" extreme Clio critiques, with the host-side runtime (ObjPlace and its per-device successor) supplying the management Clio put in hardware.
evidenceQuotes: Environment. We evaluated Clio in our local cluster of four CNs and four MNs (Xilinx ZCU106 boards), all connected to an Nvidia 40 Gbps VPI switch. Each CN is a Dell PowerEdge R740 server

equipped with a Xeon Gold 5128 CPU and a 40 Gbps Nvidia ConnectX-3 NIC, with two of them also having an Nvidia BlueField SmartNIC [48]. We also include results from CloudLab [14] with the Nvidia ConnectX-5 NIC.
We prototyped CBoard with a low-cost ($2495 retail price) Xilinx MPSoC board [82] and build the hardware fast path (which is anticipated to be built in ASIC) with FPGA.

Our prototyping board consists of a small FPGA with 504K logic cells (LUTs) and 4.75 MB FPGA memory (BRAM), a quad-core ARM Cortex-A53 processor, two 10 Gbps SFP+ ports connected to the FPGA, and 2 GB of off-chip on-board memory.

The PDM model has been adopted by a set of coherent interconnect proposals [15, 24], HPE’s Memory-Driven Computing project [20, 29, 31, 77]. ... In addition to the above problems, none of the coherent interconnects or HPE’s Memory-Driven Computing have been fully built. (ref [15] = CXL Consortium; CXL appears nowhere else in the paper)
Our FPGA prototype of Clio demonstrates that each memory node can achieve 100 Gbps throughput and an end-to-end latency of 2.5 μs at median and 3.2 μs at the 99th percentile.
Clio’s default asynchronous APIs quickly reach the line rate of our testbed (9.4 Gbps maximum throughput).
For Clio, we map a large range of VAs (up to 4 TB) to a small physical memory space, as our testbed only has 2 GB physical memory.
