papers.title: CXL-ANNS: Software-Hardware Collaborative Memory Disaggregation and Computation for Billion-Scale Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.venue: USENIX ATC
papers.numCXLDevices: FPGA prototype (functional validation only): 4 ANNS EPs behind 1 CXL switch; gem5 simulation (all reported performance numbers): 4 EPs default, 8 for Meta-S, more in 4B-vector and multi-host scalability tests
papers.mainProblem: Billion-point graph-based ANNS needs tens of TB of working memory (e.g., Microsoft 40TB+, Alibaba TB-scale). Existing fixes either compress vectors (product quantization — fails to reach recall@k 0.9 on many workloads) or tier to SSD/PMEM (DiskANN/HM-ANN — 35.9x/77.6x lower QPS than a DRAM-only oracle). Naively placing all data in a CXL memory pool preserves accuracy and capacity but is 3.9x slower than the oracle because every access pays CXL flit-conversion/far-memory latency.
papers.mainIdea: Software-hardware collaborative design over a switched CXL memory pool: (1) relationship-aware graph caching — nodes within the innermost edge hops from the entry node are kept in local DRAM, the rest in the CXL pool; (2) ANNS-behavior-aware prefetching of likely-next nodes (82.3% of next-iteration visits come from the candidate array); (3) collaborative kNN search — each CXL endpoint (EP) contains a domain-specific accelerator (DSA) that computes distances near-memory while the host RC does graph traverse and candidate update, with hardware-config-aware sharding of the embedding table across EPs; (4) dependency relaxation splitting candidate update into urgent/deferrable subtasks for fine-granular scheduling.
papers.hardwareEnv: Two-part methodology. Real FPGA prototype (functional validation): 16nm FPGA implementing a custom CXL CPU adapted from a RISC-V core, 4 ANNS EPs each with four memory controllers (each a DIMM channel with 256GB DRAM), connected via a CXL switch; Linux 5.15.36 kernel driver; FAISS v1.7.2. Evaluation testbed (gem5 full-system simulation, cycle-cross-validated against prototype, Table 1): CXL CPU = 40 O3 cores, ARM v8, 3.6GHz, 64KiB/2MiB L1/L2 per core; local memory 128GiB DDR4-3200; CXL memory pool = 1 CXL switch, 256GiB/device DDR4-3200; storage 4x Intel Optane 900P 480GB (for DiskANN/HM-ANN baselines); CXL-ANNS DSA = 1GHz, 10 ANNS PE/device, 2 distance-calc units/PE. No production CXL ASIC anywhere in the paper.
papers.evalSetup: Simulation-based studies on six 1-billion-vector datasets from the BigANN benchmark: BigANN (128d), Yandex-T (200d, angular), Yandex-D (96d), Meta-S (256d, 8 devices), MS-T (100d), MS-S (100d). Target accuracy recall@k = 0.9 per BigANN guidance; k = 1/5/10 (k=10 primary). Metrics: QPS, query latency with breakdown (graph traverse / distance calc / candidate update / interface), resource utilization. Scalability tests: synthetic 4B-vector Yandex-D (3B noise-augmented vectors) with more EPs; multi-host test splitting EP HDM/PEs across up to 6 CXL hosts, with and without doubling EP count.
papers.baselines: Comp = product quantization (compression approach); Hr-D = DiskANN and Hr-H = HM-ANN (hierarchical approaches, both on Intel Optane); Orcl = oracle DRAM-only system with unlimited local DRAM; internal ablation variants: Base (all data in CXL pool, CPU does everything), EPAx (+EP-side distance acceleration), Cache (+relationship-aware caching/prefetch), CXLA (full system +fine-granular scheduling).
papers.keyFindings: CXL-ANNS achieves 111.1x higher QPS and 93.3% lower query latency than the tested state-of-the-art billion-scale ANNS methods, and beats even the DRAM-only oracle by 68.0% (latency) and 3.8x (throughput). Pure CXL pooling without the co-design (Base) is 3.9x slower than oracle (graph traverse 2.6x, distance calc 4.3x longer) but already 9.4x/20.3x higher QPS than DiskANN/HM-ANN. EP-side distance acceleration (EPAx) cuts distance-calculation time 119.4x and query latency 7.5x vs Base, with interface overhead only 5.4% of Base's distance-calc latency. Comp fails to reach recall@k 0.9 on 7 workload configs. At 4B vectors CXLA stays 2.7x faster than oracle; multi-host QPS scales to 4 hosts then drops at 6 hosts due to PE shortage (fixed by doubling EPs). Doorbell/notification overhead grows with EP count.
papers.limitations: All reported performance numbers come from gem5 simulation, not the real prototype — the authors admit "the prototype system does not offer the flexibility needed to explore various ANNS design spaces" and that there was a "lack of a publicly available, fully functional CXL system". No production CXL silicon; CXL latency characteristics are those of their own FPGA/RISC-V prototype. The design requires custom hardware (DSA inside EPs, a custom CXL CPU, CXL switch) that does not exist in commodity CXL 1.1/2.0 memory expanders, so results are not reproducible on passive devices like CZ120. Single-workload domain (graph ANNS only), single-tenant: no interference, QoS, or co-runner experiments; the multi-host test statically partitions EP resources rather than studying contention. Static/read-only datasets — no graph updates/insertions. Industry-supported work (Panmnesia), with GPU baselines discussed only qualitatively.
papers.openQuestions: How the design performs on real CXL ASIC expanders with production latency/bandwidth profiles and without in-EP compute; dynamic index updates and mutable datasets; contention and fairness when the CXL pool is shared by uncoordinated tenants (their multi-host scheme assumes cooperative static partitioning); quantitative comparison against GPU-accelerated ANNS; energy and cost analysis of DSA-equipped EPs; behavior under bandwidth saturation of individual EPs (per-device interference is never measured).
evidenceQuotes: Given the lack of a publicly available, fully functional CXL system, we constructed and validated the CXL-ANNS software and hardware in an operational real system (Figure 21). This hardware prototype is based on a 16nm FPGA. To develop our CXL CPU prototype, we adapted the RISC-V CPU [55]. The prototype integrates 4 ANNS EPs, each equipped with four memory controllers, linked to the CXL CPU via a CXL switch. The system's software for the prototype, including the kernel driver, is compatible with Linux 5.15.36.

Unfortunately, the prototype system does not offer the flexibility needed to explore various ANNS design spaces. As a remedy, we also established a hardware-validated full-system simulator [29] that represents CXL-ANNS, which was utilized for evaluation. This model replicates all operational cycles extracted from the hardware prototype and is crossvalidated with our real system at the cycle level. We conducted simulation-based studies in this evaluation, the system details of which are outlined in Table 1.
Although our system by default uses 4 EPs, our system increases their count for specific workloads (e.g., Meta-S) that necessitate larger memory spaces (more than 2TB) compared to others.

Table 1 (Simulation setup): '40 O3 cores, ARM v8, 3.6GHz / L1/L2 $: 64KiB/2MiB per core' ... 'Local memory 128GiB, DDR4-3200' ... 'CXL memory pool: 1 CXL switch, 256GiB/device, DDR4-3200' ... 'Storage: 4x Intel Optane 900P 480 GB' ... 'CXL-ANNS: 1 GHz, 10 ANNS PE/device, 2 distance calc. unit/PE'
in our prototype, an EP has four memory controllers, each having a DIMM channel that has 256GB DRAM modules

Our empirical evaluation results show that CXL-ANNS exhibits 111.1x higher QPS with 93.3% lower query latency than state-of-the-art ANNS platforms that we tested. CXL-ANNS also outperforms an oracle ANNS system that has DRAM-only (with unlimited storage capacity) by 68.0% and 3.8x, in terms of latency and throughput, respectively.
it exhibits 3.9x slower search latency than the oracle, on average
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Limited direct transferability: CXL-ANNS's evaluation is gem5 simulation of custom DSA-equipped EPs behind a CXL switch, not passive expanders like the requester's 4x CZ120, and it never runs on production silicon. Still, it is one of the few papers that treats multiple CXL devices as separately commanded, separately sharded resources (per-EP doorbells, hardware-config-aware sharding, per-device PE counts), and it shows per-device interface/notification overhead growing with device count — a data point for the requester's per-device-scheduling direction. Its hop-count-based hot/cold placement (inner-hop graph nodes in local DRAM, rest in CXL) is a workload-specific instance of the sensitivity-driven placement ObjPlace already generalizes, so it serves as related work to position against rather than a method to reuse. It contains no interference, QoS, or multi-tenant measurements, leaving the requester's CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference angle untouched.

papers.title: Pond: CXL-Based Memory Pooling Systems for Cloud Platforms
papers.venue: ASPLOS 2023 (28th ACM International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems, Volume 2; DOI 10.1145/3575693.3578835)
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no physical CXL devices; pool emulated via remote NUMA socket of 2-socket servers; multi-host pool savings from trace-driven simulation; the EMC pool ASIC is a proposed design, not built)
papers.mainProblem: DRAM is ~50% of Azure server cost and heavily wasted: 3-27% of memory is stranded at the 95th percentile (outliers 36%) because VM cores exhaust before memory, plus much VM memory is never touched. Cross-host memory pooling could cut DRAM provisioning, but must satisfy cloud constraints: opaque VMs (no guest cooperation, no page-fault-based tiering), NUMA-local-like performance, and low host overhead.
papers.mainIdea: Pond: small CXL memory pools spanning 8-16 sockets (analysis of 100-cluster production traces shows this captures most pooling benefit while an estimated 70-90ns is added over NUMA-local DRAM, vs >180ns for rack-scale). A proposed multi-headed External Memory Controller (EMC) ASIC exposes pool DRAM to multiple hosts via x8 CXL ports; memory is explicitly moved between hosts at 1GB-slice granularity. VMs see pool memory as a zero-core virtual NUMA (zNUMA) node so guest OSes naturally bias allocations to local DRAM. Two ML models drive the local/pool split per VM: a GBM predicting untouched memory from VM metadata/history, and a RandomForest predicting latency sensitivity from core PMU counters; a QoS monitor detects mispredictions and migrates VMs back to all-local memory.
papers.hardwareEnv: Azure production servers plus similarly configured lab servers: either 2x Intel Skylake 8157M sockets with 384GB DDR4 each (measured 78ns NUMA-local / 142ns remote latency = 182%; 80GB/s local / 30GB/s remote bandwidth, "3/4 of a CXL x8 link"), or 2x AMD EPYC 7452 sockets with 512GB DDR4 each (115ns local / 255ns remote = 222%). CXL pool emulated by disabling all cores in one socket and using its memory cross-socket; hyper-threading, turbo-boost, C-states disabled in BIOS. Modified Azure hypervisor instantiates zNUMA topologies; no kernel version stated. No physical CXL device or EMC hardware; CXL port latency (25ns round-trip) cited from Intel measurements, not measured by the authors.
papers.evalSetup: 158 workloads: Redis, VoltDB, TPC-H on MySQL, Spark, GAPBS, SPLASH2x, SPEC CPU, PARSEC, plus 13 proprietary Azure internal workloads; each run fully on emulated pool memory under 182% and 222% latency increases and compared to NUMA-local placement. zNUMA behavior validated with four internal workloads on production nodes (access-bit scans, PMU accesses to zNUMA). ML models trained/evaluated on production resource logs (100-fold validation). End-to-end DRAM savings from a second-granularity simulator replaying VM traces from 100 randomly selected production clusters across 34 datacenters over 75 days.
papers.baselines: Performance baseline: VMs entirely backed by same-NUMA-node (NUMA-local) DRAM. DRAM-savings baselines: a "Static" policy allocating a fixed pool fraction per VM (3% savings vs Pond's 7-9%) and Pond's individual models vs its combined model. Prediction baselines: threshold heuristics on "Memory bound" and "DRAM bound" PMU metrics vs the RandomForest. Latency/architecture comparison: CXL-switch-based pool designs vs the multi-headed EMC.
papers.keyFindings: (1) Pooling across 8-16 sockets captures most benefit; estimated CXL latency adder 70-90ns for that scale, >180ns rack-scale. (2) Under 182% latency, 26% of 158 workloads see <1% slowdown, +17% see <5%, but 21% suffer >25%; under 222%: 23% <1%, 14% <5%, >37% suffer >25%. (3) zNUMA works: the video workload sends <0.25% of memory accesses to the zNUMA node. (4) GBM untouched-memory model is 5x more accurate than a static policy; identifies 25% untouched memory while overpredicting only 4% of VMs; RandomForest can place ~30% of workloads with controlled false positives. (5) End-to-end (Finding #9): at a 16-socket pool, Pond cuts overall DRAM requirements by 9% (182% latency) and 7% (222%), vs 3% for Static, with performance within the 1-5% degradation margin; headline claim: 7% DRAM cost reduction with performance within 1-5% of same-NUMA-node allocations. (6) First public characterization of stranding: 3-27% at p95, outliers 36%.
papers.limitations: No CXL hardware anywhere in the evaluation: latency is emulated with a remote NUMA socket (142ns/255ns), which the authors note differs from real CXL (FPGA prototypes report higher latency; 70ns ASIC overhead is an industry expectation, cited from Intel, not measured). The EMC pool ASIC is a paper design; no multi-host pooling was ever run on hardware — all cross-host DRAM savings come from trace-driven simulation. Cross-socket emulation gives 30GB/s remote bandwidth and inherits coherence-fabric behavior, so CXL bandwidth contention/interference is not studied at all; no multi-tenant co-runner interference experiments. Authors' own admissions: CXL was "still a year from broad deployment"; ATS/PRI devices for page-fault-based approaches "not yet broadly available"; ~20% of VMs lack history for predictions; opaque VMs mean production performance cannot be directly observed; mispredictions require QoS-monitor mitigation (memory migration costs). Emulated latencies (182%/222%) exceed their own 70-90ns estimate, conservatively conflating pool distance effects.
papers.openQuestions: Validation on real CXL silicon of the 25ns-port/70-90ns end-to-end estimates. Bandwidth contention and interference among VMs/hosts sharing EMC ports and DDR5 channels — entirely untested (no QoS/tail-latency-under-contention experiments). Management of multiple discrete CXL devices per host (Pond assumes one logical pool device per host). Dynamic tiering/hot-page migration between local and pool memory (explicitly out of scope; static allocation at VM start only). Behavior at 32-64 socket switched pools. Robustness of ML predictions to adversarial/shifting customer behavior. Memory offlining/reassignment speed at scale (only simulated: <1-10GB/s for 99.99-99.999% of VM starts).
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Pond is the canonical cloud-pooling motivation paper but contains zero real CXL: everything is remote-NUMA emulation plus trace simulation, so the requester's real 4x CZ120 testbed directly tests Pond-era assumptions — e.g., measured 277ns load-to-use (1.53x DRAM) sits between Pond's 182% and 222% emulation points, but Pond's 30GB/s cross-socket "pool" bandwidth and lack of any co-runner experiments miss exactly the 2.0-2.13x CXL bandwidth-contention slowdown the requester measured. Pond treats the pool as one flat logical device per host with a VM-granularity static local/pool split; per-device scheduling, CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference, and tail-aware multi-tenant QoS are precisely what it leaves open, making it the natural motivating citation and contrast point for the candidate per-device direction. Pond's PMU-based latency-sensitivity RandomForest is also a useful VM-granularity analog (and baseline contrast) to ObjPlace's object-granularity bandwidth-sensitivity signals.
evidenceQuotes: We run experiments on production servers at Azure and similarly-configured lab servers. The production servers use either two Intel Skylake 8157M sockets with each 384GB of DDR4, or two AMD EPYC 7452 sockets with each 512GB of DDR4.
we emulate a single-socket system with a CXL pool on a two-socket server by disabling all cores in one socket, while keeping its memory accessible from the other socket. This memory mimics the pool.
On Intel, we measure 78ns NUMA-local latency and 80GB/s bandwidth and 142ns remote latency and 30GB/s bandwidth (3/4 of a CXL ×8 link).

To characterize the performance impact of CXL latency for typical workloads in Azure’s datacenters, we evaluate 158 workloads under two scenarios of emulated CXL access latencies: 182% and 222% increase in memory latency, respectively.
A new external memory controller (EMC) ASIC implements the pool using multiple DDR5 channels accessed through a collection of CXL ports running at PCIe 5 speeds.
We evaluate the effectiveness of pooling using simulations based on VM traces from 100 production clusters.

Intel measures round-trip CXL port traversals at 25ns [68] which, when combined with expected controller-side latencies, leads to an end-to-end overhead of 70ns for CXL reads in a basic topology, compared to NUMA-local DRAM reads.
Finding #9: At a pool size of 16 sockets, Pond reduces overall DRAM requirements by 9% and 7% under 182% and 222% latency increases, respectively. Static reduces DRAM by 3%.
couldNotVerify: Exact kernel/hypervisor version (paper says modified Azure hypervisor; no kernel version stated)
Whether any EMC silicon was ever fabricated (paper describes it as a design; no fabrication claim found)

papers.title: HeMem: Scalable Tiered Memory Management for Big Data Applications and Real NVM
papers.venue: SOSP (ACM SIGOPS 28th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles), SOSP '21, October 26-29 2021, Virtual Event, Germany
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no CXL hardware; slow tier is Intel Optane DC persistent memory: 6 NVM DIMMs = 768 GB on the single evaluated socket, alongside 6 DRAM DIMMs = 192 GB)
papers.mainProblem: Commercially available DRAM+NVM (Intel Optane DC) tiered servers raise capacity up to 8x but, if managed badly, cut bandwidth up to 7x and inflate latency up to 63%. Existing tiered-memory managers fail on real NVM: hardware Memory Mode (direct-mapped DRAM cache) suffers conflict misses and has no app visibility or policy flexibility; OS/kernel approaches (Nimble, HeteroOS) were designed/evaluated on emulated NVM, rely on page-table access/dirty-bit scanning + TLB shootdowns that do not scale to terabytes (seconds per scan), ignore Optane's asymmetric read/write bandwidth (write BW saturates at 4 threads, DRAM random write is 10.7x higher), and do sequential scan+migration on one kernel thread.
papers.mainIdea: HeMem, a user-level library tiered-memory manager designed from scratch for real NVM: (1) asynchronous memory-access sampling via Intel PEBS CPU counters (NVM loads, DRAM loads, all stores; ~1 sample per 5,000 accesses) instead of page-table scans, processed by a dedicated PEBS thread into hot/cold FIFO lists at huge-page granularity with periodic "cooling"; (2) asynchronous batched migration on a 10ms policy thread, offloaded to an I/OAT DMA engine, with reads allowed during migration via userfaultfd write-protection; (3) NVM-aware policies: write-heavy pages prioritized for DRAM (asymmetric NVM bandwidth), small/ephemeral allocations left in DRAM (only ranges >1 GB managed), 1 GB DRAM kept free for new allocations; (4) flexibility: per-application user-level policy (e.g., pinning a priority tenant's data in DRAM), works with unmodified apps via LD_PRELOAD, mmap interception, and DAX-file-backed DRAM/NVM.
papers.hardwareEnv: Single socket of a dual-socket Intel Cascade Lake-SP system @ 2.2 GHz, 24 cores per socket, 100 GbE Mellanox ConnectX-5 NIC. Per socket: 192 GB DDR4 DRAM (6 DIMMs) + 768 GB Intel Optane DC NVM (6 DIMMs), populating all 6 memory channels. Debian 10.9, Linux kernel 5.1.0rc4 with two userfaultfd patches plus 1,337 lines of custom kernel code (userfaultfd DAX fault forwarding, ioatdma copy API). NVM in App-Direct mode exposed as a DAX file; DRAM also carved out as a DAX file via memmap. Measured tiers (Table 1): DDR4 82 ns R/W latency, 107/80 GB/s R/W; Optane DC 175/94 ns, 32/11.2 GB/s R/W. All benchmarks pinned to one NUMA node; no CXL hardware anywhere.
papers.evalSetup: (a) GUPS microbenchmark (16 threads, 1B updates each, 8-byte objects): uniform random up to 256 GB working sets; 90/10 skewed hot-set variant with 512 GB working set and 1-256 GB hot sets; dynamic hot-set shift (4 GB of hot set swapped at t=150s); thread-scalability to 24 threads; asymmetric read/write skew (128 GB write-only region); overhead breakdown (Opt/PEBS/PT-Scan variants) and sensitivity studies of PEBS sampling period, hot threshold, cooling threshold. (b) Silo in-memory database running TPC-C, 16 threads, 16-1,728 warehouses (864 fit in DRAM). (c) FlexKVS (Memcached-compatible) key-value store, 8 server threads + 48-thread client, 4 KB values, 90% GET/10% SET, 20% hot keys getting 90% of accesses, working sets 16 GB-700 GB; latency at 30% load on the TAS network stack; a 2-instance priority experiment (prioritized 16 GB instance pinned to DRAM vs 500 GB regular instance). (d) GAP benchmark betweenness centrality on Kronecker graphs of 2^28 (fits DRAM) and 2^29 vertices (exceeds DRAM), 15 iterations, plus NVM write (wear) counting.
papers.baselines: Intel Optane DC Memory Mode (MM, hardware tiering with DRAM as direct-mapped cache); Linux Nimble page management (ASPLOS'19 kernel tiering, 4 migration threads); X-Mem (EuroSys'16 language-level tiering, emulated by mmap-ing large heap structures into NVM); NVM-only and DRAM-only placements; HeMem ablations (HeMem-PT-Async page-table-scanning variant, copy-threads vs DMA).
papers.keyFindings: Silo TPC-C: up to 13%, 82%, 400% higher throughput than MM, Nimble, X-Mem (MM beats HeMem by 17% once warehouses exceed DRAM). FlexKVS at 700 GB working set: 14%/15%/17% higher throughput than MM/Nimble/X-Mem; 75% lower median and 28% lower 90p latency than MM (up to 69% lower tail); priority isolation gives the prioritized instance 47% lower median and 16% lower 99p latency than MM with ~no harm to the regular instance. GAP BC: 93% faster than MM on average when the graph fits DRAM; 58% (vs MM) and 36% (vs Nimble) faster at 2^29 vertices; NVM-only is 16-17x worse. GUPS: 3.2x MM at 128 GB uniform working set; up to 2x MM for hot sets >8 GB; Nimble reaches only 25% of MM's GUPS; page-table scanning (M.Sync) achieves only 18% of optimal and overestimates the hot set at up to 300 GB. NVM wear: 10x fewer NVM writes than MM. Sampling 0.02% of accesses (1/5,000) suffices; PEBS overhead is within 5.9% of hand-optimal placement.
papers.limitations: No CXL hardware at all - the slow tier is Optane DC NVM, whose properties (asymmetric read/write bandwidth, 256 B media granularity, wear) drive several design choices that do not transfer directly to CXL DRAM. Authors explicitly scope out multi-node effects: "NUMA effects of tiered memory are beyond the scope of this paper" - everything is pinned to one socket, so there is no notion of multiple slow-tier devices, cross-device placement, or inter-device interference; the 6 NVM DIMMs are one flat interleaved DAX-backed pool. X-Mem baseline is emulated, not run. HeMem admits it only helps workloads with a hot set ("Applications that access memory uniformly see little benefit... when their working set exceeds DRAM capacity") and only manages large (>1 GB) long-lived anonymous ranges - kernel objects, program text, and page cache are unmanaged. Isolation evaluation is a single 2-instance FlexKVS priority experiment, not a real multi-tenant study; no bandwidth-contention/interference characterization between co-runners. Requires a patched kernel (userfaultfd write-protect + DAX + ioatdma) and statically preallocated DAX carve-outs of both DRAM and NVM; PEBS is Intel-specific. Tracking is at huge-page (2 MB) granularity only.
papers.openQuestions: Authors explicitly punt on: dynamic tiered memory allocation shared with kernel anonymous memory ("It is yet unclear how Linux will integrate NVM into anonymous memory management"); global cross-process tiered memory management (sketched as a userspace daemon coordinating per-process HeMem instances, not built); kernel-object and page-cache tiering; shared tiered memory across processes (only cooperative sketch); NUMA/multi-socket tiering. Obviously untested from today's perspective: any CXL-attached tier, more than one slow-tier device managed independently, bandwidth interference between tenants sharing the slow tier, and tail-latency QoS under contention beyond the single 2-instance priority demo.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: HeMem is a canonical pre-CXL tiering baseline (PEBS sampling instead of page-table scans, async DMA migration, write-asymmetry-aware placement, priority tenant pinned to DRAM) that any ObjPlace extension or per-device placement system on the c28 box will be compared against; its 2 MB-page, access-frequency-driven policy is the "hotness" strawman that ObjPlace's bandwidth-sensitivity/skew/phase signals go beyond. Critically for the 4x CZ120 direction, HeMem treats the slow tier as one flat interleaved pool on one socket and declares NUMA effects out of scope, so per-device scheduling, CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference, and multi-tenant bandwidth QoS are completely unaddressed - a citable gap. Some Optane-specific machinery (write-heavy page prioritization due to 11.2 GB/s NVM write bandwidth, wear reduction) does not map to CZ120 CXL DRAM, but the low per-device bandwidth concern (~35.5 GiB/s per region on c28) makes HeMem's "spare bandwidth for background migration" and migration-rate-cap (10 GB/s) ideas directly reusable. Its FlexKVS priority experiment (47% median / 16% tail-latency win by reserving DRAM for one tenant) is the primitive 2-tenant precedent that a tail-aware, multi-device CXL QoS system would generalize.
evidenceQuotes: We run our evaluation on a single socket of a dual-socket Intel Cascade Lake-SP system running at 2.2GHz with 24 cores per socket and a 100 GbE ConnectX-5 Mellanox NIC. Each socket has 192 GB of DDR4 DRAM and 768 GB of Intel Optane DC NVM. To leverage all 6 memory channels, there are 6 DIMMs of DRAM and NVM per socket. The machine runs Debian 10.9 with Linux kernel version 5.1.0rc4.

NUMA effects of tiered memory are beyond the scope of this paper. Hence, we run each benchmark pinned to a single NUMA node. All evaluated tiered memory management systems support this mode of operation.
We use NVM in App-Direct mode and expose it via a DAX file to user-space. Our prototype also manages DRAM via a DAX file, which we reserve via the kernel memmap command-line argument.

We study existing hardware and software tiered memory management systems on the recently available Intel Optane DC NVM with big data applications and find that no existing system maximizes application performance on real NVM.

A deployment of the Silo [36] in-memory database running TPC-C [1], attains up to 13%, 82%, and 400% higher throughput with with HeMem than with Intel Optane DC memory mode (MM), Linux nimble memory management (Nimble), and X-Mem, respectively.
Table 1: Main memory technology comparison. | DDR4 DRAM 82 ns 107 / 80 1x | Optane DC [3] 175 / 94 ns 32 / 11.2 8x
HeMem provides up to 16% better tail-latency for a high-priority task and reduces NVM wear by making up to 10x fewer writes to NVM than MM.
couldNotVerify: The ACM DL published version (dl.acm.org) returned HTTP 403; analysis is based on the CC-BY accepted manuscript retrieved from NSF PAR (par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10337601), which carries the SOSP '21 copyright block, ACM artifact badges, and page numbers 392-407, so content should be identical to the published version.

papers.title: Optimizing System Memory Bandwidth with Micron CXL Memory Expansion Modules on Intel Xeon 6 Processors
papers.venue: arXiv (industry white paper, Micron Technology + Intel; IEEE template, not peer-reviewed)
papers.mainProblem: CXL has mostly been pitched for capacity expansion; its bandwidth-expansion value for bandwidth-hungry HPC/AI workloads on real, many-lane CXL systems is unquantified, and DRAM vs CXL tiers have different bandwidth characteristics depending on the read/write ratio, making it unclear how to split traffic between them for maximum system bandwidth.
papers.mainIdea: Populate an Intel Xeon 6 6900P (Granite Rapids AP) with 8x Micron CZ122 E3.S x8 CXL modules brought up as ONE unified CXL NUMA node alongside 12-channel DDR5-6400 (node 0), then use the Linux v6.9+ weighted (software page-level) NUMA interleaving feature to place M pages on DRAM for every N pages on CXL, sweeping the DRAM:CXL weight ratio per workload read:write mix to find the bandwidth-optimal split (e.g., 3:1 for read-only, 5:2 for mixed read/write).
papers.hardwareEnv: Intel "Avenue City" platform; Intel Xeon 6 6900P series (Granite Rapids AP), 128 P-cores, supports 6x16 (96) PCIe 5.0 lanes with any four x16 usable as CXL 2.0 Type-3 links. DRAM: 12x Micron DDR5 64 GB RDIMMs at 6400 MT/s (all 12 channels populated, HEX mode, 768 GB total) = NUMA node 0. CXL: 8x Micron CZ122 128 GB E3.S (Gen5 x8) modules occupying 64 PCIe lanes (~1 TB total; 2 devices per x16 link; 4 cards direct to backplane, 4 via riser cards in two CME slots), all brought up as a single NUMA node 1. OS: Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9.4, kernel 6.11.6 with weighted memory interleaving support. Small 64 GB DRAM modules deliberately chosen to focus on bandwidth rather than capacity.
papers.evalSetup: (1) Intel MLC microbenchmark at multiple read:write ratios (read-only R; 2W:1R; 1W:1W; 2R:1W non-temporal; 1R:1W; 3R:1W), sweeping the DRAM:CXL weighted-interleave page ratio (1:0, 1:1, 2:1, 5:2, 3:1, 4:1, 9:1, 0:1) and reporting bandwidth plus loaded-latency curves. (2) AI: Meta-Llama3-8B-Instruct inference via Intel Extensions for PyTorch (IPEX), bfloat16, batch size 1 (output token latency); FAISS vector search on Microsoft Turing-ANNS 1B x 100-dim vectors with OPQ128_256-IVF65536_HNSW32-PQ128x4fsr index, nprobe=4096, efSearch=512. (3) HPC: OpenFOAM drivaerFastback (~200M cells), HPCG (192^3), Xcompact3D (3D Taylor-Green vortex), POT3D, STREAM Triad. Each workload run standalone; best static interleave weight reported per workload.
papers.baselines: DRAM-only (12-channel DDR5-6400, interleave weight 1:0) is the sole baseline for every workload; CXL-only (0:1) also measured in the MLC tables. No external tiering/placement systems (TPP, AutoNUMA, Memstrata, etc.) are compared — only the vendor's own weighted-interleave configurations against DRAM-only.
papers.keyFindings: MLC: DRAM-only read-only = 556 GB/s; CXL-only read-only = 205 GB/s across all 8 devices (~26 GB/s/device); DRAM loses 20% at 1:1 R:W while CXL-only gains slightly on mixed R/W (214 GB/s at 1R:1W, a claimed 48% theoretical additive gain over DRAM). Best DRAM+CXL: read-only 690 GB/s at 3:1 (+24%); 2W:1R 636 GB/s at 5:2 (+34%); 1W:1R 621 GB/s (+39%); 2R:1W non-temporal 607 GB/s at 5:2 (+30%). At max load DRAM+CXL also cuts loaded latency ~21% vs DRAM-only; optimal weight shifts from 9:1 (light load) to 3:1 (heavy load). Applications: Llama-3-8B token latency 42.91→36.83 ms (+17%, 3:1); FAISS 0.545→0.442 ms/query (+23%, 2:1); OpenFOAM +22% (5:2); HPCG 92→117 GFlops/s (+27%, 3:1); Xcompact3D +25% (5:2); POT3D 687→539 s (+27%, 5:2). Geometric mean speedup across HPC+AI workloads: 24%. CXL shows an 8% bandwidth drop under non-temporal writes.
papers.limitations: All 8 devices are fused into one NUMA node — zero per-device measurement, no cross-device or device-level interference analysis, and the paper never explains how traffic is spread among the 8 devices within node 1 (hardware root-port interleave vs page striping). Interleave weights are static and hand-tuned per workload offline; the authors themselves note weights "may need to be adjusted based on the read-to-write ratio," with no dynamic/automatic mechanism. Every workload runs alone: no multi-tenant, no co-runner, no isolation or QoS experiments; latency is only MLC loaded latency, no application tail-latency. Vendor-authored (Micron+Intel) marketing-adjacent white paper, not peer-reviewed; footnote admits "Performance results are derived from testing in the specified configuration... Results may vary, so it is recommended to reconfirm them in your setting." Single platform, single CPU vendor; only bandwidth-bound workloads chosen (capacity dimension deliberately excluded via small 64 GB DIMMs). Minor internal inconsistency: W5 table header says (1W,1W) while text calls it (1W,1R) and cites 5:2 though the table highlights 2:1.
papers.openQuestions: Explicitly punted: only "future research and development efforts should continue to explore and refine this integration" — nothing concrete. Obviously untested: dynamic/phase-aware weight adaptation instead of static per-workload ratios; treating the 8 devices as anything other than one pooled node (per-device placement, per-device bandwidth allocation, failure/QoS domains); interference between co-located workloads sharing the CXL node; tail latency under contention; capacity-driven tiering combined with bandwidth interleaving; behavior when CXL devices are asymmetrically loaded; AMD platforms.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: This is the scaled-up vendor sibling of the requester's testbed — same Micron CZ12x silicon family (8x CZ122 vs their 4x CZ120), and it confirms that even Micron/Intel's flagship demo fuses ALL devices into a single NUMA node and tunes only a global DRAM:CXL page ratio: direct evidence that per-device scheduling, CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference, and multi-tenant isolation (the requester's candidate direction) are unexplored even by the vendors, with zero co-runner or tail-latency data here. The per-device bandwidth calibration is useful: 205 GB/s read-only over 8 Gen5 x8 devices (~26 GB/s/device) brackets the requester's ~35.5 GiB/s per 2-device x8 region and shows aggregate CXL bandwidth scaling roughly linearly when pooled. The kernel weighted-interleaving sweep (optimal 3:1 read-only, 5:2 mixed, shifting with load) is a mandatory, easily reproducible baseline for ObjPlace — ObjPlace's object-granularity, phase/pressure-driven placement should be positioned against exactly this static page-ratio approach, whose per-workload hand tuning is the paper's admitted weakness.

papers.title: CXL-Interplay: Unraveling and Characterizing CXL Interference in Modern Computer Systems (DAC'25); arXiv preprint titled "CXL-Interference: Analysis and Characterization in Modern Computer Systems" (2411.18308) is the same paper
papers.venue: DAC 2025 (62nd ACM/IEEE Design Automation Conference), DOI 10.1109/DAC63849.2025.11132607; arXiv:2411.18308 v1 2024-11-27
papers.numCXLDevices: System A: 1 (Montage ASIC 64GB); System B: 1 (Intel Agilex FPGA 32GB DDR4-2400)
papers.mainProblem: CXL memory coexists with main memory (MMEM) and storage (SSD) in real servers, but the mutual performance interference between CXL traffic and MMEM/SSD traffic — a shared-uncore "noisy neighbor" problem — is unstudied on real CXL hardware; prior CXL characterization work profiles CXL in isolation and simulators inject fixed delays that ignore interference.
papers.mainIdea: Build CXL-Interplay: a configurable microbenchmark suite (ld/st/ntst via cxlMemTest crossed with FIO randread/randwrite) plus tailored real applications, run on two real CXL testbeds (one Montage ASIC device, one Intel Agilex FPGA device) to systematically map the CXL-vs-MMEM and CXL-vs-SSD interference matrix; perform reverse-reasoning root-cause analysis with uncore PMU counters (TOR occupancy/inserts, new CXL counters) and kernel-function profiling; then evaluate software mitigations (cgroups CPU quota, frequency scaling, Intel MBA) and discuss device-side hardware regulation.
papers.hardwareEnv: Two Intel Sapphire Rapids testbeds, each with exactly ONE CXL 1.1 memory expander attached to socket 0 as a CPU-less NUMA node 2. System A: 4th Gen Xeon Platinum 4.0 GHz, 48 physical cores/socket, 1TB 8-channel DDR5-4800 per socket, SAS SSD, Montage ASIC CXL device 64GB, XFS, CentOS 7. System B: 4th Gen Xeon Gold 4.0 GHz, 32 physical cores/socket, 256GB 8-channel DDR5-4800 per socket, NVMe PCIe 4.0 MLC SSD, Intel Agilex FPGA CXL device 32GB DDR4-2400, XFS, Ubuntu 22.04.4 LTS. Two CPU NUMA nodes joined by UPI; figure shows CXL 1.1 off a PCIe 5.0 port; link width and kernel versions not stated. Hyper-threading disabled, CPU locked to 2GHz for microbenchmarks.
papers.evalSetup: Microbenchmarks: memory ops (load, store, non-temporal store via cxlMemTest) cross-run against storage ops (FIO libaio, iodepth 16, 4KB blocks, 20s randread/randwrite), sweeping all thread counts, main and interfering processes pinned to separate cores of the same NUMA node; case studies on sequential-vs-random SSD access and MOVDIR64B. Real applications in 4 interference types (A: filesystem apps under CXL traffic; B: CXL apps under SSD traffic; C: MMEM apps under CXL traffic; D: CXL apps under MMEM traffic): Filebench fileserver/varmail, RocksDB, MLPerf Storage, GAPBS PageRank, Redis (50/50 read-update), TinyLlama LLM inference. Root-cause via uncore PMU counters (unc_cha_tor_occupancy/inserts.ia_miss, cxlcm_txc_pack_buf_inserts.mem_data) and kernel-function profiling. Mitigation experiments: cgroups CPU-quota throttling, frequency scaling, Intel MBA bandwidth restriction.
papers.baselines: No system baselines (characterization paper). Positioned against prior characterization work in Table I: emulation-based works (Memtis, TPP-style, CXLMemSim), Sun et al. MICRO'23, Tang et al. EuroSys'24, Liu & Wang arXiv'24 — none of which study interference or regulation on real devices. Mitigation methods compared against each other: cgroups CPU quota vs frequency scaling vs Intel MBA (plus discussed-only: Intel CAT, AMD SMBA, device-side latency injection).
papers.keyFindings: (1) CXL non-temporal stores devastate co-running MMEM/SSD bandwidth: up to 93.2% degradation; CXL ld/st alone cause >40% MMEM interference on System B. (2) Root cause: CXL traffic congests the Table of Requests (TOR) between cores and LLC — unc_cha_tor_occupancy.ia_miss rises 4090x, inserts 155x, L2-miss latency 15.2x, while L3-miss latency stays ~1.01x. (3) SSD sequential writes suffer more than random (80.9% vs 54.5% loss) due to larger LLC/DDIO occupancy; MOVDIR64B interferes less than ntst. (4) Asymmetry: MMEM/SSD have mild impact on CXL (SSD up to only ~12%), and CXL st can even be boosted by MMEM traffic; RocksDB gains up to +21.2% under CXL ld background (24% fewer memory instructions). (5) Real apps: up to ~90% decline for filesystem apps under CXL ntst; GAPBS up to 20.8x slowdown under CXL traffic. (6) Mitigations: cgroups quota restores MMEM to 190 GB/s (~92%); Intel MBA restores 99%/95%/98% across three apps by cutting CXL bandwidth just 5 GB/s (intro: "restore bandwidth of the MMEM by 204GB per second, which reaches 99% of its original level"); frequency scaling recovers only 30-52%.
papers.limitations: Only ONE CXL device per testbed — no CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference, no interleaved multi-device regions, no pooling. Intel Sapphire Rapids only; root-cause counters (TOR/CHA) and mitigations (Intel MBA, DDIO reasoning) are Intel-uncore-specific, so transferability to AMD is unshown (authors note AMD's SMBA for CXL "has not been released"). CXL 1.1 devices of small capacity (64GB/32GB). No multi-tenant/VM scenarios — interference pairs are single co-running processes pinned to node 0. Bandwidth-focused; no tail-latency distributions. Authors admit: MBA restriction is coarse (can only cut CXL bandwidth to ~half due to I/O block configuration) and unresponsive (takes seconds); cache partitioning (CAT) ineffective against ntst; hardware device-side latency-injection solution is only discussed, not implemented, and is vendor-specific; some app results were unstable and reported as 0. Several explanations are hedged as presumptions ("presumably", "we hypothesize").
papers.openQuestions: Interference BETWEEN multiple CXL devices (never tested); behavior under CXL 2.0/3.x, switches, and pooled/multi-headed devices; AMD and ARM platforms; device-side fine-grained MBA-like regulation (takeaway H2 is a proposal only); specialized TOR for slow-tier memory (H1, hardware proposal only); responsive/fast-acting bandwidth regulation; tail-latency and QoS SLOs rather than bandwidth recovery; multi-tenant isolation policies built on their insights; root cause of the RocksDB promotion effect is only partially explained (system-specific).
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Directly relevant as the closest prior art on real-hardware CXL interference, but it only characterizes CXL-vs-MMEM and CXL-vs-SSD on single-device Intel testbeds — it never measures CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference, so the requester's candidate direction (per-device placement, cross-device interference, multi-tenant QoS across 4 CZ120s) remains unclaimed. The requester's observed 2.0-2.13x slowdown of a CXL victim under a CXL co-runner is a different axis (contention within/across CXL devices) than this paper's headline result (CXL ntst crushing DRAM bandwidth via TOR congestion), and its reverse-reasoning methodology (uncore TOR/CHA occupancy counters) is a useful template but is Intel-Sapphire-Rapids-specific — the AMD Turin host needs a different PMU story, and the paper itself notes AMD's CXL-targeted SMBA regulator is unreleased, which is an open tooling gap on the requester's platform. Its finding that ntst/write-combining traffic is the dominant aggressor suggests a concrete aggressor dimension to add to ObjPlace's interference model and to any per-device scheduler; its cgroups/MBA mitigation results give ready software baselines to compare a QoS mechanism against.
evidenceQuotes: System A has SAS SSD and an ASIC-based CXL memory device manufactured by Montage. System B consists of NVMe SSD and an Intel FPGA-based CXL memory device.

TABLE II row: 'CXL memory device — Montage ASIC 64GB [System A] — Intel Agilex FPGA 32GB DDR4-2400 [System B]'; other rows: CPU '4th Gen Xeon Platinum 4.0 GHz' / '4th Gen Xeon Gold 4.0 GHz'; Memory per socket '1TB, 8 Channel, DDR5-4800' / '256GB, 8 Channel, DDR5-4800'; Storage 'SAS SSD' / 'NVMe PCIe 4.0 MLC SSD'; OS 'CentOS 7' / 'Ubuntu 22.04.4 LTS'

we develop a configurable microbenchmark and systematically go through the basic interference condition of CXL with MMEM and SSD system using two different real CXL hardware setups
To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to characterize CXL interference on real CXL hardware.

a) The bandwidth of MMEM/SSD suffers significant interference when CXL performs ntst, reaching up to 93.2%. b) CXL ld and st can also be disruptive to MMEM, especially on System B, where over 40% interference is observed.

papers.title: Systematic CXL Memory Characterization and Performance Analysis at Scale (Melody)
papers.venue: ASPLOS 2025 (ASPLOS '25, March 30-April 3, 2025, Rotterdam; DOI 10.1145/3676641.3715987)
papers.numCXLDevices: 4 distinct devices characterized (CXL-A/B/C/D from different vendors: 3 ASIC + 1 FPGA); one experiment additionally hardware-interleaves two CXL-D units, implying at least 5 physical units on hand
papers.mainProblem: The performance implications of CXL memory across devices, latency regimes, processors, and workloads are underexplored: prior CXL studies use only average latency/bandwidth on small workload sets and overlook (i) CXL latency stability (tail latencies), (ii) CPU tolerance to prolonged CXL latencies at scale, and (iii) a systematic way to attribute workload slowdowns to root causes under black-box CXL memory controllers.
papers.mainIdea: Melody: the largest CXL characterization to date — 265 workloads x 4 real CXL devices x 7 memory latency configurations (140-410ns, three of them NUMA-simulated) x 5 Intel CPU platforms — providing the first disclosure and analysis of CXL tail latencies (via a custom cacheline-level microbenchmark, MIO), plus Spa, a differential stall-cycle root-cause analysis method using only 9 CPU performance counters that decomposes CXL-induced slowdown into store-buffer / L1 / L2 / L3 / DRAM / core components (including a first quantification of CPU prefetcher inefficiency under CXL).
papers.hardwareEnv: Five 2-to-8-socket Intel servers: SPR2S (Sapphire Rapids, 8xDDR5, 128GB, 114ns/218GB/s local, 32 cores @2.1GHz, 60MB L3), EMR2S (Emerald Rapids, 8xDDR5, 128GB, 111ns/246GB/s, 32c, 160MB L3), EMR2S' (8xDDR5, 1.5TB, 117ns/236GB/s, 52c @2.3GHz, 260MB L3), SKX2S (Skylake, 6xDDR4, 96GB, 90ns), SKX8S (8-socket Skylake, 6xDDR4, 410ns remote). CXL devices (vendors anonymized): CXL-A ASIC, CXL 1.1 x8, 2xDDR4, 128GB, 214ns, 24GB/s (32GB/s peak mixed R/W); CXL-B ASIC, x8, 1xDDR5, 128GB, 271ns, 22GB/s (26 peak); CXL-C FPGA, x8, 2xDDR4, 16GB, 394ns, 18GB/s (21 peak); CXL-D ASIC, x16 PCIe5, 2xDDR5, 756GB, 239ns, 52GB/s (59 peak). All devices are CXL 2.0-capable but run in CXL 1.1 mode (CPU limitation). CXL-A/B/C hosted on SPR2S/EMR2S, CXL-D on EMR2S'. Three extra latency points (140ns, 190ns via lowered uncore frequency, 410ns) are NUMA-emulated on SKX. No kernel version stated.
papers.evalSetup: 265 workloads: SPEC CPU 2017, PARSEC, GAPBS, PBBS, CloudSuite, Phoronix, Spark, Redis+YCSB, VoltDB, GPT-2, MLPerf, DLRM, Llama-7B (llama.cpp). Each workload runs with memory bound entirely to local DRAM, NUMA, or one CXL device at a time ('worst-case' placement; tiering/interleaving deliberately excluded, except one experiment interleaving two CXL-D units at 104GB/s). Slowdown S = (P_DRAM/P_CXL - 1)*100% vs local DRAM. Device-level: Intel MLC loaded-latency sweeps; custom MIO pointer-chase microbenchmark for per-request tail latency CDFs (prefetchers disabled), with AVX read/write background noise threads; 1ms latency sampling across 112 workloads. Spa validated by comparing 9-counter stall-based slowdown estimates against measured application-level slowdowns on NUMA/CXL-A/CXL-B. Note: CXL-C has only 16GB DRAM, limiting it to 60 of the 265 workloads. Artifacts at github.com/MoatLab/Melody.
papers.baselines: Not a system paper, so no system baselines. Reference points: socket-local DRAM (slowdown baseline), 1-hop NUMA, 2-hop NUMA (SKX8S 410ns), CXL+NUMA (CXL accessed from remote socket), and cross-device comparison among CXL-A/B/C/D. Spa is positioned against Intel Top-down Microarchitecture Analysis (TMA) and prior heuristic/LLC-miss-based correlation methods.
papers.keyFindings: (1) First disclosure of CXL tail latencies: 3 of 4 devices show unstable microsecond-level tails even under low (<50%) bandwidth utilization — CXL-B/C p99.9-p50 gaps up to ~160ns (50% over median), p99.99/p99.999 reaching 1us (CXL-B/C) and >700ns (CXL-A/D), vs stable local/NUMA (45ns/61ns p99.9-p50); under load, CXL-A/B spike from ~350ns to ~1.2us and CXL-C to 3us. Average latency rises >=60ns at only 50-86% utilization on CXL vs 90-95% for local/NUMA. (2) Devices are heterogeneous: peak bandwidth occurs at different R/W ratios per device (2:1 for CXL-A, 3:1/4:1 for CXL-D); FPGA CXL-C cannot exploit bidirectional links. (3) Tails propagate to applications (Redis YCSB-C p99+ blows up on CXL-C at low bandwidth); CXL+NUMA causes surprise slowdowns (520.omnetpp 2.9x at <1GB/s; 10 other workloads 33-283%) traced to tail latency. (4) Workload tolerance: 94/87/80% of workloads see <50% slowdown on CXL-D/A/B (vs 98% NUMA); 60/54/32% see <10%; a 7% 'tail' of bandwidth-bound workloads suffers 1.5-5.8x on CXL-A/B; interleaving 2x CXL-D (104GB/s) nearly closes the gap to NUMA. (5) Prefetching does not hide CXL latency: cache slowdown is caused by reduced L2 prefetcher timeliness/coverage (2-38% L2PF-L3-miss reduction, offset by L1PF misses, Pearson 0.99). (6) Spa attributes slowdowns with <5% error for >95% of workloads using 9 counters; a Spa+Pin case study moved two 2GB hot objects to DRAM, cutting slowdown 13%->2%. Verified per task hint: yes, the paper documents unstable microsecond tails on real CXL and explicitly punts mitigation ('as an initial step... to raise awareness'), deferring fixes to future CPUs, CXL MC designs, and system software; devices ARE studied individually (each characterized/run separately, on separate hosts for CXL-D), never co-managed.
papers.limitations: Authors' own admissions: tail-latency root causes remain speculative due to black-box CXL MCs — 'no tools exist to pinpoint tail latencies', white-box breakdown deferred to CXL 3.0 CPMU counters; thermal stress testing stopped at 70C to avoid damaging devices; CXL-C's 16GB capacity limited it to 60/265 workloads; 3 of 7 latency points are NUMA-emulated, not real CXL. Evident from methodology: vendors are anonymized (CXL-A/B/C/D), so results cannot be mapped to specific products (e.g., Micron CZ120); Intel-only hosts running CXL 1.1 mode — no AMD (requester's EPYC Turin) and no CXL 2.0 features; Spa's 9 counters are Intel-specific; characterization only, no mitigation mechanism built for the tails it discovers; no multi-tenant runs — 'noise' experiments are self-inflicted microbenchmark co-runners on one device, not tenant workloads; no cross-device (CXL-to-CXL) interference study; per-device measurement only, no per-device placement/scheduling; no kernel/OS configuration details.
papers.openQuestions: Explicitly punted: mitigating CXL tail latencies (framed as Implications: 'Future CPUs need to be improved to tolerate CXL's unpredictable latencies', 'CXL MC designs need to prioritize latency predictability', 'System designers need to account for tail latency impact'); white-box per-request latency decomposition awaiting CXL 3.0 CPMU; thermal throttling as a tail cause left unresolved. Untested: tiering and software interleaving policies (excluded by design), multi-device management, QoS enforcement across tenants sharing a device, cross-device interference, AMD platforms, CXL 2.0/switch topologies (switch numbers taken from public sources, not measured).
evidenceQuotes: Melody builds on an extensive evaluation spanning 265 workloads, 4 real CXL devices, 7 latency levels, and 5 CPU platforms.

We use 4 CXL memory expanders from different vendors (CXL-A, CXL-B, CXL-C, CXL-D). CXL devices are hosted on SPR/EMR servers: CXL-A, CXL-B, and CXL-C on SPR2S/EMR2S, and CXL-D on EMR2S' (remote host).

All our CXL devices operate in CXL 1.1 mode as type-3 memory expanders (CXL.io+CXL.mem). CXL-C is FPGA-based (lowest performance) while the rest are ASICs. CXL-D utilizes 16x PCIe 5 lanes and 2 memory channels, providing the highest CXL bandwidth of 52GB/s.

We use NUMA to simulate 3 additional CXL latency configurations of 140ns and 190ns on SKX2S (190ns achieved via lowering uncore frequency, not shown in the table), and 410ns on SKX8S [32, 34]. These setups provide a total of 7 latency configurations
We discover some CXL devices exhibit significant µs-level tail latencies even under low device bandwidth utilization.
In contrast, CXL-A and CXL-B see latency spikes from ∼350ns to ∼1.2µs, and CXL-C reaches 3µs when injected delay drops from 700 to 500 cycles.
We run workloads using local, NUMA or CXL memory to focus on analyzing the “worst-case” CXL setup, excluding more complex configurations like tiering or interleaving.
We also test workloads on two CXL-D devices with hardware interleaving, effectively doubling the bandwidth to 104GB/s.

Currently, no tools exist to pinpoint tail latencies. A future approach could involve a white-box analysis... As an initial step, we demonstrate and quantify the impact of CXL tail latency to raise awareness within the systems community.
Implication #1: From software/hardware design perspectives, there is a need to address CXL tail latencies. (a) Future CPUs need to be improved to tolerate CXL's unpredictable latencies
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Directly load-bearing for the requester's candidate direction: Melody proves on real silicon that CXL devices differ sharply in tail-latency stability and R/W-ratio behavior (3 of 4 devices show microsecond tails at <50% utilization), which strengthens the case that four CZ120s should not be treated as one flat pool — but Melody only characterizes devices individually and explicitly punts mitigation, per-device QoS, multi-tenant isolation, and cross-device interference, leaving exactly the requester's proposed territory open. Caveats: Melody is Intel/CXL-1.1 and anonymizes vendors, so its per-device numbers do not transfer to the AMD Turin + CZ120 (CXL 2.0) box, and all four requester devices are the same model, so cross-vendor heterogeneity arguments weaken to per-region/interleave-config heterogeneity. Melody's 2x CXL-D hardware-interleaving result (bandwidth doubling nearly closes the NUMA gap) is a direct comparison point for the requester's interleave_ways=2 region, and Spa's 9-counter differential-stall attribution is a reusable diagnosis technique for ObjPlace's bandwidth-sensitivity signals — worth citing as the characterization foundation the requester's system builds beyond.

papers.title: Beluga: A CXL-Based Memory Architecture for Scalable and Efficient LLM KVCache Management
papers.venue: SIGMOD 2026 (arXiv:2511.20172; Alibaba)
papers.numCXLDevices: 32 CXL memory devices (32 × 256 GB DDR5-4800, 8 TB total) in a switched pool behind 2 × XConn XC50256 CXL 2.0 switch chips; the paper explicitly states interleaving across '32 memory devices', contradicting the analyst's 'never states the number' — though it does not break down controllers per device
papers.mainProblem: LLM serving needs huge KVCache capacity beyond GPU HBM; existing offload/pooling paths use RDMA, which "was fundamentally designed as a networking protocol, not a memory bus," causing extra data movement through host memory, high control-path overhead (request prep, completion polling, cross-component synchronization), and high TTFT for cache reuse.
papers.mainIdea: Beluga: a rack-scale CXL 2.0 switched memory pool (XConn XC50256, up to 16 servers sharing 8 TB) exposed to each host as DAX-mapped contiguous physical address space, with both CPUs and GPUs directly load/store or P2P-DMA accessing pool memory (cudaMemcpy P2P + custom CUDA kernels for fine-grained non-contiguous access), software interleaving at 2 MB granularity across CXL devices for bandwidth, a lightweight CXL-based RPC (shared-memory producer-consumer) replacing RDMA for metadata/control, and a KVCache management layer (Beluga-KV) integrated with vLLM. Claimed first system letting GPUs directly access large switched CXL memory pools.
papers.hardwareEnv: Per server: 2 × Intel Xeon Platinum 8575C, 2 TB DRAM (32 × DDR5-4800 64 GB), 8 × NVIDIA H20 (96 GB), 2 × PCIe 5.0 x16 CXL adapters; Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 6.2.0-1015. Pool: XConn XC50256 dual-chip CXL 2.0 switch (256 PCIe 5.0 lanes, 2 TB/s forwarding per chip), memory box with 8 TB (32 × DDR5-4800 256 GB), up to 16 servers, 1 TB/s aggregate. Measured: CPU read from CXL 46.2 GB/s per adapter; GPU access 26 GB/s (Root Complex bottleneck vs 55.4 GB/s theoretical); CXL-RPC roundtrip 2.11 us vs RDMA-RC 8.39 us.
papers.evalSetup: Microbenchmarks (CPU/GPU latency and bandwidth to CXL pool vs DRAM/RDMA, 16 KB ops); end-to-end LLM serving with vLLM (V1, v0.8.5) + LMCache v0.3.1 on Qwen-32B (default, unquantized) and Llama-3.1-8B using LV-Eval long-context QA traces (>15K tokens; LV-Eval-2K/4K/8K variants); KVCache transfer/read comparisons against RDMA-based KV pools.
papers.baselines: MoonCake (v3.2), NVIDIA Dynamo (v0.4.1), vLLM V1 v0.8.5 with LMCache v0.3.1, local-DRAM and RDMA-based memory pool configurations.
papers.keyFindings: GPUs/CPUs can use a switched CXL 2.0 pool at near-local efficiency: CXL-RPC roundtrip 2.11 us vs 8.39 us RDMA-RC; GPU H2D copy from CXL 11.73 us vs 10.32 us from CPU DRAM (16 KB). End-to-end: 89.6% TTFT reduction and 7.35x throughput improvement in vLLM vs RDMA-based cache-hit path; 95.9% KVCache read latency reduction for sparse access; 4.79x improvement over MoonCake. GPU bandwidth to pool capped at 26 GB/s per adapter by Root Complex (vs 46.2 GB/s CPU reads), mitigated via multiple adapters and 2 MB software interleaving.
papers.limitations: Authors admit CXL-RPC "provides lower reliability guarantees compared to RDMA transport protocols" (reliability pushed to upper layers) and that GPU access is Root-Complex-bottlenecked (26 GB/s vs 55.4 GB/s theoretical). Methodological: exotic testbed (XConn switch + custom 8 TB memory box) that few labs can reproduce; number and model of the actual CXL memory controllers never disclosed; pool treated as one flat interleaved address space — no per-device measurement, no study of inter-host or inter-device interference/contention on the shared pool; no multi-tenant QoS/isolation evaluation; hardware interleaving deferred to future Granite Rapids CPUs; evaluation centered on one workload family (LV-Eval) and cache-hit scenarios.

papers.title: Exploring and Evaluating Real-world CXL: Use Cases and System Adoption
papers.numCXLDevices: testbed A: 1, testbed B: 1, testbed C: 1 (three different vendor devices, one per system; 3 total across three separate machines)
papers.mainProblem: CXL memory performance characteristics "remain largely unclear due to the limited availability of production hardware"; unclear what the real use cases are (HPC apps, LLM training/inference), how CXL interacts with existing OS memory tiering and page-interleaving mechanisms, and how software should place data across DRAM + CXL.
papers.mainIdea: Characterize three genuine (production ASIC) CXL 1.1 memory-expansion devices from three different vendors on three servers (AMD Genoa + two Intel SPR-class), evaluate HPC (NPB, XSBench) and LLM (ZeRO-Offload training, FlexGen inference) workloads, study the interplay between memory tiering (AutoNUMA/TPP) and page interleaving, and propose object-level interleaving (OLI): per-data-object placement that interleaves bandwidth-sensitive large objects across DRAM+CXL while pinning latency-sensitive objects to local DRAM.
papers.hardwareEnv: Three separate testbeds, each with ONE CXL device exposed as a CPU-less NUMA node over PCIe 5.0 x16 (32 GT/s), CXL 1.1. System A: 2x AMD EPYC 9354 @3.8GHz (32c, 512MB LLC each), 12x DDR5-4800 per socket (768GB/socket, 460.8 GB/s), CXL device single-channel DDR5-4800 128GB (38.4 GB/s), Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 6.2.15. System B: 2x Intel Xeon Platinum 8470 @2.0GHz (52c), 8x DDR5-4800 per socket (1TB/socket), CXL device single-channel DDR5-8000 64GB (64 GB/s), Fedora 36, kernel 6.6.0-rc5. System C: 2x Intel Xeon Gold 6438Y+ @2.0GHz (32c), 8x DDR5-4800 per socket (512GB/socket), CXL device dual-channel DDR5-6200 128GB (48.4 GB/s), Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 6.2.15. Vendor names of the three devices are not given in the testbed table (only "three CXL devices from three vendors"); Micron, Samsung, Astera Labs are mentioned elsewhere in the text.
papers.evalSetup: Intel MLC microbenchmarks for latency/bandwidth vs local DRAM (LDRAM) and remote-socket DRAM (RDRAM); 7 HPC benchmarks (NPB BT/LU/CG/MG/SP/FT + XSBench) under different placement policies (first-touch, uniform page interleaving, OLI, LDRAM-preferred with capped fast memory 64/128GB); LLM training (BERT, GPT-2 via ZeRO-Offload) and inference (LLaMA, OPT via FlexGen); kernel tiering comparison of AutoNUMA, Tiering-0.8, TPP.
papers.baselines: First-touch NUMA allocation; uniform (page-level) interleaving; LDRAM-preferred placement; RDRAM placement; NVMe offload (for FlexGen); kernel tiering systems AutoNUMA, Tiering-0.8, and TPP.
papers.keyFindings: (1) CXL latency is "comparable to a two-hop-away NUMA node": +153 ns (System A) to +211 ns (System B) over local DRAM. (2) CXL bandwidth is only 17.1% (A) and 46.4% (B) of remote-socket DRAM bandwidth and saturates with >=8 threads. (3) Proposed object-level interleaving (OLI) is 65% better than uniform interleaving on average; with sufficient LDRAM it cuts fast-memory usage 32% at <1% performance loss vs LDRAM-only; with insufficient LDRAM (64GB) it beats LDRAM-preferred by 1.42x avg (up to 2.35x on BT) and uniform interleaving by 1.32x avg. (4) LLM training with CXL offload brings little benefit or up to 16% degradation; LLM inference (FlexGen) LDRAM+CXL beats LDRAM+NVMe by 24% (LLaMA) / 20% (OPT) but is only ~3% different from RDRAM. (5) No single tiering strategy (AutoNUMA/Tiering/TPP) wins across all workloads, and page migration integrates poorly with static interleaving.
papers.limitations: Each testbed has only ONE CXL device — no multi-device, no cross-CXL-device interference, no pooling, no multi-tenant experiments. CXL 1.1 only (no CXL 2.0 features, no P2P GPU access; authors note GPU-CXL path bottlenecked by PCIe). Vendor identities of the three devices are not disclosed in the testbed table. Could not evaluate largest LLMs (e.g., GPT-3 175B) due to GPU memory limits. OLI object selection uses a simple heuristic (>=10% footprint + access intensity) and results are single-application runs; no co-runner contention or QoS study. Tiering results show no universal winner but no fix is built.
papers.openQuestions: How page migration / dynamic tiering should coexist with (static) interleaving policies; exploiting CXL 3.0+ peer-to-peer for GPU-CXL data paths in LLM serving; automatic/online identification of bandwidth- vs latency-sensitive objects; behavior with multiple CXL devices per host, device-level interleaving, contention among co-running tenants — all untested.

papers.title: Dissecting CXL Memory Performance at Scale: Analysis, Modeling, and Optimization (SupMario / Alto)
papers.venue: Under this title the work exists only as an arXiv preprint (Sep 2024, no journal-ref on arXiv). The ASPLOS'25 publication from the same group/testbed was retitled 'Systematic CXL Memory Characterization and Performance Analysis at Scale' with the framework renamed Melody, a different author list (adds Yuyue Wang, Marie Nguyen, Xun Jian, Sam H. Noh; drops Hanchen Xu), 5 CPU platforms instead of 4, and it drops the SupMario/Alto modeling+tiering content (introduces 'Spa' instead). Saying the 'Dissecting...' SupMario/Alto paper is ASPLOS'25 conflates two related but non-identical papers.
papers.numCXLDevices: 4 distinct CXL device models (CXL-A ASIC 128GB, CXL-B ASIC 128GB, CXL-C FPGA 16GB, CXL-D ASIC 768GB on a remote machine) + 3 zNUMA/uncore-emulated latency points = 7 latency configs — BUT the paper additionally uses a SECOND physical CXL-D unit in a 'CXL-D*' configuration (two CXL-Ds hardware-interleaved), so at least 5 physical devices appear in the evaluation, not 4 total.
papers.mainProblem: Lack of systematic understanding of how real CXL memory devices (with widely varying latency/bandwidth) affect application performance, how to predict per-workload slowdown from CPU counters, and how to optimize page placement/tiering — existing tiering systems (e.g., TPP) and naive interleaving are latency/bandwidth-oblivious.
papers.mainIdea: SupMario: a large-scale characterization (265 workloads x 4 real CXL devices x 7 latency configs x 4 Intel platforms) that distills workload slowdown into a performance model built on just 12 CPU performance counters (DRAM/cache/store slowdown components), then uses the insights for two optimizations: a "best-shot" weighted page interleaving policy and Alto, a regulated ("amortized memory latency"-driven) page tiering policy.
papers.hardwareEnv: Four Intel servers: SPR2S (Sapphire Rapids, 2-socket, 16 cores/socket, 2.1GHz, 256GB DDR5-4800, 114ns local latency), EMR2S (Emerald Rapids, 2-socket, 16 cores/socket, 256GB DDR5-4800, 111ns), SKX2S (Skylake 2-socket, 192GB DDR4, 90ns), SKX8S (Skylake 8-socket, 384GB DDR4, 81ns). CXL devices: CXL-A (ASIC, CXL 1.1, x8, 2xDDR4, 128GB, 214ns, 24GB/s), CXL-B (ASIC, CXL 1.1, x8, 2xDDR5, 128GB, 271ns, 22GB/s), CXL-C (FPGA, CXL 1.1, x8, 2xDDR4, 16GB, 394ns, 18GB/s), CXL-D (ASIC, CXL 1.1, x16, 4xDDR5, 768GB, 239ns, 52GB/s, hosted on a remote machine). Extra latency points (140-410ns) via zNUMA on Skylake plus uncore-frequency throttling. Each CXL device exposed as a zero-core NUMA (zNUMA) node. Kernel version not captured in the fetched text.
papers.evalSetup: 265 workloads: SPEC CPU 2017 (43 analyzed in detail), CloudSuite, Phoronix, GAPBS, PBBS, Spark, PARSEC, and ML workloads (GPT-2, Llama, MLPerf). Each workload run with memory bound to local DRAM vs. the CXL zNUMA node (and emulated latency configs); slowdown measured and modeled from 12 CPU perf counters (11 on Skylake). Optimizations evaluated: best-shot weighted DRAM/CXL page interleaving vs 1:1 round-robin, and Alto tiering vs TPP.
papers.baselines: TPP (kernel memory tiering) for Alto; traditional 1:1 round-robin DRAM/CXL interleaving for the best-shot interleaving policy; local-DRAM and NUMA configurations as reference points for the slowdown model.
papers.keyFindings: (1) Real CXL devices vary widely: 214-394ns load latency, 18-52GB/s per device. (2) CXL tail latency is much worse than DRAM (DRAM p99.9-p50 gap only 45-61ns; CXL-B/C gaps ~160ns). (3) On EMR nearly half the workloads see no slowdown on CXL; 32 workloads see <5% slowdown; but 4 workloads needing >24GB/s see >50% slowdown. (4) A 12-counter linear model predicts slowdown within 10% for >99% of NUMA cases and 91-94% of CXL cases. (5) Best-shot weighted interleaving beats 1:1 interleaving; Alto achieves up to 177% improvement over TPP for latency-sensitive workloads.
papers.limitations: Authors admit: "These devices function as black boxes to us, as we do not have access to their internal implementation details"; some needed perf counters are impractical/unavailable (L1-prefetch share of LFB hits; missing SQ prefetch counters degrade accuracy on SPR/EMR); CXL-C is only 16GB, limiting workload coverage. Methodological gaps for the requester's purposes: each CXL device is characterized alone on its host — no multi-device-per-host configuration, no CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference, no multi-tenant co-location study; 3 of the 7 latency configurations are NUMA/uncore-throttling emulation, not real CXL; all-Intel platforms (no AMD Genoa/Turin); the tiering/interleaving evaluation is single-workload-at-a-time, not consolidated tenants.
papers.openQuestions: How multiple CXL devices behave when attached to and shared on one host (per-device scheduling, cross-device interference, hardware interleaving across devices); tail-latency QoS under co-running tenants; behavior on AMD hosts and CXL 2.0 devices; extending the counter-based slowdown model to contended/multi-tenant scenarios; sub-page or object-granularity placement (they operate at page granularity).
evidenceQuotes: SupMario is based on extensive evaluation of 265 workloads spanning 4 real CXL devices within 7 memory latency configurations across 4 processor platforms.
CXL memory seamlessly integrates into systems as cacheable, byte-addressable memory within a zero-core NUMA (zNUMA) node (i.e., CPU-less NUMA)
