papers.title: Tiered Memory Management: Access Latency is the Key! (Colloid)
papers.venue: SOSP 2024
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no physical CXL device; alternate tier is remote-socket DDR4 over UPI, with uncore-frequency throttling used to sweep the latency ratio 1.9x-2.7x)
papers.mainProblem: Existing tiering systems (HeMem, TPP, MEMTIS) always pack hottest pages into the default (DRAM) tier, assuming its latency is always lower; under memory-interconnect contention the default tier's loaded latency can inflate 5x (2.4-2.5x above the alternate tier), making these systems up to 2.3-2.46x worse than optimal.
papers.mainIdea: Colloid: page placement should balance the average LOADED access latencies of the tiers, not maximize hot-page packing in the default tier. It measures per-tier loaded latency online via CHA occupancy/rate counters (Little's law style, sampled at microsecond scale by a dedicated spin-polling core in a kernel module) and a placement algorithm that migrates a fraction of pages (chosen by access probability, estimated via time-to-hint-fault) to equalize tier latencies, including demoting HOT pages to the alternate tier when the default tier is contended. Integrated into HeMem, TPP (Linux v6.3, ~315 LOC), and MEMTIS.
papers.hardwareEnv: Dual-socket server, Intel Xeon Platinum 8362 per socket (32 cores, 1.25MB L2/core, 48MB LLC), 8x 3200MHz DDR4 channels/socket (205 GB/s theoretical), UPI 75 GB/s each direction. CPUs of one socket only; default tier = local DDR (32GB, 70ns unloaded), alternate tier = remote-socket memory (96GB, 135ns unloaded, 1.9x ratio) standing in for CXL. Uncore frequency of remote socket reduced in one experiment to emulate 1.9x-2.7x latency ratios. Linux kernel v6.3 (TPP upstreamed + improvements), THP enabled. No CXL device present.
papers.evalSetup: GUPS (from HeMem, 72GB working set, 24GB hot set, 90/10 skew, 15 app cores) under controlled memory-interconnect contention from an antagonist on cores 16-30 (0x/1x/2x/3x intensity = 0/5/10/15 cores = 0/51/65/70% bandwidth in isolation); best-case placement found by manual mbind sweep of hot-set fraction in increments of 10%. Sensitivity: alternate-tier unloaded latency (uncore throttling), object sizes, core counts, R/W ratios. Dynamic experiments for convergence time under time-varying workload/contention. Real applications on 15 cores: GAPBS PageRank on Twitter graph (~12.6GB default tier = 1/3 WSS), Silo with YCSB-C (400M KV pairs, ~60GB, Zipfian, 15B lookups), CacheLib RAM-only with CacheBench HeMemKV workload (~75GB, 90/10 GET/UPDATE).
papers.baselines: HeMem (SOSP'21), TPP (ASPLOS'23, upstreamed in Linux v6.3), MEMTIS (SOSP'23) — each evaluated with vs. without Colloid, plus a manually-derived best-case placement. Related-work comparison (not run) to Carrefour and BATMAN.
papers.keyFindings: (1) Under contention, default-tier loaded latency inflates up to 5x unloaded (2.4x higher than alternate tier); existing systems are up to 2.3x (HeMem), 2.36x (TPP), 2.46x (MEMTIS) worse than optimal. (2) Colloid improves steady-state GUPS throughput 1.2-2.3x (HeMem), 1.35-2.35x (TPP), 1.29-2.3x (MEMTIS), reaching within 3%/8%/13% of best-case regardless of contention intensity. (3) Benefits persist with alternate-tier unloaded latency up to 2.7x default. (4) Real apps: GAPBS 1.05-2.12x, Silo/YCSB-C 1.08-1.25x, CacheLib 1.37-1.93x improvements at higher contention. (5) Migration overhead small (<0.7% of app throughput for HeMem; <1.6% TPP, 4.5% MEMTIS); no impact on convergence time. Implementation ~315 LOC on TPP; open source at github.com/host-architecture/colloid.
papers.limitations: No real CXL hardware anywhere in the evaluation — the alternate tier is remote-socket DDR4 over UPI, with uncore throttling to emulate higher latency ratios (authors note throttling also lowers bandwidth, making results conservative). Two tiers only; no multi-device or multi-CXL-node scenarios. Contention is generated by a synthetic antagonist pinned to the default tier; contention on the alternate tier is explicitly out of scope ("does not break the assumption"). No multi-tenant/QoS evaluation — the antagonist is a fixed traffic generator, not a co-tenant with its own SLO. Requires a dedicated spin-polling core and Intel CHA uncore counters (Intel-specific; discussion focuses on Intel processors). Placement is page-granularity via existing tiering systems; cacheline-granularity/hardware-managed integration left as future work.
papers.openQuestions: Behavior on real CXL ASIC devices with different loaded-latency/bandwidth curves than a UPI remote socket. Contention arising on the CXL/alternate tier itself (the exact phenomenon the requester measured: CXL co-runner slowing a CXL victim 2x) is assumed away. More than two tiers / multiple independent CXL devices with per-device latency balancing. Multi-tenant fairness: Colloid balances aggregate latency but does not isolate tenants. Portability of the CHA-counter latency measurement to AMD (EPYC) platforms. Integration with hardware-managed tiering (flat memory mode, DRAM caches).
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Highly relevant conceptually but methodologically complementary: Colloid's core claim — under interconnect contention, loaded latency, not unloaded latency, should drive placement — directly matches the requester's finding that a CXL co-runner inflates a CXL victim 2.0-2.13x, and it is a mandatory baseline/citation for any latency- or contention-aware placement system. However, Colloid is entirely NUMA-emulated (remote Xeon socket over UPI, zero CXL devices), assumes exactly two tiers, and explicitly scopes out contention on the alternate tier — precisely where the requester's 4x CZ120 testbed sees the problem (per-region ~35.5 GiB/s saturating at 4 threads). Extending latency-balancing to per-device placement across independently schedulable CXL devices, on real ASIC silicon, with CXL-side contention and multi-tenant QoS, is exactly the gap Colloid leaves open; also its Intel CHA-counter latency probe does not directly port to the EPYC 9745 host. ObjPlace's object-granularity, bandwidth-sensitivity-driven placement is a finer-grained, sensitivity-aware contrast to Colloid's page-granularity latency equalization.
evidenceQuotes: We use a dual-socket server, with each socket having an Intel Xeon Platinum 8362 CPU with 32 cores, 1.25MB L2 cache per-core, 48MB LLC, and 8× 3200MHz DDR4 memory channels with one DIMM attached per channel.

We use processors only on one of the sockets; the default tier is the locally-attached memory of the socket (32GB capacity, and 70ns unloaded latency), and the alternate tier is the memory attached to the other socket (96GB capacity, and 135ns unloaded latency).

In our evaluation so far, the unloaded latency of our alternate tier is 1.9× the default tier latency, roughly matching the current CXL-attached memory latency ratio. To better understand Colloid behavior under a wider range of realistic unloaded latencies of tiered memory deployments, we increase the unloaded latency on our servers by reducing the uncore frequency of the remote socket only for this experiment.
Based on latencies reported for real CXL hardware [54, 62], a 5× inflation in default tier access latency would correspond to 2.5× higher latency than the alternate tier.

We implement Colloid on top of TPP in Linux kernel v6.3 with ∼315 lines of code. We implement Colloid access latency measurement in a kernel module that runs a spin polling thread which samples CHA counters at microsecond-scale
Colloid provides increasingly larger benefits in terms of steady-state throughput: 1.2−2.3× for HeMem, 1.35−2.35× for TPP and 1.29 − 2.3× for MEMTIS.

We focus on memory interconnect contention on the default tier; memory interconnect contention on the alternate tier does not break the assumption of default tier latency being lower than the alternate tier latency—existing systems already perform ideal page placement under such a regime.
papers.verifyNote: Fetched the author-hosted PDF (601.7KB) and converted it with pdftotext; read Section 2.1 (Experimental Setup) and the latency-sweep paragraph directly. All three analyst evidence quotes are verbatim in the paper. Attempted refutation checks: searched full text for a second testbed, real CXL expander hardware, Optane, FPGA-based CXL, or per-device NUMA interleaving — none present; CXL is mentioned only as motivation/related work and as the latency ratio the remote-socket setup emulates. The 1.9x-2.7x uncore-frequency-throttling sweep claim is confirmed verbatim.

papers.title: M5: Mastering Page Migration and Memory Management for CXL-based Tiered Memory Systems
papers.venue: ASPLOS 2025 (30th ACM ASPLOS, Volume 2, Rotterdam, pp. 604-621, DOI 10.1145/3676641.3711999)
papers.numCXLDevices: 1 (one Intel Agilex-7 I-Series development kit with 8GB on-board DDR4 DRAM)
papers.mainProblem: CXL DRAM has 2-3x longer access latency than DDR DRAM, so tiered-memory systems need page migration; but CPU-driven hot-page identification (Autonuma/ANB hint faults, DAMON PTE scanning, PEBS sampling) is imprecise (identifies warm pages as hot) and costly enough that migration can degrade application performance. There was also no ground-truth way to count every page/word access in CXL DRAM to even evaluate these solutions.
papers.mainIdea: Exploit the CXL device controller itself (device-driven / near-memory profiling): implement Page Access Counter (PAC) and Word Access Counter (WAC) in an FPGA CXL controller to count every access to every 4KB page and 64B word in CXL DRAM (ground truth); use PAC/WAC to show ANB/DAMON find pages with only 21%/29% of the access counts of true hot pages and that many hot pages are sparse (86% of Redis pages have <=16/64 words accessed). Then build M5: hardware CM-Sketch/Space-Saving-based top-K Hot Page Tracker (HPT) and Hot Word Tracker (HWT) in the CXL controller, plus an M5-manager kernel-side interface (Nominator/Elector/Promoter) for building migration policies that avoid migrating sparse pages.
papers.hardwareEnv: Dual-socket server: 2x Intel Xeon 6430 (4th-gen Xeon Scalable / Sapphire Rapids) @2.1 GHz, 32 cores + 60 MB LLC per CPU, hyper-threading disabled; 4x DDR5-4800 channels per socket. CXL device: one Intel Agilex-7 I-Series FPGA development kit with hardened CXL x16 endpoint IP and a DDR4-2666 controller with 8GB on-board DRAM. Kernels: M5 in Linux 6.5; ANB baseline on Linux 5.19; DAMON baseline on Linux 6.11. ASIC projections of the trackers synthesized in 7nm logic; larger-N tracker preciseness evaluated in a trace-driven simulator (FPGA limited to N<=50 at 400MHz).
papers.evalSetup: 12 memory-intensive benchmarks sized to ~8GB footprint (matching CXL capacity): 4 SPECrate CPU2017 (mcf_r, cactuBSSN_r, fotonik3d_r, roms_r; 8 instances each), 6 GAP graph kernels (BFS, SSSP, PR, CC, BC, TC on Twitter/Google graphs), Liblinear (KDD2012), Redis 6.0.16 with YCSB-A. All pages initially allocated on CXL DRAM; DDR DRAM capped at 3GB (~50% of pages migratable); CPU cores hot-unplugged to match benchmark threads and LLC partitioned proportionally via Intel CAT so migration daemons contend with the workload. Metrics: access-count ratio of identified hot pages vs PAC ground truth, kernel CPU cycles, and end-to-end performance (p99 latency inverse for Redis).
papers.baselines: ANB (Autonuma Balancing, Linux 5.19), DAMON (Linux 6.11), and no-page-migration; discussion-level comparisons to Memtis, TPP, Intel Flat Memory Mode, and concurrent work NeoMem.
papers.keyFindings: (1) ANB and DAMON identify hot pages with only 21% and 29% of the access counts of the true top-K hot pages determined by PAC. (2) Hot pages are often sparse: 86% of Redis pages have <=16 of 64 words accessed. (3) Hot-page identification overhead is large: kernel CPU cycles increase up to 487%; DAMON degrades Redis by 16% by continuing PTE scans at equilibrium. (4) M5 identifies on average 47% hotter pages and gives 20%/14% higher performance than ANB/DAMON (106% over no migration) even with a simple y=x^n policy; Redis gains 10%/43% over ANB/DAMON with the HWT-driven policy at virtually no profiling cost. (5) CM-Sketch top-K tracker in 7nm ASIC costs ~0.01% of the chip area of an 8GB DRAM module's dies.
papers.limitations: Single FPGA CXL device with only 8GB DDR4-2666 on-board DRAM — much smaller capacity, older DRAM, and different latency/bandwidth profile than production CXL ASICs; no multi-device, no interleaving, no pooling. Requires custom hardware in the CXL controller (PAC/WAC/HPT/HWT) that no shipping ASIC device provides; ASIC results are synthesis projections and large-N tracker precision is simulator-based (FPGA capped at N=50 @400MHz). Authors admit: benchmarks do not use huge pages (2MB tracking is future work); M5-manager policy is a deliberately simple sample (best n chosen by hand-tuning per benchmark, adaptive f_default "out of intended scope"); ANB/DAMON/M5 run on three different kernel versions (5.19/6.11/6.5). Single-workload runs only — no multi-tenant or co-location experiments; no bandwidth-interference study.
papers.openQuestions: Adaptive migration policies on top of HPT/HWT (they only demo a hand-tuned sample policy); huge-page (2MB) hot tracking; scaling trackers to larger capacities (>128K CM-Sketch entries via per-rank tracker instances is only sketched); word-level migration/caching synergy with Intel Flat Memory Mode; whether commodity CXL ASIC vendors will expose such device-side profiling counters; behavior under multi-tenant contention and across multiple CXL devices is untested.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: M5 is device-side profiling on a single 8GB FPGA prototype, so nothing in its evaluation speaks to multi-device questions — no per-device placement, interleaving, or CXL-to-CXL interference. Its relevance to the CZ120 testbed is conceptual and as a foil: it argues host-side hotness tracking (ANB/DAMON/PEBS) is imprecise and expensive, which supports ObjPlace-style application/object-level signals over kernel page-fault/PTE-scan tiering, but its proposed fix (custom counters in the CXL controller) is unavailable on Micron CZ120 silicon. For the per-device-scheduling direction, M5 is useful related work to cite for "hot-page identification cost/precision" and NeoMem as concurrent device-side tracking, and its finding that migration overhead can outweigh benefit strengthens a case for coarser object-granularity, bandwidth-aware placement on real multi-device hardware.

We connect the server to the latest Intel Agilex-7 I-Series development kit [22] (or simply Agilex7 henceforth), which serves as a CXL development platform in this work. Agilex7 is integrated with a hardened CXL ×16 endpoint IP and a DDR4-2666 DRAM controller connected to 8GB of on-board DRAM.

papers.title: Oasis: Pooling PCIe Devices Over CXL to Boost Utilization
papers.venue: SOSP 2025
papers.numCXLDevices: 1 (one multi-headed CXL 2.0 memory pool device, 256 GB DDR5-4800, connected to two hosts via x8 lanes each; vendor/model undisclosed for confidentiality)
papers.mainProblem: PCIe devices (NICs, SSDs) are heavily underutilized in cloud datacenters — Azure data shows P99.99 rack NIC-bandwidth utilization of allocated bandwidth is only 20%, 33% of SSD capacity and 27% of NIC bandwidth are stranded, and redundant NICs for failover lower utilization further. Existing pooling options (PCIe switches, RDMA disaggregation) are expensive or inflexible.
papers.mainIdea: Since CXL memory pools are already being deployed for memory TCO reasons, reuse them as a data path to pool PCIe devices entirely in software: a shared (non-cache-coherent) CXL memory region carries I/O buffers (DMA'd by devices, load/store by CPUs) and a novel message channel optimized for non-coherent CXL memory (careful cache-line invalidations to "unblock" prefetching, 29x message throughput vs cache-bypass baselines). A common datapath plus per-device-class engines (network engine implemented; storage engine designed only) and a pod-wide allocator handle mapping, load balancing, and NIC failover across host boundaries.
papers.hardwareEnv: Main testbed: two AMD 5th-gen EPYC hosts (EPYC 9825 144-core and EPYC 9015 8-core), each 768 GB DDR5-5600 local memory + 100 Gbit Mellanox ConnectX-5 NIC; both connected via x8 CXL 2.0 lanes to ONE shared multi-headed CXL 2.0 memory device with 256 GB DDR5-4800 (vendor confidential; raw latency undisclosed, reported as 2.29x local DDR5 on EPYC). Ubuntu 24.04, Linux 6.8.0, CXL exposed as DAX via hmem (CXL driver patched out because it cannot parse the device's HDM decoder). Microbenchmarks used a dual-socket Intel Xeon 8592 with each socket connected to the same CXL pooling device via x8 lanes (non-coherent ranges). Network: 100 Gbit Arista 7060X switch; Xeon 8592 + CX5 as load driver.
papers.evalSetup: Message-channel microbenchmarks (16 B messages, throughput/latency across coherence strategies) on the dual-socket Xeon; end-to-end NIC pooling on the two-AMD-host + one-CXL-device pod: web applications (Python HTTP server, Rust Rocket, nginx, Apache Tomcat), memcached (75 B and 1500 B packets, P50/P90/P99 latency vs throughput), replay of a production Azure network packet trace for utilization multiplexing, and NIC-failure injection for failover timing.
papers.baselines: Junction (state-of-the-art kernel-bypass container networking) using a host-local NIC; baseline non-coherent message channels using cache-bypass (CLFLUSHOPT/MFENCE + CLWB, non-temporal ops) from prior work (e.g., HydraRPC-style designs); implicit comparison to PCIe-switch and RDMA-based pooling on cost/flexibility grounds.
papers.keyFindings: Oasis datapath adds only 4-7 us per packet (single-digit us) vs typical 50-110 us cloud network latency; its non-coherent CXL message channel achieves 29x higher throughput than cache-bypassing designs (baseline reached only 3.0 MOp/s vs the 14.0 MOp/s needed for 7.0 MOp/s I/O); replaying a production Azure trace, Oasis improves aggregated NIC bandwidth utilization by 2x with negligible overhead; transparent NIC failover completes in 38 ms. Also reports CXL idle load-to-use latency 2.29x local DDR5 on AMD 5th-gen EPYC, and that MWAIT/MONITOR-based polling optimizations from HydraRPC do not work on a real non-coherent CXL 2.0 pool.
papers.limitations: Authors' own admissions (Section 6): single-threaded datapath per frontend/backend driver underutilizes high-bandwidth devices; evaluation matches only a single 100 Gbps NIC to a x8 CXL link ("production systems use eight times as many CXL lanes... Unfortunately, these systems are not available to us"); single Arista switch "vastly oversimplifies production networks" (no VIP/DIP load-balancer integration); load rebalancing only at instance start/failure; CXL link/cable failures not tolerated (redundant pod topologies left to future work); storage (SSD) engine is designed but NOT implemented — only NIC pooling is evaluated; raw CXL device latency undisclosed. Methodological limits: only 2 hosts and 1 CXL pool device (no scale-out pod), one-way message-channel measurements done on a dual-socket single host rather than two hosts, no multi-tenant QoS experiments (QoS via Intel RDT only discussed).
papers.openQuestions: Sharded multi-channel datapath scaling beyond one I/O core; SSD/storage-engine implementation and other device classes (accelerators); resilient CXL pod topologies for CXL link failures; QoS/bandwidth partitioning when bandwidth-hungry CXL uses (e.g., OLAP) share links with Oasis; advanced burstiness-exploiting load-balancing policies; integration with cloud load balancers (VIP-to-DIP remapping); behavior with CXL 3.0 back-invalidation coherence (which vendors doubt will ship); larger pods with multiple MHDs / more hosts.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Orthogonal to the requester's tiering/placement work: Oasis uses one multi-headed CXL pool device as a cross-host I/O datapath, not as tiered memory, and never manages multiple CXL devices independently — so it neither anticipates nor conflicts with a per-device placement / CXL-to-CXL interference direction on the 4x CZ120 box. Useful pieces: their finding that non-coherent CXL access patterns (invalidation-aware prefetching) dominate performance, their 2.29x DDR5 latency number on 5th-gen EPYC (vs the requester's 1.53x on Turin), and their explicit punt on "QoS control for CXL bandwidth" when co-located uses saturate links — which directly names the interference/QoS gap the requester's candidate direction targets. It is also evidence that SOSP-level CXL papers can succeed with a single device, meaning per-device multi-CXL management remains open territory.
evidenceQuotes: Our evaluation setup consists of two AMD hosts and one CXL 2.0 memory device. The first host uses an AMD EPYC 9825 144-core CPU, while the second uses an AMD EPYC 9015 8-core CPU.

Each host has 768 GB of local DDR5-5600 memory and a 100 Gbit Mellanox ConnectX-5 (CX5) NIC. The two hosts are connected to one CXL device, each with ×8 lanes. The CXL device has 256 GB DDR5-4800 memory, which is exposed to both hosts. Due to confidentiality requirements, we do not disclose the raw access latency of the CXL device.

Oasis is the first end-to-end prototype that empirically supports this argument with off-the-shelf CXL 2.0 devices, delivering immediate benefits in total cost of ownership (TCO), near-native performance, and tens-of-milliseconds failover time.

We run Ubuntu 24.04 with Linux 6.8.0 on both hosts and configure the kernel to expose CXL memory as DAX devices [33]. Because the Linux CXL driver cannot recognize the HDM decoder of our CXL device, we apply a small patch to disable the CXL driver and instead use hmem [15] to expose the CXL memory as DAX devices.
The system is an Intel Xeon 8592 dual-socket server, with each socket connected to the CXL pooling device via ×8 lanes. The CXL memory ranges exposed to the two sockets are not cache coherent.
Our evaluation shows that Oasis improves the NIC utilization by 2× and handles NIC failover with only a 38 ms interruption.
The cost of Oasis is an added 4–7 µs of overhead per network packet, a modest overhead compared to typical cloud network latencies of 50–110 µs.
our own measurements on AMD 5th Gen EPYC show 2.29× higher latency.

Raw CXL access latency of the device (deliberately undisclosed; only normalized 2.29x vs DDR5 given)

papers.title: Tiered Memory Management Beyond Hotness
papers.venue: OSDI (19th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation)
papers.numCXLDevices: testbed SKX (CloudLab Skylake): 0 (NUMA/uncore-throttling emulation); testbed SPR (Sapphire Rapids): 1 (one ASIC-based 128 GB CXL expander, PCIe 5 x8)
papers.mainProblem: Existing tiered-memory systems (TPP, NBT, Nomad, Colloid, HeMem...) use access frequency ("hotness") to decide DRAM vs CXL placement, but hot data is not always performance-critical: memory-level parallelism (MLP) masks slow-tier latency, so per-access performance impact varies up to 4x across workloads. Hotness-based policies also mis-place data at allocation time and generate excessive, sometimes harmful page migrations (TPP up to 482% slowdown, worse than running entirely on CXL).
papers.mainIdea: Introduce Amortized Offcore Latency (AOL) = memory access latency / MLP combined with CPU stall cycles, a metric validated across 56 workloads that captures true performance impact of memory accesses. Two AOL-driven mechanisms: SOAR, an offline profile-guided static object allocation policy that ranks objects by accumulated AOL-based performance contribution and places top-ranked objects in the fast tier (no runtime migration); and ALTO, a lightweight kernel-side page-migration regulation layer (~30 LOC kernel-side per system) that throttles promotions when AOL is low (high MLP means latency is masked), integrated on top of TPP, NBT, Nomad, and Colloid.
papers.hardwareEnv: Two platforms. (1) "SKX": CloudLab dual-socket Intel Skylake, two 10-core CPUs, 96 GB DDR4 per socket; CXL emulated by lowering uncore frequency and disabling cores on one NUMA node, yielding 90/190 ns (2.1x) latency and 49/17 GB/s bandwidth. (2) "SPR": local Intel Sapphire Rapids server, 32-core CPU per socket, 192 GB DDR5 DRAM, one ASIC-based 128 GB CXL memory expander over PCIe 5 x8; 114/271 ns (2.4x) latency, 218/26 GB/s bandwidth. CXL vendor/model and kernel version not stated in the text I read.
papers.evalSetup: Workloads span graph analytics (GAPBS: bc-urand, bc-kron, bc-twitter, sssp-kron, tc-twitter), machine learning (GPT-2 inference), caching (Redis), and HPC (bwaves); 8 threads by default, RSS 8-35 GB, bandwidth usage 2.3-21 GB/s, fast/slow-tier ratios swept 10-90% of RSS. Performance reported as slowdown relative to fast-tier(DRAM)-only. Bandwidth-contention experiments use Intel MLC co-runners (0-9 threads, ~8 GB/s each, up to 98% of fast-tier bandwidth, 2x inflated latency) on SKX. Sensitivity studies over AOL thresholds and sampling intervals (100ms-1s).
papers.baselines: TPP, Linux NUMA Balancing Tiering (NBT), Nomad, Colloid (TPP-based implementation), and NoTier (first-touch-only); DRAM-only and CXL-only bounds.
papers.keyFindings: (1) SOAR+ALTO outperform four state-of-the-art tiering designs by up to 12.4x, underperforming in a few cases by no more than 3%. (2) On real CXL (SPR), SOAR worst-case slowdown is 42% for bc-urand vs Nomad up to 588% and Colloid up to 92%; SOAR keeps <20% slowdown with up to 90% slow-tier memory on SKX. (3) ALTO+TPP outperforms TPP by 2-471% (SKX) and 2-178% (CXL); ALTO+NBT 1-23%, ALTO+Nomad 0-35%, ALTO+Colloid 0-18% on CXL. (4) ALTO cuts page promotions by up to 127.4x (e.g., 1.6M to 190K pages for TPP). (5) Under bandwidth contention, all hotness-based tiering underperforms NoTier; SOAR beats second-best by 4-41%, but gains shrink from 33% to 4% at 9 MLC threads; ALTO+Colloid loses 3% under extreme contention unless AOL thresholds are re-tuned (33% to 23% slowdown after tuning).
papers.limitations: Authors admit: ALTO's default AOL thresholds degrade under extreme bandwidth contention (Alto+Colloid -3% vs Colloid at 9 MLC threads) and need contention-dependent tuning ("Developing an auto-tuning mechanism for AOL thresholds ... is an interesting direction for future work"). Methodology weaknesses: SOAR requires offline profiling of each workload (profile-guided, static placement — no adaptation to unseen inputs at runtime discussed as a deployment mode); only ONE physical CXL device on the real testbed, half the experiments on uncore-throttled NUMA emulation; bandwidth-contention experiments run only on the emulated SKX platform with synthetic MLC traffic, not real CXL; no multi-tenant experiments (single foreground workload plus MLC noise); workloads deliberately do not saturate fast-tier bandwidth ("in our setup, none of the workloads saturate fast-tier bandwidth"); no CXL device model/vendor or kernel version disclosed.
papers.openQuestions: Auto-tuning AOL thresholds under varying bandwidth contention (explicitly punted). Untested: multiple CXL devices, per-device placement or cross-CXL-device interference, multi-tenant isolation/QoS, tail latency (all results are runtime slowdown), online (non-profile-guided) object placement, virtualized environments, larger-than-128GB CXL capacities, AMD platforms (AOL is built on Intel offcore latency/occupancy PMU events — portability to AMD EPYC counters is not addressed).
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Directly competing prior work for ObjPlace: SOAR is also object-granularity DRAM/CXL placement, but driven by an MLP-aware latency metric (AOL) rather than bandwidth-sensitivity/skew/phase/pressure — the requester must differentiate against it and ideally compare or incorporate AOL/MLP-awareness. Its bandwidth-contention results (hotness-based tiering underperforms NoTier under contention; AOL thresholds break at 2x inflated latency) corroborate the requester's 2.0-2.13x CXL co-runner slowdown finding, but SoarAlto only injects synthetic MLC noise on an emulated NUMA platform and never runs contention on real CXL. Its real testbed has exactly one 128 GB CXL device, so per-device scheduling, CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference, and multi-tenant tail QoS on 4x CZ120 remain completely open — the requester's candidate direction is not covered here. Caveat: AOL relies on Intel offcore PMU events; reproducing it on the AMD EPYC 9745 testbed would require mapping to AMD equivalents.
evidenceQuotes: We evaluate Soar and Alto on two platforms. The first is a CloudLab dual-socket Intel Skylake server ("SKX") with two 10-core CPUs and 96 GB DDR4 DRAM per socket [52]. We emulate CXL by lowering the uncore frequency and disabling cores on one NUMA node, resulting in fast/slow-tier latencies of 90/190 ns (2.1x) and bandwidths of 49/17 GB/s.

The second platform is a local Intel Sapphire Rapids server ("SPR"), with a 32-core CPU per socket, 192 GB DDR5 DRAM, and an ASIC-based 128 GB CXL memory expander (PCIe 5 x8). Fast/slow-tier latencies are 114/271 ns (2.4x), and bandwidths are 218/26 GB/s.
These results reaffirm that Soar is effective and robust across both emulated and real CXL environments.
Soar and Alto outperform four state-of-the-art tiering designs across a diverse set of workloads by up to 12.4x, while underperforming in a few cases by no more than 3%.
This requires tuning AOL thresholds based on contention levels. Developing an auto-tuning mechanism for AOL thresholds for such scenarios is an interesting direction for future work.

papers.title: Managing Memory Tiers with CXL in Virtualized Environments (Intel Flat Memory Mode + Memstrata)
papers.venue: OSDI (18th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation)
papers.numCXLDevices: 3 (three CXL cards, each a preproduction Astera Labs Leo CXL Smart Memory Controller holding two DDR5-4800 DIMMs)
papers.mainProblem: Cloud providers want CXL memory to cut DRAM cost/carbon, but software-managed tiering (e.g., TPP, Hyperswap-style page migration) is impractical in virtualized clouds: the hypervisor cannot see guest access patterns, access-bit scanning burns nearly a whole core per VM, and CXL's ~2x latency causes large, workload-dependent slowdowns that violate cloud SLOs in opaque multi-tenant VMs.
papers.mainIdea: Two-part solution: (1) Intel Flat Memory Mode — the first hardware-managed, cache-line-granularity tiering between local DRAM and CXL memory in the memory controller, with a 1:1 DRAM:CXL capacity ratio where each physical line maps to one of two locations (local or CXL), plus a "mixed mode" carving out dedicated local-only memory; (2) Memstrata — a lightweight host-userspace multi-tenant allocator that uses page coloring to give conflicting page pairs to the same VM (eliminating inter-VM contention on local-DRAM slots) and an online hardware-counter-based slowdown estimator to detect outlier VMs and migrate dedicated local pages to them via a page-exchange syscall.
papers.hardwareEnv: Single-socket pre-production Intel Xeon 6 processor implementing Flat Memory Mode; 128 GB DDR5 local memory + 128 GB DDR5 CXL memory. CXL attached via three CXL cards (preproduction Astera Labs Leo CXL Smart Memory Controllers), each with two DDR5-4800 DIMMs and an x16 PCIe5 CXL link; CXL idle latency ~200-220% of local, ~50 GB/s max bandwidth per card. Software: Ubuntu 22.04, modified Linux 5.19 (2729 LOC kernel changes), QEMU/KVM 6.2. Core count/frequency/cache sizes withheld for confidentiality. Separate latency characterization (2.02x load-to-use) done on 5th Gen Xeon.
papers.evalSetup: 115 workloads across web (DaCapo, Renaissance, Ruby YJIT, DeathStarBench), database (TPC-C/Silo, TPC-H/PostgreSQL), ML (DLRM), KV stores (YCSB on FASTER, Redis, memcached), big data (HiBench/Spark), graph (GAP), and SPEC CPU 2017 — each run inside a VM on Linux/KVM with VM size rounded to cloud sizes (2-64 GB), under four settings: local-only, CXL-only, 100% hardware-tiered, and mixed mode (33% dedicated local + 67% HW-tiered => 67% DRAM / 33% CXL). Multi-VM experiments: 6 VMs with workload mix matching Azure's internal composition (web 31%, big data 32%, ML 11%), 1/6 to 4/6 outlier VMs; workloads >32 GB excluded due to the 128 GB local-memory prototype. Hyperthreading and frequency scaling disabled, 1:1 vCPU pinning.
papers.baselines: Local-DRAM-only (upper bound X+Y local); CXL-memory-only; hardware-tiered without Memstrata; TPP (state-of-the-art software tiering, configured with 50% local memory); random vs. hotness-based (DAMON) dedicated-page allocation; Intel 2LM/Optane memory mode discussed as prior hardware tiering; Pond discussed as static-placement prior work.
papers.keyFindings: CXL load-to-use latency measured at 2.02x local DDR5. With 100% hardware-tiered memory, 73% of the 115 workloads see <=5% slowdown and 86% <=10%; mixed mode further improves, but outliers remain at up to 34% (mixed) / 50% (HW-tiered only, e.g., 649.fotonik3d_s with 41% local-miss ratio). Hardware tiering cuts FASTER/YCSB-C slowdown from 25% to 4% vs CXL-only. TPP consumes nearly a full CPU core per VM for access scanning and still underperforms. In realistic multi-VM runs, Memstrata reduces worst-case slowdown from 35% (>30%) to below 6% without hurting other VMs, and hardware+Memstrata provides 1:1 capacity use of DRAM and CXL (unlike 2LM's inclusive cache wasting the CXL tier).
papers.limitations: Authors' own: CPU and CXL cards are pre-production, detailed specs withheld for confidentiality ("core count, frequency, and CPU cache sizes may not reflect those of the final product"); per-VM local-miss-rate counters "not implemented in the current prototype" so slowdown estimation relies on proxy per-core events covering only demand loads; page coloring assumes static VM memory sizes and needs redesign for non-virtualized/dynamic processes; workloads >32 GB excluded; no public VM traces used (workload mix synthesized from Azure statistics). Methodology-evident: requires new Intel silicon (fixed 1:1 DRAM:CXL ratio baked into hardware), CXL devices are fused by cache-line interleaving so no per-device visibility, no study of CXL bandwidth contention across devices, single socket only, and hotness within CXL tier is invisible to software.
papers.openQuestions: How Flat Memory Mode behaves at DRAM:CXL ratios other than 1:1; per-device CXL management, cross-device interference, and bandwidth-driven placement (interleaving is fixed in hardware); extension to non-virtualized processes with dynamic footprints (sketched but unimplemented); interaction with memory pooling/multi-headed devices (Pond-style); behavior with slower DDR4-backed CXL only argued, not measured; accuracy of the slowdown estimator when non-demand-load traffic (prefetches, stores) dominates.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Memstrata is the requester's stated primary inspiration and the closest multi-tenant CXL-tiering baseline, but its hardware treats the 3 CXL cards as one cache-line-interleaved pool behind the memory controller — exactly the opposite of the candidate per-device direction, and it requires special pre-production Xeon 6 silicon the requester lacks. On the requester's stock AMD Turin + 4x CZ120 box, Memstrata's page-coloring/slot-conflict mechanism does not apply, but its slowdown-estimator + dedicated-page-migration pattern maps directly onto ObjPlace-style software placement and onto per-VM/tenant outlier detection. The paper's gap — no per-device visibility, no CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference study, no bandwidth-contention isolation (which the requester already measured at 2.0-2.13x victim slowdown) — is precisely the territory the 4-independent-device direction would occupy; citing Memstrata as "pools devices, cannot isolate CXL bandwidth interference" is a clean positioning hook.
evidenceQuotes: Experimental setup. We use a pre-production Intel® Xeon® 6 Processor that implements Intel® Flat Memory Mode. Our test server contains a single socket with 128GB DDR5 local memory and 128GB DDR5 CXL memory. The CXL memory is attached via three CXL cards, which each hold two DDR5-4800 DIMMs and offer an x16 PCIe5 CXL connection. We use a preproduction Astera Labs Leo CXL Smart Memory Controller [22].

Request interleaving. To achieve maximum bandwidth, we interleave local memory requests across memory channels and interleave CXL memory requests across CXL devices at cache line granularity within the same NUMA node.
The idle latency of the CXL memory is roughly 200-220% the latency of the local memory, and the max bandwidth per CXL card is around 50 GB/s [91].
we measure that CXL memory has 2.02× the load-to-use latency of local DDR5 on the 5th Gen Intel® Xeon® Processor.
In multi-VM experiments on prototype hardware, Memstrata is able to identify performance outliers and reduce their degradation from above 30% to below 6%, providing consistent performance
Since the CPU is pre-production, the core count, frequency, and CPU cache sizes may not reflect those of the final product. For confidentiality, we cannot share the detailed technical specification.
Overall, with only hardware-tiered memory, 73% of the workloads experience no more than 5% slowdown, and 86% experience no more than 10% slowdown.

Some figure axis values (e.g., Figure 9b latency scale) omitted in the paper itself

papers.title: MTTM: Dynamic Fast Memory Partitioning with Bandwidth Optimization for Multi-tenant Cloud
papers.venue: EuroSys 2026 (21st European Conference on Computer Systems); acceptance rate 16.9%. Authors: Changjun Lee, Sangjin Choi, Youngjin Kwon (KAIST, CASYS lab). DOI 10.1145/3767295.3769371.
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no physical CXL device; slow tier = remote NUMA socket DRAM with bandwidth-throttling-based latency emulation)
papers.mainProblem: In multi-tenant tiered-memory clouds, prior work optimizes page movement between tiers but leaves the distribution of the fast tier's (local DRAM) capacity among competing tenants underexplored. Bandwidth utilization is critically impacted by "memory request rejection," which depends on how local DRAM is partitioned across tenants — bad partitioning wastes fast-tier bandwidth and hurts aggregate performance.
papers.mainIdea: MTTM, a Linux-kernel tiered memory system (CONFIG_MTTM, Linux 5.15.145) that implements DRAM-sensitivity-based partitioning of fast memory among tenants: it allocates fast-tier DRAM capacity according to each workload's characteristics (how much its performance depends on DRAM) and dynamically adjusts each tenant's local-DRAM allocation at runtime to mitigate memory request rejection and improve fast-tier bandwidth utilization.
papers.hardwareEnv: Two-socket server: 2x 24-core Intel Xeon Gold 5220R @ 2.20 GHz, 6x 32 GB DRAM per socket (192 GB/socket). Fast tier = local DRAM (socket 0); slow tier = remote DRAM on socket 1 posing as CXL memory (socket-1 CPUs removed via isolcpus=24-47). Slow-memory latency emulated by combining Quartz-style uncore-register (0x190) bandwidth throttling with intel-cmt-cat membw traffic saturation, calibrated with Intel MLC to a target idle latency (example: 300 ns). Kernel: Linux 5.15.145 with CONFIG_MTTM=y, NUMA_BALANCING off. No physical CXL, Optane, or FPGA device.
papers.evalSetup: Nine cloud workloads run as co-located tenants (cgroup-based multi-tenant mixes plus single-tenant runs): GAPBS (pre-generated -g 28 graph), XSBench, Btree (vmitosis-workloads), X-Index with YCSB-generated data (5.9 GB load / 22 GB transaction), SPEC CPU 2017, CPU DLRM inference (ISCA'23 reproduction setup), Silo, and GUPS. Experiments sweep workload mixes, memory configurations (local:remote ratios), and remote-memory access latencies (figures 8-16 in artifact scripts); metrics include performance, bandwidth, and request-rejection ratio.
papers.baselines: Local (all-DRAM), static partitioning, Memstrata (policy emulation on the MTTM kernel), vTMM (emulation), Memtis (its own 5.15.19-htmm kernel), TPP and Colloid (Colloid 6.3.0 kernel).
papers.keyFindings: Per the abstract, MTTM shows clear performance improvements over state-of-the-art tiered-memory baselines (Memtis, TPP, Colloid, Memstrata/vTMM emulations, static) across various workload mixes, memory configurations, and remote-memory latencies, by partitioning fast-tier DRAM by DRAM-sensitivity and dynamically adjusting allocations to reduce memory request rejection. Exact speedup numbers could not be verified (paper text paywalled); the artifact confirms the full comparison matrix (Figs 8-16) exists and that Fig 11 alone takes several days to reproduce.
papers.limitations: No real CXL hardware at all: the slow tier is remote-socket DRAM with uncore bandwidth throttling + traffic saturation to hit a target latency. The authors' own emulation README admits: latency and bandwidth of slow memory cannot be controlled simultaneously; the PCIe throttle register value does not survive reboots and must be recalibrated each boot; validation on real hardware was done only on Optane DC (results not public), not CXL. Single emulated slow node — no notion of multiple slow-tier devices, no CXL-to-CXL interference. Baselines Memstrata and vTMM are re-implemented as policy emulations rather than the original systems. Kernel is dated (5.15.145). Xeon Gold 5220R (Cascade Lake) has no CXL support, so device-side behaviors (CXL controller queuing, on-device bandwidth ceilings) are absent from the study.
papers.openQuestions: Whether DRAM-sensitivity-based partitioning holds on real CXL silicon, where slow-tier bandwidth is per-device-limited (~35 GB/s per CZ120 region) rather than an emulated remote socket sharing the same memory controllers. Multi-device slow tiers (partitioning tenants across several CXL devices, cross-device interference) are entirely untested. Tail latency / QoS SLOs are not the stated focus (throughput/bandwidth-utilization oriented). Interaction with huge pages, GPU/LLM workloads, and >2-tier hierarchies unaddressed.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Highly relevant as the closest recent multi-tenant fast-tier-partitioning competitor (EuroSys'26, same Memstrata lineage the requester tracks), but it partitions the DRAM tier, treats the slow tier as one homogeneous emulated node, and has zero real CXL hardware — its Cascade Lake + throttled-remote-socket emulation cannot reproduce the per-device 35.5 GiB/s ceilings and 2.0-2.13x CXL co-runner slowdowns the requester measured on real CZ120s. This leaves the requester's candidate direction (per-device CXL placement, CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference, tail-aware multi-tenant isolation across 4 independent devices) untouched: MTTM answers "how much DRAM does each tenant get" while the requester can answer "which CXL device does each tenant/object get." MTTM's DRAM-sensitivity metric and request-rejection signal are directly reusable ideas to compare against or extend in ObjPlace on real hardware, and MTTM is an obvious baseline to emulate (its kernel and scripts are public).

papers.title: Nomad: Non-Exclusive Memory Tiering via Transactional Page Migration
papers.venue: OSDI (18th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation)
papers.numCXLDevices: Platform A: 1 (Agilex-7 FPGA CXL, 16 GB); Platform B: 1 (same FPGA device on engineering-sample SPR); Platform C: 0 CXL (6x Optane 100 PM modules); Platform D: 4 (256 GB pre-market Micron CXL modules)
papers.mainProblem: State-of-the-art tiered-memory systems (TPP, Memtis, AutoNUMA, Nimble) use exclusive tiering — every page lives in exactly one tier — so under fast-memory pressure they thrash: pages ping-pong between tiers via synchronous page migration that sits on the program's critical path (PTE lock, unmap, TLB shootdown, copy, remap), causing severe performance collapse.
papers.mainIdea: Non-exclusive memory tiering: recently promoted pages keep a shadow copy in slow memory ("page shadowing"), so demotion of a clean page degenerates to remapping instead of a copy. Promotion uses "transactional page migration" (TPM): the page is copied asynchronously while still mapped and accessible; after the copy, the kernel checks (via PTE dirty bit) whether the page was written during the copy — if so the transaction aborts and retries later. Implemented as Linux kernel patches (v5.13-rc6); shadow pages are reclaimed first under memory pressure.
papers.hardwareEnv: Four testbeds (Table 1), one socket enabled, fast tier capped at 16 GB DRAM to match the FPGA device. Platform A: COTS 4th-gen Xeon Gold 2.1 GHz (Sapphire Rapids), 16 GB DDR5 + 16 GB Agilex-7 FPGA-based CXL device (read latency 316 vs 854 cycles). Platform B: engineering-sample 4th-gen Xeon Platinum 3.5 GHz + same FPGA CXL (226 vs 737 cycles). Platform C: 2nd-gen Xeon Gold 3.9 GHz, 16 GB DDR4 + 6x Intel Optane 100 256 GB PM (249 vs 1077 cycles). Platform D: AMD Genoa 9634 3.7 GHz (84 cores used), 16 GB DDR5 + 4x 256 GB pre-market Micron CXL modules exposed as a single CPU-less NUMA node (391 vs 712 cycles). Kernels: Linux v5.13-rc6 for Nomad/TPP; v5.15.19 for Memtis. Slow tier also capped to 16 GB on C/D for micro-benchmarks (limit lifted for real applications).
papers.evalSetup: Micro-benchmarks: custom Zipfian-access workloads with working-set size (WSS) smaller than, close to, and larger than the 16 GB fast tier, measuring read/write bandwidth over time (transient vs stable phase). Real applications: Redis under YCSB (50/50 read/write), PageRank graph computation, and Liblinear ML training, with small vs large RSS relative to fast memory. Also measured TPM transaction success:abort ratios (e.g., Redis on platform D 278.2:1; Liblinear on platform C 1:1.9).
papers.baselines: TPP (Meta's Transparent Page Placement, kernel-patch version from Linux community discussions), Memtis (PEBS-sampling-based; both Memtis-Default and Memtis-QuickCool variants; not runnable on AMD platform D), and a no-migration baseline. AutoNUMA/Nimble/AutoTiering discussed as related work.
papers.keyFindings: Up to 6x performance improvement over TPP under memory pressure/thrashing; consistently outperforms Memtis by up to 130% when the WSS fits in fast memory. Migration itself is shown to be detrimental under pressure: when WSS exceeds fast-tier capacity, even Nomad is sub-optimal versus disabling migration entirely and accessing pages in place. Page-fault-based tracking (TPP/Nomad) vs PEBS-based sampling (Memtis) trade off differently across platforms; TPM transactions succeed at high rates for read-mostly workloads (Redis 278:1 on platform D) but abort heavily for write-intensive ones (Liblinear 1:1.9 on platform C).
papers.limitations: Authors admit: TPM is disabled for multi-mapped pages (falls back to synchronous Linux migration); Nomad under severe thrashing is still worse than no migration at all; shadow pages consume slow-tier capacity. Methodology weaknesses: fast tier artificially capped at 16 GB DRAM everywhere (to match the 16 GB FPGA device) and slow tier also capped to 16 GB for micro-benchmarks — tiny relative to real 1 TB-class CXL deployments; Memtis could not be compared on the AMD/Micron platform; the 4 Micron devices on platform D are fused into one CPU-less NUMA node and never measured or managed per-device; artifact explicitly requires exactly one CPU node plus one CPU-less node ('If the system has more NUMA nodes, the operating system might encounter unexpected errors'); single-workload runs only — no multi-tenant, no interference or QoS experiments; no bandwidth-contention study.
papers.openQuestions: Authors explicitly punt on the migration policy: detecting thrashing is easy but deciding when to resume migration requires estimating a WSS spanning tiers (global memory tracking is 'prohibitively expensive'); they plan to extend Nomad to unilaterally throttle promotions and monitor demotions. Untested: multiple independent CXL devices/NUMA nodes, cross-device interference, bandwidth contention between co-runners, multi-tenant isolation, huge pages beyond their setup, and integration with hardware sampling (IBS on AMD).
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Nomad's platform D is essentially the requester's hardware one generation earlier: an AMD EPYC (Genoa 9634) with 4x 256 GB pre-market Micron CXL modules — but Nomad fuses all four into a single CPU-less NUMA node and its artifact explicitly breaks with more NUMA nodes, so it provides zero coverage of per-device placement, CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference, or multi-tenant QoS — direct evidence the requester's candidate direction is untouched by this line of work. Nomad is complementary rather than competing with ObjPlace: it is a page-granularity kernel migration *mechanism*, while ObjPlace does object-granularity placement in a runtime; Nomad's central finding that page migration is actively harmful under fast-tier pressure (best strategy: leave data in place) supports ObjPlace's pressure/phase-driven placement-over-migration philosophy and is a strong citation for it. TPP/Memtis/Nomad also form the natural kernel-tiering baseline set for the requester's evaluations on the same Micron CZ-class hardware.
evidenceQuotes: Platform D had an AMD Genoa 9634 processor and four 256 GB Micron’s (pre-market) CXL memory modules. This platform allowed us to evaluate Nomad with more realistic CXL memory configurations.

Platform A was built with commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) Intel Sapphire Rapids processors and a 16 GB Agelix-7 Agilex-7 FPGA-based CXL memory device [agilex]. • Platform B featured an engineering sample of the Intel Sapphire Rapids processors with the same FPGA-based CXL memory device. (note: arXiv HTML v2 contains tracked-changes duplications such as 'Agelix-7 Agilex-7')
Platform C included an Intel Alder Cascade Lake processor and six 128 256 GB 100 series Intel Optane Persistent Memory. (tracked-changes text; Table 1 row reads 'Optane 100 256 GB DDR-T ×6')
Table 1 row: 'Capacity tier (CXL or PM Memory) Agilex 7 16 GB DDR4 | Agilex 7 16 GB DDR4 | Optane 100 256 GB DDR-T ×6 | Micron CXL memory 256GB ×4'
From the perspective of OS memory management, CXL memory or PM appears to be a remote, CPUless memory node, similar to a multi-socket non-uniform memory access (NUMA) node.

To reproduce the results in the paper, the system under test requires one NUMA node with a CPU and another CPU-less NUMA node. If the system has more NUMA nodes, the operating system might encounter unexpected errors.
We evaluated both TPP and Nomad on Linux kernel v5.13-rc6 and ran Memtis on kernel v5.15.19, the kernel version upon which Memtis was built and released.
Nomad is able to achieve up to 6x performance improvement over the state-of-the-art transparent page placement (TPP) approach in Linux when under memory pressure.
Since the FPGA-based CXL memory device had only 16 GB of memory, we configured local DRAM to 16 GB for all platforms
When the program’s working set exceeds the capacity of the fast tier, the most effective strategy is to access pages directly from their initial placement, completely disabling page migration.

papers.title: Cosmos: A CXL-Based Full In-Memory System for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.venue: IEEE Computer Architecture Letters (CAL)
papers.numCXLDevices: 4 (simulated devices, 256GB each, 1TB total; no physical CXL hardware)
papers.mainProblem: RAG demands high-throughput, low-latency ANNS over billion-scale vector databases; conventional DRAM/SSD tiers hit capacity/latency limits, and specialized accelerators or RDMA clusters lack flexibility or add network overhead. Plain CXL memory expansion suffers from host-side compute bottlenecks and PCIe traffic when the host must traverse graphs and compute distances over data in CXL memory.
papers.mainIdea: Cosmos is a near-data-processing CXL memory device architecture: programmable general-purpose cores (GPCs) embedded in CXL memory controllers execute the entire ANNS pipeline (graph traversal, distance computation, candidate updates) locally, eliminating host intervention and PCIe traffic. It adds (1) rank-level parallel distance computation that partitions vector dimensions across DRAM ranks to exploit internal DRAM parallelism/bandwidth, and (2) an adjacency-aware cluster placement algorithm that assigns graph clusters to devices by proximity, balancing load and enabling parallel search across the four devices; the host dispatches queries via a CXL switch to relevant devices, which return local top-k results.
papers.hardwareEnv: No physical testbed — evaluation via a custom simulator integrated with Ramulator. Modeled system: 1TB CXL memory from four CXL devices, each with four DDR5-4800 channels and two ranks of 16Gb x4 DRAM chips per channel (256GB per device). Host CPU model, kernel, and CXL link width not specified.
papers.evalSetup: Trace-driven simulation: node-visit traces extracted from 10,000 queries each on SIFT1B and DEEP1B (BigANN benchmark) injected into the Ramulator-integrated simulator, modeling graph traversal, distance calculation, and candidate-update operations on the modeled GPC-equipped CXL devices.
papers.baselines: Base (host-side computation over plain CXL memory expansion); DRAM-only (unlimited DRAM capacity); CXL-ANNS (prior state-of-the-art CXL-based ANNS system); round-robin (RR) cluster placement as the placement baseline.
papers.keyFindings: Cosmos achieves up to 6.72x higher throughput than the Base CXL system on SIFT1B (5.35x on DEEP1B) and 2.35x over CXL-ANNS. Adjacency-aware cluster placement yields consistently lower load-imbalance ratio (LIR) than round-robin placement across devices. Rank-level parallel distance computation exploits DRAM internal parallelism otherwise wasted behind the narrow CXL link.
papers.limitations: Entirely simulation-based (Ramulator); no real CXL silicon, FPGA prototype, or measured link latencies — the GPC-in-CXL-controller hardware does not exist in any shipping device. Only one application (graph-based ANNS) and two datasets; no multi-tenant or interference experiments; no energy/area cost analysis of the GPCs visible; host CPU and CXL link modeling details are thin (short 4-page CAL letter format). Authors state no explicit limitations section.
papers.openQuestions: Feasibility/cost of embedding programmable cores in production CXL memory controllers; behavior under real CXL link latencies and contention; sharing GPC-equipped devices among multiple tenants/workloads; handling index updates/inserts; generalization beyond ANNS; validation on real hardware — all unaddressed.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Low direct relevance for systems-software work on the requester's real 4x CZ120 testbed: Cosmos assumes hypothetical compute-in-CXL hardware and evaluates purely in Ramulator simulation, so none of its mechanisms are runnable on commodity CZ120 expanders. However, it is a useful conceptual citation for the candidate direction of treating each CXL device independently — its adjacency-aware cluster placement explicitly distributes data across four separate CXL devices for load balancing, directly analogous to per-device placement/load-balancing of ANNS or KV data across the requester's four devices. It also motivates that cross-device load imbalance matters (their LIR metric), which the requester could measure with real CXL-to-CXL interference numbers that this paper cannot provide.
evidenceQuotes: To evaluate the performance of Cosmos quantitatively, we developed a simulator integrated with Ramulator.
Our setup models a 1TB CXL memory comprising four CXL devices, each with four DDR5-4800 channels and two ranks of 16Gb ×4 DRAM chips per channel (256GB per device).
Cosmos integrates programmable general-purpose cores (GPCs) in CXL memory controllers for local ANNS execution, eliminating host intervention and PCIe traffic during search.
We propose adjacency-aware cluster placement algorithm that assigns clusters based on proximity, balancing load and enabling parallel search.
The host dispatches queries via the switch to relevant CXL devices. Each device performs local ANNS using its GPC...and returns local top-k results.
couldNotVerify: Exact CXL link latency parameters and host-side simulator configuration (not surfaced in fetched HTML summary)
Whether the CAL camera-ready differs from arXiv v1

papers.title: NeoMem: Hardware/Software Co-Design for CXL-Native Memory Tiering
papers.venue: MICRO 2024
papers.mainProblem: OS-level memory tiering on CXL heterogeneous memory needs accurate, low-overhead hot-page profiling, but existing software methods (PTE-scan, NUMA hint faults, PEBS/PMU sampling) have low resolution, high fault overhead, or vendor-specific low-frequency sampling, because the CPU accesses CXL memory via plain load/stores with no OS visibility into access patterns.
papers.mainIdea: Move profiling into the CXL device itself: NeoProf, a hardware unit in the CXL memory controller, tracks page hotness with a Count-Min Sketch (default W=512K, D=2, 16-bit counters), hot-bit filtering, a 64-bin access-frequency histogram, and a bandwidth/read-write state monitor; a co-designed Linux kernel daemon (kernel v6.3) reads NeoProf and drives promotion/demotion with a dynamic hotness threshold based on top-p% frequency distribution, bandwidth utilization, ping-pong severity, sketch error bounds, and migration quotas.
papers.hardwareEnv: Single-socket Intel Xeon 6430 @ 2.10 GHz, 32 cores (HT disabled), 60 MB LLC, 4x 32GB DDR5-4800 DRAM. CXL device: one Intel Agilex I-Series FPGA Dev Kit @ 400 MHz with hard CXL 1.1 IP on PCIe Gen5 x16, hosting 16 GB 2-channel DDR4-2666, exposed as a CPU-less NUMA node. CXL latency ~430 ns, ~3.6x local DDR. Linux kernel v6.3.
papers.evalSetup: Eight benchmarks run with 32 threads (RSS 10.3–19.7 GB against 16 GB CXL + throttled/limited DRAM tier): DeathStarBench, PageRank, XSBench, GUPS, Silo, Btree, SPEC-2017 603.bwaves and 654.roms. Metrics: end-to-end speedup vs tiering baselines, plus profiler overhead (GUPS slowdown with NeoProf on).
papers.baselines: First-touch NUMA, AutoNUMA (Linux v6.3), TPP, PTE-scan and PEBS-based tiering, Memtis.
papers.keyFindings: NeoMem achieves 32%–67% geomean speedup over existing tiering solutions (TPP, AutoNUMA, PTE-scan, PEBS variants); 1.58x geomean speedup over Memtis; 1.19x–1.67x speedup on DeathStarBench; NeoProf profiling overhead is negligible (0.021% slowdown on GUPS). Device-side sketch profiling gives full-resolution access counts without CPU-side sampling cost.
papers.limitations: Authors' own admissions: "constrained by a single 16GB CXL memory device due to hardware limitations"; multi-device scenarios, interleaving effects, and virtualized environments are all deferred to future work. Methodological weaknesses: FPGA prototype at CXL 1.1 with 430 ns latency (3.6x DRAM) — much worse than production ASICs (~1.5x), so speedups over baselines may be inflated relative to real silicon; only 16 GB CXL capacity forces small working sets; single-tenant runs only, no QoS/interference study; requires custom hardware in the CXL controller, not deployable on off-the-shelf devices like CZ120.
papers.openQuestions: How device-side profiling composes across multiple CXL devices (per-device NeoProf instances, cross-device promotion arbitration, interleaved regions); how interleaving affects tiering performance (explicitly unanswered); behavior in virtualized/multi-tenant settings; whether the approach works at realistic ASIC latencies and hundreds-of-GB capacities; standardization path for exposing device-side telemetry (e.g., via CXL 3.x hot-page tracking proposals).
evidenceQuotes: One Intel® Agilex I-Series FPGA Dev Kit @400 MHz. Hard CXL 1.1 IP on PCIe Gen5 x16. 16GB 2-Channel DDR4-2666 DRAM
we are constrained by a single 16GB CXL memory device due to hardware limitations
The evaluation in multi-device scenarios to our future work
CXL memories are usually exposed to the OS as CPU-less NUMA nodes
Single socket Intel® Xeon 6430 CPU @ 2.10GHz, 32 Cores, hyperthreading disabled. 60MB Shared LLC. 32GB DDR5 4800MHz x 4
Intel's CXL memory prototype exhibits a latency of approximately 430 ns, around 3.6× that of faster CPU-attached DDR-DRAM
NeoMem achieves 32%∼67% geomean speedup over several existing memory tiering solutions
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: NeoMem is single-device FPGA (CXL 1.1, 16 GB, 430 ns = 3.6x DRAM) and explicitly punts on multi-device and interleaving, so it does not compete with a 4x CZ120 per-device-scheduling direction — it actually motivates it: the open questions it lists (multi-device, interleaving effects) are exactly the requester's candidate territory. Its device-side telemetry idea (per-device bandwidth utilization, read/write ratio, hot-page histograms) is the kind of signal ObjPlace approximates in software; the requester cannot add hardware to CZ120s, but per-device counters/perf events could serve as a poor-man's NeoProf for per-device placement and CXL-to-CXL interference detection. Note NeoMem is page-granularity kernel tiering, orthogonal to ObjPlace's object granularity; citing it as the hardware-assisted-profiling point in the design space is the main use. Its 3.6x-latency FPGA numbers should not be used as a performance comparison point against the requester's 1.53x ASIC measurements.
couldNotVerify: Exact DRAM-tier size restriction used during tiering runs (how DRAM was limited relative to 10.3–19.7 GB RSS) was not captured verbatim

papers.title: Towards an Adaptable Systems Architecture for Memory Tiering at Warehouse-Scale (TMTS)
papers.venue: ASPLOS 2023 (Volume 3)
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (tier2 is a variant of Intel Optane Persistent Memory DIMMs; no CXL devices in any testbed)
papers.mainProblem: DRAM dominates infrastructure spend in warehouse-scale computers; the paper asks how to transparently replace a fraction (25%) of DRAM with a cheaper, slower, directly-addressable second memory tier across a highly multi-tenant fleet of thousands of production services while keeping aggregate performance degradation under 5% and meeting per-application SLOs — without page faults (unlike swap/zswap) and without application modification.
papers.mainIdea: TMTS (Transparent Memory Tiering System): a four-layer architecture — hardware (tiers exposed as NUMA nodes), kernel mechanisms (A-bit page scanning, cold-page demotion, page migration), a userspace policy daemon (ufard) that consumes kernel BPF ring-buffer events plus precise PMU sampling (PEBS/IBS on tier2 LLC-miss loads) for fast fault-less hot-page promotion, and tier-aware Borg cluster scheduling. Proxy metrics STRR (secondary-tier residency ratio, driven toward 25%) and STAR (secondary-tier access ratio, kept below ~0.5%) steer adaptive demotion/promotion policies; live A/B testing (2200 experimental vs 1000 control servers) evaluates policies at scale. Additional adaptive layers: STAR-directed demotion control loops, scheduling hints classifying jobs tiering-friendly/unfriendly, and application-hinted cold allocation via TCMalloc's new-operator cold hints.
papers.hardwareEnv: Production Google fleet: 2-socket Intel Xeon servers (Cascade Lake mentioned for the Optane DIMM controller), DDR4 DIMMs as tier1 and "a variant of Intel Optane Persistent Memory" DIMMs as tier2 at 25% of machine memory capacity, sharing memory channels with DRAM. Measured tier2: sequential read 6.9 GB/s, sequential write 2.2 GB/s, random read 1.8 GB/s, random write 0.5 GB/s per DIMM; ~325 ns idle read latency; <1/10 of DDR4 channel bandwidth. Linux kernel with in-kernel A-bit scanner, BPF, and a custom promotion syscall (no kernel version given). No CXL hardware anywhere; tier2 enumerated as NUMA nodes.
papers.evalSetup: Deployed nearly two years in production. A/B methodology: 2200 experimental (2-tier, 75% DDR4 + 25% Optane) and 1000 control (1-tier all-DDR4) servers across 6 clusters running hundreds of thousands of production services; >100K distinct jobs (~1M HILS instances, 330M non-HILS), experiments typically ~4 weeks, 5% false-positive-rate confidence intervals; policy studies on 300-machine slices over 2-week or 5-week windows. Case studies: Spanner (distributed database, HILS) and a TensorFlow ML training pipeline. Metrics: STAR, STRR, per-job IPC normalized to control machines, memory utilization, TLB misses.
papers.baselines: 1-tier all-DRAM control machines (primary baseline via A/B); internal policy variants (2m_2m vs 8m_2m demotion; 60s vs 30s vs 60s+PMU promotion; NUMA jailing on/off; scheduling hints on/off). Compared qualitatively (not experimentally) to swap/zswap fault-based approaches, Nimble, HeteroOS, Thermostat, AutoTiering, HeMem, TMO, Pond in related work.
papers.keyFindings: (1) Sustains <5% aggregate performance degradation while replacing 25% of DRAM with Optane: median job IPC impact 2.3% (P5 ~7%) in the main study; 3.5% aggregate in a larger 1000-machine study. (2) Median STAR kept below 0.5% (P95 <1.5%) while STRR approaches 25% at >75% memory utilization; tier2 access ratio below 1% at socket level in >99% of instances. (3) Cold memory coverage >50%, averaging 75% — much higher than swap-based solutions. (4) PMU-sampling promotion cuts promotion latency to <1 s median (vs ~13 s/25 s for scan-only) and reduces STAR 45% at median, 44% at P95 vs 60s scan policy. (5) NUMA jailing (no remote-socket demotion) is essential: remote demotion elevated tail DRAM latency by orders of magnitude and caused kernel soft lockups. (6) Hugepage coverage drops 45%→30% on 2-tier machines, +7% TLB misses, ~1.5% of the perf impact; TCMalloc cold-allocation hints raised Spanner cold-memory identification 10%→42% and cut query latency 2%. (7) Tier-aware scheduling hints cut STAR 30% and improved latency-sensitive performance 4%. (8) System overhead ~1% CPU.
papers.limitations: Authors' own: tier2 is Optane, whose controller buffer stalls the shared memory channel and inflates DRAM latency (1.5% perf impact) — they explicitly "expect the introduction of CXL-based memory to mitigate this impact"; hardware cannot filter PMU sampling of stores, only loads (pragmatic, imperfect detector); constraints (no direct tier2 allocation, no remote-socket demotion) are artifacts of the Optane implementation; bandwidth-intensive ML workloads with unpredictable access remain unfriendly (up to 50% IPC degradation, >80% of severe bandwidth-saturation events). Methodological: no CXL hardware at all, so latency/bandwidth/interference profile differs from CXL expanders; single tier2 media type and fixed 25% ratio; Google-internal infrastructure (Borg, ufard, custom syscall) not open-source or reproducible; per-machine effects cannot be isolated due to scheduling dynamics; only two tiers evaluated though the design claims extensibility.
papers.openQuestions: Explicitly punted: adapting policies to CXL-attached memory and multi-tier (>2) hierarchies ("expandable to handle more than two tiers or alternative memory hierarchies, such as CXL attached devices" — untested); incorporating environmental signals such as tier2 bandwidth saturation into demotion control loops; compiler/PGO-generated allocation hints; cluster-level tiering-aware scheduling policies as an open research avenue; handling of bandwidth-bound noisy-neighbor workloads on the constrained tier2 remains unsolved; what STAR/STRR targets look like when media latency/bandwidth profiles change (e.g., CXL).
evidenceQuotes: Our deployment uses a variant of Intel Optane Persistent Memory as tier2. Such tier2 DIMMs have highly constrained bandwidth, supporting < 1/10 the memory bandwidth of the DDR4 channels typically on Intel Xeon Scalable Processors.
We use 2-socket Intel Xeon servers with DDR4 DIMMs as tier1 and a variant of Optane DIMMs as tier2.
We expect the introduction of CXL-based memory [1] to mitigate this impact.

Linux enumerates and initializes tier2 memory devices as NUMA memory nodes. TMTS defines a new tiered hierarchy over memory nodes. This results in two groupings for the current deployment, but is expandable to handle more than two tiers or alternative memory hierarchies, such as CXL attached devices.
It sustains less than 5% overall performance degradation while replacing 25% of DRAM with a much slower medium.

We performed a series of A/B experiments using 2200 experimental servers and 1000 control servers deployed across 6 clusters spread geographically and serving hundreds of thousands of production services daily
The measured idle read access latency is about 325ns
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: TMTS is the canonical warehouse-scale transparent-tiering baseline (with Memstrata and TPP) that any per-device CXL placement paper must position against, but its tier2 is Optane DIMMs sharing DDR4 channels — it never touches real CXL and explicitly defers CXL to future work, so it says nothing about per-device management, cross-device interference, or interleaved regions like the requester's 2-way CZ120 node. Its treatment of tier2 as a single opaque NUMA grouping, its acknowledged failure mode on bandwidth-bound unpredictable workloads (>80% of bandwidth-saturation events, up to 50% IPC loss), and its lack of any per-device bandwidth-contention control are exactly the gaps the requester's candidate direction (independently schedulable CXL devices, CXL-to-CXL interference, tail-aware QoS) targets. Its reusable ideas for the 4-device box: STAR/STRR-style proxy metrics per device, PMU-sampling-driven fast promotion, and tiering-friendly/unfriendly job classification for scheduler co-location — complementary to ObjPlace's object-granularity bandwidth-sensitivity signals. Note it is page-granularity and kernel/userspace-daemon based, contrasting with ObjPlace's object-granularity runtime.
couldNotVerify: Exact number of Optane DIMMs per server and per-DIMM capacity (paper gives only 25% capacity ratio and per-DIMM bandwidth table)
Linux kernel version

papers.title: TraCT: Disaggregated LLM Serving with CXL Shared Memory KV Cache at Rack-Scale
papers.venue: arXiv (cs.DC preprint)
papers.numCXLDevices: 1 (one SK hynix Niagara 2.0 multi-headed pooled-memory device shared between 2 servers)
papers.mainProblem: In disaggregated (prefill/decode-split) LLM serving, transferring KV-cache tensors between prefill and decode nodes over RDMA/NIC (e.g., Dynamo's NIXL/UCX) is a bandwidth and latency bottleneck, and DRAM-resident prefix caches (LMCache) are capacity-limited and node-local. Additionally, CXL Type-3 devices lack cross-host atomics/coherence, so conventional synchronization cannot be extended across hosts sharing a CXL memory pool.
papers.mainIdea: Place the KV cache in a rack-scale CXL shared-memory pool that multiple serving nodes attach to: prefill workers DMA KV blocks GPU-to-CXL and decode workers fetch CXL-to-GPU directly (the CXL DAX region is pinned via CUDA host-memory registration so GPU DMA engines bypass intermediate buffers and the network entirely). Software solves the missing cross-host coherence/atomics with a two-tier inter-node synchronization mechanism: per-node pthread-style local locks in DRAM ensure only one process per node contends for a global lock array in CXL memory, managed by a dedicated lock manager marking slots IDLE/WAITING/LOCKED. A shared prefix cache in CXL (LRU eviction) serves both nodes.
papers.hardwareEnv: 2 servers, each with an NVIDIA A6000 GPU (48 GB GDDR) and 512 GB host DRAM; baseline interconnect 100 Gbps Mellanox MT2892 NIC. CXL: one SK hynix Niagara 2.0, a second-generation CXL Type-3 multi-headed pooled-memory device (FPGA-based prototype per SK hynix public materials; the paper itself does not state FPGA/ASIC), exposed as a DAX region; measured 640 ns access latency and 10.1 GB/s bandwidth via Intel MLC; 64 GB configured as shared memory between workers. CPU models, kernel version, and CXL link width not stated in the paper.
papers.evalSetup: Two-server disaggregated serving: Server 1 runs the benchmark client, decode, and all runtime components; Server 2 runs only prefill. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B. Workloads: (a) static workloads with fixed output length (3 tokens) and input lengths swept over 1500/3000/4500/6000 tokens to control KV transfer volume; (b) synthetic workloads: three request sets from Dynamo's built-in data generator with varying unique prefix lengths.
papers.baselines: (1) NVIDIA Dynamo runtime with NIXL/UCX KV transfer over 100 Gbps RDMA NIC (no prefix caching); (2) LMCache with a 48 GB DRAM-resident prefix cache; TraCT uses a 48 GB CXL-resident shared cache.
papers.keyFindings: Verbatim headline: "TraCT reduces average TTFT by up to 9.8x, lowers P99 latency by up to 6.2x, and improves peak throughput by up to 1.6x" versus the RDMA/LMCache baselines. For pure KV transfer without caching, TraCT is comparable to NIXL despite the Niagara device's modest 10.1 GB/s bandwidth, because GPU-CXL DMA avoids network stack overheads; the big wins come from the shared CXL prefix cache eliminating both re-prefill and network transfer.
papers.limitations: Authors admit only that the LRU eviction policy is naive ("exploring more advanced policies is left to future work"). Evident from methodology: single FPGA-prototype pooled device (640 ns / 10.1 GB/s — far slower than production ASIC expanders), only 2 servers despite the "rack-scale" title, one small 8B model on a single A6000 per node, no multi-tenant or interference experiments, CPU/kernel/CXL-spec details unreported, 64 GB of pool used. No per-device placement question arises since there is one device.
papers.openQuestions: Scaling beyond 2 hosts (Niagara 2.0 supports up to 8) untested; behavior with production-grade ASIC CXL bandwidth/latency unknown; contention on the shared global lock array and on device bandwidth when many nodes serve concurrently; smarter-than-LRU shared-cache eviction; multi-tenant isolation and QoS on the shared pool; larger models / multi-GPU nodes.
evidenceQuotes: For the CXL experiments, we employ a Niagara 2.0 device, a second-generation CXL Type-3 memory expander that provides byte-addressable, load/store–accessible memory through the CXL.mem interface.

Niagara exposes its capacity to the host as a DAX memory region and functions as a high-capacity, moderate-latency memory tier. In our setup, it delivers an access latency of 640 ns and a bandwidth of 10.1 GB/s, measured using Intel's Memory Latency Checker (MLC). We configured 64 GB of space of Niagara for shared memory between workers.
Each server is equipped with an NVIDIA A6000 GPU (48 GB GDDR) and 512 GB of host DRAM. For the baseline (NIXL/UCX) configuration, the servers are interconnected using a 100 Gbps Mellanox MT2892 NIC.

Our evaluation environment is configured with 2 servers. Server 1 executes the benchmark client and all runtime components aside from prefill worker. Server 2 is provisioned to perform only prefill tasks.
TraCT reduces average TTFT by up to 9.8x, lowers P99 latency by up to 6.2x, and improves peak throughput by up to 1.6x
CXL Type-3 devices do not expose cross-node atomic operations, so traditional synchronization primitives cannot be directly extended across hosts
exploring more advanced policies is left to future work
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: TraCT targets multi-host sharing of one pooled CXL device (SK hynix Niagara 2.0 FPGA prototype, 640 ns / 10.1 GB/s) for KV-cache exchange, whereas the requester's testbed is single-host with 4 production Micron CZ120 ASICs (277 ns, ~35.5 GiB/s per region) — the hardware regimes and problems are nearly orthogonal. It offers no per-device placement, cross-device interference, or QoS treatment: one device, two hosts, no multi-tenant runs, so it does not preempt the candidate direction of treating each CXL device as an independently schedulable resource. It is useful as related work showing (a) KV cache is a natural CXL-resident object class for an ObjPlace-style placement runtime, and (b) GPU-CXL direct DMA via CUDA host registration works, which the requester could reuse on c28's 4060 Ti for KV-cache baselines. Its software cross-host locking is irrelevant to a single-host multi-device setup.

Whether Niagara 2.0 is FPGA-based is not stated in the paper itself; classified real-fpga based on SK hynix's public description of Niagara as a 4U FPGA-based multi-port CXL prototype
Whether the Niagara device is physically attached to both servers simultaneously is not explicitly stated in the evaluation section, though the shared-memory design implies it
