papers.title: CXL Memory Performance for In-Memory Data Processing
papers.venue: PVLDB (VLDB 2025), Vol. 18, No. 9, pp. 3119-3133
papers.numCXLDevices: 4 (four Seagate Composable Memory Appliance (CMA) FPGA-based blades, each treated as one CXL device; each blade hosts 8x 128 GiB DDR4-1866)
papers.mainProblem: Efficiently using CXL-attached memory in in-memory database systems requires knowing how DB operations (scans, B+tree index ops, full analytical workloads) behave on real CXL memory, and specifically how placing/interleaving data across MULTIPLE real CXL devices affects performance - prior studies used a single device or emulation.
papers.mainIdea: An in-depth experimental study on a server with four real x16 PCIe Gen5 CXL 1.1 memory expansion devices, each exposed as a separate NUMA node: microbenchmarks (CXL-Bench, successor of PerMA-Bench) for throughput/latency scaling over 1-4 devices via round-robin page interleaving with mbind, TMA bottleneck analysis of vectorized column scans and BTreeOLC, and TPC-H on Hyrise with page-interleaving and access-frequency-based column placement strategies, plus an economic (TCO) analysis.
papers.hardwareEnv: Supermicro SYS-741GE-TNRT server; 2x Intel 5th Gen Xeon Scalable Gold 6542Y (24 cores each); 8x 32 GB DDR5-4800 per CPU; Ubuntu 24.04, Kernel 6.13. CXL: four Seagate Composable Memory Appliance (CMA) Blade prototypes, FPGA-based Type 3 memory expansion, PCIe Gen5 x16 CXL 1.1, each blade with four DDR4 channels x 2 DIMMs = 8x 128 GiB DDR4-1866 (1 TiB/blade). Each blade configured as a separate memory-only NUMA node. Interconnect table: DDR 64-bit 5.2 GT/s 41.6 GB/s per channel; CXL x16 32 GT/s 64 GB/s per link.
papers.evalSetup: (1) CXL-Bench microbenchmarks: sequential/random reads/writes, 8 B-8 KiB access sizes, 1-48 threads, 7 GiB regions pinned via mbind to CPU / remote-CPU / 1-4 CXL NUMA nodes (round-robin page interleaving for >=2 devices); latency percentiles via dependent-chain 8-B accesses. (2) AVX-512 filtering column scan (512 MiB columns, selectivity 0.1%/100%) with placements CPU / CXL-1 / CXL-4 / ColumnsCXL (columns in CXL, TID writes to CPU), plus hybrid share-of-columns sweeps; Intel VTune TMA bottleneck breakdown. (3) BTreeOLC with YCSB read-heavy (95/5) and write-heavy (5/95) Zipfian workloads, 100 M ops on 100 M records, node sizes 256 B-4 KiB. (4) TPC-H SF 100 on Hyrise, 10 clients running all 22 queries in random order for 20 minutes; placement via polymorphic memory resources with linear allocators: round-robin/weighted page interleaving and top-n access-frequency column placement.
papers.baselines: All-in-CPU-memory (local DDR5) placement is the primary baseline throughout; remote-CPU (cross-socket UPI) memory as a second reference in latency/throughput microbenchmarks; single-CXL-device placement as baseline for 2/3/4-device scaling. Systems used: CXL-Bench (their tool), BTreeOLC (Muhlig et al. implementation), Hyrise DBMS. No external competing systems compared.
papers.keyFindings: One CXL device sustains ~38-40 GB/s reads (vs ~260 GB/s CPU memory sequential reads) and ~13.5-18 GB/s writes. Round-robin page interleaving across devices scales bandwidth: sequential 4 KiB reads at 24 threads reach 1.9x/2.3x/2.5x with 2/3/4 devices; writes 2x/3x/3.7x. Latency: average random-read latency 520 ns on CXL (vs ~200-ish CPU; sequential reads average 65 ns CXL vs 45 ns CPU because the hardware prefetcher hides latency); 99.9th percentile random reads ~785 ns above CPU median. Scans: 100%-selectivity scan all-in-CXL is 10 GB/s on one device; writing TIDs to CPU memory instead gives 4x (40 GB/s); four devices reach 42 GB/s (4x one device) and 92 GB/s at 0.1% selectivity (2.3x). B+tree: all-CXL achieves 38%/40% (read-heavy) and 25%/39% (write-heavy) of CPU baseline with 1/4 devices - multiple devices help write-heavy (+57%) far more than read-heavy (+6%). TPC-H on Hyrise: all-in-CXL round-robin across 1-4 devices gives 71-73% of baseline, and multiple devices give <2% gain because the workload is latency-bound; a 2:1 CPU:CXL page ratio gives 87%; keeping the 16 most-accessed columns in CPU memory (over 80% of table data in CXL) gives 94% (abstract states >80% data in CXL at 85% performance). Economics: one CXL device cuts cost up to 61% for 4-5 TiB demands; 46-64% for 4-8 TiB.
papers.limitations: Authors admit: the FPGA-based CMA blade design "is not performance-optimized for production" (so absolute CXL bandwidth/latency understate ASIC devices); "finding an optimal placement strategy is not the focus of this work"; TPC-H has less access skew than real workloads. Evident from methodology: CXL 1.1 devices only (no CXL 2.0 features, no hardware interleaving studied); single host, single DBMS process - no multi-tenant runs, no interference or QoS study between co-running workloads on different devices, no measurement of CXL-to-CXL cross-device contention (devices are only used cooperatively via interleaving); DDR4-1866 backing memory makes per-device bandwidth low relative to the x16 link; placement strategies are static/offline (access counters collected in a prior run); no OS/kernel tiering (e.g., TPP/AutoNUMA) comparison.
papers.openQuestions: Authors explicitly punt on: developing lightweight online approaches for identifying hot data and optimal placement granularities (table/column/page) as future work; co-design between database systems and operating systems; software prefetching for random CXL accesses; shared CXL memory across multiple compute nodes (spilling large intermediate results) as a new use case. Untested: per-device scheduling/isolation, interference between independent tenants on separate devices, dynamic/phase-aware migration, behavior with production ASIC devices, transactional workloads.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: This is the closest published testbed to the requester's: 4 real CXL devices, each a separate NUMA node on one host, with software round-robin/weighted page interleaving across them - directly validating that 4-device bandwidth aggregation (2.5x reads, 3.7x writes) is real, but also showing latency-bound workloads (TPC-H/Hyrise) gain <2% from extra devices, a useful decision criterion for ObjPlace-style placement. Their devices are FPGA blades with DDR4 (per-device ~38 GB/s reads), so per-device numbers roughly match the requester's CZ120 regions but latency (520 ns avg random read) is worse than the requester's 277 ns ASIC measurement. Critically, they only use the 4 devices cooperatively (interleave to add bandwidth for one workload) and never study cross-device interference, per-device QoS, or multi-tenant isolation - the requester's candidate direction of treating each device as an independently schedulable resource remains unclaimed by this paper and can cite it as motivation that multi-device CXL testbeds exist but are only exploited for bandwidth pooling.
evidenceQuotes: The server is attached to four Seagate Composable Memory Appliance (CMA) Blade prototypes [23, 55]. Each CMA blade is an FPGA-based memory expansion solution. The FPGA-based design is not performance-optimized for production. A CMA blade supports PCIe Gen5 x16 CXL 1.1 specification connectivity. Each blade has four DDR4 channels with two DIMMs connected per channel. We refer to a blade as a CXL device.

Table 2: Specifications of the evaluation server. ... CPUs: 2x Intel 5th Gen Xeon Scalable Gold 6542Y with 24 cores ... Memory: 8x 32 GB DDR5 with a speed of 4800 MT/s ... OS: Ubuntu 24.04, Kernel 6.13
We use CXL-Bench with a memory region of 7 GiB pinned to a set of the CXL devices' NUMA nodes. This results in a round-robin interleaving of pages with two or more devices.
When using multiple CXL devices, this allows interleaving pages across all devices, assuming that each device is configured as a separate NUMA node.
In this paper, we experimentally evaluate and analyze CXL memory performance with four x16 PCIe/CXL memory expansion devices directly attached to a CPU.

For sequential 4 KiB reads with 24 threads (matching the core count), the throughput achieves 1.9x, 2.3x, and 2.5x with two, three, and four devices compared to one device (with 38 GB/s). For sequential 4 KiB writes with 24 threads, the throughput achieves 2x, 3x, and 3.7x compared to one device (with 13.5 GB/s).
Our TPC-H evaluation shows that placing table columns based on access frequencies allows storing over 80% of the table data in CXL memory with a performance of 85% of a local-memory-only solution.

Placing all segments in CXL memory with a round-robin page interleaving across one to four devices yields 71% to 73% (i.e., 27.5 Q/h/c to 28 Q/h/c) of the baseline throughput. Using multiple devices does not show significant throughput increases (< 2%) over one CXL device.

papers.title: CXL-SpecKV: A Disaggregated FPGA Speculative KV-Cache for Datacenter LLM Serving
papers.venue: FPGA 2026 (ACM/SIGDA Int'l Symposium on FPGAs; also arXiv:2512.11920)
papers.numCXLDevices: 4 (4x Intel Agilex-7 FPGAs, each with a CXL 2.0 controller / attached Type-3 expander memory)
papers.mainProblem: KV-caches for autoregressive LLM decoding consume huge GPU HBM, capping batch sizes and throughput; existing offload paths (CPU DRAM, NVMe) add too much latency to be practical for datacenter serving.
papers.mainIdea: Disaggregate the KV-cache onto CXL 2.0-attached FPGA memory: a CXL Memory Manager transparently offloads KV blocks to FPGA-attached memory (64-256GB/device), a lightweight speculative prefetcher predicts which KV blocks future tokens will need (95% top-4 accuracy) and prefetches them ahead of the GPU, and an FPGA Cache Engine does inline compression/decompression (~3.2x) and address translation, hiding CXL latency behind speculation.
papers.hardwareEnv: Claimed testbed: 8x NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs (NVLink), 4x Intel Agilex-7 FPGAs (933K ALMs, 64GB HBM each) with CXL 2.0 controllers (64GB/s per x16 link, T_CXL<400ns), dual-socket Intel Sapphire Rapids CPUs (96 cores, 1TB DDR5), Ubuntu 22.04; GPU-FPGA link is PCIe Gen4 x16; FPGA connects to a CXL 2.0 Type-3 memory expander; Intel CXL IP v1.2 in cache mode. No kernel version given. Note: the paper never explicitly states results were measured on this hardware vs modeled.
papers.evalSetup: LLM serving workloads across LLaMA-2/3 (7B-70B), Qwen (1.8B-72B), Mistral/Mixtral, Gemma, CodeLLaMA; workload classes: chatbot (128/256 tokens), summarization (1024-2048 in / 128-256 out), code generation, QA. Metrics: throughput, TTFT, per-token latency, P99, memory expansion, cost-performance, J/token, multi-GPU scaling.
papers.baselines: GPU-Only (vLLM), CPU Offload (FlexGen), NVMe Offload, Compression-Only (INT8), CXL-NoSpec (ablation without speculative prefetch)
papers.keyFindings: Up to 3.2x throughput vs GPU-only (2.4x average) via 4-8x larger batches; +8.2% per-token decode latency and +4.2% TTFT overhead (P99 +12.3% from prefetch misses); 8x KV capacity expansion (24x with compression); 95% top-4 prefetch accuracy (87.2% precision); 3.21x average compression; 2.8x memory cost reduction, 1.75x cost-performance, 1.90x better J/token; 87% parallel efficiency at 8 GPUs. Code at github.com/FastLM/CXL-SpecKV (kernel driver, C++ host stack, Verilog RTL).
papers.limitations: Authors: P99 latency +12.3% from prefetch misses; 12.8% over-prefetch bandwidth waste; no dedicated limitations section. Methodological weaknesses: the paper NEVER explicitly states that the evaluation ran on the described physical testbed (no statement distinguishing measured hardware results from projection/modeling); no per-CXL-device breakdown or cross-device interference analysis despite 4 devices; no multi-tenant experiments; CXL memory is FPGA-attached prototype memory, not production CXL ASIC expanders, so latency/bandwidth characteristics differ from commodity devices; the two-author paper claims an unusually large testbed (8xA100 + 4x Agilex-7), and authors (Dong Liu, Yanxuan Yu / FastLM) have a very high-volume arXiv output pattern, warranting caution about result reproducibility.
papers.openQuestions: Authors punt on: fine-tuning/training workloads, CXL 3.0 (128GB/s, memory-side caching), heterogeneous memory tiers (HBM/DDR/NVM), and security/isolation for shared CXL memory. Untested: contention between co-located tenants on the CXL pool, per-device scheduling, behavior on production CXL ASIC expanders, tail-latency QoS under interference.
evidenceQuotes: Our platform consists of 8× NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs (1.6TB/s HBM, 312 TFLOPS FP16) with NVLink, 4× Intel Agilex-7 FPGAs (933K ALMs, 64GB HBM per device, 1.6TB/s bandwidth) with CXL 2.0 controllers (64GB/s per x16 link, T_CXL<400ns latency), and dual-socket Sapphire Rapids CPUs (96 cores, 1TB DDR5) running Ubuntu 22.04.
The A100 GPU connects to the Agilex-7 FPGA via PCIe Gen4×16, and the FPGA connects to a CXL 2.0 Type-3 memory expander.

CXL Memory Pool: Large-capacity FPGA-attached memory (64-256GB per device) connected via CXL 2.0 interface provides the main KV-cache storage. This memory is organized as a cache-coherent shared resource accessible to both GPU and FPGA.
Our code implementation has been open-sourced at https://github.com/FastLM/CXL-SpecKV
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Low-to-moderate relevance. CXL-SpecKV's "CXL" is FPGA-attached prototype memory behind Agilex-7 CXL 2.0 controllers, pooled as one cache-coherent KV store — a very different substrate from the requester's 4x Micron CZ120 ASIC expanders, and it never studies per-device behavior, cross-device interference, or multi-tenant isolation, leaving the requester's candidate direction (each CXL device as an independently schedulable resource) untouched. papers.title: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation (IKS — Intelligent Knowledge Store)
papers.venue: ASPLOS 2025 (30th ACM Int'l Conf. on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems, Vol. 1)
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 physical CXL devices; 1 proposed IKS device modeled via a cycle-approximate simulator (RTL-synthesis timing) and emulated end-to-end as a remote CPU socket (NUMA emulation) on a two-socket Sapphire Rapids server
papers.mainProblem: Retrieval (nearest-neighbor search over large vector databases) is a growing bottleneck in RAG inference: exact nearest-neighbor search (ENNS) on CPUs over 100s-of-GB corpora is memory-bandwidth-bound and slow, while ANNS (e.g., HNSW) trades accuracy and forces sending more, lower-quality documents to the generative model, inflating end-to-end inference time. GPUs have too little HBM capacity per dollar to hold large vector DBs.
papers.mainIdea: IKS: a type-2 CXL memory-expander/accelerator card with 512 GB of LPDDR5X (8 packages) and 8 near-memory accelerators (64 PEs each, 1 GHz) that offloads exact vector search. A novel host-accelerator interface built on CXL.cache uses cache-coherent shared-memory offload contexts and doorbell registers (umwait-based notification) instead of MMIO/interrupts; the device's DRAM is simultaneously disaggregated as ordinary memory expansion via CXL.mem so capacity is not stranded.
papers.hardwareEnv: Host testbed: two servers with Intel 4th-gen Xeon (Xeon 4416+, 16 cores @ 2.0 GHz, 37.5 MB L3, 2x AVX-512 FMA), 512 GB DDR5-4000 across 8 channels (256 GB/s), Ubuntu 22.04.3, Linux 5.15.0-88-generic; NVIDIA H100 SXM for GPU baselines; Intel AMX baseline on same CPU. IKS itself is NOT built: NMA RTL synthesized with Synopsys DC at TSMC 16nm; IKS (emulated) modeled at 1.1 TB/s, 69.9 TFlop/s; end-to-end runs emulate IKS as a CXL device on a remote CPU socket of a two-socket Sapphire Rapids machine.
papers.evalSetup: ENNS traces fed into a cycle-approximate simulator (RTL timing + LPDDR5X access timing + PCIe/CXL timing + measured software-stack overheads for top-K aggregation and umwait). End-to-end RAG pipelines: FiDT5, Llama-8B, Llama-70B over Wikipedia-based vector databases (50 GB and 512 GB), Google Natural Questions queries; retrieval quality vs. count studied for exact vs. approximate search. CXL.cache interface benefits measured on a real two-socket Sapphire Rapids machine (coherent shared memory vs. non-temporal writes mimicking CXL.io). Artifact: iks_simulator on GitHub + modified FAISS.
papers.baselines: CPU ENNS on Intel Sapphire Rapids (FAISS, AVX-512), Intel AMX (BFloat16), NVIDIA H100 GPUs (1-8x), ANNS (HNSW) variants.
papers.keyFindings: IKS achieves 13.4-27.9x faster exact nearest-neighbor search over a 512 GB vector database vs. Sapphire Rapids CPU, giving 1.7-26.3x lower end-to-end RAG inference time (up to 2.0-49x vs. Sapphire Rapids accelerators per conclusion). Outperforms 1 H100 GPU by 2.6x and 4.6x at batch sizes 1 and 16 for retrieval. Cache-coherent CXL.cache offload-context communication gives 1.6x higher throughput than non-temporal writes mimicking the PCIe MMIO (CXL.io) datapath. Exact retrieval lets the generator consume fewer, higher-quality documents, so paying for ENNS can reduce total inference time at equal accuracy.
papers.limitations: No real CXL hardware anywhere in the loop: the device exists only as synthesized RTL + a cycle-approximate simulator, and end-to-end numbers splice simulated retrieval latency into runs where IKS is emulated as a remote NUMA socket — real CXL link behavior (contention, controller queuing, coherence traffic under load) is untested. Single proposed device; no multi-device, multi-tenant, or interference experiments; the memory-disaggregation claim (CXL.mem expansion for co-running apps) is asserted but not evaluated with co-runners. Authors admit: if a dataset is amenable to clustering, the ENNS-ANNS accuracy gap shrinks (weakening the case for exact search), and NMA chip utilization is low for batch sizes under 64. CXL.cache (type-2) devices are essentially unavailable commercially, limiting near-term realizability.
papers.openQuestions: Behavior when the same IKS DRAM is concurrently used as CXL.mem expansion by other tenants while NMAs scan it (bandwidth interference between search and expansion traffic) is unaddressed. Scaling across multiple IKS cards per host, cross-device coordination, and QoS are not studied. Real-silicon validation of the CXL.cache doorbell/shared-context interface (measured only via socket-to-socket coherence as a proxy) remains open, as does ANNS-on-IKS and dynamic exact/approximate selection.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Low direct relevance to your 4x CZ120 testbed: IKS is a proposed custom type-2 (CXL.cache) near-memory accelerator evaluated purely in simulation/NUMA-emulation, not a study of real CXL.mem expanders, and it never exercises multiple devices or cross-device interference. It is useful as related work in two ways: (1) it quantifies that large-vector-DB search is bandwidth-bound on host memory, which supports your bandwidth-sensitivity-driven ObjPlace placement story for RAG/vector workloads on CZ120s; (2) its "disaggregate the device DRAM so it isn't stranded" claim is asserted without co-runner experiments — exactly the search-traffic-vs-expansion-traffic interference question your victim/co-runner measurements can answer on real hardware. Cite it for RAG-retrieval motivation and for the contrast between simulated NDP proposals and real multi-device CXL characterization; it does not compete with a per-device placement/QoS direction.
evidenceQuotes: To evaluate the performance of the IKS, we developed a simulator (see appendix A) and fed ENNS traces into it to obtain the retrieval time of IKS. The simulator is a cycle-approximate performance model that utilizes timing parameters from the RTL synthesis, LPDDR5X access timing, PCIe/CXL timing [43; 81], along with calculations of real software stack overhead (top-K aggregation and umwait() overhead). It emulates an IKS as a CXL device running on a remote CPU socket.
We implemented the RTL design of the Near-Memory Accelerator (NMA) used in IKS and synthesized it using Synopsys Design Compiler targeting TSMC's 16nm technology node.
We ran the experiments on two servers equipped with Intel Xeon 4th generation CPUs and one NVIDIA H100 GPU

papers.title: CXL-Bench: Benchmarking Shared CXL Memory Access
papers.venue: ADMS workshop @ VLDB 2025 (16th Int'l Workshop on Accelerating Analytics and Data Management Systems)
papers.numCXLDevices: 1 (one Seagate Composable Memory Appliance blade with 8x 128 GiB DDR4 DIMMs, two CXL 1.1 ports, one port per server)
papers.mainProblem: Database developers lack a way to quantify access performance across increasingly heterogeneous memory paths (local/remote socket, multi-die, CXL device memory), and in particular do not know how multiple servers simultaneously accessing one shared CXL memory device affect each other's latency/bandwidth, or how expensive (un)mapping shared CXL regions is.
papers.mainIdea: CXL-Bench: a highly configurable open-source microbenchmark framework (extending PerMA-Bench) covering scalar/vector/streaming loads and stores, cache instructions (clwb/clflush/clflushopt), CAS/FAA atomics, mmap/unmap latency, NUMA-node vs devdax character-device abstractions, thread pinning, interleaved/partitioned placement, and a distributed mode that time-synchronizes workloads on multiple servers attached to one shared CXL device. Demonstrated by characterizing two servers sharing one CXL 1.1 device in devdax mode.
papers.hardwareEnv: Server EMR: Supermicro SYS-741GE-TNRT, 2x Intel Xeon Gold 6542Y (24 cores/CPU, Emerald Rapids), 8x 32 GB DDR5-4800 (1 DPC), Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.13.0. Server GNR: Avenue City Platform, 1x Intel Xeon 6 engineering sample (96 cores, Granite Rapids), 12x 16 GB DDR5-5600, same OS/kernel. CXL device: FPGA-based Seagate Composable Memory Appliance (CMA) Blade prototype, 4 DDR4 channels x 2 DPC = 8x 128 GiB DIMMs at 1866 MT/s, data interleaved across all 8 DIMMs, PCIe Gen5 x16 CXL 1.1 (64 GB/s per port), two ports each connected to one server; configured as character device in devdax mode (/dev/dax2.0), not as a NUMA node.
papers.evalSetup: Microbenchmarks only, via CXL-Bench distributed mode: a "main" workload on EMR measures latency (10 M ops, sample every 1000th -> 10 000 samples) or throughput (10 s runs, 1-48 threads) of 64 B vector/streaming vector loads and stores plus CAS/FAA atomics against 16 GiB (also 64 GiB) devdax regions, with and without a "background" workload on GNR doing continuous sequential vector reads to the same device (same-offset and disjoint 512 GiB-offset variants). Separate experiment: mmap/unmap latency for 16-128 GiB devdax regions vs anonymous shared/private regions (MAP_POPULATE, 5 repetitions averaged).
papers.baselines: No system baselines (it is itself a benchmark tool). Comparisons are internal: with vs without cross-server background load; vector vs streaming-vector instructions; devdax mmap vs anonymous shared/private mmap. Framework is compared qualitatively to PerMA-Bench in related work.
papers.keyFindings: (1) Cross-HOST interference on one shared device: with GNR background reads, EMR median random load latency rises ~70% (480/490 ns -> 820/830 ns; p99 860 -> 1270 ns), and load throughput drops ~50%; store latencies are unaffected but store throughput drops significantly. Interference persists even when the two hosts use disjoint regions (offset 512 GiB), because the device interleaves data across all 8 DIMMs. (2) Streaming vector stores reach ~40 GB/s, 2.4x higher than regular vector stores (16.5 GB/s max), by avoiding RFO reads. (3) Uncached CAS/FAA latency is dominated by memory access latency (500-550 ns unloaded, 800-850 ns loaded; <50 ns p90 if cache line pre-loaded); atomics on CXL 1.x/2.0 shared memory trigger no cross-host coherence. (4) devdax mmap of 128 GiB takes ~1 s vs 40 s/26 s for anonymous shared/private; unmap <0.1 s — frequent CXL region re-allocation is feasible.
papers.limitations: Single CXL device only — no multi-device experiments at all, and CXL 1.1 only (no coherent sharing, no pooling/DCD). Device is an FPGA prototype (Seagate CMA) with DDR4 at 1866 MT/s, so absolute numbers (480 ns loads, ~40 GB/s) may not transfer to production ASICs like CZ120. Only one interference pattern tested (background = sequential vector reads from one server); no write-heavy or mixed background loads, no >2 hosts despite the discussion of hundreds of cores. Microbenchmarks only — no application/database workloads in this paper. Fixed 64 B access size in the load/store experiments; asymmetric servers (2-socket EMR vs 1-socket GNR ES) with main workload always on EMR. No QoS/isolation mechanism proposed, only measurement.
papers.openQuestions: Authors explicitly punt on how to distribute data across memory tiers to avoid oversubscribing CXL/memory controllers ("one needs to carefully distribute data") — no placement policy given. Untested: interference among multiple CXL devices; more than two hosts; per-region hardware QoS or bandwidth partitioning on the device; behavior of CXL 2.0/3.x pooling, DCD, and hardware coherent sharing; whether findings hold on ASIC devices; application-level (DBMS) impact of the measured interference; manual erasure cost of reused devdax pages.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Adjacent but orthogonal axis of interference: this paper shows contention between two HOSTS on ONE shared CXL device, whereas the requester's candidate direction is contention/scheduling ACROSS 4 devices under one host — so it does not occupy that niche and can be cited as evidence that device-internal controllers/DIMM interleaving are the contention point (interference persisted even for disjoint regions because the device interleaves across all DIMMs; analogous to the requester's 2-way root-decoder interleave coupling their two online CZ120s). The ~70% load-latency and ~50% throughput degradation numbers on a shared device complement the requester's 2.0-2.13x victim slowdown and support the argument that per-device (non-interleaved) management is needed for isolation. The devdax fast-mmap result (1 s for 128 GiB) is directly relevant to per-device dynamic re-allocation in an ObjPlace extension, and note two of the requester's CZ120s already host famfs on devdax. Caveats for citation: FPGA prototype with DDR4, CXL 1.1, Intel hosts — absolute numbers differ from the requester's ASIC CZ120/EPYC Turin setup.
evidenceQuotes: The CXL memory device is an FPGA-based Seagate Composable Memory Appliance (CMA) Blade prototype [14, 30] with four DDR4 memory channels and two DIMMs per channel (DPC). Data stored on the device is interleaved across all eight DIMMs. The CMA supports the PCIe Gen5 x16 CXL 1.1 specification connectivity. One CMA has two ports. Each port can be connected to a separate server for a shared memory setup. We refer to a single blade as CXL device in the remainder of this work.

We demonstrate the utility of CXL-Bench by quantifying memory access characteristics of two servers accessing a shared CXL 1.1 memory device. Our results show that memory accesses of one server to the device affect the access performance of another server accessing the same device.

The CXL device is configured as character device in devdax mode. Its physical memory is mapped into the virtual memory address space using the mmap system call, as shown in Listing 1. In this example code, the CXL device path is /dev/dax2.0.
Without background load, the median latencies for vector loads and streaming vector loads are 480 ns and 490 ns. ... With background load, the median latencies increase to 820 ns and 830 ns.
With sequential read load on the CXL device generated by the GNR server, the achieved throughput is reduced by approximately 50%.
Changing the start offset of the background workload's memory region (to 512 GiB) so that the regions of the main and background workload are disjoint yields the same latencies.
Vector stores achieve a maximum of 16.5 GB/s. The throughput of streaming stores is by 2.4× higher, reaching a plateau of approximately 40 GB/s.
For 128 GiB, mapping the character device takes only one second while allocating anonymous memory regions takes 40 seconds and 26 seconds in shared and private mode.

papers.title: Mercury: QoS-Aware Tiered Memory System
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.OS), arXiv:2412.08938
papers.numCXLDevices: real-CXL testbed: 2 (Astera Labs memory expansion cards); emulation testbed: 0 (remote NUMA socket with uncore throttling)
papers.mainProblem: Existing tiered memory systems (TPP, Colloid, etc.) optimize aggregate performance but lack QoS support, so when multiple applications with different priorities/SLOs share a CXL-tiered machine, memory-capacity contention on the fast tier and bandwidth interference within/across tiers cause SLO violations for latency- and bandwidth-sensitive workloads.
papers.mainIdea: Mercury adds QoS to tiered memory via: (1) per-tier page reclamation enabling application-level per-tier capacity allocation (instead of global/node-level reclamation), (2) intra- and inter-tier bandwidth-interference mitigation, (3) a proactive admission control algorithm tailored for tiered memory that decides whether a new app's SLO can be satisfied before admitting it, and (4) real-time adaptation to dynamic requirement changes. Implemented in Linux kernel v6.6 plus ~3000 LoC C++ user-space components.
papers.hardwareEnv: Real-CXL testbed: dual-socket AMD Genoa servers, 96 physical cores and 12 DDR5 channels per socket, 768GB DDR5 per socket + 256GB CXL memory (1.8TB total) supplied by two Astera Labs memory expansion cards with 2 DDR5 channels each, each card on x16 PCIe lanes (x32 total). Emulation testbed: dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6330 (56 physical cores), 512GB DDR4 per socket, remote socket used as slow tier with uncore frequency tuned down to match measured real-CXL latency. Linux kernel v6.6.
papers.evalSetup: Multi-tenant co-location experiments over 80 workloads across seven categories (databases, ML, KV stores/Redis, Spark, graph processing, SPEC CPU 2017, web apps, VectorDB), running applications simultaneously with assigned priorities and SLOs (latency targets for latency-sensitive apps, bandwidth targets for bandwidth-intensive ones); scenarios cover local-memory contention, bandwidth interference, combined contention+interference, and long-running dynamic adaptation.
papers.baselines: TPP (Transparent Page Placement) and Colloid
papers.keyFindings: Under local-memory contention Mercury cuts foreground max slowdown from 29% to 12% and VectorDB slowdown from 75% to 14%; up to 40% improvement over TPP for ML workloads under bandwidth interference; 53.4% performance improvement for VectorDB under combined contention+interference; 8.4x longer SLO-satisfaction time for Redis vs TPP; overall 14.9% and 20.3% improvement vs TPP and Colloid respectively.
papers.limitations: The two Astera Labs CXL cards are managed only as an abstract slow "tier" — no per-device visibility, no CXL-device-to-CXL-device interference study, and the paper never states how the two cards are exposed as NUMA nodes. Part of the evaluation runs on NUMA emulation (Intel socket with uncore throttling), not real CXL. Admission control simply rejects inadmissible apps ("the user should adjust the SLO or deploy it on another machine"), i.e., no graceful degradation. QoS mechanisms are page-granularity kernel reclamation, so per-object placement effects are out of scope. Not (yet) upstreamed; authors only plan to "share our design with the Linux community for open discussion after the paper's publication".
papers.openQuestions: How QoS/isolation should work when multiple CXL devices are managed independently rather than as one tier; cross-CXL-device bandwidth interference; scaling beyond two tiers/two devices; interaction with object-granularity placement runtimes; behavior with CXL switches/pooling across hosts; SLO negotiation instead of hard admission rejection.
evidenceQuotes: CXL memory enabled via two Astera Labs memory expansion cards with 2 DDR5 channels. Each card connects via x16 PCIe lanes (x32 lanes in total).
The servers have a 1.8TB memory footprint with 768GB DDR5 per socket and 256GB CXL memory.

We run these experiments on dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6330 servers with 56 physical CPU cores where each socket contains 512GB DDR4 memory. For controlling the environmental setup, we use the remote socket as the slow tier, with uncore frequency tuned down to match the memory access latency in our real CXL hardware.
In a CXL-enabled tiered memory system, memory nodes appear to the system as separate NUMA nodes ... assume that each tier consists of one or multiple NUMA nodes.
Mercury enables per-tier page reclamation for application-level resource management ... a novel admission control algorithm tailored for tiered memory.
couldNotVerify: Whether the two Astera Labs cards are exposed as one interleaved NUMA node or two separate NUMA nodes — the paper (per fetched text) does not state this; deviceTreatment=multi-device-pooled is inferred from the paper managing CXL as a single slow tier with per-tier (not per-device) mechanisms.
CXL device capacity per card and link generation (only total 256GB CXL and x16 PCIe per card stated in fetched text).
Which experiments ran on the real-CXL vs the emulated testbed (the split is stated to exist but I could not attribute every result).
Exact author-written future-work/limitations section text beyond the quotes fetched.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Highly relevant as the closest QoS-for-tiered-memory baseline: Mercury does per-tier capacity allocation, bandwidth-interference mitigation, and admission control on real CXL (2 Astera Labs cards) plus emulation — but it collapses all CXL devices into one abstract slow tier and never manages or measures devices independently, leaving the requester's candidate direction (per-device placement, CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference, per-device tail-aware QoS on 4x CZ120) unclaimed. It validates the requester's own observation that CXL bandwidth interference (their 2.0-2.13x victim slowdown) is the key QoS problem, and its TPP/Colloid baselines and 80-workload multi-tenant methodology are a useful evaluation template. A per-device, object-granularity QoS system (ObjPlace extension) would be positioned as finer-grained than Mercury's page/tier-level kernel mechanisms; expect reviewers to demand a Mercury/Colloid comparison.
papers.verifyNote: Verified directly against the arXiv HTML full text (downloaded and grepped, plus WebFetch of the abs page). All analyst quotes are verbatim except the first, which drops the word 'is' ("CXL memory is enabled via..."). One nuance for deviceTreatment: 'multi-device-pooled' is supported at the tier level (two cards -> one 256GB CXL tier), but the paper is silent on whether the two Astera cards are interleaved into a single NUMA node or exposed as multiple nodes within the tier. Also note many evaluation experiments (e.g., 5.3 'follows the same workload setup as depicted in Figure 5', the 80-workload suite) appear to run on the Xeon Gold NUMA-emulation testbed, so 'mixed' is the right realCXL label.

papers.title: Architectural and System Implications of CXL-enabled Tiered Memory (MIKU)
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.AR, cs.ET); no conference venue stated
papers.numCXLDevices: Platform A: 2 (256GB Micron pre-market each), Platform B: 4 (256GB Micron pre-market each)
papers.mainProblem: Tiered DDR+CXL memory suffers severe, previously uncharacterized cross-tier interference: CXL devices have limited hardware-level parallelism (few in-flight requests) and the CPU's shared on-chip request path (CHA/IRQ→ToR queuing) dispatches DDR and CXL requests at the same rate, so slow CXL requests back up shared queues and unfairly throttle fast DDR traffic — DDR bandwidth can drop by up to 81% (performance loss up to 89%) under heavy CXL load, and CXL latency rises by nearly an order of magnitude.
papers.mainIdea: MIKU, a dynamic memory-request control mechanism that prioritizes DDR requests and serves CXL requests best-effort: it estimates memory-request service time / queuing pressure via hardware performance counters (Intel PMU) and dynamically throttles the CXL-request issue rate using CPU quota adjustment (Linux cgroups) or Intel RDT Memory Bandwidth Allocation (MIKU-MBA), preserving near-peak DDR throughput while keeping CXL performance high — a pure software prototype on commodity hardware, no hardware changes.
papers.hardwareEnv: Two real testbeds with pre-market Micron CXL ASIC memory expanders. Platform A: two sockets, processor from "vendor A" (anonymized, Intel-implied given CHA/IRQ/ToR and RDT usage), 8x 32GB DDR5-4800 DIMMs per socket, two 256GB Micron pre-market CXL devices, PCIe Gen5 x8. Platform B: single socket, processor from "vendor B" (anonymized), 12x 16GB DDR5-4800 DIMMs, four 256GB Micron pre-market CXL devices, PCIe Gen5 x8. DDR hardware-interleaved; CXL devices software-interleaved via Linux weighted interleaving with equal weights. Kernel version not stated.
papers.evalSetup: Micro-benchmarks: lat-test (pointer chasing, load-to-use latency) and bw-test (sequential accesses, bandwidth) run as DDR/CXL co-runners to expose cross-tier queuing interference. Real applications: LLM serving (LLaMA models, prefill/decode phases), Apache Spark running TPC-H queries, and a concurrent hash table (dashmap) driven by a YCSB dataset. Workloads placed on DDR vs CXL tiers concurrently to measure interference and MIKU's mitigation.
papers.baselines: DataRacing (unthrottled co-running, no control); MIKU (CPU-quota-based throttling); MIKU-MBA (variant using Intel Memory Bandwidth Allocation); Opt (each workload run in isolation, no interference — upper bound).
papers.keyFindings: (1) Disparity in memory-tier parallelism lets CXL traffic reduce DDR bandwidth by up to 81%; DDR performance loss up to 89% under co-running heavy CXL load. (2) CXL latency rises nearly an order of magnitude under load because requests accumulate in shared IRQ/ToR queues — cores issue DDR and CXL requests at the same rate even though DDR completes faster, creating unfair dispatch that hurts the faster tier. (3) MIKU recovers near-peak DDR throughput while keeping CXL best-effort: achieves at least 81% of optimal performance on DDR across workloads and 89% of optimal LLM decode performance. (4) Findings hold on two vendors' CPUs and both 2-device and 4-device Micron CXL configurations.
papers.limitations: Authors' own: MIKU is most effective when workloads alternate between DDR and CXL phases every tens of seconds or longer; stabilization takes ~6-7 seconds, so fast-phase-changing workloads are poorly served; they punt architectural fixes (token-based differential request scheduling) to future work. Methodological: CPU vendors are anonymized ("vendor A/B") so exact CHA/queue microarchitecture is unverifiable; kernel version and CXL device model not stated; CXL devices are always pooled via equal-weight software interleaving — no per-device analysis, no CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference study, no multi-tenant isolation experiments; throttling is coarse (cgroup CPU quota / MBA acts on cores, not on CXL traffic specifically), which can collaterally slow non-memory work of throttled tasks.
papers.openQuestions: Hardware-level fixes (differential/token-based request scheduling in the CHA) are explicitly left for future investigation. Untested: per-CXL-device scheduling and interference (devices only ever used as an interleaved pool), fairness among multiple CXL tenants (only DDR-vs-CXL fairness is addressed), tail-latency SLO enforcement rather than throughput recovery, behavior on kernels with hardware tiering (e.g., TPP/weighted autotiering) migrating pages mid-run, and fast phase-alternating workloads (<10s phases).
evidenceQuotes: Platform A was equipped with two sockets, each featuring a processor from vendor A, 8 DDR DIMMs (32GB each), and two 256GB Micron's (pre-market) CXL memory devices.
Platform B had a single socket equipped with a processor from vendor B, 12 DDR DIMMs (16GB each), and four 256GB Micron's (pre-market) CXL memory devices.
On both platforms, hardware interleaving was applied to all DDRs, while CXL memory devices were interleaved in software using Linux's weighted interleaving (ker, [2023]), with equal weights.

The disparity in handling concurrent memory requests, particularly under heavy load, between memory tiers leads to unfair memory request processing for the faster memory tier. This imbalance can significantly reduce DDR memory bandwidth, by as much as 81%.
CXL memory requests gradually accumulate in the IRQ because cores issue DDR and CXL requests to the IRQ at the same rate, even though DDR requests are completed more quickly at the ToR.
MIKU achieves 89% of the optimal decode performance.
MIKU achieves at least 81% of the optimal performance on DDR.
MIKU is most effective for workloads that alternate between DDR and CXL memory accesses every tens of seconds or longer.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Highly relevant: Platform B is nearly the requester's exact box — a single-socket non-Intel ("vendor B") CPU with four 256GB pre-market Micron CXL devices (almost certainly CZ120s, same as the requester's EPYC 9745 + 4x CZ120). It gives an architectural mechanism (limited CXL device parallelism + unfair shared-queue dispatch) that explains the requester's own observation that a CXL co-runner slows a CXL victim 2.0-2.13x and that per-region bandwidth saturates at only 4 threads. Crucially, MIKU always pools the 4 devices via equal-weight software interleaving and never studies per-device placement or CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference — leaving the requester's candidate direction (each CXL device as an independently schedulable resource, per-device QoS, multi-tenant isolation) open; MIKU's core-level cgroup/MBA throttling is also a natural baseline for a per-device tail-aware QoS system and complements ObjPlace's object-granularity placement.

papers.title: PACT: A Criticality-First Design for Tiered Memory
papers.venue: ASPLOS 2026 (31st ACM ASPLOS, Volume 2; Best Paper honorable mention per search snippet)
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no physical CXL device; CXL emulated by uncore-throttling the remote NUMA socket of a dual-socket Skylake to 190ns)
papers.mainProblem: Existing tiered-memory systems place/migrate pages by access frequency ("hotness"), but frequency does not predict actual performance cost: pages with identical access frequency can differ in stall contribution by up to 65x because MLP/latency-tolerance varies. Coarse per-core stall counters lack the per-page, per-tier granularity needed to place pages by true performance impact.
papers.mainIdea: Introduce PAC (Page Access Criticality): estimate each page's contribution to LLC-miss-induced CPU stalls online via an MLP-aware analytical model using only 4 standard CPU performance counters (per-tier stalls modeled from LLC misses, latency, and TOR-occupancy-derived MLP; Pearson >0.98), attributing 20ms stall windows proportionally to PEBS-sampled page accesses. PACT is a Linux 5.15 tiering system where PAC drives placement: eager demotion (via MGLRU, proactively freeing fast-tier space) plus adaptive promotion using dynamic binning over a hash table + priority queues, avoiding global sorting and static hot/cold thresholds. Samples only slow-tier load accesses; ~25 bytes per tracked 4KB page (0.6% overhead).
papers.hardwareEnv: Dual-socket Intel Skylake server on CloudLab; each socket a 10-core Xeon at 2.2GHz with 96GB DDR4 (52GB/s, 90ns local; cross-socket NUMA 32GB/s, 140ns). CXL emulated by reducing remote-NUMA-node uncore frequency to raise latency to 190ns (2.1x DRAM). Implemented on Linux 5.15 (incorporating modules/fixes from TPP). No real CXL silicon anywhere in the paper.
papers.evalSetup: 13 memory-intensive workloads: graph analytics (GAPBS), GPT-2 inference, in-memory databases, SPEC CPU 2017 HPC; 8 threads each, RSS 6.6-40GB, bandwidth demand 6-45GB/s. Varied 7 fast/slow tier ratios from 8:1 to 1:8, 4KB vs THP, memory pressure, plus sensitivity analyses and a controlled colocation microbenchmark (Figure 12). Metric: runtime slowdown normalized to DRAM-only ideal; also migration counts. Motivation study profiled Masim, GUPS, tc-twitter on the 190ns emulated tier; model validation over 96 workloads across three latency configs (90/140/190ns).
papers.baselines: Soar and Alto, Memtis, Colloid, Nomad, TPP, Linux NUMA Balancing Tiering (NBT), plus NoTier (first-touch) and DRAM-only/CXL-only reference lines.
papers.keyFindings: Frequency-identical pages differ in criticality by up to 65x. PACT achieves up to 61% improvement over the second-best system across 13 workloads and 7 tier ratios; when not best, it trails the winner by 4.1% on average (max 11.8%). Up to 50x (50.1x/40.6x cited) fewer migrations and up to 10.4x fewer promotions than second-best; outperforms Colloid by up to 33% and Nomad by over 500% across 12 workloads; average improvements 9.95% (1:2 ratio) and 10.66% (2:1) with peaks of 57%/61%. Under colocation microbenchmarks PACT still beats prior policies. Per-tier stall model reaches Pearson 0.98 vs 0.82-0.89 for raw LLC-miss counts.
papers.limitations: Authors admit: proportional stall attribution breaks down when heterogeneous access streams share a tier (e.g., multi-tenant CXL memory) — latency-bound and streaming accesses get frequency-diluted criticality; finer-grained stall observability is left as future work, as is latency-weighted attribution and systematic exploration of PAC cooling mechanisms. Methodology weaknesses: entirely NUMA-emulated CXL (uncore throttling to 190ns) on an old dual-socket Skylake — no real CXL device, so no CXL-specific bandwidth ceilings, controller queuing, or head-of-line effects; single slow tier only (no multi-device or per-device treatment); PEBS-dependent (Intel-only counters, e.g., TOR occupancy); demotion delegated to LRU rather than PAC-driven; single-workload runs except one colocation microbenchmark.
papers.openQuestions: PAC estimation under multi-tenant/colocated tiers (explicitly punted, needs finer stall attribution such as latency-weighted PAC or CXL 3.2 CHMU-based sampling). Behavior on real CXL ASICs where bandwidth contention (not just latency) dominates is untested. Multiple slow tiers / multiple independently managed CXL devices are never considered — the design assumes one fast and one slow tier. Portability beyond Intel PEBS/TOR counters (e.g., AMD) is unaddressed.
evidenceQuotes: Testbed. We evaluate PACT on a dual-socket Intel Skylake server on CloudLab [15]. Each socket contains a 10-core Xeon CPU (2.2GHz) with 96GB DDR4, providing 52GB/s bandwidth and 90ns access latency for local memory access. Cross-socket NUMA accesses exhibit 32GB/s bandwidth and 140ns latency. To emulate CXL memory, we reduce remote NUMA node uncore frequency, increasing access latency to 190ns (2.1× DRAM latency), consistent with measured CXL device characteristics and prior work [30, 32, 37, 51, 53].
We use three memory configurations: local DRAM (90ns), NUMA (140ns), and simulated CXL with CPUless NUMA (190ns).
we profile three applications on an emulated CXL device with 190ns latency (§5): Masim [9], GUPS [4], and tc-twitter from GAPBS [13].
The limitations of proportional attribution arise when multiple, heterogeneous memory access patterns are colocated within the same memory tier, such as multi-tenant CXL memory deployments.
We implement PACT on Linux 5.15 and incorporate several modules from TPP [37], including fixes to improve the reliability of LRU-based page demotion.

Across these settings, PACT achieves strong performance improvements, by up to 61% over the second-best system. In cases where PACT is not the top performer, it closely tracks the best-performing baseline, with an average gap of 4.1% and a maximum gap of 11.8%.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Highly relevant as the state-of-the-art frequency-vs-criticality tiering baseline for ObjPlace: PAC's insight (bandwidth/latency-tolerance, not hotness, drives cost) aligns directly with ObjPlace's bandwidth-sensitivity/skew/phase signals, but PACT works at page granularity in-kernel while ObjPlace works at object granularity in userspace — a clean positioning contrast. Critically, PACT is evaluated only on uncore-throttled NUMA emulation with zero real CXL devices and a single slow tier, so it never sees the requester's measured CXL bandwidth cliffs (35.5 GiB/s per region, 2.0-2.13x co-runner slowdown) or per-device effects. The authors themselves flag multi-tenant/colocated CXL as an open observability gap — exactly the per-device interference and QoS direction the requester is considering on 4x CZ120, so PACT strengthens rather than closes that gap. Note PACT is PEBS/TOR-counter (Intel) based; porting its stall model to the requester's AMD EPYC 9745 (IBS instead of PEBS) is nontrivial and a potential differentiator.
papers.verifyNote: Fetched the primary-source PDF from the author's Virginia Tech page (people.cs.vt.edu/jinshu/docs/papers/PACT_ASPLOS.pdf) and extracted full text with pdftotext. The testbed section (§5.1) matches the analyst's quotes exactly. No physical CXL device anywhere in the paper — CXL is emulated by reducing remote NUMA node uncore frequency on a dual-socket Skylake CloudLab server, raising latency to 190ns; the profiling section (§2) likewise uses 'an emulated CXL device with 190ns latency'. Searched for a second testbed / FPGA / ASIC / real CXL hardware: none present. Could not independently confirm the 'Best Paper honorable mention' claim from the PDF itself (not part of the checked fields).

papers.title: Performance Characterizations and Usage Guidelines of Samsung CXL Memory Module Hybrid Prototype
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2503.22017, cs.AR)
papers.mainProblem: DRAM alone cannot economically serve data-intensive workloads that need both large capacity and persistence; Samsung's CMM-H (a CXL Type-3 hybrid device with a DRAM cache in front of NAND flash, load/store accessible without block-I/O overheads) had no public performance characterization, so users lacked guidance on which workloads it suits.
papers.mainIdea: First public comprehensive characterization of the FPGA-based CMM-H prototype: microbenchmark latency/tail-latency/bandwidth studies plus application studies (SPEC CPU2017, LLaMA 3.c, XSBench, RocksDB, Redis) in three usage modes (sole memory, memory expander alongside DRAM, persistent memory with compiler-enforced idempotent processing replacing WAL), distilled into boxed usage guidelines.
papers.hardwareEnv: Dual-socket server, 2x AMD EPYC 9454 @2.75 GHz (48 cores/socket, 256 MB LLC per CPU), 512 GB DDR5-4800 (256 GB/socket), Ubuntu 22.04.4, Linux kernel 6.8.0-49, HT and boost disabled, GCC 11.4.0. CXL device: one Samsung CMM-H E3.L PoC built on a Xilinx/AMD Versal XCVM1802 FPGA — CXL 1.1 Type 3 (CXL.io/CXL.mem) over PCIe Gen4 x8; 1 TB Samsung TLC NAND backing store fronted by a 16 GB 8-way LRU DRAM cache with 4 KB blocks (internal cache-to-NAND link PCIe Gen4 x4, 40 W). Exposed as a CPU-less NUMA node.
papers.evalSetup: Microbenchmarks: Intel MLC v3.11b pointer-chasing (1800 MB region); custom assembly kernels of 16 64-byte accesses in temporal/non-temporal load/store variants; tail latency measured over 20M runs per region size (99.99th/99.999th/max); bandwidth via multithreaded random 64-byte reads/writes. Applications: SPEC CPU2017 (ref inputs), LLaMA 3.c running LLaMA 3.2 1B (4740 MB footprint, 1-32 threads), XSBench with 10 footprints from 80 MB to 40.9 GB, RocksDB 9.9.3 db_bench (1M KV pairs), Redis 7.4.1 redis-benchmark (200K requests, 10 KB values); placement forced with numactl page binding plus CPU pinning; persistence experiments recompile RocksDB/Redis with idempotent processing (Clang/LLVM 13.0.1) to drop WAL/logging. Memory-expander mode interleaves pages between DDR5-L and CMM-H at varying ratios.
papers.baselines: Local DRAM (DDR5-L) and remote-socket DRAM (DDR5-R, cross-NUMA); no Optane comparison ("not supported on our AMD CPUs-based testbed"). For persistence: conventional WAL/AOF-logging RocksDB/Redis vs. CMM-H idempotent variants.
papers.keyFindings: MLC idle latency: CMM-H 728.9 ns vs DDR5-L 122.9 ns (5.9x); fine-grained kernels 1.2x-5.9x slower, but non-temporal stores nearly match DRAM (16.0 vs 13.5 ns) and nt-st is ~7x faster than temporal st on CMM-H. Tail latency comparable to DRAM while footprint fits the 16 GB device DRAM cache, then spikes to 15-20 us at 32 GB footprints. Peak bandwidth only ~4.5 GB/s vs ~219 GB/s DDR5-L (~48x gap), saturating at 4 threads (loads) / 2 threads (stores). SPEC CPU2017: negligible impact at low memory pressure; bwaves 3.73x slowdown on CMM-H under high pressure. LLaMA 3: 4% (4 threads) to 48% (32 threads) throughput loss. XSBench: 1.58x-5.56x slowdown, DRAM-cache hit rate falling 99.97%->97.62%. As memory expander, 80% of DDR5-L performance with a 50/50 page split. As persistent memory with idempotent processing (no WAL), RocksDB gains up to 2.2x (fillseq) / 4.59x (deleteseq) and Redis 1.67x-1.71x over logged baselines.
papers.limitations: Authors' own: FPGA PoC, not ASIC ("planning the next generation CMM-H products based on ASIC implementation to deliver lower latency and higher bandwidth"); sequential tag lookup and unmodified PCIe Gen4 x4 NAND SSD architecture limit bandwidth; 8-way/4KB DRAM cache causes conflict misses at large footprints; no Optane baseline (AMD testbed); idempotent-persistence gains require recompilation with a special compiler. Methodological: single device only — no multi-device, no interleaving, no device-to-device or co-runner interference study; no multi-tenant or QoS experiments; CXL 1.1 only; idle-latency-centric microbenchmarks (no loaded-latency curves vs. injected bandwidth reported like MLC loaded-latency); no OS tiering system actually evaluated (only suggested).
papers.openQuestions: Automatic OS/VM memory tiering onto CMM-H is repeatedly recommended but not built or measured; software coalescing of random writes to 4 KB granularity is suggested but unimplemented; behavior of the future ASIC version, multi-device scaling, contention between co-running tenants on the device DRAM cache, and CXL 2.0+ features (pooling, hotplug) are all untested.
evidenceQuotes: E3.L form-factor PoC device which is based on Versal XCVM1802 FPGA
v1.1, CXL.io/CXL.mem (Type 3)
CMM-H is exposed as a CPU-less NUMA node to the upper-level software stack
16 GB 8-way associative DRAM cache, which uses an LRU replacement policy
2x AMD EPYC 9454 CPUs @2.75 GHz, 48 cores
Ubuntu 22.04.4 LTS with Linux kernel 6.8.0-49
PCIe Gen 4 x8 interface
Intel Memory Latency Checker (MLC) v3.11b, which performs pointer-chasing in a (1800 MB) memory region
bwaves suffers a 1.37x and 3.73x slowdown on DDR5-R and CMM-H, respectively
we are planning the next generation CMM-H products based on ASIC implementation to deliver lower latency and higher bandwidth

papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Different device class from the requester's testbed: CMM-H is a flash-backed hybrid FPGA prototype (16 GB DRAM cache + 1 TB NAND, ~4.5 GB/s, 729 ns idle latency) versus the requester's 4x all-DRAM Micron CZ120 ASICs (~277 ns, ~35.5 GiB/s per region), so its absolute numbers do not transfer. Its value is methodological: a template for characterization structure (idle vs tail latency across footprint, nt-load/store variants, thread-scaling bandwidth saturation, per-app footprint sweeps with numactl binding) that the requester could replicate per-device and cross-device. It is single-device and CXL 1.1 with zero interference, multi-tenant, or multi-device content, so it leaves the requester's candidate direction (per-device scheduling, CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference, tail-aware QoS) entirely open — useful as related work showing the gap. The extreme thread-saturation behavior (BW saturates at 2-4 threads) echoes and corroborates the requester's own 4-thread saturation observation on CZ120 regions.

papers.title: Equilibria: Fair Multi-Tenant CXL Memory Tiering At Scale
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2602.08800); from CMU + Meta (Zhao, Gholkar, Maruf, Dhanotia, Weiner, Price, Skarlatos et al.)
papers.numCXLDevices: unknown — exact count of physical expanders per server never stated; two testbeds (large: 256GB CXL, small: 64GB CXL); production servers use "a single x8 or x16 PCIe controller to connect CXL memory", suggesting one expander per server
papers.mainProblem: Existing OS memory tiering for CXL (TPP/upstream Linux) is single-tenant-oriented: in multi-tenant container colocation it lacks per-container fair-share controls, causes fairness violations and performance variability (noisy neighbors thrashing pages between tiers), and offers insufficient per-container observability of tiered-memory usage for diagnosing issues at datacenter scale.
papers.mainIdea: Equilibria, an OS (Linux kernel) framework for fair multi-tenant CXL tiering: per-container "lower protection" (local memory protected from demotion) and "upper bound" (max local memory before forced demotion) knobs; regulated demotion (containers under protection exempt; overage-proportional scanning d_scan = n_lru(n_cgroup - n_protection)/n_cgroup) and regulated promotion (fourth-power throttle p_scan = p_base * min(n_protection^4/n_cgroup^4, 1/16)); thrashing suppression via a hash-table sample of recently promoted pages with adaptive promotion-rate halving/doubling every 5s; new per-cgroup tier-usage and promotion/demotion counters for observability. Patches partially upstreamed to Linux; being deployed fleet-wide at Meta.
papers.hardwareEnv: Two Meta production-class single-socket AMD Turin-generation servers with real CXL 2.0 Type 3 memory expanders built from recycled decommissioned DDR4 DRAM. Large server: 768GB local DDR5 + 256GB DDR4-as-CXL (3:1 ratio), unloaded CXL latency 252ns. Small server: 256GB local DDR5 + 64GB DDR4-as-CXL. CXL presented as memory-only NUMA domain(s); production connects CXL via a single x8 or x16 PCIe controller. Linux kernel 6.11 base.
papers.evalSetup: Three Meta production workloads — Cache (replayed production traces, 2 colocated instances), Web (application server, live production requests, 5 instances across two partitions), CI (build/test service, live, 4 instances/server) — plus DCPerf benchmarks SparkBench and TaoBench (3 TaoBench + 1 SparkBench colocated). Multi-tenant colocation on the small and large CXL servers; validation microbenchmarks with 3 instances per container setup.
papers.baselines: Upstream Linux kernel memory tiering derived from TPP (the state-of-the-art Linux solution). No direct comparison against Memtis, Pond, Memstrata, or other research tiering systems.
papers.keyFindings: Up to 52% performance improvement over Linux/TPP on production workloads and 1.7x on benchmarks (SparkBench 11.2 vs 4.2 queries/hour). For colocated Cache instances, partition B's average P99 latency drops 47% and A's 52% vs Linux; Web partition B gains 8% throughput. Fairness controls eliminate noisy-neighbor thrashing between colocated containers. Production apps use only 1-3 GB/s of CXL bandwidth, so the design targets capacity fairness, not bandwidth arbitration. Patches shared with Linux community, subset accepted upstream; fleet-wide Meta deployment underway.
papers.limitations: Authors admit no quantitative evaluation of the observability component, and that current CPUs/memory hardware lack support for low-overhead page migration/hotness tracking. Methodology weaknesses: number of physical CXL devices never stated and per-device behavior never examined — CXL is treated as one opaque capacity tier; bandwidth contention on the CXL link is explicitly declared out of scope ("additional memory bandwidth from CXL memory has limited practical use in current deployments") and no bandwidth-interference scenarios are evaluated; CXL media is recycled DDR4 (Meta-specific cost model, not commodity CZ120-class DDR5 expanders); max colocation tested is ~4-5 instances; only TPP/Linux as baseline.
papers.openQuestions: Bandwidth-driven inter-tenant interference on CXL (the paper measures only 1-3 GB/s CXL use and punts on bandwidth arbitration entirely); per-device or multi-device CXL management and cross-device interference; hardware-assisted hotness tracking/migration (stated as future vision); fairness for bandwidth-bound rather than capacity-bound workloads; behavior beyond ~4-5 colocated containers; VM (non-container) tenancy.
evidenceQuotes: We performed experiments on two types of Meta servers equipped with CXL memory, denoted as small and large servers. Both are single-socket servers with CPUs of the AMD Turin generation. The large server features a local to CXL memory ratio of 3:1, including 768GB of local DDR5 memory and 256GB of DDR4 DRAM as CXL memory. It has an unloaded CXL memory access latency of 252ns.
The CXL memory expanders used in the evaluation are CXL 2.0 Type 3 devices, using recycled previously-decommissioned DDR4 memory.
Therefore, we continue to use a single x8 or x16 PCIe controller to connect CXL memory across several generations of servers.
CXL memory is attached to a host system, where it is presented as memory-only NUMA domains.
Equilibria improves performance over the state-of-the-art Linux solution, TPP, by up to 52% and 1.7× for production workloads and benchmarks, respectively.
additional memory bandwidth from CXL memory has limited practical use in current deployments

Although we do not provide a quantitative evaluation of the container-level observability of memory tiering provided by Equilibria, most of the evaluation and motivation studies in this paper are only possible because of it.

Whether CXL is exposed as one or multiple NUMA nodes on the testbeds (paper says 'memory-only NUMA domains' generically)

papers.title: HybridTier: an Adaptive and Lightweight CXL-Memory Tiering System
papers.venue: ASPLOS 2025 (Proceedings of the 30th ACM International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems, Volume 3, ASPLOS '25), DOI 10.1145/3676642.3736119
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no physical CXL devices; CXL emulated with the remote socket's DDR4 of a two-socket system)
papers.mainProblem: High-performance memory tiering between fast DRAM and slower CXL memory requires (1) adapting to skewed but dynamically shifting data-hotness distributions and (2) keeping the tiering system's own metadata memory and CPU-cache overhead low; prior systems (TPP, AutoNUMA, Memtis, classic caching policies ARC/TwoQ) fail on one or both, adapting slowly to hotness shifts and paying large per-page metadata/cache-miss costs.
papers.mainIdea: A userspace (LD_PRELOAD-injected) per-process tiering runtime that samples accesses via Intel PEBS and tracks hotness probabilistically with two blocked Counting Bloom Filters (4-bit counters capped at 15): a long-term "frequency" tracker (high cooling period) and a short-term "momentum" tracker (low cooling period). Pages with high frequency OR high momentum are promoted, letting the system both capture stable hot sets and quickly promote newly-hot pages; probabilistic tracking trades small inaccuracy for 2.0-7.8x less metadata memory and 1.7-3.5x fewer cache misses. Supports 4KB pages and 2MB THP.
papers.hardwareEnv: Two-socket server; each socket a 16-core Intel Xeon 4314 (Ice Lake) with 512GB DDR4. CXL emulated as the remote NUMA node: emulated idle latency 124ns, bandwidth 34 GB/s. Linux kernel v6.2 for AutoNUMA and HybridTier. No CXL device model/link width - no real CXL hardware present.
papers.evalSetup: Workloads: CacheLib (CDN and social-graph traces), GAP graph kernels (BFS, CC, PR), SPEC CPU 2017 (603.bwaves, 654.roms), Silo in-memory database, XGBoost. All experiments use 16 threads pinned to the 16 physical cores of the local socket; application memory split between local DRAM (fast tier) and remote-socket DRAM emulating CXL (slow tier), with varying fast-tier size ratios.
papers.baselines: TPP, AutoNUMA (Linux kernel tiering), Memtis, and caching policies ARC and TwoQ.
papers.keyFindings: On average HybridTier outperforms TPP, AutoNUMA, Memtis, ARC, and TwoQ by 32%, 11%, 29%, 50%, and 40% respectively; achieves 2.0-7.8x less metadata memory overhead and 1.7-3.5x fewer cache misses than prior tiering systems; adapts to hotness-distribution shifts 3.2x faster (3.2x less time to adapt).
papers.limitations: Evaluation is entirely on NUMA emulation (remote-socket DDR4, 124ns idle latency) - no production CXL silicon, so real CXL controller effects (higher load-to-use latency ratios like the requester's 1.53x, bandwidth saturation at low thread counts, contention behavior) are untested; authors justify this by noting many CXL devices "are not commercially available on the market" (paper predates wide CZ120 availability). Single emulated slow tier - no multiple CXL devices, no per-device management, no bandwidth-interference or co-runner analysis, no multi-tenant evaluation (global tiering via a "central HybridTier controller" is only sketched in Discussion). Per-process userspace design requires PEBS (Intel-specific; requester's box is AMD EPYC, which would need IBS instead). One-time-only access patterns (scans, pointer chasing) require manual tuning of the momentum threshold. No dedicated limitations section.
papers.openQuestions: How the CBF frequency/momentum approach behaves on real CXL ASICs where latency and especially bandwidth contention differ from a remote NUMA socket; global/multi-tenant tiering (explicitly punted to a hypothetical central controller); multiple independent CXL devices and inter-device placement; bandwidth-aware (not just latency/hotness-aware) placement; AMD/IBS-based access sampling; interaction with famfs or shared CXL memory.
evidenceQuotes: Similar to recent works, we use a remote NUMA node on a two-socket system to emulate CXL. The emulated CXL memory has idle latency of 124ns and bandwidth of 34 GB/s
Each socket has a 16-core Intel Xeon 4314 processor and 512GB of DDR4 memory.
HybridTier tracks memory accesses using counting bloom filters (CBFs), a probabilistically data structure that trades higher memory efficiency for lower tracking accuracy.
HybridTier utilizes Intel Processor Event-Based Sampling (PEBS), where each access sample contains the virtual memory address being accessed.
On average, HybridTier outperforms TPP, AutoNUMA, Memtis, ARC, and TwoQ by 32%, 11%, 29%, 50%, and 40%
For AutoNUMA, HybridTier, we use Linux kernel v6.2.
To support global memory tiering (e.g., multi-tenant VM, co-located applications), one could use a central HybridTier controller.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Direct competitor in hotness-driven DRAM/CXL tiering, but evaluated purely on remote-NUMA emulation (124ns, 34 GB/s remote DDR4) - it never sees real CXL contention effects like the requester's measured 2.0-2.13x slowdown of a bandwidth-bound victim under a CXL co-runner, nor the 1.53x load-to-use latency gap on CZ120s. It manages one flat slow tier per process and explicitly does not address multiple CXL devices, per-device placement, bandwidth interference, or multi-tenancy - exactly the gap the requester's candidate direction (per-device scheduling, CXL-to-CXL interference, multi-tenant QoS on 4x CZ120) targets. Its PEBS-based probabilistic (CBF frequency+momentum) tracking is a useful lightweight-telemetry baseline for ObjPlace, though on the AMD EPYC 9745 it would need IBS rather than PEBS. Strong differentiation angle: real-ASIC multi-device results vs HybridTier's single emulated tier.

papers.title: OBASE: Object-Based Address-Space Engineering to Improve Memory Tiering
papers.venue: OSDI 2026 (also arXiv:2603.00378)
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no CXL hardware; slow tier is 4x 128GB Intel Optane DC Persistent Memory 100 modules exposed as a separate NUMA node)
papers.mainProblem: Hotness fragmentation: memory allocators in unmanaged languages (C/C++) place objects by size class, not access pattern, so hot and cold objects are interleaved within the same 4KB pages. A single hot cache line marks a whole page active, trapping cold bytes in DRAM; the authors' analysis of six Google production workload traces shows up to 97% of bytes in active pages are cold and unreclaimable, defeating page-granularity tiering/reclamation backends (TPP, AutoNUMA, Memtis, kswapd, cgroups, TMO).
papers.mainIdea: "Address-space engineering": a compiler-runtime system (OBASE) that dynamically reorganizes virtual memory so hot objects cluster into uniformly hot pages and cold objects into uniformly cold pages. Objects are accessed via 'guides' (tagged indirection pointers, 16 upper bits repurposed for hotness/lock metadata); pointer instrumentation tracks per-object access; an Object Collector scans every 120s and migrates objects between NEW/HOT/COLD virtual heaps using a lock-free two-phase CAS protocol safe under concurrency (concurrent access vetoes migration via CAS failure). OBASE acts as an object-aware frontend for unmodified page-aware OS backends; a feedback controller adapts the cold threshold to hold promotion rate at 1%.
papers.hardwareEnv: Intel Xeon Gold 5218 (16 cores, SMT disabled, performance governor), Ubuntu 22.04, Linux kernel 6.12. Fast tier: 2x 16GB DDR4-2400 DRAM. Slow tier: 4x 128GB Intel Optane DC Persistent Memory 100 modules at 2666 MHz, configured in Memory Mode and exposed as a separate NUMA node to emulate first-generation CXL memory (~2.5x DRAM latency). All six memory devices on distinct channels. Swap experiments use a 512GB Intel P4800X Optane SSD. No real CXL device anywhere in the testbed.
papers.evalSetup: CrestDB, an in-memory KV store the authors built integrating ten concurrent data structures (hash tables, skiplists, B+Trees, ART, MassTree, etc., many from ASCYLIB), 6 server + 6 client threads over Unix domain sockets. Workloads: YCSB A/B/C with Zipfian keys (10M keys, 30B keys / 1024B values, 13 GiB; tiering runs use 50M keys, 67 GiB), plus four production trace replays: Meta CacheLib, Meta DBench Mixgraph, Twitter Cluster 7 and Cluster 23. Tiering experiments vary DRAM:slow-tier ratio 1:4 / 1:8 / 1:16 by shrinking DRAM budget; scalability measured 2-32 threads.
papers.baselines: Six OS backends run with vs. without OBASE as frontend: reclamation - Linux kswapd, cgroup memory limits, Meta TMO (PSI-based); tiering - TPP, Linux AutoNUMA, Memtis (PEBS-based). Also an uninstrumented DRAM-only baseline for overhead, and a CXL(slow-tier)-only baseline for tiering normalization. Object-level far-memory systems AIFM and MIRA are discussed but explicitly NOT compared ("they target custom runtimes").
papers.keyFindings: Page utilization improves 2-4x (baseline 18-20% to 40-80%) across all ten data structures; RSS drops 65-72% (12.4 GiB to 3.5-4.0 GiB for YCSB-B 10M keys). With OBASE all reclamation backends reach the aggressive 4 GiB RSS with no throughput loss (without it, cgroup loses 38% throughput; TMO stalls at 6.5 GiB). Tiering: hot set compacts from 16.3 GiB @21% utilization to 6.33 GiB @57%; TPP gains 16% at 1:16 (1.25x to 1.45x), AutoNUMA gains 12-29%, Memtis 3-10%; OBASE at ratio 1:X roughly matches baseline at 1:(X/2), i.e. same performance with half the DRAM. Runtime overhead 2-5% throughput (avg 2.5%), +5% p90 latency, flat from 2 to 32 threads; guide dereference RMW costs 4-5ns. Production traces: 1.8-3.4x utilization gain, 36-58% RSS reduction, +15-30% savings on top of TMO; controller converges in ~25 min and re-converges after workload shifts.
papers.limitations: Authors' own: requires developer annotation of relocatable pointers and applies only to pointer-based data structures; hardware-aware tuning of the promotion-rate target is left to future work; OBASE cannot determine which tier a page occupies (backend-agnostic by necessity). Methodology weaknesses: NO real CXL hardware - slow tier is Optane PMEM 100 declared "representative of emerging CXL-attached memory deployments"; single old 16-core Xeon Gold 5218 host; evaluation entirely on the authors' own CrestDB KV store (no unmodified real applications end-to-end); single-tenant runs only, no interference or bandwidth-contention study; Optane emulates latency but not CXL bandwidth characteristics; no comparison against object-level runtimes (AIFM/MIRA); 2-4x/70% headline numbers are on synthetic YCSB, production traces show smaller 36-58% reductions.
papers.openQuestions: How OBASE behaves on real CXL silicon where bandwidth (not just latency) is the constraint; hardware-aware promotion-rate tuning (explicitly punted); multi-tenant / co-runner interference; whether annotation burden is acceptable for large real codebases (only CrestDB evaluated); extension to multiple slow tiers or per-device placement (the paper treats the slow tier as one monolithic NUMA node); interaction with huge pages; applicability beyond pointer-based KV structures (arrays, ML tensors).
evidenceQuotes: All experiments run on an Intel Xeon Gold 5218 (16 cores, SMT disabled) configured in performance governor mode with Ubuntu 22.04 and Linux kernel 6.12. The memory subsystem comprises two tiers: a fast tier of 2×16 GB DDR4 DRAM modules at 2400 MHz, and a slow tier of 4×128 GB Intel Optane DC Persistent Memory 100 modules at 2666 MHz.

We configure Optane PMEM in Memory Mode and expose it as a separate NUMA node, creating a two-tier hierarchy representative of emerging CXL-attached memory deployments [40, 42]. The Optane tier provides approximately 2.5× higher access latency than local DRAM [55], consistent with first-generation CXL memory characteristics [49].
Our analysis of Google production workloads shows that up to 97% of the bytes in active pages are cold and unreclaimable.

We evaluate OBASE with ten concurrent pointer-based data structures and six state-of-the-art reclamation and tiering backends [14, 38, 42, 51, 53]. Using key-value store workloads (YCSB) and production traces (Meta, Twitter), we demonstrate that OBASE improves page utilization (by 2-4x) and achieves higher memory savings (up to 70%)
The approach has limitations: it requires developer annotation of relocatable pointers and applies only to pointer-based structures.

The optimal promotion rate is hardware-dependent: faster secondary tiers can tolerate higher cold-access fractions, while much slower tiers may require more conservative thresholds; exploring such hardware-aware tuning is left to future work.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Directly validates ObjPlace's core premise from an independent OSDI'26 team: object-granularity (not page-granularity) hotness management is the right frontend for DRAM/CXL tiering, and their 97%-cold-bytes Google analysis is a strong motivation citation. However, OBASE is latency/capacity-driven and evaluated only on Optane-emulated CXL on one Xeon with one monolithic slow NUMA node - it never touches real CXL silicon, bandwidth contention, or multiple devices, exactly the gaps the requester's CZ120 testbed exposes (35.5 GiB/s per-region saturation, 2x co-runner slowdown). ObjPlace must differentiate on bandwidth-sensitivity-driven placement on real hardware, and the candidate per-device/interference direction is untouched by OBASE, which explicitly cannot even tell which tier a page occupies. Its lock-free object-migration protocol and tagged-guide indirection are reusable mechanism ideas if ObjPlace needs safe concurrent object relocation.
