papers.title: vTMM: Tiered Memory Management for Virtual Machines
papers.venue: EuroSys 2023 (Proceedings of the Eighteenth European Conference on Computer Systems, pp. 283-297)
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no physical CXL device; "CXL-Memory system" = remote-socket DRAM on a dual-socket machine; second testbed uses real Intel Optane DC PMem, not CXL)
papers.mainIdea: vTMM, a hypervisor-level tiered memory manager that exploits virtualization hardware: (1) tracks page accesses cheaply with Intel Page-Modification Logging (PML) plus a multi-level-queue GPT scanner (scan only dirty guest page tables); (2) quantifies page "temperature" (weighted read/write page-degree) and classifies hot/cold pages in O(n) with bucket sorting; (3) migrates pages in parallel (4 threads) using PML with negligible access pause; (4) transparently resizes each VM's fast-memory share via the 2D (EPT) page tables, enabling a dynamic FMem pool across co-running VMs (island mode = fixed per-VM FMem; pool mode = demand-driven repartitioning); (5) hybrid-grained huge-page support (track THP at 4KB granularity, split/merge in software).
papers.hardwareEnv: Dual-socket Intel Cascade Lake-SP, 2.2 GHz, 24 cores/48 threads per socket; VMs pinned to one socket; Ubuntu 18.04, Linux kernel 5.4.142 (host and guest), QEMU 3.1.0. Testbed 1 (real DRAM+NVM): 32 GB local DRAM (FMem) + 192 GB Intel Optane DC PMem in App Direct mode mounted as a NUMA node (SMem). Testbed 2 ("CXL-Memory"): 32 GB local DRAM + 192 GB remote-socket DRAM as SMem — no CXL hardware at all. Their Table 1: DRAM 81/82 ns R/W latency, 120/82 GB/s R/W BW; "CXL-Memory" 153/162 ns, 97/63 GB/s; PMem 310/94 ns, 37/13 GB/s.
papers.evalSetup: Single-VM and multi-VM experiments under QEMU/KVM. Workloads: SPEC CPU 2017 649.fotonik3d_s, graph500, Redis, GAPBS page rank (PR) and betweenness centrality (BC), random-access microbenchmarks; regular-page VMs (8 cores, 40 GB = 8 GB FMem + 32 GB SMem each, 4 co-running VMs) and THP VMs (16 cores, 16 GB FMem + 64 GB SMem, 2 co-running VMs). Modular evaluation of tracking overhead/accuracy, sorting, migration speed/pause, DRAM-size sensitivity, THP, and multi-VM co-running in island vs pool mode. Most results shown on the DRAM+NVM system; multi-VM results also shown for the NUMA-simulated CXL system ("results are basically the same").
papers.baselines: Linux AutoNUMA (NUMA balancing), Intel Optane Memory Mode (hardware DRAM-cache, "MM"), Nimble Page Management (OS-level tiering); HeMem and DAMON discussed qualitatively; DRAM-only VM as upper bound.
papers.keyFindings: Multi-VM co-running: vTMM improves DRAM+NVM system performance by 50-140% and the (emulated) CXL-Memory system by 16-40%. Regular-page 4-VM runs: island mode beats AutoNUMA/MM by 35%/17% geomean; pool mode adds another 12% by dynamically reallocating FMem (e.g., 3 VMs release 1.5-2 GB each to a hot VM); on the CXL system pool/island give 16%/15%. Huge-page runs: vTMM outperforms AutoNUMA, MM, Nimble by 140%, 14.1%, 590% on DRAM+NVM and AutoNUMA/Nimble by 39.5%/49.4% on the CXL system. Motivation: tiered-memory VM slows up to 2.37x (fotonik3d) under AutoNUMA vs DRAM-only. MM (DRAM cache) degrades badly under co-running due to cache pollution (redis miss ratio 6.52%->16.89% going from 1 to 2 VMs). Measured read:write migration weights 1:3 (NVM), 2:3 (remote-DRAM "CXL").
papers.limitations: CXL results are entirely from remote-NUMA-socket DRAM emulation ("NUMA-simulated CXL-Memory system") — no real CXL device, so no CXL port/controller contention, no real CXL bandwidth ceiling (their emulated tier has 97/63 GB/s, far above real CZ120-class devices), and read/write asymmetry of real CXL memory is not captured. Only one slow tier and effectively one slow "device"; no per-device management or cross-device interference. Requires Intel PML (VMX hardware feature) — not portable to AMD hosts like the requester's EPYC. Small scale: at most 4 co-running VMs, 32 GB FMem. Space-limited reporting: most results shown only for DRAM+NVM, with the claim results "are basically the same" on the emulated CXL system. No tail-latency/SLO analysis (throughput/runtime metrics only); no admitted-limitations section in the paper.
papers.openQuestions: Behavior on real CXL ASICs (different latency/bandwidth/asymmetry than a remote socket) is untested. Bandwidth interference between VMs on the slow tier is only indirectly observed (migration traffic hurting co-runners), never managed — no bandwidth-aware placement or QoS. Multi-device CXL (independent devices, interleaving choices) is out of scope. Applicability without PML (AMD, or CXL-native hotness telemetry) is unaddressed; the authors' later TOCS'24 extension (Hardware-Software Collaborative Tiered-Memory Management Framework for Virtualization) continues this line. Scalability beyond 4 VMs and tail-latency-sensitive workloads remain open.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: vTMM is a VM-granularity analog of what the requester is exploring: it dynamically repartitions scarce fast memory among competing tenants (its "pool mode" is essentially multi-tenant FMem scheduling) and explicitly motivates performance isolation. But its "CXL" is a remote NUMA socket with 97/63 GB/s — it never sees real per-device bandwidth ceilings like the requester's ~35.5 GiB/s-per-region CZ120s, never models CXL-side co-runner interference (the 2.0-2.13x victim slowdown the requester measured), and treats the slow tier as one monolithic node, so per-device placement and CXL-to-CXL interference are untouched. It also depends on Intel PML, unavailable on the requester's AMD Turin host. Useful as a baseline/related-work citation for multi-tenant fast-memory pooling and as evidence that the "one flat slow tier, emulated" methodology dominates prior work — strengthening the novelty of treating 4 real devices as independently schedulable resources.
evidenceQuotes: We evaluate vTMM on a real DRAM+NVM system and a simulated CXL-Memory system.
We run our evaluation on a dual-socket Intel Cascade LakeSP system running at 2.2 GHz with 24 cores/48 threads per socket.

(1) Real DRAM+NVM system has 32 GB of local DRAM (FMem) and 192 GB PMem (SMem). The system enables the APP direct mode [24] and mounts PMem as a NUMA node. (2) NUMA-simulated CXL-Memory system has 32GB local DRAM (FMem) and 192 GB of remote DRAM (SMem).
The access latency and bandwidth to CXL-Memory listed in Table 1 are similar to the remote latency and bandwidth on a dual-socket system [34].
In the NUMAsimulated CXL-Memory system composed of local DRAM and remote DRAM, the ratio is 2 : 3.
Multi-VM co-running results show that vTMM improves the performance of a DRAM+NVM system by 50% − 140% and a CXL-Memory system by 16% − 40%, respectively.

Overall, in the DRAM+NVM system, vTMM outperforms AutoNUMA, MM and Nimble by 140%, 14.1% and 590%, respectively. Similarly, vTMM still performs the best on CXLMemory system and outperforms AutoNUMA and Nimble by 39.5% and 49.4%, respectively.

papers.title: A Three-Tier Buffer Manager Integrating CXL Device Memory for Database Systems
papers.venue: HardBD & Active workshop (co-located with ICDE)
papers.mainProblem: Three-tier buffer managers exist for DRAM/PMem/SSD (HyMem, Spitfire) but rely on invasive pointer swizzling and none integrate byte-addressable CXL device memory as a middle tier between local DRAM and SSD in a DBMS buffer pool.
papers.mainIdea: A three-tier (local DRAM / CXL device memory / SSD) buffer manager that combines vmcache-style virtual-memory-based page-identifier translation (mmap + madvise(MADV_DONTNEED), mbind/move_pages across NUMA nodes) with Zhou et al.'s probabilistic page-migration policy (probabilities Lr, Lw, Cr, Cw) and variable power-of-two page sizes (4 KiB-2 MiB), integrated into the in-memory DBMS Hyrise without pointer swizzling.
papers.hardwareEnv: Dual-socket 4th Gen Intel Xeon (Sapphire Rapids), 48 cores/socket; 256 GiB (8x32 GiB) DDR5 on socket 0 as local memory; one Seagate Technology CXL 1.1 Type 3 device prototype attached via PCIe/CXL x8 Gen4 to node 0, FPGA-based (Bittware Xilinx VU13P) memory controller with 64 GiB (4x16 GiB) DDR4-2400; Micron Crucial CT500P1SSD8 500 GB NVMe SSD; pre-released Linux kernel 6.3.0-060300rc1-generic. MLC: local 125.5 ns idle latency / 224.3 GB/s; CXL device 557 ns / 9.4 GB/s.
papers.evalSetup: YCSB-based microbenchmarks (Update Heavy ~ YCSB A: 50/50 lookup/update; Read Mostly ~ YCSB B: 95/5; Scan ~ YCSB E: full page scans + 5% updates) with zipfian skew, 64 B tuples accessed via AVX-512 load/store (_mm512_load_si512, _mm512_stream_si512). Scalability: fixed 2 GiB database, 1-48 threads, buffer pool entirely on local vs. entirely on CXL memory, pinned to NUMA node 0, hyper-threading and NUMA balancing off. Migration-policy study: 2 GiB local + 4 GiB CXL buffer pools, database 1-8 GiB, 48 threads, Eager (probability 1.0) vs Lazy (0.2) three-tier policies vs two-tier setups.
papers.baselines: Two-tier configurations of their own buffer manager: Local Memory-SSD and CXL Device Memory-SSD; eager vs lazy probabilistic migration policies. No external systems (HyMem/Spitfire/vmcache discussed as related work only, not run).
papers.keyFindings: Point-lookup-dominated workloads (Update Heavy, Read Mostly) show similar throughput on local and CXL device memory despite 557 ns vs 125.5 ns latency; Scan on local memory is up to 2x faster at low thread counts but converges to CXL throughput as threads increase; latencies ~300 ns at low threads to 28 us at 48 threads for lookups. Three-tier (2 GiB local + 4 GiB CXL = 6 GiB pool) sustains high throughput for databases up to combined capacity, while two-tier throughput collapses once the pool spills to SSD; lazy policy generally beats eager (except a tipping point at 6 GiB DB for Update Heavy). move_pages between volatile tiers is a bottleneck; mbind with MPOL_MF_MOVE doubles page-movement throughput. Scalability is limited by their implementation (false sharing on frame arrays, tbb::concurrent_queue contention).
papers.limitations: Authors admit: results are bound to the prototype's characteristics (9.4 GB/s, 557 ns - far below production CXL devices); "our work is limited to a single device prototype"; achieved performance is limited by their buffer manager implementation (false sharing, queue contention); optimal migration probabilities require per-hardware tuning; OS page-movement syscalls are serialized/single-threaded. Methodological weaknesses: only one CXL device, only YCSB-style microbenchmarks (no TPC-C/TPC-H or full Hyrise query workloads evaluated), no multi-tenant or interference experiments, buffer pools artificially small (2/4 GiB), workshop-length evaluation.
papers.openQuestions: Explicitly punted: improving buffer manager scalability; evaluating impact of storing data on CXL memory in a three-tier vs two-tier storage hierarchy; how different throughput/latency characteristics of (production) CXL Type 3 devices influence three-tier buffer manager design; multi-threaded page migration without kernel modifications (thread-local buffer copy scheme is proposed but not evaluated). Untested: multiple CXL devices, device-level bandwidth contention, multi-tenant isolation, real query workloads.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Marginal to the requester's multi-device direction: this is a single FPGA-prototype device (9.4 GB/s, 557 ns) treated as one NUMA node, so it says nothing about per-device scheduling or CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference on the 4x CZ120 testbed. It is useful as a related-work datapoint for object/page placement across DRAM/CXL (probabilistic migration probabilities as an alternative policy to ObjPlace's sensitivity/skew/phase signals) and for the practical finding that move_pages is a migration bottleneck while mbind(MPOL_MF_MOVE) doubles movement throughput - directly relevant to ObjPlace's migration path. Its observation that latency-insensitive point-lookup workloads run equally well on CXL echoes the requester's bandwidth-vs-latency sensitivity distinction, but its prototype bandwidth (9.4 GB/s) is far below the CZ120s' 35.5 GiB/s/region, limiting quantitative transfer. The paper explicitly names multi-device CXL characteristics as future work, supporting the novelty of a per-device treatment.
evidenceQuotes: A CXL 1.1 Type 3 device prototype provided by Seagate Technology LLC is attached via a PCIe/CXL x8 Gen4 connection to node 0.
The device is an FPGA-based (Bittware Xilinx VU13P) memory controller containing 64 GiB (4 x 16 GiB) DDR4 DIMMs with a speed of 2400 MT/s.

While our work is limited to a single device prototype, future work needs to evaluate how different throughput and latency characteristics of CXL Type 3 devices influence the quality of three-tier buffer manager designs.

We conduct the experiments on a dual-socket platform with 4th Generation Intel Xeon CPUs (Sapphire Rapids), each having 48 cores. The server has 256 GiB (8 x 32 GiB) DDR5 DIMMs on the first socket (NUMA node 0), which we use as local memory in the experiments.
For CXL device memory, we observe 557 ns and 9.4 GB/s. Note that we use a preliminary CXL device prototype.
The OS is a pre-released Linux kernel version 6.3.0-060300rc1-generic to support CXL memory.
Experiments suggest that the performance of move_pages between volatile tiers is a limitation and that using mbind with the MPOL_MF_MOVE flag doubles the page movement throughput.

papers.title: Clove: Object-Level CXL Memory Management in Managed Runtimes
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2605.20370)
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no physical CXL device; remote NUMA socket of a dual-socket CloudLab c6420 used as the "CXL" tier)
papers.mainProblem: Page-based tiered-memory management (TPP, Memtis, HybridTier) is granularity-mismatched for CXL: hot and cold objects share 4KB pages, so page-level hotness tracking and migration waste fast-tier DRAM capacity and migration bandwidth. Object-level management for CXL-tiered memory is underexplored because CXL's load/store interface and tight performance budget make per-object tracking/relocation seemingly too expensive, and prior object-level approaches target unmanaged languages with bespoke runtimes or compiler support.
papers.mainIdea: Clove extends existing managed runtimes (JVM prototype) with the missing pieces for object-level tiering — profile-guided object hotness tracking and object relocation policies — reusing mechanisms managed runtimes already have (GC-style object relocation, dynamic code generation). It layers on top of an underlying page-based migration system (TPP/Memtis/HybridTier), packing hot objects onto pages so the page tier system keeps them in fast memory.
papers.hardwareEnv: CloudLab c6420 dual-socket machine: Intel Xeon Gold 6142 CPUs, 192 GB DDR4 per socket. CXL is emulated: application/runtime threads pinned to the local socket with taskset; the remote socket's memory serves as the slow "CXL" tier; tiering ratios enforced via local-memory ballooning (Memtis methodology). Kernel version not captured. No real CXL device of any kind.
papers.evalSetup: Java applications on the modified JVM: Ehcache (YCSB-C plus Twitter production cache traces, 160 GB and 120 GB footprints), JGraphT PageRank (120 GB), H2 relational DB with TPC-C (120 GB); synthetic HotWarm and Zipfian(0.99) microbenchmarks (~100 GB). Tiering ratios: 10%, 20%, 50% of memory local (fast tier), enforced by ballooning on the emulated two-socket testbed.
papers.baselines: TPP, Memtis, HybridTier — three open-source page-based tiered-memory systems, used both as baselines and as the underlying page-migration substrate for Clove; plus an ideal oracle for fast-tier hit ratio.
papers.keyFindings: Clove reduces application slowdown by 22-84% vs page-based systems: Twitter-Large 29-59%, Twitter-Medium 43-63%, PageRank 47-84%, H2/TPC-C 22-47%; synthetic HotWarm 29-59% latency reduction at 20% local ratio. Fast-tier hit ratio 11-45 percentage points above Memtis and only 4-5 points below an oracle. Overheads: online profiler <1%; hotness tracking ~5.5% if always on, near-zero with periodic activation. Demonstrates that JVM object relocation + dynamic code generation make object-granularity tiering practical at CXL-like latencies.
papers.limitations: Entirely NUMA-emulated — no real CXL silicon, so real device latency/bandwidth asymmetry, on-device controller behavior, and bandwidth contention effects are untested; zero physical CXL devices, so nothing about multi-device or per-device behavior. Authors' own scoping: targets memory-intensive apps whose hot sets evolve over minutes/hours; workloads where hotness of millions/billions of objects shifts every few seconds are out of scope; off-heap memory is not managed; adaptive parameter tuning deferred to future work. JVM-only prototype; single-application runs (no multi-tenant/interference evaluation).
papers.openQuestions: Behavior on real CXL hardware (bandwidth saturation, contention) is untested. No multi-tenant or co-runner interference study. Extension beyond the JVM to other managed runtimes, off-heap/native memory, rapidly-shifting hot sets, and automatic parameter tuning are explicitly left open. Nothing on multiple CXL devices, pooling, or per-device scheduling.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Clove is the closest external competitor/companion to the requester's ObjPlace: both argue for object-granularity DRAM/CXL placement, and Clove's 22-84% wins over TPP/Memtis/HybridTier validate the object-level thesis — it must be cited and differentiated. Key differentiators for the requester: Clove is NUMA-emulated with zero real CXL devices, single-tenant, and hotness-driven only; ObjPlace runs on 4x real CZ120s and can add bandwidth-sensitivity, contention, and per-device dimensions Clove cannot see under emulation (e.g., the requester's measured 2.0-2.13x CXL co-runner slowdown). Clove says nothing about multi-device independence, cross-device interference, or QoS, leaving the candidate per-device-scheduling direction untouched.

We use a dual-socket system to emulate a CXL-based tiered memory architecture, following the methodology in prior work (Lee et al., 2023; Amaro et al., 2023; Song et al., 2025). Application and runtime threads are pinned to the local socket using taskset... tiering ratios are enforced using the local-memory ballooning mechanism used in prior work (Lee et al., 2023).

We evaluate three open-source, page-based tiered-memory management systems—TPP (Maruf et al., 2023), Memtis (Lee et al., 2023...), and HybridTier (Song et al., 2025)—as both baselines for comparison and as the underlying page migration systems for Clove.
We test three different tiering ratios, where 10%, 20%, or 50% of memory is local...

Target applications [are] memory-intensive applications whose hot sets evolve over minutes or hours... Extreme workloads in which the hotness of millions or billions of objects changes every few seconds are outside our scope.

papers.title: TierScape: Harnessing Multiple Compressed Tiers to Tame Server Memory TCO (arXiv v1 title: "Taming Server Memory TCO with Multiple Software-Defined Compressed Tiers")
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no CXL devices; far tier is Intel Optane DC PMM, 1.6 TB, flat mode)
papers.mainProblem: Memory is 33-50% of server TCO; existing 2-tier cold-data solutions (DRAM + one zswap compressed tier, as in Google's production setup) force a coarse trade-off between TCO savings and performance because a single compressed tier cannot serve both warm and cold data well.
papers.mainIdea: Create N software-defined compressed memory tiers by combining different compression algorithms (lz4/lzo/deflate), allocators (zbud/zsmalloc), and backing media (DRAM/Optane/potentially CXL) via a modified multi-pool zswap; a userspace TS-Daemon profiles 2MB-region hotness with Intel PEBS and places/migrates pages across tiers using either a waterfall policy or an analytical performance-vs-TCO cost model, putting warm data in low-latency compressed tiers and cold data in max-TCO-savings tiers.
papers.hardwareEnv: 2-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6252N (24 cores/socket, 2-way HT, 96 logical CPUs), 384 GB DRAM near tier, 1.6 TB Intel Optane DC PMM in flat (volatile) mode as far media, Fedora 30, modified Linux kernel 5.17. No CXL hardware.
papers.evalSetup: Five workloads: Memcached (44 GB) and Redis (41 GB) driven by memtier with Gaussian key-access distributions, BFS (18 GB), PageRank (18 GB), XSBench (119 GB). 120 s profiling windows, 100 s warm-up; TS-Daemon samples hotness via Intel PEBS at 2 MB granularity. Five compressed tier configs tested: T1 zbud/lz4/DRAM, T2 zbud/lz4/Optane, T3 zsmalloc/lz4/Optane, T4 zsmalloc/lzo/DRAM, T5 zsmalloc/deflate/Optane.
papers.baselines: 2-Tier zswap (Google production-style: DRAM + zsmalloc/lzo/DRAM) at conservative/moderate/aggressive coldness thresholds (2T-C/2T-M/2T-A), vs TierScape 6-tier waterfall (6T-WF) and 6-tier analytical-model (6T-AM) variants.
papers.keyFindings: Overall 22-40 percentage-point higher memory TCO savings than 2-tier at performance parity or 2-10% better performance. Redis: 6T-AM-0.1 gets 64.10% TCO savings at 14.37% slowdown vs 2T-A's 34.84% savings at 18.33% slowdown. PageRank: 6T-WF-C 40.78% savings/13.09% slowdown vs 2T-C 24.86%/21.82%. BFS: 6T-AM-0.1 is 4.05 pp faster than 2T-M at ~63% TCO savings. TS-Daemon overhead 1.2-7% CPU.
papers.limitations: Authors admit: waterfall model needs N profiling windows for cold pages to reach the last tier; no prefetching ("pages that the prefetcher fails to identify still incur high access latency"); naive migration path (decompress then recompress); analytical model assumes stable access patterns. Methodological: no CXL hardware at all — far media is Optane PMM (discontinued product); single-server, apparently single-workload-at-a-time runs (no multi-tenant experiments); TCO savings computed via an analytical cost model rather than measured dollar costs; arXiv v1 read here may differ from the EuroSys'26 camera-ready.
papers.openQuestions: How the multi-tier design behaves when compressed pools are backed by actual CXL memory (latency/bandwidth characteristics differ from Optane); interaction with hardware tiering/interleaving; multi-tenant contention on compression CPU and far-media bandwidth; prefetching from compressed tiers; whether the PEBS-based profiler works on AMD platforms (PEBS is Intel-specific).
evidenceQuotes: Intel Xeon Gold 6252N with 2 sockets, 24 cores per socket, and 2-way HT for a total of 96 cores. It has a DRAM-based near-memory tier with 384 GB capacity and a far-memory tier with Intel's Optane DC PMM configured in flat mode (i.e., as volatile main memory) with 1.6 TB capacity. We run Fedora 30 and use a modified Linux kernel, 5.17.
Using cheaper and denser memory, such as NVMMs or CXL-attached memory, to store compressed pages increases memory TCO savings
storing compressed pages on DRAM offers the lowest possible media access latency and hence suits low latency tiers
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Marginal for the requester's 4x CZ120 per-device-scheduling direction: TierScape never touches CXL hardware (Optane stands in as far media) and manages software-defined compressed tiers, not physical devices, so it says nothing about cross-device interference, per-device bandwidth, or multi-tenant QoS on real CXL. Its useful ideas for ObjPlace are orthogonal: an analytical cost model trading performance vs TCO for placement decisions, and the observation that backing media choice per tier matters — the requester could treat each CZ120 (or famfs region) as a distinct backing medium for compressed or uncompressed tiers. It also confirms EuroSys'26 has no real-CXL multi-device competitor in this space.

papers.title: Vistara: Making CXL Real—Full Path from ASIC Design and OS Support to Hyperscale Deployment
papers.venue: ISCA 2026 (Industry Session)
papers.numCXLDevices: 2 per server (2x Meta in-house Vistara CXL 2.0 Type-3 ASICs per MemServer node, 128GB DDR4 each = 256GB CXL per server); deployed fleet-wide across millions of servers
papers.mainProblem: ~40% of Meta's millions of servers are memory-capacity bound; DRAM dominates fleet embodied carbon (69%); decommissioned DDR4 DIMMs outlive servers but cannot be reused in DDR5-only platforms; and six years after CXL's introduction no large-scale production deployment had been reported, leaving CXL's real-world viability (tail latency, tiering-software overhead) contested.
papers.mainIdea: Hardware-software co-design: a first-party CXL 2.0 Type-3 memory-expander ASIC (Vistara) optimized for reusing recycled DDR4 RDIMMs at low power (~9W, ~50ns idle ASIC latency), integrated 2-per-node into a memory-optimized AMD Turin "MemServer" (768GB DDR5 + 256GB CXL DDR4 = 1TB), with both devices interleaved at 256B at the CPU host-bridge and exposed as ONE CPU-less NUMA node managed by upstream-Linux tiering (TPP + TMO, ZONE_MOVABLE, weighted interleave, cgroup cpuset.mems opt-out, per-container Fair Share tier accounting). Deployed at hyperscale across diverse production services; the paper refutes CXL misconceptions (unstable tail latency, high TPP overhead).
papers.hardwareEnv: MemServer: single-socket AMD Turin (Zen5), 158 cores / 316 SMT threads @ ~3GHz, 300W TDP; 768GB DDR5-6400 across 12 channels (614 GB/s peak, ~130ns idle); 2x Vistara ASICs each on PCIe Gen5 x8 (chip supports x16, deployed x8), each with 2 independent 72-bit DDR4 channels @ 2400 MT/s (chip max 3200), 4x32GB reclaimed RDIMMs per ASIC = 256GB CXL total, ~76 GB/s CXL peak, ~250ns CXL idle latency, 256B host-bridge interleave across the 2 devices, ~50W total CXL power. Kernel: upstream Linux with TPP, ZONE_MOVABLE onlining via CXL driver, numa_demotion_enabled=1, numa_balancing=2, zone_reclaim_mode=7; exact kernel version not stated.
papers.evalSetup: Production A/B testing on MemServer nodes serving live traffic: identically configured nodes differ only in CXL enabled/disabled via cpuset.mems cgroup; production load balancer splits traffic evenly; each experiment runs at least one week. Workloads: CacheA/CacheB (distributed caches), Spark, Cosco (shuffle), FtStoreX (data warehouse), CI + Devmachine (DevInfra), ML Parameter Server (5.1-20TB recommendation models), plus HHVM Web and DPP for iso-capacity local:CXL ratio sensitivity (3:1, 2:1, 1:1). Microbenchmarks: Intel MLC bandwidth/latency sweeps with threads pinned per NUMA node; latency-CDF tail study at 1-100 threads; synthetic hot-footprint knee-of-curve stress test; multi-tenant fairness test stacking two CacheA containers (~2.5M QPS, ~430GB each).
papers.baselines: (1) Identical MemServer with CXL disabled (cgroup opt-out) under A/B production traffic; (2) iso-capacity all-local-DRAM configuration for the ratio-sensitivity study; (3) baseline TPP vs their Fair Share per-container tier accounting for the multi-tenant study; (4) implicit comparisons against prior findings: FPGA tail-latency anomalies [Liu et al.] and reported TPP overheads [Zhong et al. OSDI'24].
papers.keyFindings: Up to 25% server-count reduction for disaggregated ML inference (parameter servers use 25% less compute capacity, 4-12% throughput gain at 5.1-20TB models); CacheB average query time -29%; CacheA +33% sustainable QPS with 5-10x longer retention age; Spark/CI/Devmachine +25-33% executors/jobs/VMs per server; OOM job failures -33% (data warehouse) and -50% for some ML workloads. Device characterization: CXL 48 GB/s all-read (62% of theoretical) vs native 497 GB/s; latency 269ns CXL vs 169ns native at 10% BW util (372 vs 234 at 60%); tail-latency CDF of CXL closely tracks local DRAM even at 100 threads, refuting FPGA-based instability claims; TPP overheads <0.5%. Knee-of-curve: performance flat until ~75% hot footprint (+22% latency at 100% hot, 34 GB/s CXL BW); production workloads draw 10-100x less CXL BW than local BW. Multi-tenant: baseline TPP lets one container hold 90% local vs neighbor's 70% (20% P99 skew; 65% QPS drop + OOM-kill under noisy neighbor); their Fair Share per-container local-DRAM bounds improve P99 by 1.6-1.8x and cap the noisy-neighbor QPS dip at 12%. 3:1 and 2:1 local:CXL ratios show <1% regression vs all-local; 1:1 degrades (Web -6% requests, +9% latency; DPP -19% throughput).
papers.limitations: Authors' own: DDR4-2400 + x8 links give ~10x lower bandwidth and ~60% higher latency than local; workloads at/above the 75%-hot knee need x16 links or DDR5-based CXL devices; regressions emerge at 1:1 local:CXL. Methodological: the 2 devices are always fused by 256B host-bridge interleaving into one CPU-less NUMA node — no per-device measurement, management, or cross-device interference study; results are Meta-internal production workloads on a custom ASIC, not reproducible externally; kernel version and Fair Share implementation details are not given; multi-tenant evaluation covers only two co-located instances of the same cache workload on one node; no cross-host pooling/sharing (expansion only); the paper's "CXL is fine" conclusions are conditioned on cold-page-dominated, capacity-bound workloads that keep CXL bandwidth under ~10% utilization.
papers.openQuestions: More aggressive local:CXL ratios beyond 3:1 (explicitly flagged as future opportunity); CXL memory compression as an emerging use case requiring more balanced bandwidth/capacity; higher-bandwidth (x16 / DDR5) devices for bandwidth-sensitive workloads; behavior of bandwidth-bound (not capacity-bound) workloads on CXL is deliberately out of scope (such workloads opt out); per-device scheduling, device-level QoS, and CXL-to-CXL interference between independently exposed devices are never considered; generalization of Fair Share to heterogeneous multi-tenant mixes untested.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Highly relevant positioning citation: Vistara's production platform is nearly isomorphic to the requester's testbed (single-socket AMD Turin, DDR5 local + multiple real CXL 2.0 expanders interleaved at the host bridge into one CPU-less NUMA node) — but Meta permanently pools its 2 devices at 256B granularity and manages them as a single tier, never treating devices as independently schedulable resources; this leaves the requester's per-device placement / cross-device CXL-interference direction open. Vistara's Fair Share multi-tenant result is the closest overlap: Meta confirms tiered-memory noisy-neighbor problems (65% QPS drop, OOM-kill) and fixes them with per-container local-DRAM accounting, so a new system must differentiate by operating at device granularity (CXL-to-CXL contention, per-device tail QoS), not just per-container DRAM shares. Caveat for motivation: Meta argues production capacity-bound workloads draw <10% CXL bandwidth and sit below the 75%-hot knee, and that TPP overhead is <0.5% making complex OS solutions unnecessary — the requester's bandwidth-interference results (2.0-2.13x victim slowdown at ~35.5 GiB/s/region) must therefore be framed as targeting the bandwidth-sensitive / high-hot-fraction / multi-tenant regime that Vistara explicitly opts out of or identifies as its degradation regime.
evidenceQuotes: The Vistara ASIC is Meta’s first-generation, custom CXL memory expander, designed to address the growing memory capacity needs in datacenters.

At its core, the Vistara ASIC is designed to bridge DDR4 memory to host processors via a CXL 2.0/1.1compliant PCIe Gen5 x16 interface. Each Vistara ASIC integrates two independent 72-bit DDR4 memory channels, supporting speeds up to 3200 MT/s and up to 256GB per chip with 64GB DIMMs.
CXL memory expansion is enabled by two Vistara ASICs per node, each connected via a PCIe Gen5 x8 interface.
With two Vistara ASICs per board, this enables 256GB of CXL-attached DDR4 memory expansion in production.

To ensure balanced utilization of the CXL links and minimize contention, memory accesses are interleaved across Vistara devices at a 256-byte granularity at the CPU host-bridge. This means consecutive memory blocks are alternately mapped across both Vistara CXL modules.
CXL-attached memory is exposed to the OS as a distinct, CPU-less NUMA node, separate from the local DRAM nodes directly attached to the processor.

All production experiments are conducted on MemServer nodes. This is a single-socket AMD Turin machine (158 cores, 2-way SMT, ≈3 GHz) with 768 GB local DDR5-6400 and 256 GB CXL-attached DDR4-2400 (2× Vistara ASICs), totaling 1 TB per server.
We have deployed our CXL solution in hyperscale infrastructure with millions of servers, across a variety of production workloads
Under the same noisyneighbor scenario, Fair Share limits Container A’s worst-case QPS dip to 12% (recovering within seconds) and eliminates the OOM risk entirely.

papers.title: Data Tiering in Heterogeneous Memory Systems (X-Mem)
papers.venue: EuroSys
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no CXL; NVM emulated via Intel HMEP — separate physical memory range with custom BIOS + CPU-microcode latency/bandwidth throttling)
papers.mainProblem: Whether replacing most DRAM with cheaper, higher-capacity but slower NVM (PCM/RRAM, 2-4x latency, 1/8-1/4 bandwidth) causes unacceptable application slowdown, and how to place application data across DRAM/NVM tiers to avoid it. Naive page-cache/paging approaches fail because objects with different access patterns share pages and paging overheads are unacceptable for directly-attached memory.
papers.mainIdea: Object/data-structure-granularity tiering: an extended allocator API (xmalloc with a per-data-structure tag) that segregates objects of each tagged data structure into disjoint memory regions (built on per-tag jemalloc instances, mapped to tiers via mbind, entirely in user space); an offline Pin-based profiler that classifies each data structure's access pattern (sequential/streaming vs. random vs. pointer-chasing) — because effective latency on out-of-order CPUs depends on pattern, not just access frequency ("hotness" alone is insufficient); and a greedy placement optimizer that uses the resulting tag-to-priority map to decide which structures go in scarce DRAM vs. NVM.
papers.hardwareEnv: Intel Hybrid Memory Emulation Platform (HMEP): 2-socket Intel Xeon E5-4620, 8 cores per socket @ 2.6 GHz, hyperthreading disabled, 4 DDR3 channels per CPU, memory interleaved across CPUs; measured DRAM latency 150 ns, bandwidth 37-40 GB/s. NVM emulated via custom BIOS (separate physical range) + custom CPU microcode (configurable latency 300-600 ns and bandwidth down to 5 GB/s). Network apps driven by a dedicated client machine over direct 10 GigE links. No CXL hardware; no kernel version stated.
papers.evalSetup: Three applications modified with 10-50 LOC each to tag large data structures via the X-Mem API: MemC3 key-value store (Facebook-like trace), VoltDB in-memory database (TPC-C), GraphMat graph analytics (PageRank on Twitter dataset; plus GraphLab, X-Stream, Galois in the motivating study). NVM emulator swept over latency 300/450/600 ns and bandwidth 40/20/10/5 GB/s; DRAM fraction varied (e.g., 1/2 down to 1/16 of footprint). Offline profile run (Pin tracing) produces tag-to-priority map used in production runs.
papers.baselines: DRAM-only (all data in DRAM, best case); NVM-only (all data in emulated NVM, worst case); frequency-based/manual placements ("based on the access frequencies alone and/or our understanding of the applications"); all possible placement permutations exhaustively for GraphMat; discussion vs. AutoNUMA-style co-location and DRAM-as-cache paging.
papers.keyFindings: With DRAM at only 6% of footprint (GraphMat) or 25% (VoltDB, MemC3) and NVM at 4x latency / 1/8 bandwidth of DRAM, X-Mem-guided placement yields only 13-40% slowdown vs. DRAM-only; unguided worst-case placement suffers 1.5-5.9x slowdown on the same configuration. Assuming NVM is 5x cheaper per bit, hybrid gives 2-2.8x better performance/$ than DRAM-only (1/2-DRAM config: 1.5-1.7x better perf/$ within 9% of DRAM-only performance). Access pattern matters, not just frequency: NVM-only slowdown up to 6x for bandwidth-sensitive streaming apps. For GraphMat, the automatic placement beat all exhaustively-enumerated alternatives (one instance 1.0-5.8x better). Pin profiling overhead up to 40x (offline only).
papers.limitations: Authors admit: static offline classification assumes homogeneous behavior within a data structure and must be redone if workload behavior changes (they suggest shadow-infrastructure re-profiling); Pin tracing is up to 40x slowdown, unusable online (they punt to hoped-for x86 ISA/hardware profiling extensions); manual tagging of data structures required (compiler automation left as future work). Methodological: NVM is emulated (custom BIOS/microcode), not real device silicon; single-node, single-application runs — no multi-tenant or interference experiments; placement is static at classification time, no phase-adaptive migration; pre-CXL, so no coherent-device link effects (no port/link contention, no per-device topology).
papers.openQuestions: Online/low-overhead profiling and real-time placement (explicitly deferred to hardware extensions); per-object heterogeneity within a tagged data structure (skew inside a structure); dynamic workload adaptation/re-classification; automation of tagging; behavior on real NVM or CXL devices; multi-tenant contention on the slow tier; write-endurance-aware placement beyond their brief device-wear discussion.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: This is the foundational ancestor of ObjPlace: allocator-tag object-granularity DRAM/slow-tier placement driven by access-pattern classification (streaming vs. pointer-chasing vs. random), directly anticipating ObjPlace's bandwidth-sensitivity-driven placement — cite it as the origin of the object-tiering paradigm and differentiate on real CXL silicon, online profiling, and phase/pressure adaptivity. Its key insight that effective latency depends on access pattern (bandwidth-bound streaming suffers most on the slow tier) matches the requester's own 2.0-2.13x bandwidth-victim result on CZ120s. It offers nothing on the candidate next direction: single emulated slow tier, zero devices, no per-device scheduling, no cross-device interference, no multi-tenancy — so treating 4 CZ120s as independently schedulable resources is untouched territory relative to this paper.
evidenceQuotes: We perform all experiments on a hybrid memory emulator (§5.1) that runs at full speed.

The hybrid memory emulation platform (HMEP) [39] was built by Intel to support the exploration of software stacks for hybrid memory systems. HMEP enables the study of hybrid memory with real-world applications by implementing – (i) separate physical memory ranges for DRAM and emulated NVM (using a custom BIOS), and (ii) fine-grained emulation of configurable latency and bandwidth for NVM (using custom CPU microcode).

HMEP is restricted to Intel proprietary Xeon E5-4620 platforms, with each of its two processors containing eight 2.6 GHz cores. Hyperthreading is disabled. Each CPU supports four DDR3 channels and memory is interleaved across the CPUs. The measured DRAM latency and bandwidth on the system are 150ns and 37GB/s, respectively.

With such guided placement and with DRAM constituting only 6% of the total memory footprint for GraphMat and 25% for VoltDB and MemC3 (remaining memory is NVM with 4× higher latency and 8× lower bandwidth than DRAM), we show that our target applications demonstrate only a 13% to 40% slowdown.

these applications see, in the worst case, 1.5× to 5.9× slowdown on the same configuration. Based on a realistic assumption that NVM will be 5× cheaper (per bit) than DRAM, this hybrid solution also results in 2× to 2.8× better performance/$ than a DRAM-only system.
Memory tracing (with Pin) during the profiling step can significantly slow down the application (up to 40× in our tests), and is therefore suited only for offline use and not for production.

papers.title: TierBPF: Page Migration Admission Control for Tiered Memory via eBPF
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2604.12300)
papers.numCXLDevices: CXL testbed: 1 (single CXL Type-3 memory expansion device, 128 GB DDR4, PCIe 5.0; vendor/model not stated); PMEM testbed: 0 (Optane, no CXL)
papers.mainProblem: Existing kernel memory-tiering systems (AutoNUMA, TPP, Colloid, MEMTIS) make page migration decisions that ignore (1) page size — migrating whole 2 MB THPs wastes scarce fast-tier capacity when intra-THP access is skewed, while splitting to 4 KB destroys TLB coverage — and (2) the underlying memory architecture — e.g., CXL's full-duplex PCIe link vs. Optane PMEM's half-duplex DDR bus means a promotion policy tuned for one substrate can hurt on another. Per-page profiling (MEMTIS-style) also has runtime/memory overhead that scales with working-set size (up to 15% runtime overhead cited).
papers.mainIdea: Add three eBPF hooks on the kernel's NUMA migration path — mTHP split-order selection, subpage hot/cold classification, and duplex-aware migration admission — so users can load custom, architecture-aware migration policies without kernel modification. Profiling runs entirely in-kernel as an eBPF program attached to hardware-event sampling (no perf ring buffer / user-space round trip), using blocked counting Bloom filters and per-THP heat histograms whose overhead is independent of working-set size. Policies: split THPs to intermediate mTHP sizes and migrate only hot subfolios (entropy-based uniformity check falls back to whole-THP migration); on CXL, defer promotion of pages whose read/write class does not match the dominant direction of current CXL traffic (BalanceTraffic).
papers.hardwareEnv: Two servers. (1) CXL server (default): dual-socket AMD EPYC 9555 (64 cores/socket), 8x32 GB DDR5 DRAM per socket; Socket 0 connects to one CXL Type-3 Memory Expansion device (128 GB DDR4) over PCIe 5.0 (full-duplex); only Socket 0 used to isolate migration effects from cross-socket NUMA. AMD IBS for hardware event sampling at 4,000 samples/sec per CPU. (2) PMEM server: dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6252 (24 cores/socket), 6x16 GB DDR4 DRAM fast tier + 6x128 GB Intel Optane PMEM slow tier per socket. Linux kernel v6.12 (vanilla for AutoNUMA; TPP and Colloid re-implemented on v6.12 with ~270 and additional LOC).
papers.evalSetup: 17 memory-intensive benchmarks: 12 GAPBS graph workloads (bc/bfs/cc/pr on Twitter, uniform-random, Web graphs), Silo-YCSB in-memory DB, and 4 NPB HPC kernels (LU, SP, CG, MG; working sets 12-76 GB). GAPBS/NPB run with 12 threads, Silo with 8; cgroup-based CPU/memory limits for reproducibility. Bandwidth-contention experiments run a non-temporal-store antagonist pinned to separate cores on the CXL/slow tier at ~0, 5, 10, 20 GB/s. THP enabled (always/always/inherit), numa_balancing=2, demotion enabled.
papers.baselines: Integrated into and compared against unmodified AutoNUMA (Linux v6.12), TPP (re-implemented on v6.12), and Colloid (TPP-based, with AMD Data Fabric counters replacing Intel CHA monitoring) on the CXL server; additionally compared against MEMTIS on the PMEM server (MEMTIS cannot run on the AMD CXL server because it needs Intel PEBS; AMD IBS lacks equivalent counters).
papers.keyFindings: On the CXL server, mTHP-splitting TierBPF improves geomean throughput across 17 workloads by 12.3% (AutoNUMA), 17.7% (TPP), 7.4% (Colloid); individual gains up to 30% (bc-twitter on AutoNUMA), 29% (CG on TPP), up to 75% cited across all experiments. Splitting benefits are contention-dependent: geomean gain is only 3.4% at 0 GB/s and -0.1% at 5 GB/s background CXL traffic, 7.0% at 10 GB/s, and clear/consistent at 20 GB/s. The duplex-aware admission policy (BalanceTraffic) gives 5.2%/4.7% geomean under moderate 10 GB/s contention but is counterproductive under 20 GB/s (Split+BalanceTraffic drops TPP's gain from 17.7% to 1.8%). On PMEM, TierBPF-enhanced AutoNUMA beats baseline by 7.1% geomean and outperforms MEMTIS on 11 of 15 workloads (up to 26%); MEMTIS's 4 KB all-or-nothing splitting degrades MG.D by 7% and LU.D by 8% via TLB-miss inflation (3.26 vs 2.90 vs 2.22 L2 DTLB misses/1K instr for MEMTIS/TierBPF/AutoNUMA on LU.D).
papers.limitations: Authors' own: two-tier configurations only — "more than two memory tiers or CXL-SSD ... could be implemented in the future"; BalanceTraffic admission control hurts under high (20 GB/s) contention and gives only modest standalone gains (3.2% geomean on TPP, 10 of 17 workloads degrade without Split); MEMTIS comparison only possible on the Intel/PMEM box. Evident from methodology: only ONE physical CXL device (vendor/model never named) — no multi-device, cross-device, or pooled scenarios; single-socket runs only (cross-socket NUMA deliberately excluded); no multi-tenant experiments (contention is a synthetic streaming antagonist, not co-located tenants); single-benchmark-at-a-time runs; no LLM or latency-SLO workloads; no tail-latency metrics (throughput only); Silo crashes at 12 threads (run at 8).
papers.openQuestions: Extension to more than two tiers and CXL-SSD substrates is explicitly punted to future work. Untested: per-device policies when multiple CXL devices are present; interaction of the admission hook with real multi-tenant contention rather than a synthetic stressor; how BalanceTraffic should adapt or disable itself as contention crosses the ~10-20 GB/s regime (they show it flips from helpful to harmful but leave the adaptive policy open); behavior on GPU/inference workloads; whether the duplex-aware policy holds on multi-headed or switched CXL topologies.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Directly relevant as mechanism, not as multi-device precedent: TierBPF uses a single unnamed 128 GB CXL device on AMD EPYC (very close to your EPYC 9745 + CZ120 box) and never treats devices independently, so your per-device placement / CXL-to-CXL interference direction remains open. Its duplex-aware admission hook — monitoring live CXL read/write channel traffic and deferring mismatched promotions — is a policy you could generalize per-device across your 4x CZ120s, and its finding that traffic-balancing helps at 10 GB/s but backfires at 20 GB/s contention maps onto your measured 2.0-2.13x co-runner slowdown regime. Note it operates at page granularity inside the kernel, complementary to (and a potential competing baseline framing for) ObjPlace's object-granularity user-level placement; its eBPF-hook architecture is a plausible implementation substrate for per-device QoS policies. Their working-set-independent bCBF profiling is also relevant if ObjPlace's profiling cost scales with object count.
evidenceQuotes: A server with CXL memory expansion with dual-socket AMD EPYC 9555s (64 cores per socket). Each socket has 8×32 GB DDR5 DRAM as local memory. Socket 0 connects to a CXL Type-3 Memory Expansion device (128 GB DDR4) over PCIe 5.0, providing a full-duplex link.
A server with Intel Optane PMEM with dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6252 (24 cores per socket). Each socket has 6×16 GB DDR4 DRAM as the fast tier and 6×128 GB Intel Optane PMEM as the slow tier.
By default, we use the CXL server. To isolate the impact of page migration from cross-socket NUMA effects, we use Socket 0 only, following prior efforts in [12, 21, 50].
Across all 17 workloads, TierBPF improves the geomean throughput of AutoNUMA by 12.3%, TPP by 17.7%, and Colloid by 7.4%.

On AutoNUMA, enabling Split alone improves geomean performance by 12.3%, while Split+BalanceTraffic reduces the gain to 6.6%. The effect is more pronounced on TPP: Split alone achieves 17.7% geomean throughput improvement, whereas Split+BalanceTraffic yields only 1.8%.
TierBPF enables sufficient flexibility to develop novel policies in diverse environments, such as more than two memory tiers or CXL-SSD, which could be implemented in the future.
couldNotVerify: Vendor/model and CXL spec revision of the CXL Type-3 device is never stated (only '128 GB DDR4 over PCIe 5.0'), so real-asic vs real-fpga cannot be distinguished from the text; realCXL is set to 'mixed' because evaluation spans one real CXL device plus an Optane PMEM platform.

The '75%' per-workload maximum is stated in abstract/intro; the largest individual number visible in the evaluation text I extracted was 36% (bc-twitter on PMEM) — the 75% case likely appears in a figure I could not read.
Paper text in section 6.5 refers to 'FlexTier-enhanced AutoNUMA', apparently a leftover earlier system name for TierBPF.

papers.title: Finding NEMO: Nimble and Expressive Memory Observability
papers.venue: OSDI (USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation)
papers.mainProblem: OSes managing heterogeneous multi-tier memory hierarchies need memory-usage measurements for placement/control decisions, but existing HW/SW tracking mechanisms (e.g., PEBS/PMU sampling, page-table scanning) force difficult tradeoffs between coverage, timeliness, granularity, flexibility, and CPU overhead.
papers.mainIdea: NEMO: a programmable hardware memory-telemetry engine placed in server memory controllers that gives OS subsystems policy-specific views of memory behavior via flexible telemetry rules that filter memory operations, map accesses to counters, and apply simple per-counter state updates; prototyped in an FPGA-based CXL-attached memory expander and plugged into HeMem, MEMTIS, and Linux noisy-neighbor detection.
papers.hardwareEnv: Not verifiable: full text embargoed. Only known from abstract: prototype implemented on an FPGA-based CXL-attached memory expander. CPU model, DRAM config, FPGA board, CXL link width, capacity, and kernel version unknown.
papers.evalSetup: From abstract only: three use cases evaluated against state-of-the-art memory-management systems — (1) hot-set change reaction in HeMem, (2) THP splitting in MEMTIS, (3) noisy-neighbor detection in Linux — with end-to-end workloads including key-value stores and databases. Detailed workload/run methodology unverified (embargoed).
papers.baselines: HeMem (PEBS-sampling-based tiering), MEMTIS, and stock Linux telemetry/noisy-neighbor detection mechanisms (per abstract); exact baseline configurations unverified.
papers.keyFindings: Per abstract: NEMO speeds up HeMem's reaction to hot-set changes by 5x, accelerates THP splitting in MEMTIS by 10.4x, and detects noisy neighbors in Linux with 350x lower overhead; these telemetry improvements yield up to 1.7x higher throughput and 23% lower latency across key-value stores and databases.
papers.limitations: Could not read methodology/evaluation sections (paper embargoed until OSDI '26 opens proceedings), so author-admitted limitations are unknown. Evident from the abstract: the prototype is an FPGA CXL expander, not production ASIC silicon, so absolute latency/bandwidth are not representative of devices like CZ120; NEMO requires new memory-controller hardware, so it is not deployable on existing servers; telemetry appears device-side (CXL expander MC), so DRAM-side accesses presumably still need other mechanisms unless host MCs also adopt NEMO.
papers.openQuestions: Unknown from available text. Obvious untested/unstated questions: behavior with multiple CXL devices (per-device telemetry aggregation, cross-device interference attribution); adoption path into production host/CXL memory controllers; multi-tenant isolation enforcement (abstract covers detection of noisy neighbors, not mitigation); scalability of rule/counter state at TB-scale capacity.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Highly relevant conceptually: NEMO argues the device/MC side is the right place for hotness and interference telemetry, exactly the observability layer ObjPlace currently approximates from the host (bandwidth-sensitivity/skew/phase signals). Its noisy-neighbor detection at 350x lower overhead speaks directly to the requester's measured 2.0-2.13x CXL co-runner slowdown and the candidate per-device QoS/interference direction — NEMO provides detection, leaving per-device placement, CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference management, and mitigation policy open. However, NEMO needs a programmable FPGA memory expander; the requester's Micron CZ120 ASICs expose no such telemetry (at best CXL 2.0 CPMU-style counters), so on their testbed NEMO is a positioning/related-work anchor and a motivation for host-side or multi-device software techniques rather than a reusable mechanism. Caveat: this judgment rests on the abstract only; the full paper is embargoed as of 2026-07-07.
evidenceQuotes: We prototype NEMO on an FPGA-based CXL-attached memory expander.

We present NEMO, a nimble and expressive hardware memory telemetry engine for server memory controllers (MCs) that gives OS subsystems policy-specific views of memory behavior. NEMO enables flexible telemetry rules that filter memory operations, map accesses to counters, and apply simple updates to per-counter state.

it speeds up HeMem’s reaction to hot-set changes by 5×, accelerates THP splitting in MEMTIS by 10.4×, and detects noisy neighbors in Linux with 350× lower overhead. These telemetry improvements yield up to 1.7× higher throughput and 23% lower latency across key-value stores and databases.

Shihang Li and Matthew Giordano, University of Washington; Tushar Garg, Meta; Rohan Kadekodi, University of Washington; Daniel S. Berger, University of Washington and Microsoft Azure; Baris Kasikci, Thomas Anderson, and Simon Peter, University of Washington

papers.title: Harvesting Sub-Microsecond CXL Memory Stalls with LiteSwitch
papers.venue: OSDI
papers.numCXLDevices: unknown
papers.mainProblem: CXL memory access latency is "typically 3x or more" than local DRAM, and each access is a sub-microsecond stall — too short for interrupt-based or profiling-based stall-harvesting techniques — so CPUs waste large numbers of idle cycles on CXL-induced memory stalls, degrading application performance.
papers.mainIdea: Hardware-software co-design: (1) a hardware mechanism ("location-dependent memory branching", LDMB, per the dissertation abstract) that detects a CXL-induced long-latency memory stall online with near-perfect accuracy and delivers control to software via direct branching; (2) an ultra-fast software switch path (Bundled Handoff scavenger-thread selection + xstate-aware context switching that skips unnecessary SIMD/FP save/restore) that switches to another ready thread in under 20 ns — an order of magnitude faster than a conventional context switch — so stalls longer than ~200 ns can be harvested with no application changes.
papers.keyFindings: From the official abstract only: with a sufficient number of available threads per core, LiteSwitch "recovers up to 80% of the performance lost due to CXL access latency"; thread switch completes "in under 20 nanoseconds, an order of magnitude faster than conventional context switches"; harvestable stalls are sub-microsecond but ">200 nanoseconds"; no application changes required. The dissertation abstract adds that evaluation covers "representative workloads and CXL latency settings" (plural latency settings — suggesting configurable/injected CXL latency rather than one fixed real device, but this is inference, not verified).
papers.limitations: Full text unavailable, so limitations are partly inferred: (1) LDMB is a proposed hardware mechanism that does not exist in any shipping CPU, so the evaluation almost certainly cannot run end-to-end on production CXL silicon — deployment requires CPU-vendor changes; (2) the "up to 80%" recovery is conditioned on "a sufficient number of available threads per core", i.e., it needs abundant thread-level parallelism (scavenger threads) to harvest into; (3) evaluation spans "CXL latency settings", implying tuned/emulated latency points rather than measured multi-device hardware behavior; (4) nothing in any available abstract mentions multiple CXL devices, bandwidth contention, interference, or multi-tenancy — the focus is per-access latency hiding only.
papers.openQuestions: How LDMB would be realized in real CPUs and whether real production CXL devices (with latency ~1.5x DRAM, not 3x) still leave enough stall time above the ~200 ns harvesting threshold; behavior under bandwidth saturation and cross-tenant contention (stall durations become variable and long); interaction with placement/tiering systems that reduce CXL accesses instead of hiding them; correctness/security of sub-20 ns user-level thread switching in multi-tenant settings. All untestable here until the paper text is released.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Complementary, not competing, with ObjPlace: LiteSwitch hides CXL latency by switching threads during individual stalls, whereas ObjPlace avoids CXL accesses via object placement — a paper could cite it as the latency-hiding alternative in related work. It requires a new hardware mechanism (LDMB), so it cannot run on the requester's EPYC 9745 + CZ120 testbed, and it says nothing about per-device scheduling, CXL-to-CXL interference, or multi-tenant QoS — the requester's candidate direction is untouched by it. Notably, its premise is "3x or more" CXL latency, while the requester measures only 1.53x (277 ns vs 185 ns); that gap is a useful data point arguing that on real Turin+CZ120 hardware the harvestable stall window (>200 ns) is thin, and that bandwidth contention (their 2.0-2.13x victim slowdown), not per-access latency, is the bigger problem — a potential positioning angle against LiteSwitch.
evidenceQuotes: USENIX abstract: "However, CXL memory incurs sub-microsecond latency that is typically 3× or more compared to local memory, exacerbating memory-induced CPU stalls and degrading application performance."

USENIX abstract: "(1) a hardware mechanism that precisely identifies a CXL-induced memory stall and exposes it to software with near-perfect accuracy and minimal overhead; (2) an ultra-fast software path that switches to another ready thread for harvesting in under 20 nanoseconds, an order of magnitude faster than conventional context switches."

USENIX abstract: "The evaluation demonstrates that with a sufficient number of available threads per core, LiteSwitch recovers up to 80% of the performance lost due to CXL access latency, enabling the adoption of CXL memory without prohibitive slowdowns."

Princeton FPO abstract: "On the hardware side, location-dependent memory branching (LDMB) detects long-latency accesses online and delivers control via direct branching. On the software side, Bundled Handoff provides fast scavenger selection, and xstate-aware context switching avoids unnecessary SIMD/FP save/restore overhead. Evaluation shows substantial slowdown reductions across representative workloads and CXL latency settings."
Yuhong Zhong CV: "Harvesting Sub-Microsecond CXL Memory Stalls with LiteSwitch / Nanqinqin Li, Yuhong Zhong, Asaf Cidon, Michael J. Freedman / OSDI 2026 ... Acceptance rate: 20%"

papers.title: CARINA: An Efficient CXL-Oriented Embedding Serving System for Recommendation Models
papers.venue: SIGMOD 2025 (PACMMOD Vol. 3, No. 3, paper pp. 1-29, DOI 10.1145/3725274)
papers.numCXLDevices: unknown
papers.mainProblem: Embedding-based recommendation models (ERMs) need huge memory for embedding tables and generate massive embedding-read traffic; running DRAM-designed ERM serving systems directly on CXL memory performs poorly because CXL bandwidth is much lower than DRAM and easily saturated, and NUMA effects in modern CXL servers make it worse.
papers.mainIdea: Carina, an ERM serving system co-designed for DRAM+CXL heterogeneous memory: (1) balance access across memory devices by keeping hot (high-frequency) embeddings in DRAM and explicitly placing embedding tables across NUMA nodes; (2) bandwidth-aware task execution that decomposes each request batch into fine-grained tasks and schedules them to cap real-time CXL bandwidth utilization and avoid instantaneous saturation.
papers.hardwareEnv: Could not verify. Abstract states evaluation "under real CXL devices" on servers with NUMA architecture, but the paper is closed-access (no arXiv/author PDF); CPU model, DRAM config, CXL device vendor/model/capacity/link width, and kernel version could not be read.
papers.evalSetup: Could not verify beyond the abstract: evaluation of ERM serving throughput and request latency on real CXL devices against a CXL-oblivious baseline. Specific workloads/datasets (e.g., which recommendation models or traces) not readable.
papers.baselines: A "CXL-oblivious baseline" (a DRAM-based ERM serving system run unmodified on CXL) per the abstract; full baseline list not verifiable.
papers.keyFindings: Carina outperforms a CXL-oblivious baseline by an average of 5.38x in system throughput and 4.04x in request latency on real CXL devices. Core diagnosis: CXL bandwidth (not latency) is the bottleneck for ERM serving and can be instantaneously saturated; hot/cold DRAM/CXL placement plus rate-controlled fine-grained task scheduling recovers the loss.
papers.limitations: Full text unreadable this session, so authors' own admissions unknown. From what is verifiable: the headline comparison is against a CXL-oblivious baseline (naively running a DRAM system on CXL), which inflates speedups relative to stronger tiering baselines; number of CXL devices, device type, and whether multi-tenant or tail-latency scenarios were tested are all unverifiable.
papers.openQuestions: Whether Carina manages multiple CXL devices independently (per-device placement/scheduling) or treats CXL as one flat pool; behavior under multi-tenant contention and CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference; generality beyond embedding serving. These cannot be confirmed without the full text.
evidenceQuotes: We evaluate Carina under real CXL devices and find that it outperforms a CXL-oblivious baseline by an average of 5.38x and 4.04x in system throughput and request latency, respectively.

directly running DRAM-based ERM serving systems on CXL yields poor performance because the bandwidth of CXL is notably lower than DRAM and can be easily saturated, making CXL memory the bottleneck. The non-uniform memory access (NUMA) architecture in modern CXL servers further decreased the system performance.

Carina balances the memory access from different memory devices by storing hot embeddings with high access frequencies on DRAM and specifying the placement of embedding tables on the NUMA nodes. Moreover, Carina adopts bandwidth-aware task execution, which decomposes each batch of ERM requests into fine-grained tasks and schedules the tasks to control the real-time utilization of CXL bandwidth to avoid instantaneous saturation.

papers.title: ArtMem: Adaptive Migration in Reinforcement Learning-Enabled Tiered Memory
papers.venue: ISCA (52nd Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture), Tokyo — note: ISCA 2025, pp. 405-418, NOT ISCA 2026 as the tasking hint believed
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 CXL devices. The slow tier is 4x 128GB Intel persistent memory modules (512GB PM) on one socket; fast tier is 4x 16GB DDR4 (64GB DRAM).
papers.mainProblem: Existing tiered-memory management systems perform inconsistently across workloads, fail to adjust migration strategies when fast-tier access rates are low, and do not dynamically tune migration scope to workload patterns.
papers.mainIdea: ArtMem is an RL-driven (tabular Q-learning) tiered-memory manager: a modified Linux kernel (5.15.19, Memtis/htmm-lineage PEBS-sampling design with per-cgroup hot/cold tracking) exposes the fast-tier hit ratio via a cgroup file, and a userspace Q-learning agent observes the hit-ratio decile as state, chooses a migration-scope action (0 to 512Ki pages, i.e., quota sizes 4096..524288 pages x 4KB written back to memory.action_show every 10s), with reward = hit-ratio decile minus a threshold, thereby adaptively tuning migration aggressiveness/scope to increase fast-tier accesses while reducing unnecessary migrations.
papers.hardwareEnv: Could not read the paper's testbed section. From the artifact: Intel x86 server (PEBS events MEM_LOAD_L3_MISS_RETIRED.LOCAL_DRAM, MEM_INST_RETIRED.ALL_STORES/ALL_LOADS), Linux kernel 5.15.19-artmem (same base version as Memtis SOSP'23), DRAM tier ending at phys 0x207fffffff (~130 GB) and a 'PM' slow tier spanning 0x2080000000-0x11c7fffffff (~1 TB), CPUS_PER_SOCKET=8. No CXL device model, DRAM/CXL capacities, or emulation method verifiable from the paper itself.
papers.evalSetup: Not verifiable this session. Abstract states evaluation "over diverse workloads"; a third-party citing paper (ICPP'25 'Leave No One Behind') evaluates ArtMem alongside Memtis/TPP/Nomad on ML/graph benchmarks, but ArtMem's own workload list, footprint ratios, and run methodology could not be read.
papers.baselines: Abstract says ArtMem "outperforms state-of-the-art tiering systems"; exact baseline names not verifiable (Memtis lineage of the code and contemporaneous papers suggest Memtis/TPP/AutoNUMA/Nomad-class baselines, but this is inference, not verified). Author README admits "A comparison with MGLRU is currently missing."
papers.keyFindings: Per the publisher abstract (via Semantic Scholar/OpenAlex): ArtMem achieves 35%-172% performance improvements over diverse workloads vs. state-of-the-art tiering systems while reducing unnecessary migrations (the author lab page states "35% to 191%" — discrepancy unresolved). Design finding: system-level feedback (access frequency, recency, migration counts) fed to an RL agent enables better page placement and fewer wasted migrations than static-heuristic tiering.
papers.limitations: Authors' own (GitHub README): "Several magic numbers and manually tuned parameters make configuration less convenient" and "A comparison with MGLRU is currently missing." From the artifact: tabular Q-learning with a coarse 10-bucket hit-ratio state and 10-second decision epoch; hardcoded physical address ranges for the DRAM/PM tiers (single fast + single slow tier only, no per-device awareness); single-cgroup focus with no evident multi-tenant evaluation; slow tier appears to be PM/Optane-class rather than real CXL silicon (unconfirmed). Full-text limitations section unread.
papers.openQuestions: Whether the RL policy transfers to real CXL ASIC latency/bandwidth profiles (vs. the PM-style tier in the artifact); multi-application/multi-tenant fairness (explicitly taken up by the follow-on ICPP'25 'Leave No One Behind' paper that benchmarks ArtMem); handling of more than two tiers or multiple independently addressable slow devices; MGLRU comparison; sensitivity to the many hand-tuned magic numbers (PEBS period lists, 10s epoch, reward threshold).
evidenceQuotes: From author lab page (chaselab.wiki/publication/2025-artmem): ArtMem "outperforms state-of-the-art tiering systems, achieving performance improvements ranging from 35% to 191%, over diverse workloads."

From Semantic Scholar record of the ACM abstract: ArtMem is "an RL-driven framework" that "dynamically manages tiered memory systems and adapts to workload evolution," achieving "35% - 172% performance improvements over diverse workloads."

From artifact kernel/include/linux/artmem.h (verbatim code): "#define DRAM_ADDR_END 0x207fffffff" / "#define PM_ADDR_START 0x2080000000" / "#define PM_ADDR_END 0x11c7fffffff" / "#define DRAM_LLC_LOAD_MISS  0x1d3 // MEM_LOAD_L3_MISS_RETIRED.LOCAL_DRAM" — a two-tier DRAM + 'PM' physical layout on an Intel PEBS machine; no CXL identifiers anywhere in the artifact.
From artifact kernel/Makefile (verbatim): "VERSION = 5 / PATCHLEVEL = 15 / SUBLEVEL = 19 / EXTRAVERSION = -artmem" — same 5.15.19 base kernel as Memtis (SOSP'23, Optane testbed).

From artifact Q-Learning/env.py (verbatim): "self.action_space = [0, 4096, 8192, 16384, 32768, 65536, 131072, 262144, 524288]" and "cat /sys/fs/cgroup/artmem/memory.hit_ratio_show" — userspace Q-learning agent picks migration-scope actions from kernel-exported hit ratio.

papers.title: CXL and the Return of Scale-Up Database Engines
papers.venue: PVLDB (Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment), Vol. 17, No. 10, pp. 2568-2575
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (vision paper; no evaluation testbed of its own — all numbers cited from prior work by Intel [Sun et al. MICRO'23], Meta [TPP], and Microsoft [Pond])
papers.mainProblem: Scale-out database architectures dominated the last two decades because cloud servers could only grow by adding whole machines over slow, non-coherent networks (PCIe/RDMA); PCIe's bandwidth/latency and lack of coherence erode accelerator benefits and force batching, while per-server memory limits cause stranded memory and inelastic, hard-to-migrate database engines.
papers.mainIdea: Vision: CXL's coherent cxl.mem/cxl.cache sub-protocols and CXL 2.0/3.x switches enable three architectures — (a) local memory expansion managed by the database buffer pool (not the OS), (b) far-memory pooling where a buffer pool lives in switched, shared CXL memory so engines spawn/migrate without warm-up, and (c) full rack-scale disaggregation turning the rack into one shared-memory machine — plus coherent near-data processing (active memory regions in the CXL controller) and heterogeneous device pooling; together these revive scale-up database engines and turn distributed-systems problems back into single-machine ones.
papers.hardwareEnv: None. No testbed of any kind; the paper cites third-party characterizations (Intel micro-benchmarks: CXL load ~35% slower than remote NUMA; Meta: ~64 GB/s CXL bandwidth; Microsoft Pond: 26% of 158 workloads <1% penalty).
papers.evalSetup: No evaluation. Section 2.4 'CXL Performance Characterization' is a literature summary of Intel (Sun et al., MICRO'23), Meta (TPP, ASPLOS'23), and Microsoft (Pond, ASPLOS'23) results; the rest of the paper is architectural argument plus enumerated research questions.
papers.baselines: None run. Rhetorical comparisons only: CXL vs RDMA (latency ~200-400 ns vs a few microseconds, 'a difference of at least 2.5x'; NICs waste >20% of PCIe lane bandwidth), CXL vs PCIe copies, CXL NDP vs non-coherent NDP (Oracle SPARC S7 DAX, Farview), scale-up vs scale-out/replication+sharding databases.
papers.keyFindings: All secondhand: (1) CXL load latency ~200-400 ns, ~35% over remote NUMA (Intel); NUMA load bandwidth 70% efficient vs 46% over CXL. (2) Meta: CXL as cold-page tier gives ~64 GB/s with latency only slightly above NUMA. (3) Microsoft: 26% of 158 workloads <1% penalty, +17% <5%; TPC-H overheads mostly <20%, query-dependent. (4) CXL coherence domain scales to 4096 devices (rack scale). Positions: database engines, not the OS, should place pages across tiers; OLTP on DRAM + OLAP structures on CXL avoids interference; disaggregated buffer pools enable elastic/serverless and easy migration; coherent NDP lets host and accelerator share the lock table and work in parallel.
papers.limitations: It is explicitly a position paper: zero implementation, zero measurements, no testbed, no multi-device or interference data. Key enabling features it relies on (CXL 3.0/3.1 memory sharing, GIM/GFAM, peer-to-peer, multi-rack fabrics, switch silicon at scale) were not commercially available in 2024. Authors note modeling CXL as NUMA 'can be inaccurate' and that bandwidth 'highly depends on the expander's characteristics', but do not measure this. They acknowledge cost/complexity critiques (Levis et al. 'A Case Against CXL Memory Pooling') only argumentatively. Nothing on per-device bandwidth contention, tail latency, QoS, or multi-tenant isolation — the interference problem is only implied ('OLTP and OLAP data structures would not interfere with each other', asserted, not shown).
papers.openQuestions: Explicit research questions: are expanders fast enough for OLTP or only OLAP; do data structures need redesign for CXL non-uniformity and should they span DRAM+CXL with adaptive placement; byte-addressable allocation vs paging-block-device use; how do hashing/sorting/indexing behave at rack scale where coherence invalidation traffic may dominate; scheduling rack-scale resources across competing queries; engine- vs thread-level elasticity granularity; what to offload to coherent NDP; how to compose/balance pooled heterogeneous devices. Untouched entirely: multi-device management, interference/QoS, fault handling beyond citing CXL RAS.
evidenceQuotes: Alberto Lerner and Gustavo Alonso. CXL and the Return of Scale-Up Database Engines. PVLDB, 17(10): 2568 - 2575, 2024. doi:10.14778/3675034.3675047

Preliminary benchmarks by Microsoft, Meta, and Intel about CXL memory performance are already available (resp., [31, 34, 52]). The perceived latency for CXL memory access is slightly higher than that for remote NUMA access, roughly in the 200–400 nanoseconds range.

The micro-benchmarks from Intel investigate both latency and bandwidth [52]. Regarding latency, executing a load instruction against a given type of CXL-attached memory can take just 35% longer than the equivalent NUMA memory access.

In this paper, we describe why such architectural transformations are now possible, how they benefit emerging heterogeneous hardware platforms for data-intensive systems, and the associated research challenges.
We note, however, that simply modeling CXL memory as NUMA can be inaccurate. The number of memory controllers in an expander and, thus, available bandwidth varies from product to product.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Useful as motivation/related-work framing, not as a technical baseline: it argues application-level (engine-level) placement across DRAM/CXL tiers beats OS paging, which directly supports the ObjPlace thesis, and its admission that 'modeling CXL memory as NUMA can be inaccurate' because per-expander controller/bandwidth characteristics vary is a citable hook for treating each CZ120 (or region) as a distinct resource. It contains no measurements of multi-device contention, per-device scheduling, or QoS, so the requester's per-device interference and tail-aware isolation direction fills a gap this vision paper only gestures at (its scheduling-across-competing-queries question). Good citation for positioning a systems paper on multi-tenant CXL placement at a DB or systems venue.

papers.title: A CXL-Powered Database System: Opportunities and Challenges
papers.venue: ICDE (author-hosted PDF; IEEE Xplore record 10597964)
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 — pure vision/position paper, no evaluation testbed of any kind
papers.mainProblem: Distributed DBMSs are constrained by limited interconnect capacity, communication speed, and bandwidth; static CPU-memory coupling causes resource stranding, slow disk-log-based fault recovery, and index designs ill-suited to far memory. The paper asks how CXL (1.1/2.0/3.0/3.1) should reshape next-generation DBMS design.
papers.mainIdea: A vision paper identifying four opportunity areas for CXL in DBMS — (1) hybrid buffer pools spanning near/far/pooled/shared memory, (2) elastic memory scaling via switch-managed dynamic allocation, (3) fast recovery via far-memory checkpoints/dirty-page lists/force-commit with PMEM, (4) CXL-aware index design (B+ tree node placement, dynamic allocation, concurrency via switch coherence) — and enumerating 12 concrete research challenges across them (e.g., dynamic page allocation modeled as graph partitioning, unified near/far latency cost models, dual checkpoints, hot/cold tiering agents).
papers.hardwareEnv: None. No testbed, no measurements. The paper describes CXL product timelines (Intel Sapphire Rapids, Agilex 7 FPGAs, Samsung CXL Memory Expander for CXL 1.1; XConn CXL 2.0 switch + Samsung expanders + MemVerge/H3 2TB pooled demo) purely as industry context, citing others' work.
papers.evalSetup: No evaluation section exists. The paper contains only architecture figures (Fig. 1-12 are conceptual diagrams: rack memory hierarchy, hybrid buffer pool, page directories, dual checkpoint, dirty-page sync, force commit) and cites prior empirical studies (DaMoN'22 Ahn et al., DaMoN'23 Lee et al., Pond, TPP, DirectCXL) for performance claims.
papers.baselines: None — no experiments, hence no baselines.
papers.keyFindings: No measured results. Contributions are taxonomic: 4 opportunities (buffer pool scaling, elastic memory allocation, fast recovery from far memory, efficient index design) and 12 named challenges (hybrid buffer pool construction; dynamic data page allocation; fine-grained memory sharing for multi-write consistency; elastic hybrid buffer pool; near-far memory allocation; automatic hot-cold tiering; dual checkpoint mechanisms; dirty-page synchronization in shared memory; force commit with CXL+PMEM; B+ tree node memory allocation; dynamic memory allocation for data modifications; index concurrency for structure updates). Quantitative claims are all secondhand (e.g., sub-microsecond latency for KB-scale shared-memory page updates, cited to a CXL tutorial).
papers.limitations: Entirely speculative: no hardware, no prototype, no measurements — all performance assumptions (sub-us shared-memory updates, switch-mediated coherence) come from CXL Consortium white papers and a tutorial, and much of the vision (CXL 2.0 switches, 3.0 fabric/shared memory, dynamic capacity reallocation) depends on hardware that at writing was not in mass production ("expected to launch from Q2 2025 through end of 2026 or later"). Authors themselves defer type-2 devices, GPUs, and CXL-TSP security to future work. No discussion of multi-device direct-attach expansion topologies, per-device bandwidth contention, or interference — the paper treats far memory as a monolithic layer.
papers.openQuestions: All 12 challenges are explicitly open: how to allocate pages across near/far/shared buffer pools; unified latency cost model for near/far memory; predicting memory reallocation latency; hot/cold tiering agents (ML-based); dual checkpoint consistency; whether force-commit over CXL+PMEM keeps transaction latency acceptable; CXL-aware B+ tree placement and OCC-based concurrent index updates. Also punted: type-2/GPU devices, TEE/CXL-TSP security, and any empirical validation.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Useful only as motivation/citation fodder, not as a technical baseline: it argues DBMS buffer pools, tiering, and indexes should become CXL-aware, which supports the requester's ObjPlace framing, but it offers zero measurements and treats CXL memory as one homogeneous "far buffer pool" behind (mostly hypothetical) switches. It never considers direct-attached multi-device topologies like the 4x CZ120 box, per-device bandwidth saturation (~35.5 GiB/s/region), or CXL-to-CXL interference, so the candidate direction of per-device scheduling/isolation is untouched here — the paper's tiering/hot-cold challenges (#2, #6) could even be cited as validation that device-granular placement is an open problem. Its DB-workload angle (buffer pools, B+ trees) suggests database workloads as an evaluation domain where per-device QoS claims would resonate.
evidenceQuotes: This paper explores the significant potential of employing CXL in constructing next-generation DBMS. Through a thorough analysis of CXL's key characteristics, this paper identifies emerging opportunities, particularly in buffer pool expansion, memory elasticity, swift data recovery, and index optimization.
Contribution. This paper presents a list of challenges when leveraging CXL protocols in DBMS design from four aspects.
We argue that the next wave in DBMS innovation should consider CXL. Solving the challenges proposed in this paper will move DBMS design to the next frontier.
Products based on this version are expected to launch from the second quarter of 2025 through the end of 2026 or later.

The first study [21] evaluated CXL memory with OLTP and OLAP workloads, finding that reasonable data allocation can mitigate the throughput impact. (performance evidence is secondhand citation; the paper runs no experiments of its own)
