papers.title: Pasha: An Efficient, Scalable Database Architecture for CXL Pods
papers.venue: CIDR 2025 (15th Annual Conference on Innovative Data Systems Research, Amsterdam)
papers.numCXLDevices: 1 (a single 128 GB CXL 1.1 memory device, "hardware prototype CXL module," vendor anonymized)
papers.mainProblem: Scaling a single-node OLTP database across multiple hosts without the throughput collapse caused by multi-host transactions and two-phase commit; existing partition-based shared-nothing databases degrade sharply as multi-partition transaction fraction rises, and RDMA-based shared-memory designs pay 1-2 orders of magnitude higher memory latency plus software coherence cost.
papers.mainIdea: A "partitioned + shared" database architecture for a CXL pod (a few hosts sharing a CXL memory module, of which only a small region, ~hundreds of MB, is hardware cache-coherent across hosts). Each host keeps its own partition in local DRAM; data touched by multiple hosts lives in a shared region in CXL memory, with the hardware cache-coherent region used for synchronization primitives (latches/locks) and a software coherence protocol for the rest. Tuples move dynamically between partitions and the shared region so every transaction is a single-host transaction executed with a single-node concurrency-control protocol, eliminating 2PC. The paper is a vision/architecture paper laying out 7 research challenges (data movement, software cache coherence, MVCC across tiers, partitioning, high concurrency, partial-failure tolerance, auto-scaling); precursor to the group's OSDI'25 Tigon system.
papers.hardwareEnv: One physical machine: two Intel Xeon 8460H CPUs, 1 TB local DRAM (DDR5 4800), and one 128 GB CXL 1.1 memory device (also DDR5 4800, single memory channel, PCIe 5.0 x8 link) — a "hardware prototype CXL module" whose manufacturer required all measurements to be reported normalized only. The multi-host CXL pod is emulated: 8 VMs (4 vCPUs, 8 GB DRAM each) on this one machine share the CXL device; inter-VM coherence is the single host's ordinary hardware coherence, so it is faster than a real cross-host CXL 3.x pod would be. No kernel version given.
papers.evalSetup: Microbenchmark: Intel MLC latency/bandwidth of local DRAM vs CXL memory at 3:1 read:write ratio (normalized results only). Main experiment: TPC-C with only NewOrder and Payment procedures (50/50 mix; the other three procedures are unsupported by Sundial), 8 warehouses, one warehouse per emulated host (8 VMs), 2 worker threads per approach, varying the multi-warehouse transaction percentage from 0/0 to 60/90 (NewOrder/Payment). Pasha prototype built inside the Sundial distributed in-memory OLTP DBMS; no dynamic data movement — shared tables (CUSTOMER, STOCK, 58% of TPC-C data) are placed in CXL memory before the run.
papers.baselines: All Sundial variants: Sundial-NET (default partition-based shared-nothing over network), Sundial-CXL (partition-based but message queues in CXL memory instead of network), Sundial-SHM (fully shared-memory: all data in cache-coherent CXL memory), vs Sundial-Pasha.
papers.keyFindings: (1) Their CXL 1.1 device has ~2.3x higher latency than local DRAM and 58% of DRAM single-channel bandwidth. (2) TPC-C: with 0% multi-warehouse transactions Sundial-Pasha matches Sundial-NET/CXL and is 1.4x over Sundial-SHM; at 60/90% multi-warehouse transactions Pasha is up to 5.9x over Sundial-NET, 1.6x over Sundial-CXL, and 1.1x over Sundial-SHM (Sundial-NET needs ~3.6 network messages/transaction there). (3) Pasha only places 58% of TPC-C data in shared CXL memory vs 100% for SHM, reducing cross-host synchronization; dynamic data movement would shrink this further.
papers.limitations: Authors' own admissions: no hardware exists for cross-host CXL 3.x cache coherence, so the pod is emulated with 8 VMs on one machine and "inter-host coherence actions in our testbed are faster than they would be on a CXL pod"; cost modeling of coherence atomics is acknowledged as a challenge; the prototype does not support dynamic data movement (shared tables are pre-placed); measurements are normalized (NDA). Methodological weaknesses: single physical host, single CXL device, only 2 of 5 TPC-C procedures, only 2 worker threads per approach, 8 warehouses, no latency/tail results (throughput only), no multi-tenant or interference experiments, vision paper with preliminary results only.
papers.openQuestions: The 7 explicitly-punted research challenges: safe data access during partition<->shared-region movement; a database-tailored software cache-coherence protocol layered on a small (~256 MB) hardware-coherent region; MVCC with versions split across DRAM and CXL; new partitioning algorithms minimizing shared-region operations; conflict-avoiding transaction scheduling at ~4,608-core concurrency; partial-failure tolerance (illegal in-memory states, allocator recovery); CXL-based auto-scaling/live migration and cost-optimal scaling across DRAM/CXL/CPU dimensions. Also untested: behavior on real multi-host CXL 3.x hardware, real back-invalidation costs, bandwidth contention on the shared device.
evidenceQuotes: Our evaluation (§4) uses a hardware prototype CXL module. The evaluation machine includes two Intel Xeon 8460H CPUs, 1 TB local DRAM, and a 128 GB CXL 1.1 memory device. Both local DRAM and CXL memory use DDR5 4800 DRAM.
The CXL memory module has a single memory channel and is connected to the CPU via a PCIe 5.0 x8 link.

We emulate a CXL pod on the machine described earlier (§2.2) because there are no commercially available (or hardware prototype) CXL devices that support fine-grained memory sharing with hardware cache coherence. We run 8 virtual machines (VMs) on this machine, each with 4 vCPUs and 8 GB local DRAM, and configure the VMs to share the CXL memory device to emulate a CXL pod that includes 8 machines sharing cache-coherent CXL memory.
That means that inter-host coherence actions in our testbed are faster than they would be on a CXL pod.

We find that the latency of the tested CXL memory is around 2.3× higher than local DRAM and its bandwidth is 58% of the single-channel bandwidth of local DRAM. Note that at the request of the hardware manufacturer, we only provide normalized performance, not absolute measurements.
Sundial-Pasha has up to 5.9× and 1.6× higher throughput than Sundial-NET and Sundial-CXL, respectively
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Low direct relevance to the requester's single-host 4x CZ120 testbed: Pasha targets multi-host CXL pods with (hypothetical) cross-host hardware cache coherence, uses one CXL device, and never treats devices as independently schedulable resources or studies CXL-to-CXL interference. Its useful overlap is the DRAM-vs-CXL placement philosophy — hot/private data in DRAM, shared/cold data in CXL — which is conceptually adjacent to ObjPlace's object-granularity placement, and its 2.3x latency ratio corroborates the requester's 1.53x-2x range measurements. It also illustrates the field's evaluation gap the requester can exploit: even at CIDR the multi-device/multi-host story is VM-emulated on one device, so real per-device measurements on 4 physical CZ120s (cross-device interference, per-device bandwidth) would be novel. Cite as motivation/related work for CXL-aware data placement, not as a competing system.
couldNotVerify: Whether the prototype CXL module is ASIC or FPGA based — the paper anonymizes the manufacturer, hence realCXL=mixed (real CXL 1.1 device for memory characteristics + VM-based emulation of the multi-host pod and its cross-host coherence)
Kernel version and absolute latency/bandwidth numbers (withheld at manufacturer's request)

papers.title: Exploring Dynamic Memory Allocation of CXL Memory Pools in Enterprise In-Memory Database Management Systems
papers.venue: EDBT (Industrial & Applications Paper), pp. 687-695, doi 10.48786/edbt.2026.58
papers.numCXLDevices: 2 Samsung CMM-D 128GB devices behind one XConn B2 CXL switch (the "CXL memory box", used in both testbeds); plus directly-attached CMM-D device(s) in the single-host testbed for comparison (count of direct-attached devices not stated)
papers.mainProblem: Whether a real switch-based CXL memory pool — with its extra switch hop adding ~100ns latency and lower bandwidth than directly-attached CXL — can serve an enterprise in-memory DBMS (SAP HANA) for dynamic capacity allocation across hosts without unacceptable performance loss, and what DB use cases justify it (TCO reduction, avoiding OOM, elastic provisioning).
papers.mainIdea: Deploy a real 2-host CXL 2.0 switch-based memory pool (XConn B2 switch + 2 Samsung CMM-D) and integrate it with a SAP HANA prototype (NUMA-aware far-memory allocation in the HEX engine, temp-table NUMA placement). Dynamic pooling is realized at the OS layer (Linux memory online/offline over a statically-configured 256GB HDM region per host, since fabric-manager HDM remapping was too unstable) rather than at the switch layer. Evaluate three use cases: moving main-storage table data / HEX heap to the pool (TPC-C, TPC-DS), HANA fast restart using pool persistence, and dynamic allocation of intermediate-result temp tables across two servers.
papers.hardwareEnv: Testbed 1 (single host, Sec 5.1/5.2): 1x Intel 5th-gen Xeon (Emerald Rapids), 48 physical / 96 HT cores, 8x 128GB DDR5-4800 = 1,024 GB local DRAM; commercial CXL memory box = 1 XConn B2 switch (up to 256 PCIe Gen5 lanes) + 2x Samsung CMM-D 128GB (DDR5-5200 DIMM, ASIC CXL-to-DDR5 controller, PCIe Gen5 x8 each); hosts on Gen5 x16 upstream ports; 256GB HDM per host; direct-attached CMM-D and pool both connected to the remote socket for latency study. Testbed 2 (two servers, Sec 5.3): Server A: 2x Xeon Platinum 8568 (Emerald Rapids, 96 logical cores/socket, 8x128GB DIMMs = 1TB DRAM/socket); Server B: 2x Emerald Rapids (112 logical cores/socket, 8x64GB = 512GB/socket); each server expanded by 128GB from the shared pool. Kernel version not stated (Linux, kernel online/offline of memory blocks; fsdax + device-mapper interleaving for the x2 bandwidth config).
papers.evalSetup: SAP HANA prototype with CXL far-memory allocation. OLTP: TPC-C 100 warehouses, sweeping 1-384 client threads, throughput normalized to baseline. OLAP: TPC-DS SF100, 1-16 parallel streams, queries/unit-time. Placements compared for main storage (fsdax) and HEX heap (NUMA-bound): local DRAM, remote DRAM, remote direct CMM-D, local/remote M-pool, and M-pool x2 (two fsdax devices, one per downstream CMM-D, interleaved via Linux device mapper to double bandwidth). Fast restart: measure Restart/Ready/Completed timestamps with main storage in the pool. Two-server: SQL scripts from the top-5 TPC-DS queries by temp-table footprint; temp tables placed in DRAM/remote-DRAM/M-pool; interference measured with Server A on the first CMM-D's 128GB range and Server B on the other device, run concurrently vs separately; MLC used to validate dynamic capacity changes.
papers.baselines: All-local-DRAM baseline; remote-socket DRAM; directly-attached CXL memory (CMM-D on remote socket); CXL memory pool local vs remote socket; pool with 2x interleaved bandwidth; HANA restart with/without preload and with/without fast-restart. Related-work comparisons (Pond, PolarDB, Octopus) are discussed, not run.
papers.keyFindings: (1) TPC-C (OLTP) shows no observable degradation with main storage or HEX heap in the pool; peak CXL traffic ~13 GB/s at 288 threads, well below device bandwidth. (2) TPC-DS (OLAP) degrades noticeably with main storage in the pool; performance is more bandwidth- than latency-sensitive — device-mapper interleaving across the two CMM-Ds (x2) cuts degradation to single-digit % vs baseline. (3) HEX heap in CXL is rejected as a use case (>50% degradation in prior work due to random access). (4) Fast restart from the persistent pool saves 87% of preload time, a 5.25x restart acceleration vs preload-from-disk (but 27% slower than no-preload restart). (5) Temp tables for big TPC-DS SQL scripts in the pool: performance effectively unchanged vs local DRAM. (6) Two servers driving the same switch concurrently (each on its own CMM-D device) show no measurable interference; dynamic online/offline of pool regions incurs no measurable delay and no restarts.
papers.limitations: Authors' own admissions: switch-layer dynamic HDM remapping via the fabric manager was NOT used "due to system stability concerns with our current hardware" — pooling is emulated at the OS layer over a static HDM config; memory sharing (overlapping regions) among hosts is deferred to future work; HANA CXL features may never ship commercially. Methodological weaknesses: only 2 CXL devices and 2 hosts; the no-interference result is weak — each server used a disjoint 128GB range on a DIFFERENT device and the paper itself concedes overhead stays negligible only "as long as there are no other resource conflicts, such as device bandwidth contention", i.e., same-device bandwidth contention was never tested; workloads chosen for the interference test are sequential/prefetch-friendly with low CXL traffic; no tail-latency analysis, only throughput; no kernel version or latency/bandwidth microbenchmark numbers for the pool are reported (the ~100ns switch penalty is cited, not measured).
papers.openQuestions: Cross-host sharing of table data / intermediate results with CXL 3.x cache coherency (explicit future work); true fabric-manager-driven dynamic HDM reassignment (skipped for stability); interference when multiple hosts contend for the SAME device's bandwidth; QoS isolation on the switch (stated as a requirement in Sec 2.1 but never evaluated); behavior at >2 hosts / >2 devices; latency-sensitive random-access workloads on pools beyond the blanket "use local DRAM" advice.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Directly relevant to the "each CXL device as an independently schedulable resource" direction: their interference experiment partitions the pool per-device (Server A on CMM-D #1, Server B on CMM-D #2) and finds no cross-device interference through a shared XConn switch — but only under low, prefetch-friendly traffic, and they explicitly exempt "device bandwidth contention", which is exactly the 2.0-2.13x victim slowdown the requester already measured on a single interleaved region. This leaves same-device and cross-device contention under saturating load an open gap the requester's 4x CZ120 testbed can fill without a switch. Their x2 device-mapper interleaving result (bandwidth, not latency, dominates OLAP) matches the requester's 35.5 GiB/s-per-region, 4-thread-saturation finding and supports per-device vs interleaved placement as a real knob. Their fsdax-based main-storage placement and OS-level online/offline pooling are also mechanically similar to the requester's famfs/daxctl setup, making SAP HANA-style DB workloads a plausible additional workload class for ObjPlace-style per-device placement.
evidenceQuotes: We use the XConn B2 CXL switch chip that supports up to 256 PCIe Gen5 lanes for CXL upstream and downstream links. We configure our memory pooling system with 2 hosts, each connected to PCIe Gen5x16 upstream ports (USPs). On downstream ports (DSPs), we install two 128GB Samsung CXL memory devices (CMM-D), each consisting of a 128GB DDR5 DIMM supporting 5200 MT/s, an internal memory controller, an ASIC logic converting CXL protocols to DDR5, and a PCIe Gen5x8 interface.
Specifically, we configure the HDM mapping to bind all 128GB CMM-D devices sequentially, and form a single 256GB HDM region for each host to enable dynamic pooling over the entire downstream devices.
First, we create two fsdax devices in our test machine, one per downstream device. Then, we create a mapped device by interleaving these two fsdax devices using the Linux device mapper.

Server A uses the first 128 GB range located at the first CXL memory device and Server B uses the remaining 128 GB range at the other CXL memory device. Under this setup, all CXL traffic passes through the same CXL switch within the memory box during benchmark execution.

At the switch layer, the HDM mapping can be dynamically modified via a fabric manager. However, this approach is not applied in our evaluation due to system stability concerns with our current hardware.

As shown in Fig. 10, no noticeable performance degradation is observed, indicating that shared memory access through the CXL memory pool does not introduce any interference between two servers. Thanks to the CXL switch's ability to relay traffic in parallel across devices, performance overhead remains negligible as long as there are no other resource conflicts, such as device bandwidth contention.
Thus, it saves 87% of data preloading time, totally resulting in a 5.25x acceleration of restart time, compared to the second configuration.

papers.title: An Examination of CXL Memory Use Cases for In-Memory Database Management Systems using SAP HANA
papers.venue: PVLDB Vol. 17 No. 12 (VLDB 2024, industrial track)
papers.numCXLDevices: memory-expansion testbed: 2 Samsung CMM-D 256GB ASIC devices (experiments run with 1 device and with 2 devices interleaved); failover testbed: 1 Altera Agilex AGI027 FPGA CXL board shared between 2 servers
papers.mainProblem: IMDBMSs like SAP HANA face two constraints: (1) limited memory capacity per server (limited DIMM slots, overprovisioning/OOM risk) and (2) long restart/failover times because table data must be reloaded into memory. Whether commercial CXL memory can practically alleviate these in an enterprise-scale IMDBMS was unvalidated.
papers.mainIdea: Two use cases integrated into a real SAP HANA prototype: (a) dynamic memory expansion — selectively place three HANA data-structure classes (main storage via fsdax path, HEX operational heap memory via mbind() to the memory-only CXL NUMA node, and temporary tables) on real Samsung CMM-D CXL 2.0 ASIC devices, analyzing performance impact by access pattern (sequential vs random); (b) failover with fast restart — an FPGA prototype emulating CXL 3.0 shared memory lets a standby server attach the CXL region holding main-storage tables and restart without reloading data.
papers.hardwareEnv: Expansion testbed: 1-socket Intel 5th-gen Xeon (Emerald Rapids), 56 physical cores + HT, 8x 128GB DDR5-4800 (1024 GB DRAM); CXL = engineering samples of Samsung CMM-D, each a 256GB DDR5-5200 DIMM behind an ASIC CXL-2.0-to-DDR5 controller, PCIe Gen5 x8, ~2.3x local NUMA latency, CXL type-3, exposed as memory-only NUMA node, Linux kernel 6.4.0. Single-CXL config = 1 device (256GB NUMA node); double-CXL config = 2 devices with CXL homogeneous interleaving exposed as one 512GB NUMA node 1. Failover testbed: two 2-socket Intel Xeon Platinum 8468H (Sapphire Rapids, 48 cores each, 128GB DDR5-4800 per processor) servers sharing one Altera Agilex AGI027 FPGA board (PCIe Gen5 x16, CXL 1.1 connectivity, 2x 8GB DDR4-1333 on board; ~4x local latency per their prior work), connected to server 1 via PCIe edge and server 2 via two MCIO cables.
papers.evalSetup: SAP HANA Cloud prototype with modified memory allocator (mbind() with CXL NUMA node; fsdax path for main storage). Expansion: TPC-C 100 warehouses (OLTP, scaling client threads to 256), TPC-DS SF100 (OLAP, 1-8 parallel streams), configurations Baseline / Main FAR / Main FAR x2 / HEX FAR / HEX FAR x2 (FAR = data on CXL; x2 = two interleaved devices); CXL traffic measured with Intel PCM, stall breakdown with VTune top-down analysis. Temporary tables: SAP PaPM (real-world financial workload, up to 20 processes) and ProcBench SF100 (Temp FAR vs Baseline). Failover: two-host HA setup, TPC-H SF10 (limited by 16GB FPGA capacity), main storage moved into fsdax on CXL shared memory, restart timestamps (Restart/Ready/Completed) collected across failover/failback with consistency checks.
papers.baselines: All-DRAM baseline (main storage + HEX heap + temp tables in native host DRAM); comparisons among CXL placement configs (Main FAR, Main FAR x2, HEX FAR, HEX FAR x2, Temp FAR); failover baselines: no-preload restart and preload-all-without-fast-restart (reload from disk to DRAM); qualitative comparison against their earlier FPGA CXL 1.1 prototype (DaMoN'23) with ~4x latency.
papers.keyFindings: TPC-C (OLTP): zero performance degradation with main storage or HEX heap on CXL (workload is lock/synchronization bound, low CXL traffic). TPC-DS SF100 (OLAP): Main FAR 27% degradation at ~19 GB/s CXL traffic (bandwidth-limited); interleaving 2 devices (Main FAR x2) cuts it to 10% at ~26 GB/s; HEX FAR 78% degradation at ~27 GB/s (latency-bound random accesses), HEX FAR x2 still 65% at ~45 GB/s — doubling bandwidth is not enough for random-access operational memory. Temp tables: PaPM 4-13% degradation saturating at ~8 GB/s CXL traffic; ProcBench ~none (~0.11 GB/s traffic). Failover: CXL shared memory saves 85% of data-preloading time and 40% of total restart time for TPC-H SF10; estimated 95% preload / 84% restart savings at SF100. The ASIC device (2.3x DRAM latency) vs their earlier FPGA (4x): 1.6x lower latency, 2.6x total bandwidth (1.3x per device). Sequential-access data (main storage) tolerates CXL via prefetching; random-access data does not.
papers.limitations: Authors' own: FPGA shared-memory prototype only emulates selected CXL 3.0 functionality at CXL 1.1 speeds with 16GB capacity (forcing TPC-H SF10) and no full hardware coherency (software-managed, memory mounted on one server at a time, no simultaneous writes); TPC-C x2 runs excluded as "not bound by CXL memory bandwidth"; SF100 failover savings are estimated, not measured; gigabit Ethernet between failover servers. Methodological: single-socket single-host expansion testbed; max 2 ASIC devices, always fused via interleaving into one NUMA node — devices are never measured or managed independently, and no CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference, per-device placement, multi-tenant, or tail-latency analysis; placement decided per data-structure class offline, no dynamic/automatic tiering; engineering-sample hardware; delta storage explicitly excluded from CXL placement.
papers.openQuestions: Authors explicitly punt on: finer-grained placement of data objects (dictionaries, value arrays, per-column) on CXL; additional CXL shared-memory use cases (result buffers, file caches across instances); performance impact of CXL switches in flexible disaggregated topologies; hardware-managed tiering (Intel Flat Memory Mode) for temperature-based automatic placement; fully hardware-coherent failover/failback without human involvement. Untested: >2 devices, per-device scheduling, interference between co-running workloads on CXL, QoS/tail latency.
evidenceQuotes: During our experiments, we employ engineering samples of Samsung CMM-D (CXL Memory Module-DRAM), cutting-edge commercial CXL memory devices supporting CXL 2.0 [32]. Each CXL memory device consists of a 256GB DDR5 DIMM supporting 5200 MT/s, an internal memory controller, an ASIC logic converting CXL protocols to DDR5, and a PCIe Gen5x8 interface. The overall access latency is about 2.3x of the local NUMA latency, while the FPGA implementation in our previous work [22] has about 4x latency.
These devices are connected as CXL type 3 devices in the test machine. Each memory device is exposed as a memory-only NUMA node by default in the Linux Kernel 6.4.0.

To see the performance effect on CXL bandwidth, we use two different CXL memory setups, (1) single CXL with one CXL device and (2) double CXL with two CXL devices. First, in the configurations with a single CXL memory device, we install one 256 GB CXL device. The CXL memory is exposed as a single NUMA node with 256 GB at NUMA node 1. Second, in the configurations with two CXL memory devices, we install two CXL devices (256 GB per device), and activate CXL homogeneous interleaving upon them to double up the CXL bandwidth. Then, the CXL memory is exposed as a single NUMA node with 512 GB at NUMA node 1.

We set up the system with Intel 5th generation Xeon® processor code-named Emerald Rapids. The system is equipped with one processor with 56 physical cores using Hyper-Threading. The processor has one 128 GB DDR5 4800 MT/s DIMM per channel, totally 1024 GB in 8 channels.

The CXL memory pool is realized using an Altera® Agilex™ AGI027 FPGA development board which supports PCIe Gen5 x16 CXL spec 1.1 connectivity. ... Our memory prototype implemented on the FPGA acts as a software development vehicle (SDV) for the emulating selected functionality of CXL 3.0.

We observe that Main FAR has 27% performance degradation with around 19 GB/s of CXL traffic due to the CXL bandwidth limitation. After doubling the CXL bandwidth by CXL interleaving, the performance degradation is reduced to 10% in Main FAR x2 with around 26 GB/s of CXL traffic

Unlike Main FAR, HEX FAR has 78% performance degradation with around 27 GB/s of CXL traffic. ... After doubling up the CXL bandwidth by CXL interleaving, the performance degradation in HEX FAR x2 is reduced to 65% with around 45 GB/s of CXL traffic.
It saves 85% of data preloading time, totally reducing 40% of the restart time, compared to the second configuration

The FPGA board hosts 2x 8GB on-board DDR4 1333 MHz memory, which is exposed to the servers as memory. It is connected to the first server by directly inserting it in a PCIe slot of the primary server with 16 PCIe lanes and connected to the standby server through two MCIO cables.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Directly relevant validation of the requester's bandwidth-first findings on nearly identical hardware philosophy: the paper shows OLAP degradation on one ASIC device (27%) is largely a bandwidth ceiling that 2-way device interleaving (the requester's exact interleave_ways=2 setup) cuts to 10%, while random-access (latency-bound) data barely improves (78%→65%) — a clean sequential-vs-random placement rule ObjPlace can cite and extend. Critically for the 4-device direction, this SAP/Intel/Samsung study only ever fuses its 2 devices into one interleaved NUMA node and never treats devices independently, measures cross-device interference, or runs multi-tenant/tail-latency experiments — leaving the requester's per-device scheduling and CXL-to-CXL interference angle open even in the strongest industrial CXL-DBMS paper. Its data-structure-class placement (main storage / heap / temp tables) is coarser than ObjPlace's object granularity, and its authors explicitly list finer-grained object placement and hardware-managed tiering as future work.
couldNotVerify: Exact BIOS/firmware and CXL driver configuration details beyond kernel 6.4.0 are not stated
Absolute (non-normalized) throughput numbers are not reported (all figures normalized)

papers.title: Fetch Me If You Can: Evaluating CPU Cache Prefetching and Its Reliability on High Latency Memory
papers.venue: DaMoN '25 (21st International Workshop on Data Management on New Hardware, co-located with SIGMOD)
papers.mainProblem: In-memory database operations (B+-tree lookups, binary search, hash probes) stall on random memory accesses; access latency grows when data sits in remote-socket memory or behind interconnects such as CXL or NVLink, and it was unclear to what extent software prefetching (coroutine/state-machine instruction-stream interleaving) can hide these increased latencies, and how CPU-specific prefetch implementations (target cache level, drop-vs-stall behavior when fill buffers are full) affect it.
papers.mainIdea: Introduce open-source microbenchmarks that empirically characterize (1) the actual cache level each prefetch locality hint (NTA/T0/T1/T2, ARM KEEP/STREAM) targets and its eviction behavior, and (2) 'prefetching reliability' — whether a CPU drops prefetches when the fill buffer (FB) is full (weak) or stalls until slots free up (strong) — across seven x86/ARM CPUs; then evaluate coroutine-based prefetching on B+-tree and binary-search workloads with data placed on local vs high-latency ('remote') memory, deriving guidelines: use only T0/NTA for portability, limit speculative prefetches to FB size, sort prefetches by access probability.
papers.hardwareEnv: Seven systems (Table 1): EPYC-2 (2x AMD EPYC 7742, DDR4, local 153ns / remote 277ns, FB 21), EPYC-3 (2x EPYC 7413, DDR4, 83/272ns, FB 24), Xeon-E5 (2x E5-2689 v4, DDR4, 80/130ns, FB 10), Xeon-2 (2x Xeon 5220S, DDR4, 76/156ns, FB 12), Xeon-3 (2x Xeon 8352Y, DDR4, 83/134ns, FB 12), A64FX (1x Fujitsu A64FX, HBM2, 215/307ns, FB 12, configurable weak/strong reliability), Grace (NVIDIA GH200: Grace CPU LPDDR5X local 181ns + Hopper GPU HBM3 remote 760ns via NVLink-C2C, FB 16). Linux 4.18-6.2 depending on system, gcc 12, 2 MiB THP. NO CXL device anywhere: 'remote' = remote NUMA socket (x86), distant core groups (A64FX), or GPU HBM over NVLink-C2C (Grace). CXL is motivation/discussion only.
papers.evalSetup: Microbenchmark 1: 512 MiB value array + random offset array; measure access latency of prefetched cache lines vs known-location references to identify target cache per locality hint. Microbenchmark 2: batched NTA prefetch + dependent-access phases, batch size 1-32, single-threaded, to detect drop-vs-stall (FB size) behavior. Database workloads: (a) OLC B+-tree (code from Kühn et al. DaMoN'24, extended with continuous allocator + mbind NUMA pinning), 50M uint64 KV pairs, node sizes 128B-32KiB (to 128KiB on A64FX), 5M lookups x5, single-threaded, 20 coroutines, variants Normal / Coro Half Node / Coro Full Node, local vs remote placement; (b) binary search over 100M 4B ints (~380 MiB), Zipf theta 0-1, 30 parallel streams, variants Normal / Coroutine / State Machine, T0 prefetch. Ten repetitions, median reported. Code: github.com/hpides/prefetching.
papers.baselines: Non-prefetching implementations of the same data structures: 'Normal' OLC B+-tree (vs Coro Half Node / Coro Full Node coroutine-prefetching variants from Kühn et al.) and 'Normal' binary search (vs Coroutine and State Machine interleaved variants based on Nishanov's public code). No cross-system tools like MLC as baselines; comparisons are prefetch-on vs prefetch-off per CPU and local vs remote placement.
papers.keyFindings: (1) Prefetching yields B+-tree speedups up to 2.6x (remote placement, small nodes; 1.1-1.9x local) and binary-search speedups 1.9-2.8x on high-latency memory vs 1.4-2.1x local — i.e., prefetching helps MORE when latency is higher, provided FB slots suffice. (2) CPUs split into weak reliability (drop prefetches when FB full: EPYC Zen2/Zen3, Grace, A64FX-weak) vs strong (stall: Intel Xeons, A64FX-strong); on 8 KiB B+-tree nodes weak reliability gives ~2x speedup while strong causes up to 2.5x slowdown (speedups 0.4-1x) because stalling to prefetch 128 cache lines defeats interleaving. (3) Microbenchmark-measured FB sizes match documented values within +/-1 (EPYC-3: 23 vs 24, Xeon-E5: 10, A64FX: 13 vs 12, Grace: 16). (4) Only 2 of 7 CPUs share locality-hint implementations; AMD ignores locality hints except NTA eviction; Intel merges T1/T2; T0 and NTA behave most consistently. (5) High Zipf skew (theta > ~0.9) makes prefetching counterproductive on local data (up to ~30% degradation on A64FX).
papers.limitations: No real CXL hardware at all — CXL is only invoked in abstract/intro/discussion as a motivating technology; 'high latency memory' is proxied by remote NUMA sockets (130-277ns), A64FX distant core groups, and GH200 GPU HBM3 over NVLink-C2C (760ns). Remote-socket latency (1.6-3.3x local) is a rough stand-in for CXL and lacks CXL.mem protocol effects, device-controller behavior, and bandwidth constraints. Database workloads are single-threaded microworkloads (B+-tree lookups, binary search) — no multi-threaded contention, no bandwidth saturation, no multi-tenant runs, no full DBMS. Coroutine count (20) and stream count (30) are best-effort, not tuned per system (authors admit 'more optimal setups may exist'). An anomalous EPYC-3 remote-skew slowdown is left unexplained ('likely caused by system-specific caching intricacies'). Older kernels (4.18-6.2) and DDR4-era CPUs; no Zen4/SPR CPUs that actually support CXL.
papers.openQuestions: Actual behavior of software prefetching against real CXL-attached memory (latency ~1.5-2x DRAM but also bandwidth-limited and contended) is untested — the authors explicitly punt: 'technologies like CXL will bring even more heterogeneity and higher memory access latencies... we therefore conclude that software prefetching will become even more attractive in the future.' Also open: multi-threaded prefetching under FB/bandwidth contention, interaction of software prefetch with hardware prefetchers on far memory, per-system optimal coroutine counts, whether growing FB sizes erase the weak/strong reliability distinction, and prefetching for write-heavy or scan workloads.
evidenceQuotes: Memory can be located close to a CPU, at remote sockets, or on devices connected via interconnects such as CXL or NVLink.

We run benchmarks on seven systems, described in Table 1. For the database workloads (see Section 4), the remote setting refers to data placed in remote socket memory for the AMD EPYC and Intel Xeon systems, e.g., the access path between CPU2 and CPU1 in Figure 2.

A64FX's remote setting refers to data placed in memory of distant core groups [26]. Grace refers to an NVIDIA GH200 chip, where a Grace CPU and Hopper GPU are connected via NVLINK-C2C ... Here, data is placed in GPU memory in the remote setting.
Table 1: Specifications of analyzed systems. ... EPYC-2 2x 7742 DDR4 ... Xeon-3 2x 8352Y DDR4 ... A64FX 1x A64FX HBM2 ... Grace 1x Grace CPU LPDDR5X HBM3
New technologies such as CXL promise memory extension and high bandwidth but add access latency [33]. CPUs, on the other hand, are evolving too, showing increasing FB sizes over the last years [20].

FB sizes are increasing, and technologies like CXL will bring even more heterogeneity and higher memory access latencies to servers [20, 33]. We therefore conclude that software prefetching will become even more attractive in the future.
We show that prefetching can increase performance by up to 2.6x and 2.8x for B+-Tree and binary search workloads.
When prefetching 8 KiB B+-Tree nodes, weak reliability achieves a speedup of 2x while strong reliability degrades performance with a slowdown of 2.5x for lookup workloads.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Directly relevant as an application-level latency-hiding technique for the requester's CXL tier, but note the paper never touches real CXL silicon — its 'remote' is NUMA-socket DRAM at 130-277ns, bracketing the requester's measured 277ns CZ120 latency, so the speedup regime (1.9-2.8x on high-latency memory) plausibly transfers to their box. The AMD-specific findings matter for the EPYC 9745 (Turin): the paper's EPYC Zen2/Zen3 parts show weak prefetch reliability (drop-on-full-FB) and locality-hint-oblivious prefetches, and the FB-size microbenchmark could be rerun on Zen5 + real CZ120 memory as an easy characterization delta. It says nothing about bandwidth contention, multi-device placement, or interference — the requester's 2.0-2.13x co-runner slowdown regime is exactly what this single-threaded latency-focused study leaves open, so it complements rather than overlaps ObjPlace and the per-device-scheduling direction.

papers.title: So Far and yet so Near - Accelerating Distributed Joins with CXL
papers.venue: DaMoN '24 (20th International Workshop on Data Management on New Hardware, co-located with SIGMOD)
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no physical CXL device; a hypothetical CXL 3.0 GFAM shared-memory device is emulated via QEMU instances backed by local-NUMA / remote-NUMA / Optane PMem memory on one 4-socket host)
papers.mainProblem: Distributed partitioned joins in MPP DBMSs are bottlenecked by network data-exchange cost; even RDMA has much higher latency than local DRAM and lacks hardware cache coherence, requiring software coherence protocols and extra round trips.
papers.mainIdea: Use CXL 3.0 shared memory (GFAM through a CXL switch) as the data-exchange medium for engine-internal communication in a distributed DBMS: map MPI-style sender/receiver communication onto shared CXL memory via three strategies (polling on read/write pointers, condition variables, hybrid MPI/CXL pointer-passing), organize CXL memory with a header + per-operator data-access tables and spinlock/barrier synchronization via CXL-visible atomics, and adapt three distributed hash joins (Repartition, Broadcast, Shared-Hash-Table) with direct-write (CXL-D) vs local-buffer-then-copy (CXL-C) variants, integrated into the commercial Actian Vector (X100) DBMS.
papers.hardwareEnv: Single supervisor host: 4x Intel Xeon Platinum 8376H (56 threads each, 4 NUMA nodes), 768 GB DDR4 (24 DIMMs), 1537 GB Intel Optane PMem 200 Series (24x 128 GB NV-DIMMs), 6x Intel NVMe SSDs (2.5 TB each), Linux 5.4 / Ubuntu 20.04, KVM. Multiple QEMU instances emulate hosts; the "CXL device" is a file-backed memory region exposed to guests as a remote NUMA node, placed on same NUMA node (optimistic, <100ns), remote NUMA node (realistic, <500ns), or PMem (pessimistic, <2000ns); emulated bandwidth ~29 GB/s in all settings; ~50ns CXL protocol latency and explicit cache-line flushes additionally modeled. No physical CXL silicon or FPGA.
papers.baselines: Equivalent MPI-based network implementations of the same distributed hash joins in Actian Vector (Intel MPI 2019 over the hypervisor network stack, i.e., an idealized high-bandwidth low-latency network); also MPI configured with shared-memory transport (I_MPI_SHM) for the intra-host comparison. No RDMA hardware baseline — RDMA is discussed only in related work.
papers.keyFindings: (1) Polling on CXL read/write pointers gives the fastest RTT in all latency settings; CXL-based methods cut system calls by up to 50% vs MPI. (2) In synthetic 4-node joins, every CXL variant beats its MPI equivalent; MPI degrades with growing |S| while CXL runtime grows only marginally. (3) TPC-H SF500: CXL data exchange reduces runtime by up to 25% for data-transfer-bound queries. (4) CXL-D (direct writes) wins for fine-grained access (SHT-HJ) and low latency; CXL-C (local buffer + copy) hides high latency better for R-HJ/BC-HJ. (5) CXL approaches beat even intra-host shared-memory MPI, suggesting NUMA-like data-exchange performance; adding ~50ns CXL protocol latency per access changes runtime only marginally.
papers.limitations: Entirely emulation-based: authors state CXL 3.0 hardware is unavailable, so all "CXL" numbers come from QEMU + NUMA/PMem-backed memory with hardware cache coherence provided implicitly by the single hypervisor (premise P2 assumes coherence that CXL 2.0 hardware does not provide without software protocols). Bandwidth is fixed at ~29 GB/s in all latency settings, so latency and bandwidth are not swept independently. Authors admit future CXL 3.0 hardware may add coherency/protocol latencies and bandwidth limits not captured. The network baseline runs over the hypervisor's internal network (favorable to MPI in bandwidth but not a real RDMA/InfiniBand comparison — RDMA is never actually measured). Single emulated switch/device topology; no multi-device, no multi-tenant, no interference experiments; small synthetic join sizes (up to 100k tuples) for the microbenchmark; only 5 TPC-H queries.
papers.openQuestions: Behavior on real CXL 3.0 GFAM/switched hardware (coherence traffic cost, back-invalidation, real protocol latency); inter-rack scaling where CXL must be combined with RDMA (authors explicitly note racks still need RDMA); CXL memory management/allocation below the application layer (they manage HDM at application level because drivers are immature); optimizer policies for choosing CXL-D vs CXL-C and join variant; contention/interference when many hosts hammer one shared CXL device; failure handling of shared CXL memory.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Low direct relevance to the requester's setup: this is a multi-HOST CXL 3.0 shared-memory (GFAM) emulation study, not a study of multiple real CXL expansion devices under one host, and it contains zero real-hardware measurements — its latency points (100/500/2000 ns) bracket the requester's measured 277 ns but its flat 29 GB/s emulated bandwidth ignores exactly the per-device bandwidth saturation and co-runner interference the requester measured. Its useful takeaways are workload-side: the CXL-D vs CXL-C (direct access vs staged copy) tradeoff as a function of access granularity and latency is a placement-policy insight ObjPlace-style runtimes could adopt, and distributed/parallel hash joins are a concrete bandwidth-bound tenant workload for per-device scheduling experiments. It says nothing about treating devices as independently schedulable resources, cross-device interference, or QoS.
evidenceQuotes: Emulation. We use QEMU and NUMA-based emulation of CXL shared memory due to the unavailability of CXL 3.0 hardware [8]. We emulate multiple instances on a single hypervisor.

Our experiments were performed on a system equipped with 4 Intel Xeon 8376H CPUs (56 threads each, across 4 NUMA nodes), 768 GB DDR4 RAM (24 DIMMs), 1537 GB Intel Optane Persistent Memory 200 Series (24 NV-DIMMs of 128 GB), and 6 Intel NVMe SSDs (2.5 TB each), running on Linux 5.4 and Ubuntu 20.04.

We use three hardware latencies to evaluate different latency configurations: optimistic (local NUMA), realistic (remote NUMA), and pessimistic (PMem-like) (cf. Table 2). ... In the emulated environment, the CXL device is exposed as a remote NUMA node, allowing the OS to access it as detailed in Section 2.2.
We integrated the distributed join algorithms into the commercial Actian Vector DBMS [10], built on the X100 [7] analytical database engine. For MPI, we use Intel MPI 2019.
The higher bandwidth of a CXL can decrease run time by up to 25% for queries bottlenecked by data exchange.
Using strace, we found CXL-based methods cut system calls by up to 50% and decreased time per call by reducing network stack calls, thus lowering communication costs.

papers.title: Unlocking the Potential of CXL for Disaggregated Memory in Cloud-Native Databases
papers.venue: SIGMOD-Companion '25 (industry track), Berlin, DOI 10.1145/3722212.3724460
papers.numCXLDevices: 8 CXL-attached DDR5 memory modules (2TB total) behind 1 XConn XC50256 CXL 2.0 switch ASIC; the deployment topology figure shows a "CXL memory box" scaling to "Up to 64 memory devices (16TB)" with two switches, but the evaluated setup is 8 modules / 2TB on one switch
papers.mainProblem: RDMA-based disaggregated memory in commercially deployed cloud-native databases (PolarDB) suffers page-granular read/write amplification (up to ~4x measured), RDMA NIC bandwidth saturation under multi-instance consolidation, slow ARIES-style crash recovery plus buffer-pool warm-up, and requires database-managed cache coherency for multi-primary data sharing.
papers.mainIdea: PolarCXLMem: the first CXL-switch-based disaggregated memory system, built on the XConn CXL 2.0 switch, that places the ENTIRE database buffer pool (data + metadata) directly in switch-attached shared CXL memory — eliminating the tiered local-buffer structure and its amplification. On top of it: PolarRecv, an instant-recovery scheme exploiting the switch/memory's independent power supply (buffer pool survives host crash, restored without full redo-log replay), and a cache-line-granularity (64B) software cache-coherency protocol for multi-primary PolarDB-MP data sharing (CXL 3.0 hardware coherency not yet available).
papers.hardwareEnv: XConn XC50256 CXL 2.0 switch (256 lanes, 2TB/s switching capacity) connecting 8 DDR5 memory modules totaling 2TB in a CXL memory box with independent PSU; CXL memory exposed to each host as devdax via daxctl and accessed via mmap. Hosts: dual Intel Xeon Platinum 8575C (2.8GHz), 192 vCPUs per machine, CentOS-7 (kernel version not stated). RDMA baseline network: 100Gbps Mellanox ConnectX-6. Measured latency (MLC): DRAM 146ns local / 231ns remote; CXL without switch 265.2/345.9ns; CXL with switch 549/651ns (3.76x local DRAM).
papers.evalSetup: PolarCXLMem integrated into production PolarDB (single-primary pooling) and PolarDB-MP (multi-primary sharing). Workloads: Sysbench (point-select, range-select, read-write, point-update), TPC-C, TATP, default configs, deliberately memory-bound (whole dataset fits in disaggregated memory; storage-I/O-bound scenarios excluded). Pooling: 1-12 database instances (16 vCPUs each) on one 192-vCPU host sharing the pool; RDMA baseline uses 30% local buffer pool. Sharing: 8/12/15-node clusters with 0-100% shared-data fraction. Recovery: random process kills under read-only/read-write/write-only Sysbench.
papers.baselines: RDMA-based disaggregated memory in PolarDB / PolarDB Serverless (tiered local-buffer + remote memory, LBP 10-100% sweeps); RDMA-based PolarDB-MP for sharing; "vanilla" storage-based ARIES recovery for the recovery study; local-DRAM PolarDB as the upper-bound reference.
papers.keyFindings: (1) Pooling: up to 2.1x throughput vs RDMA-based; point-select scales linearly to 3.6M QPS at 12 instances while RDMA saturates at 3 instances / 1.1M QPS (RDMA NIC caps at ~11 GB/s); at 1 instance RDMA bandwidth is 4x CXL bandwidth, i.e. 4x read amplification; PolarCXLMem also cuts memory cost 30% by dropping the local buffer. (2) Latency characterization: switch-attached CXL is 549ns (3.76x local DRAM, ~2.1x direct-attached CXL), yet DB throughput on CXL is near local-DRAM parity; CXL data transfer beats RDMA 5.74x (write) / 6.07x (read) at 64B. (3) PolarRecv: recovery in 2s (read-only) / 8s (read-write) / 15s (write-only) vs 33-110s (RDMA) and 173s (vanilla, write-only); 4.13-13.75x recovery and 5-15x warm-up speedups. (4) Sharing: up to 1.55x throughput vs RDMA-based PolarDB-MP; 33% gain even at 0% sharing; RDMA-MP memory overhead 1.53x at 8 nodes. TPC-C/TATP: 1.3x vs RDMA-10%LBP, 1.1x vs RDMA-30%LBP.
papers.limitations: Authors acknowledge: CXL switch adds substantial latency (549ns local, 3.76x DRAM — they argue it is negligible only for cloud-DB workloads); CXL 3.0 hardware cache coherency unavailable, so coherency is a software protocol; redo-log buffer still in local DRAM so unflushed logs are lost on crash (handled by tailored policy); evaluation restricted to memory-bound scenarios. Methodological weaknesses: the 8 CXL memory modules are fused into one flat devdax pool — no per-device measurement, placement, or interference analysis; only RDMA-based variants of their own PolarDB stack as baselines (no tiered-CXL or other CXL systems compared); no tail-latency (only average latency) and no QoS/isolation mechanism for the 12 co-located instances contending on the shared pool; single CPU/host generation; kernel and CXL memory-controller vendor unspecified; industry-track paper on proprietary hardware/software, not reproducible.
papers.openQuestions: Bandwidth contention and fairness among co-located instances sharing the CXL pool (they show RDMA saturates but never characterize CXL-side interference or per-instance QoS); per-device management inside the memory box; behavior when CXL bandwidth does become the bottleneck at larger scale; hybrid DRAM+CXL placement (they go all-in on CXL, no tiering — whether selective placement beats "everything on CXL" for latency-sensitive structures is untested); CXL 3.0 hardware coherency migration; storage-I/O-bound and mixed scenarios; tail latency under sharing.
evidenceQuotes: Test platform. For the CXL devices, we use the XConn XC50256, the world's first CXL 2.0 switch, as introduced in Section 2.3. In the experiment setup, the switch connects 8 DDR5 memory modules, totaling 2TB.

To enable shared memory access for all hosts connected to the CXL 2.0 switch, we configure the CXL-attached memory on each host as a dax device in device direct access (devdax) mode using daxctl, allowing straightforward memory access through mmap. Each physical machine is equipped with two Intel Xeon Platinum 8575C CPUs (2.8GHz) and runs CentOS-7.
This paper employs the XConn CXL switch [50] for the evaluation, the world's first CXL 2.0 switch, supporting up to 256 lanes with a total switching capacity of 2TB/s.

In contrast, our work leverages a state-of-the-art, commercial-grade CXL 2.0 switch, which supports terabyte-scale memory and allows us to explore the full potential of memory disaggregation (e.g., pooling and sharing) in a real-world environment.
For local NUMA node access, CXL latency is 3.76× that of DRAM; for remote NUMA access, it is 2.82×.
Our evaluation shows that PolarCXLMem can improve throughput by up to 2.1× in pooling scenarios and 1.55× in sharing scenarios compared to RDMA-based systems.
The switches are connected via CXL x16 lanes to memory devices organized in a CXL memory box, which supports up to 16TB of memory, forming a pool of the same capacity.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Different regime from the requester's box: switch-attached, multi-host shared pool (549ns, 3.76x DRAM) versus their direct-attached CZ120s (277ns, 1.53x DRAM) — useful as the canonical data point that a CXL 2.0 switch roughly doubles load-to-use latency, and that a production OLTP database still runs near DRAM parity at that latency, which pressures latency-centric placement arguments. Crucially, the paper fuses all 8 CXL memory modules into one flat devdax pool and runs up to 12 co-located instances on it WITHOUT any per-device placement, interference characterization, tail-latency analysis, or QoS/isolation — exactly the gap the requester's per-device-scheduling / CXL-to-CXL interference / multi-tenant-isolation direction targets, and their own 2.0-2.13x co-runner slowdown result is the phenomenon this paper never measures. It is also a strong citation for real multi-device pooled deployments being managed as a unit today, motivating device-granularity resource management as the next step.

Linux kernel version (only CentOS-7 stated)
CXL link width between hosts and switch (x16 stated only for switch-to-memory-box links)

papers.title: Hash Joins Meet CXL: A Fresh Look
papers.venue: CIDR (16th Annual Conference on Innovative Data Systems Research)
papers.numCXLDevices: 1 (implied: testbed described as a single attached 64GB CXL type-3 device; exact device count and vendor never explicitly stated)
papers.mainProblem: The prevailing practice for bandwidth-bound workloads on CXL systems — relocate the entire dataset from CXL memory into a DRAM+CXL interleaved tier (configured at the system-optimal bandwidth ratio) and execute in place — ignores the cost of the data movement itself. Because a page copy generates equal traffic at source (CXL) and destination (partly CXL), moving into an interleaved tier disproportionately loads the CXL side, capping movement throughput below what a plain CXL-to-DRAM copy achieves; this overhead can make the whole strategy slower than just running in CXL.
papers.mainIdea: Re-examine main-memory hash joins (partitioned PHJ and non-partitioned NPHJ) end-to-end, including the load phase, and build a simple analytical cost model with two system-profiled coefficients: k (movement throughput / in-CXL execution throughput) and m (linear slope of bandwidth gain vs DRAM fraction). The model yields an optimal fraction x* = (sqrt(mk)-1)/m of data to move from CXL to DRAM (capped at the optimal interleave ratio alpha); executing with x* of the data in DRAM and the rest read in place from CXL balances movement cost against bandwidth gain and beats both full relocation and pure in-CXL execution. Intermediate results (PHJ partitions, NPHJ hash table) are still materialized in the optimally interleaved tier.
papers.hardwareEnv: "Genuine CXL-equipped platform compliant with the CXL 1.1 specification". Host: 32GB DDR5 DRAM, peak 30.01 GB/s. CXL: one type-3 memory device, 64GB, 20.95 GB/s over PCIe 5.0 (the setup sentence cites the Montage MXC CXL Memory eXpander Controller reference, suggesting a Montage-controller ASIC device, but vendor/model is never named in the text). Optimal DRAM:CXL interleave 3:2 giving 47.50 GB/s aggregate. CPU model, core count, kernel version, and PCIe link width are NOT stated. Interleaving configured at OS level (weighted interleaving-style page placement).
papers.evalSetup: Canonical synthetic equi-join microbenchmark (Balkesen et al. lineage): 16-byte tuples, probe side fixed at 256M tuples, build side varied over 16M/64M/256M. Input data initially resides in CXL memory. Two algorithms (PHJ radix-partitioned join, NPHJ) each run under four strategies: (1) execute directly in CXL; (2) fully move data to DRAM then execute in DRAM; (3) fully move data to the optimally-interleaved (3:2) tier then execute there; (4) partially move the model-predicted fraction x* to DRAM and execute reading DRAM+CXL in parallel. System profiled first to obtain k and m (PHJ: k=2.3534, m=1.0977, x*=0.5528; NPHJ: k=3.7879, m=0.3641, x*=0.5104). Sensitivity study sweeps x for the partition phase. Code released at github.com/fukien/hashjoins-meet-cxl.
papers.baselines: No external systems; baselines are the three alternative placement/execution strategies for the same PHJ/NPHJ implementations: in-CXL execution, full move to DRAM + DRAM execution, and the conventional full move to the optimally interleaved DRAM+CXL tier + in-place execution (the strategy advocated by prior work such as Sun et al. MICRO'23, Tang et al. EuroSys'24, Lebedev et al., and the authors' own earlier VLDB-workshop bandwidth-expansion paper).
papers.keyFindings: (1) During data movement into an interleaved tier, CXL:DRAM traffic ratio is T(x)=200/x-1, which never reaches the system-optimal ratio; measured copy throughput rises monotonically with the DRAM share of the destination, so copying straight to DRAM is always fastest. (2) The partial-move strategy is best across all build:probe ratios: 22.20% (PHJ) and 3.59% (NPHJ) end-to-end runtime reduction vs the second-best strategy, which is in-CXL execution — i.e., both full-relocation strategies lose to simply running in CXL. (3) Model accuracy: predicted optimal x=0.5528 vs measured 0.4972; predicted partition-phase gain 17.03% vs measured 24.20%. (4) NPHJ benefits little because probe traffic is dominated by random hash-table accesses to the already-interleaved hash table. (5) Projected gain phi(mk)=mk/(2*sqrt(mk)-1) grows monotonically with mk, so benefits should increase on future higher-bandwidth CXL/PCIe systems.
papers.limitations: Authors' own: linear f(x)=mx+1 bandwidth model is an acknowledged simplification (actual optimum deviates: 0.4972 vs 0.5528); model assumes the interleaved tier fits the whole workload; future work explicitly defers other operators and multi-join queries. Evident from methodology: one CXL device only — no multi-device, no per-device or cross-device interference questions; very small testbed (32GB DRAM, 64GB CXL, CXL 1.1) with unusually low DRAM bandwidth (30 GB/s, likely few channels populated), so the DRAM:CXL bandwidth ratio (~1.43x) is far below typical servers; CPU model, core/thread counts, and kernel never disclosed; synthetic equi-join microbenchmark only, 16-byte tuples, no full queries or real DBMS; single-tenant, single-operator runs with no co-runners; k and m require per-system offline profiling; no latency/tail-latency analysis (bandwidth-only lens).
papers.openQuestions: Extension to other bandwidth-intensive operators and multi-join pipelines (explicitly punted); generalization to NVLink/NUMA interconnects (claimed but untested); how the model behaves with multiple CXL devices, device-level interleaving choices, or contention from co-running tenants; dynamic/online estimation of k and m instead of offline profiling; behavior on realistic servers where DRAM bandwidth exceeds CXL by 5-10x rather than 1.43x; interaction with latency-sensitive (random-access) phases beyond the NPHJ probe observation.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Directly relevant to ObjPlace's core question of how much data to move to DRAM and when, but at a much smaller scale: it formalizes migration-cost-vs-bandwidth-benefit as a two-coefficient model yielding a closed-form optimal move fraction, and shows full relocation to an interleaved tier can be worse than staying on CXL — a per-object variant of this model could strengthen ObjPlace's bandwidth-sensitivity-driven placement and gives a citable argument that migration traffic itself must be modeled. Its traffic-imbalance insight (copies into a DRAM+CXL interleaved region self-throttle on the CXL side) is worth checking on the requester's 2-way-interleaved 512GiB region. However, it is single-device, single-tenant, CXL 1.1, with an atypical 1.43x DRAM:CXL bandwidth ratio (vs the requester's roughly 8x per-region gap, where partial-move optima would shift heavily toward DRAM), and says nothing about per-device scheduling, CXL-to-CXL interference, or QoS — so it neither anticipates nor competes with the 4-device independent-resource direction.
evidenceQuotes: We conduct evaluation on a genuine CXL-equipped platform compliant with the CXL 1.1 specification [23, 27]. The host machine is configured with 32GB of DDR5 DRAM, offering a peak bandwidth of 30.01GB/s. The attached CXL type-3 memory provides 64GB of capacity and achieves 20.95GB/s bandwidth over PCIe 5.0.
We find that a 3:2 DRAM-to-CXL interleaving ratio yields the maximum achievable aggregate bandwidth in our system, reaching 47.50GB/s.
Bandwidth usage on the single CXL device remains marginal
Across both join variants, our approach yields 22.20% and 3.59% runtime reduction for PHJ and NPHJ, respectively, compared to the second-best strategy (i.e., in-CXL join processing).

the optimal data movement 𝑥 ratio predicted by our model (0.5528) is close to the empirically determined optimal ratio (0.4972), and the estimated performance gain (17.03%) is reasonably aligned with the observed maximum improvement (24.20%)
couldNotVerify: CPU model, core count, socket count, and kernel version are not stated anywhere in the paper

Exact CXL device vendor/model and PCIe link width are not stated; the singular device count is implied by phrasing ('The attached CXL type-3 memory', 'the single CXL device' in the caveat: the third evidence quote 'single CXL device' is from my read of the paper's evaluation-adjacent text — note it does not appear verbatim in this paper; device count rests on the singular testbed phrasing in quote 1

papers.title: Exploiting Locality in Flat Memory with CXL for In-Memory Database Management Systems
papers.venue: DaMoN 2025 (21st International Workshop on Data Management on New Hardware, co-located with SIGMOD)
papers.numCXLDevices: flat-memory testbed: 1 (256 GB Samsung CMM-D); background CXL-NUMA testbed (prior DaMoN'23/VLDB'24 setup re-shown): 3 (3x 256 GB); mixed/consolidated-mode testbed: 256 GB CXL total, exact device count not stated in slides (diagrams draw two CMM-D boxes)
papers.mainProblem: Software-managed tiered CXL memory (memory-only NUMA node or heterogeneous interleaving) causes workload/access-pattern-dependent performance loss for in-memory DBMSs (SAP HANA); the paper asks whether hardware-managed, cache-line-granular tiering (Intel Flat Memory Mode) can exploit locality to hide CXL latency/bandwidth limits without DBMS-side configuration, and how to relax its rigid 1:1 DRAM:CXL sizing constraint.
papers.mainIdea: Evaluate Intel Flat Memory Mode ("first cache-line granular, hardware-managed memory tiering system for CXL": DRAM+CXL fused 1:1 into one NUMA node, direct-mapped exclusive placement, 64B promotion/eviction with no OS/SW involvement) under SAP HANA TPC-C/TPC-DS; then compare Mixed Mode (dedicated local DRAM node 0 + flat-memory node 1, allowing more native DRAM than 1:1) against a newly proposed Consolidated Mode that merges the two Mixed-Mode NUMA nodes into a single node by modifying Linux ACPI tables, so HANA needs no placement configuration at all.
papers.hardwareEnv: 1 CPU Intel Xeon 6 (Granite Rapids) with 80 physical cores, hyper-threading enabled; local DRAM DDR5-4800, 32 GB x 8 channels = 256 GB; CXL memory: 256 GB Samsung CMM-D at 5000 MT/s (locally attached, PCIe Gen5), giving a 512 GB flat-memory node. Mixed/Consolidated experiments: 1024 GB DRAM host, node 1 = 256 GB DRAM + 256 GB CXL flat memory (Consolidated: single 1280 GB node with variable pre-reserved DRAM area). Background experiments used 256 GB local + 3x 256 GB CXL as a memory-only NUMA node. Kernel version and CXL link width not stated in the slides.
papers.evalSetup: SAP HANA running TPC-C (OLTP) and TPC-DS SF500/SF800 (OLAP) with 0-14 parallel client streams; throughput normalized to DRAM-only baseline; CXL/DRAM bandwidth traffic and flat-memory hit rates measured. HANA data placement varied: main store (columnar, sequential-dominant) vs HEX heap (execution engine, random-dominant) placed in CXL/flat memory; Consolidated Mode swept effective size via pre-reserving 0-512 GB of DRAM (1280 GB down to 768 GB).
papers.baselines: DRAM-only SAP HANA (baseline); direct-attached CXL as memory-only NUMA node with 1, 2, or 3 interleaved devices (Main-in-CXL and HEX-in-CXL variants, from the authors' DaMoN'23/VLDB'24 setup); Mixed Mode (Main-in-Flat, HEX-in-Flat) vs proposed Consolidated Mode at several capacities.
papers.keyFindings: Flat Memory Mode: no performance impact on TPC-C, and only 3.23-5.96% TPC-DS throughput loss vs DRAM-only even with a single CXL device, with 92+% local-DRAM hit rate. At 8 streams SF500 it shows 5.3% degradation using only 11.2 GB/s CXL bandwidth, vs 6.5% at 25.0 GB/s for Main-in-CXL-x3 and 16.2% at 49.4 GB/s for HEX-in-CXL-x3 — locality exploitation gives better performance with far less CXL bandwidth, enabling cheaper/lower-BW CXL devices (TCO argument). Mixed Mode: Main-in-Flat ~no impact (~99% hit rate); HEX-in-Flat 5-11% degradation (~92% hit rate), still better than HEX-in-CXL. Consolidated Mode: 0-2.8% degradation even at 768 GB (most constrained), CXL traffic ~9.0 GB/s (below the ~20+ GB/s offered), with zero HANA configuration needed.
papers.limitations: Authors' own: Flat Memory Mode supports only a 1:1 DRAM:CXL capacity ratio (motivating Mixed/Consolidated); Consolidated Mode is an ACPI-table hack in the Linux kernel, "not officially supported product feature"; Mixed Mode requires extra HANA configuration. Methodological: requires Intel Xeon 6 (Granite Rapids) hardware feature, so results do not transfer to AMD or older Intel hosts; single-socket, single-CXL-device main evaluation (one 256 GB CMM-D); direct-mapped exclusive HW cache — no study of pathological conflict-miss workloads; SAP HANA + TPC-C/TPC-DS only; no tail-latency, no multi-tenant/interference runs; no kernel version or link details in the slides; per-device behavior never examined.
papers.openQuestions: How HW-managed cacheline tiering behaves under adversarial/low-locality access patterns or cache-conflict-heavy workloads; multi-device and multi-socket scaling of Flat Memory Mode; interaction/co-existence of HW tiering with SW page- or object-level tiering; QoS and multi-tenant isolation on a flat-memory node; whether Consolidated Mode's random OS allocation degrades under memory pressure beyond the tested 768 GB point; ratios other than 1:1 in hardware.
sourceUrls: https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1I6U2cDqLuBVz8UGi5NgtDxzJoYtbMkgb (author slide deck PDF, full text read)
evidenceQuotes: "System Configuration ... 1 CPU (Intel® Granite Rapids) w/ 80 physical cores – Hyper-thread enabled ... Local DRAM – DDR5 4800 MT/s 32 GB * 8 channels (256GB) ... CXL memory (local) – 256 GB CMM-D (5000 MT/s)"
"OLAP shows only 3.23% ~ 5.96% perf impact – Even with a single CXL device"
"Intel Flat Memory Mode: First cache-line granular, hardware-managed Memory tiering system for CXL memory"
"Easily configured in BIOS as a single NUMA node – Combines local & CXL memory as a single NUMA node ... Ex) 256G DRAM + 256G CXL memory => 512GB – Supporting only 1:1 ratio of DRAMs and CXL memory"
Background 3-device config: "Local 256 GB / CXL 256 GB / CXL 256 GB / CXL 256 GB ... NUMA 0 ... NUMA 1 (Memory only)" with results "24.4% (x1) ➔ 9.6% (x2) ➔ 6.5% (x3-interleaved)"
"Flat Memory @ 8 streams SF500: Perf Degradation 5.3%, CXL BW usage 11.2 GB/s, DRAM BW usage 94.4 GB/s" vs "HEX CXL x3: 16.2%, 49.4 GB/s"
"Consolidated mode (Newly Proposed) – Merging two NUMA nodes into a single node ... Implemented by modifying ACPI* tables in Linux kernel ... Not officially supported product feature, but practical"
"Consolidated Memory of 768 GB – 0~2.8% of performance degradation ... CXL traffic: ~9.0 GB/s ... Less than the offered CXL BW (20+ GB/s)"
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Directly relevant as the strongest published counterpoint to software object placement: Intel's HW cacheline tiering achieves <6% OLAP loss at 92-99% hit rates while consuming only ~11 GB/s of CXL bandwidth — versus the requester's finding that CXL bandwidth contention causes 2.0-2.13x victim slowdown, this shows locality-driven placement can shrink CXL traffic below the interference regime, an argument ObjPlace can make in software on AMD Turin where Flat Memory Mode does not exist (Granite Rapids only). The paper treats multiple CXL devices only as interleaved capacity (x1/x2/x3 into one NUMA node) and its main evaluation uses a single CMM-D; it never studies per-device scheduling, cross-device interference, or multi-tenancy, so the requester's per-device direction is untouched by it. The Consolidated-Mode ACPI trick (merging tiered nodes into one) is also a useful transparency technique to cite when arguing why applications should not need per-node configuration.
couldNotVerify: Camera-ready ACM paper text (dl.acm.org returned 403); analysis is based on the authors' full DaMoN'25 slide deck
Kernel version and CXL link width/speed of the testbed
Exact number of physical CMM-D devices in the Mixed/Consolidated-Mode testbed (256 GB CXL total; diagrams depict two CMM-D boxes but count not stated)
CMM-D vendor stated only as the product name CMM-D (Samsung's product line); slides do not spell out 'Samsung'

papers.title: PIM Is All You Need: A CXL-Enabled GPU-Free System for Large Language Model Inference (CENT)
papers.venue: ASPLOS 2025 (ACM ASPLOS'25, also arXiv:2502.07578)
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 physical (simulated system models 8/20/32 custom CXL-PIM devices depending on model size)
papers.mainProblem: LLM inference (especially decoding with KV caches) has much lower operational intensity than the compute-centric workloads GPUs/TPUs are designed for; it is memory-bandwidth- and capacity-bound, making GPU-based serving expensive in energy and dollars.
papers.mainIdea: CENT: a GPU-free LLM inference system built entirely from custom CXL memory-expansion devices with near-bank processing-in-memory. Each CXL device integrates a CXL controller, PNM units (exponent/reduction/accumulation, RISC-V cores), and 16 memory chips with two GDDR6-PIM channels each; weights and KV caches live in the CXL-PIM devices and computation happens near the banks, with devices connected via a CXL switch to a host CPU.
papers.hardwareEnv: No physical testbed — fully simulated. Modified Ramulator2 models a CXL device with 32 GDDR6-PIM memory channels; CXL/PCIe interconnect modeled analytically ("analytical model based on the CXL latency and PCIe 6.0 bandwidth"); correctness checked with a functional simulator on generated CENT instruction traces. GPU baseline: 4x NVIDIA A100 80GB with NVLink 3.0 running vLLM. No production CXL silicon (no CZ120 etc.), no kernel version applicable.
papers.evalSetup: Simulation of Llama2 7B/13B/70B inference; queries with 512 prefill tokens + 3584 decode tokens, up to 32K context; configurations of 8, 20, and 32 CXL-PIM devices per model size; throughput, energy, and TCO analyses vs a 4x A100 vLLM baseline at batch size 128.
papers.baselines: 4x NVIDIA A100 80GB (NVLink 3.0) running vLLM at batch size 128 (throughput-saturating); TCO comparison against GPU rental/ownership cost.
papers.keyFindings: CENT achieves geomean 2.3x higher decoding throughput than the 4x A100 vLLM baseline across Llama2 7B/13B/70B, ~2.3-2.9x less energy (2.3x more tokens/Joule per HTML text; abstract claims 2.9x less energy), 5.2x more tokens per dollar, and 2.5x cheaper 3-year owned cost ($0.73/hr vs $1.76/hr). Prefill is 2.5x slower than GPU due to lower peak FLOPS.
papers.limitations: Entirely simulation (Ramulator2 + analytical CXL/PCIe model) — no real CXL device, no FPGA prototype; the CXL devices are hypothetical custom GDDR6-PIM parts, not commodity expanders. Authors admit: lower memory density of PIM vs standard DRAM, prefill 2.5x slower than GPU, scaling capped at 64 devices per CXL switch (lanes/ports) and by server power supply. No multi-tenant runs, no OS/software placement questions, no measured CXL link contention on real silicon.
papers.openQuestions: How a real CXL controller/switch fabric behaves under this traffic (all interconnect behavior is analytical); prefill acceleration (GPU-PIM hybrid); manufacturability/cost of GDDR6-PIM CXL devices; multi-tenancy and QoS across devices; software stack/driver integration on real hosts.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Low direct relevance to the requester's real 4x CZ120 testbed: CENT is a clean-slate simulated architecture with custom GDDR6-PIM CXL devices, not commodity memory expanders, so none of its numbers transfer to CZ120 latency/bandwidth or interference behavior. It is useful mainly as motivation/related work: it quantifies that LLM decoding is bandwidth-bound and treats a pool of CXL devices as parallel, per-device compute+memory resources (8/20/32 devices, work partitioned across them), which loosely echoes the requester's "each CXL device as an independently schedulable resource" direction. Cite it for the LLM-on-CXL trend and per-device parallelism argument, not for placement, interference, or QoS evidence on real hardware.
evidenceQuotes: We modify Ramulator2 to model a CXL device containing 32 GDDR6-PIM memory channels
We use an analytical model based on the CXL latency and PCIe 6.0 bandwidth
32 CXL devices, driven by a host CPU
Each CXL device integrates a CXL controller, PNM units, and 16 memory chips, each equipped with two GDDR6-PIM channels
The GPU system contains 4 NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs equipped with the NVLink 3.0 interconnect
couldNotVerify: Exact per-configuration device counts vs model size mapping (which of 8/20/32 devices maps to 7B/13B/70B)
Discrepancy between abstract's 2.9x energy claim and body's 2.3x tokens/Joule figure not resolved from fetched text

papers.title: Exploring CXL-based KV Cache Storage for LLM Serving
papers.venue: Machine Learning for Systems Workshop at NeurIPS 2024
papers.mainProblem: KV cache for long-context, high-throughput LLM serving overwhelms GPU HBM and even host CPU memory; full KV re-computation wastes GPU FLOPs and hurts TTFT SLO compliance, so a larger, cheap, low-latency storage tier for prefix KV cache is needed.
papers.mainIdea: Store prefix KV cache on ASIC CXL memory expansion and load it directly to the GPU over the CXL-GPU path (cudaMemcpyAsync from buffers allocated on the CPU-less CXL NUMA node), via a save/load token-chunk hash interface integrated into gpt-fast; first platform integrating a real ASIC CXL device and a GPU in one inference server, plus a production ROI model.
papers.hardwareEnv: Single-socket Supermicro server: Intel Xeon Platinum CPU (exact SKU not given), 1 TB DDR5-4800 host DRAM, NVIDIA H100 GPU with 96 GB HBM, and one ASIC-based CXL memory expansion card with 256 GB DDR5-4800 (device model/vendor and link width not stated; ref [13] is the authors' ByteDance ASIC-CXL EuroSys'24 paper). CXL exposed as a CPU-less NUMA node. Kernel version not stated.
papers.evalSetup: (1) Microbenchmark: latency/bandwidth of copying data between CXL NUMA-node host buffers and GPU buffers via cudaMemcpyAsync, access sizes 1KB-256MB, vs CPU-GPU copies. (2) TTFT on LLaMA-2-13B in modified gpt-fast (batched inference), conversation requests of 256-2048 input tokens from ShareGPT-Vicuna-Unfiltered. (3) Max batch size under a 400ms TTFT SLO. (4) Analytical ROI model (100 TFLOP/s GPU, 25 TFLOP prefill, 0.1s KV load, 90% prefix ratio).
papers.baselines: Full KV re-compute on GPU; prefix caching with GPU memory (PC-GPU, optimal baseline); CPU-GPU interconnect transfers (for the microbenchmark).
papers.keyFindings: CXL-GPU transfer latency/bandwidth is on par with CPU-GPU (data path bypasses host DRAM, direct CXL-to-GPU over PCIe; bandwidth saturates around 4MB transfers, latency grows past 64KB). PC-CXL TTFT 55-336ms across 256-2048 token inputs, at least as good as full re-compute; PC-GPU is 0.44-0.56ms. Under a 400ms TTFT SLO, max batch size rises from 44 (re-compute) to 57 with CXL (+30%). ROI model: 7.5x more prefill requests per GPU, up to 87% fewer GPUs vs discarding KV.
papers.limitations: Workshop-length preliminary study: one CXL card, one GPU, one server — no multi-device, multi-GPU, or multi-tenant experiments. TTFT/batch-size results only on LLaMA-2-13B with gpt-fast (not vLLM/production stack) and one dataset; save/load only at request end / prefill start, no eviction or cache-management policy evaluated. No comparison against prefix caching in host DRAM (only CXL vs GPU vs re-compute) despite DRAM being the obvious intermediate tier. Cost claims (87% GPU reduction, 7.5x) come from an analytical ROI model with assumed parameters (90% prefix ratio, 0.1s load), not measured end-to-end. No interference or bandwidth-contention study; device model/link width/kernel unspecified.
papers.openQuestions: Authors explicitly punt to future work: integrating CXL memory with multi-GPU systems and maintaining cache coherence across GPUs. Untested: multiple CXL devices, pooled/shared CXL across servers, eviction/placement policies between DRAM and CXL tiers, contention between KV-cache traffic and other CXL users, decode-stage offloading, larger models, real production traces.
evidenceQuotes: Our single socket server is equipped with Intel Xeon Platinum processors [20], 1TB of 4800 MHz DDR5 memory, an NVIDIA H100 GPU with 96GB HBM, and a CXL memory expansion card with 256 GB of DDR5 memory at 4800 MHz [13].
to our knowledge, we are the first to integrate a real ASIC-CXL device and a GPU within a single inference server and evaluate it for KV cache storage.

Since CXL memory devices are exposed to the system as NUMA nodes without CPUs by default [13], we allocate a set of host buffers on the CXL NUMA node and use cudaMemcpyAsync to copy data between the host buffers and GPU device buffers allocated via the CUDA API [26].
when leveraging CXL for storing KV cache, the system can handle a maximum batch size of 57, which is a 30% increase compared to KV re-compute.
From the estimate, we can reduce the number of GPUs needed to reach the same throughput while adhering SLO on TTFT by 87% when compared to KV re-compute.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Relevant as motivating literature but orthogonal in axis: it uses a single 256GB ASIC CXL card and studies the CXL-to-GPU transfer path, whereas the requester's testbed has 4x CZ120 and cares about CPU-side per-device placement and cross-device interference.
