papers.title: Bandwidth Expansion via CXL: A Pathway to Accelerating In-Memory Analytical Processing
papers.venue: ADMS workshop @ VLDB 2024 (15th Intl. Workshop on Accelerating Analytics and Data Management Systems)
papers.numCXLDevices: 1 (one Montage MXC-based CXL prototype module containing two DDR5 DIMMs behind one controller)
papers.mainProblem: Prior CXL work treats CXL memory only as a slower capacity tier (tiering/pooling), overlooking that CXL attaches via PCIe and thus adds aggregate memory bandwidth; and most prior DB-on-CXL studies used NUMA/FPGA emulation or simulation, which may not reflect real CXL device behavior for in-memory analytical (OLAP) workloads.
papers.mainIdea: Instead of DRAM-CXL tiering, interleave pages between local DRAM and a real CXL Type 3 device at a ratio matched to their bandwidth ratio (found: 3:2 DRAM:CXL) using a Linux N:M weighted-interleave mempolicy patch, thereby amalgamating DDR-channel and PCIe bandwidth to accelerate bandwidth-bound in-memory analytics.
papers.hardwareEnv: Dual-socket Intel Sapphire Rapids (32 cores/socket, 64MB LLC, 1024-entry TLB), 128GB DDR5 per socket (4x 32GB DIMMs, 35.2 GB/s per DIMM), UPI 96.0 GB/s cross-socket, run in sub-NUMA clustering (SNC) mode so local DRAM = one 32GB DDR5 DIMM at 35.2 GB/s theoretical. CXL: one early Montage MXC (Memory eXpander Controller) prototype integrating two DDR5 DIMMs, attached via 8-lane PCIe Gen5 (31.5 GB/s theoretical; ~20-21 GB/s practical, controller-limited, confirmed by Montage). Linux kernel 5.19.17 with Weiner's N:M interleave mempolicy patch; hyper-threading, prefetching, IRQ, ASLR disabled; huge pages enabled.
papers.evalSetup: Microbenchmarks plus OLAP on a single socket (32 cores): (1) peak sequential LOAD/STORE/NT-STORE throughput across 13 DRAM:CXL interleave ratios (100:0 to 0:100); (2) sequential access vs thread count (1B 4-byte records); (3) hash join (PK-FK, 256M build / 1B probe, 8-byte tuples) as random access; (4) selective column-scan reads (2B 8-byte records, 1-512 skipped records); (5) radix partitioning (1B 8-byte records, fanout 64-16384); (6) Star Schema Benchmark, 13 queries at SF=30, custom implementation from HyPer-generated query plans. Code at github.com/fukien/type3-pathway.
papers.baselines: Four memory configurations compared: local DRAM only; remote NUMA socket memory only; CXL memory only; DRAM:CXL 3:2 interleaved. For SSB, additionally a conventional DRAM-CXL tiered-memory model ("TIER": DRAM as buffer, CXL as fast disk with data movement into DRAM before query ops), representing TPP/Pond-style tiering wisdom.
papers.keyFindings: (1) Any non-zero DRAM:CXL interleave beats pure DRAM; 3:2 (matching the bandwidth ratio) is optimal. (2) Pure DRAM (SNC single channel) peaks at ~28.5 GB/s, pure CXL at ~20.1 GB/s (controller-bottlenecked); interleaved LOAD reaches ~47.5 GB/s = 1.61x DRAM, exceeding both single-path theoretical limits. (3) Hash join: interleaved up to ~1.59x DRAM; join scales to 16 threads vs 8 for others. (4) CXL (non-processor-affiliated) has better STORE/NT-STORE than remote NUMA due to lower cache-coherence maintenance overhead: hash-join build 26% faster on CXL than NUMA, but probe 24% faster on NUMA. (5) Radix partitioning: interleaving wins but only within 7.5% of DRAM (TLB thrashing bound). (6) SSB SF=30: interleaved beats DRAM on all 13 queries, mean 1.19x (Q1.x >1.4x); the TIER config performs about as poorly as pure CXL, challenging tiered-memory DBMS designs.
papers.limitations: Authors' own: CXL controller caps practical bandwidth at 20-21 GB/s well below the PCIe Gen5 link; SSB limited to SF=30 because "Our platform cannot accommodate larger workloads due to the limitations of the current 32GB local host DRAM"; SSB gains muted because SF=30 hash tables fit in the 64MB LLC; only CXL 1.1 evaluated ("Currently, only CXL 1.1 is commercially available"). Evident from methodology: exactly ONE CXL device — no multi-device interleaving, no cross-device interference, no pooling; SNC mode artificially shrinks DRAM to a single channel (35.2 GB/s), inflating the relative CXL benefit versus a full 4-channel socket; single static interleave ratio, no dynamic/object-level placement; no latency-sensitive or multi-tenant/co-runner experiments; read-mostly OLAP only, no OLTP; prototype (pre-production) Montage silicon.
papers.openQuestions: Authors punt on OLTP/transaction processing and broader database operations, TCO optimization, and larger-scale heterogeneous memory platforms (explicit future-work agenda). Untested: behavior with full DRAM channel population (non-SNC), multiple CXL devices and per-device management, adaptive/dynamic interleave ratios, interference between co-running workloads sharing the CXL link, tail latency, and CXL 2.0/3.0 switching or pooling.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Strong methodological relevance but zero multi-device content: it uses a single Montage-controller prototype and an SNC-shrunken single DRAM channel, so its headline 1.61x depends on DRAM being throttled to 35.2 GB/s — on the requester's EPYC 9745 with full 12-channel DRAM the relative bandwidth-expansion gain from one 35.5 GiB/s CXL region would be far smaller. Its key transferable findings are (a) bandwidth-ratio-matched weighted interleaving (via the same N:M mempolicy mechanism now upstream as weighted interleave) beats tiering for bandwidth-bound analytics, and (b) CXL's lack of processor affiliation gives it better store performance than remote NUMA — both directly usable as placement-policy signals in ObjPlace. It provides no evidence on per-device scheduling, CXL-to-CXL interference, or QoS, so it is prior art the requester's 4-device independent-resource direction clearly extends beyond; it can also serve as a baseline configuration (static bandwidth-ratio interleave) for ObjPlace to beat.
evidenceQuotes: We employ an initial CXL memory prototype from Montage [45], which integrates two DDR5 DIMMs as previously described. This prototype interfaces with the host system through an 8-lane PCIe Gen5 port, achieving a bandwidth of 31.5GB/s.

Our experimental platform is anchored on a dual-socket platform running Linux kernel version 5.19.17. Each socket hosts a 32-core Intel Sapphire Rapids CPU, with 64MB last-level cache (LLC) and 1024-entry translation lookaside buffer (TLB).
We have received confirmation from Montage[45] that their current technology is capable of providing a practical bandwidth limited to 20 − 21 GB/s.

our comparison encompasses four distinct memory configurations: local host memory access only (DRAM), remote NUMA memory access only (NUMA), CXL memory access only (CXL), and a DRAM-CXL interleaved setup (DRAM:CXL)

We apply a Linux patch [51] to facilitate a range of memory interleaving ratios, enabling the distribution of memory pages between a processor-bound memory node and a processor-independent memory node

the aggregated “LOAD” throughput around 47.5GB/s, which is 1.61x higher than the local DRAM configuration, and significantly surpasses the theoretical bandwidth limit of a single DDR channel (35.2GB/s)
Our platform cannot accommodate larger workloads due to the limitations of the current 32GB local host DRAM.

papers.title: PIFS-Rec: Process-In-Fabric-Switch for Large-Scale Recommendation System Inferences
papers.venue: MICRO 2024 (per ACM DL/IEEE listing; arXiv page does not state venue)
papers.numCXLDevices: characterization testbed: unknown device count ("four channels of DDR4 memory" via CXL, 256GB total; device model/vendor never stated); proposed PIFS system: simulated only (Ramulator 2.0)
papers.mainProblem: DLRM inference at datacenter scale is bottlenecked by huge, sparsely-accessed embedding tables; placing them in CXL-attached memory pools (Pond-style) incurs high latency (up to ~270 ns per access, ~37% from CXL I/O port transfers and retimer delays) and limited bandwidth, and prior near-data schemes (BEACON, RecNMP) still move data across the fabric or are DIMM-bound.
papers.mainIdea: PIFS: place lightweight processing cores at the downstream ports of a CXL fabric switch so embedding gather/pooling operations execute near the memory endpoints inside the fabric, with an FM-endpoint extension, on-switch buffering/caching (HTR), and page-management support, so only reduced results traverse upstream to the host.
papers.hardwareEnv: Characterization: dual-socket AMD Genoa, 96 physical cores/socket, 12 DDR5 channels/socket (768GB); CXL memory "enabled through four channels of DDR4 memory resulting in memory capacity of 256GB" — CXL device model, link width, and kernel version not stated. Evaluation of PIFS-Rec itself: cycle-level simulation in Ramulator 2.0 with custom cycle-accurate models (1 ns/clock) of the Process Core, FM Endpoint Extension and switch logic; no physical PIFS switch exists.
papers.evalSetup: Characterization of DLRM embedding-lookup phase on the real Genoa+CXL box with representative traces; then Ramulator 2.0 cycle-level simulation of PIFS-Rec on four DLRM configurations (RMC1–RMC4, e.g., RMC1 16K embeddings x 64B up to RMC4 1M embeddings x 128B) using Meta open-source DLRM traces.
papers.baselines: Pond (CXL pooling), Pond+PM (with page management), BEACON (in-switch/near-memory compute for recommendation), RecNMP (processing-near-memory DIMM).
papers.keyFindings: PIFS-Rec achieves 3.89x lower latency than Pond and 2.03x lower than BEACON; on-switch buffer with HTR gives 14.8% speedup on RMC4 with a 512KB cache. Characterization shows CXL pool fetch latency up to 270 ns with ~37% from CXL I/O port transfers/retimer delays, motivating in-fabric processing.
papers.limitations: The core contribution (processing in the fabric switch) is evaluated purely in simulation (Ramulator 2.0 + custom models) — no real CXL 2.0/3.x fabric switch hardware. The real-hardware part is only motivational characterization on one host whose CXL memory device(s) are never identified (model, count, link width unknown). No multi-tenant or interference experiments; no end-to-end DLRM serving with latency SLOs on real hardware; per-device management is not studied since devices sit behind an idealized simulated switch.
papers.openQuestions: How PIFS behaves with real switch silicon (no CXL 3.x fabric switches with compute exist commercially); coherence and CXL.mem protocol overheads for in-switch compute; sharing the in-switch processors across tenants/workloads; applicability beyond embedding gather (other sparse workloads); interaction with host-side tiering/page placement beyond the simple PM scheme.
evidenceQuotes: we run the embedding table lookup phase of the DLRM inference process on a dual-socket AMD Genoa system (each socket having 96 physical CPU cores and 12 channels of DDR5 memory that populates a capacity of 768GB)... Here, CXL memory is enabled through four channels of DDR4 memory resulting in memory capacity of 256GB.
we conducted cycle-level memory simulations using Ramulator 2.0 [57] for a detailed evaluation of PIFS-Rec.
Fetching a single address from memory pools can take up to 270 ns, with approximately 37% attributed to frequent CXL I/O port transfers and retimer delays.
The HA manages the CXL.mem protocol, presenting memory to the CPU as if it were on a remote NUMA node, allowing direct access via standard load/store commands.
These limitations include the risk of flex bus congestion under heavy memory traffic, increased data access latency (by over 4x compared to local DRAM), and limited bandwidth expansion capabilities.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Moderate relevance. The characterization half mirrors the requester's setup (AMD EPYC host + real CXL DDR4-backed expansion, ~270 ns CXL latency vs their 277 ns measurement — a useful corroborating data point), but the paper's contribution assumes a hypothetical compute-capable CXL fabric switch evaluated only in simulation, so it does not inform per-device placement or CXL-to-CXL interference on real CZ120s. It is best used as related work motivating that CXL fabric/port overheads dominate far-memory latency, and as a contrast point: PIFS pushes compute into the fabric, whereas the requester's candidate direction manages real, independently addressable devices from the host (ObjPlace-style), a niche PIFS leaves untouched (no multi-tenant, no per-device scheduling, no interference study).

papers.title: SIDLE: Tree-structure Aware Indexes for CXL-based Heterogeneous Memory
papers.numCXLDevices: primary testbed: 1 (one 32 GiB CXL 1.1 memory expansion card, Montage MXC controller [ref 14]); large-scale scalability testbed: 0 (downclocked remote NUMA emulation on a 1 TB dual-socket machine)
papers.mainProblem: Tree-structure indexes placed on CXL heterogeneous memory suffer ~70% slowdowns because CXL has ~2x latency / ~60% bandwidth of DRAM, and existing page-level CXL-HM placement schemes mismatch the granularity of small tree nodes, while prior NUMA/RDMA/PM index techniques don't transfer to CXL.
papers.mainIdea: SIDLE: a CXL-native, tree-structure-aware, node-grained data placement scheme/framework that matches the tree's inherent characteristics (layered structure, path-correlated hotness, node size hierarchy) to CXL-HM features. It does layer-aware allocation (upper/internal nodes preferentially in fast memory), node-granularity hotness tracking and migration that propagates along tree paths (demoting a node queues its parent; promotions follow hot paths), adaptive thresholds via a "hyper watermark" (high/low watermarks 95%/85%) that tunes fast-memory usage online, and lightweight background workers (migration trigger, cooler, watermark maintainer; 5 threads) with optimistic concurrency control for migration correctness (TLA+-verified). Developers integrate existing indexes (B+ tree, ART/PACTree-style, Masstree) with the SIDLE framework.
papers.hardwareEnv: Primary: Intel Xeon Platinum 8468V (48 cores, 395 MiB CPU cache), 32 GiB DRAM + 32 GiB CXL-attached DRAM behind one CXL 1.1 memory expansion card (Montage MXC CXL Memory eXpander Controller, ref [14]); single socket used (remote NUMA socket excluded as it is another slow tier). Link width and kernel version not stated in the text I read. Secondary (only for datasets > ~400M records): 1 TB dual-socket machine emulating CXL via downclocked remote NUMA tuned to comparable latency/bandwidth.
papers.evalSetup: Workloads: YCSB (multiple mixes: Read Only, Read Mostly, Update Heavy, With Insert, workloads A-F, short/long ranges), TPC-C for database tasks, and Alibaba Block Traces as a real-world production workload. Indexes integrated: B+ tree, radix tree (S-ART) and S-Masstree. Default 20M records with fast memory capped at 20% of total footprint (following MEMTIS/HeMem/Colloid practice); sensitivity sweeps over fast-memory ratio and dataset size 10M-4B records; concurrency scaling to 48 threads; SIDLE-Prophet (oracle pre-placement of hot paths, ~10% fast memory) used as ideal reference and its footprint as the fair budget for all systems.
papers.baselines: Baseline = default weighted allocation; TPP; MEMTIS; Caption; Random migration; PAC-L (optimized PACTree); Mass-L (optimized Masstree); SIDLE-Prophet oracle.
papers.keyFindings: Up to 71% higher throughput and up to 81% lower P99 latency vs SOTA placement (MEMTIS) and HM-optimized indexes (PACTree) on YCSB/real workloads. TPC-C: up to 133% higher throughput and 67% lower P99 than MEMTIS. Microbenchmarks: S-Masstree beats weighted-allocation baseline by 50.4-82.2%; S-ART/S-Masstree outperform baseline by 31.7-83.6% and 30.8-56.6% across YCSB mixes; Alibaba traces: up to 90.3% over baseline throughput, P99 down up to 81.2% vs MEMTIS and 63.2% vs TPP. Layer-aware allocation alone adds 2.8-28.7% throughput. Adaptive (hyper watermark) thresholds gain 1.7-16.8% over static. Scales to 48 threads (28.6-38.1x single-thread) with negligible background-worker overhead; stable from 10M to 4B records.
papers.limitations: Authors' own: SIDLE targets only software-visible cache-coherent CXL memory with latency in the same order as DRAM — ill-suited to hardware-managed-caching CXL devices (e.g., Intel Flat Memory Mode) or non-CC devices; currently two-tier only (multi-layer hierarchies left as extension); mainly targets low memory-contention scenarios (defers contention handling to Colloid); software access sampling has overhead, PEBS left as future work. Methodological: only ONE small (32 GiB) CXL 1.1 device — no multi-device, no interleaving, no cross-device or multi-tenant interference study; large-scale results rely on downclocked-NUMA emulation, not real CXL; single-socket only; no bandwidth-contention/co-runner experiments; index-specific (trees only), requires index code integration rather than transparent placement.
papers.openQuestions: Behavior under memory bandwidth contention/co-located tenants (explicitly punted to Colloid); multi-layer/multi-device tiers (only sketched: rank tiers and apply pairwise); hardware sampling (PEBS) integration; CXL 2.0/3.0 switched or pooled topologies never tested despite citing 1.5-4x latency across generations; interaction of node-grained migration with page-level OS tiering running concurrently for non-index data.
evidenceQuotes: Testbed. We run all experiments on Intel® Xeon® Platinum 8468V CPUs (48 cores), equipped with 395 MiB CPU cache, 32 GiB DRAM, and 32 GiB CXL-attached DRAM (connected through a CXL 1.1 memory expansion card [14]), except the large scale dataset scalability test (§6.4 part2). Since the remote NUMA-node is another tier of slow memory besides CXL, all experiments use a single socket
[14] 2024. CXL® Memory eXpander Controller (MXC). https://www.montagetech.com/MXC.

Datasets exceeding our CXL testbed’s memory limit (~400 M records) are evaluated on a 1 TB dual-socket machine, where we emulate CXL memory using downclocked remote NUMA [79] to achieve comparable performance (Figure 1(c)).

Evaluations show that SIDLE improves throughput by up to 71% and reduces P99 latency by up to 81% compared with state-of-the-art data placement schemes (e.g., MEMTIS) and HM-optimized tree-structure indexes (e.g., PACTree) in YCSB and real-world workloads.

SIDLE’s Scope and Limitations. SIDLE mainly targets CXL devices with software-visible, cache-coherent (CC) memory whose latency is within the same order of magnitude as local DRAM. SIDLE is ill-suited for CXL devices with hardware-managed caching [156] or lacking CC.
Note that SIDLE mainly targets scenarios with low memory contention; Colloid [130] may further enhance SIDLE when contention occurs.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: SIDLE is the strongest published validation of the requester's ObjPlace thesis from the database side: it argues explicitly that page-granularity CXL placement (TPP/MEMTIS/Caption) mismatches object (tree-node) granularity and shows large wins from object-structure-aware, node-grained placement on real CXL silicon — directly overlapping with ObjPlace's object-granularity claim, so it must be positioned against (it is index-specific and requires code integration, whereas ObjPlace is a general runtime). It offers nothing on the candidate multi-device direction: one 32 GiB CXL 1.1 card, single-device, no interleaving, and it explicitly assumes low memory contention and defers bandwidth-contention handling to Colloid — exactly the regime the requester's 2.0-2.13x co-runner slowdown measurements target. The requester's 4x CZ120 testbed could both stress-test SIDLE-style placement under contention and extend it to per-device scheduling, a gap SIDLE leaves open.

Linux kernel version not stated in the sections I extracted
Exact vendor of the memory expansion card module (only the Montage MXC controller is cited)

papers.title: Smart-Infinity: Fast Large Language Model Training using Near-Storage Processing on a Real System
papers.venue: HPCA 2024 (30th IEEE International Symposium on High-Performance Computer Architecture; Best Paper Award Honorable Mention)
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no CXL devices; up to 10 Samsung SmartSSD computational storage devices)
papers.mainProblem: Storage-offloaded LLM training (ZeRO-Infinity style, offloading optimizer state/parameters to NVMe SSDs) is bottlenecked by storage bandwidth on the host PCIe/storage path, making training of tens-of-billion-parameter models on a single node slow.
papers.mainIdea: Use near-storage processing: Samsung SmartSSD computational storage devices (NVMe SSD + Kintex UltraScale+ KU15P FPGA on the same card) execute the optimizer parameter update near the storage (SmartUpdate), removing most parameter/optimizer traffic from the host storage path; plus a transfer-handler overlap optimization and accelerator-assisted gradient compression (CSD-side decompression) to reduce write traffic.
papers.hardwareEnv: CPU: Intel Xeon Gold 6342, 2 sockets (2x48C/96T as listed); Memory: 32x32GB DDR4-3200 (1 TB); GPUs: NVIDIA A5000 (also A100 40GB and A4000 for sensitivity); Storage: up to 10 Samsung SmartSSD devices, each a 4TB NVMe SSD paired with a Xilinx Kintex UltraScale+ KU15P FPGA (522K LUTs, 984 BRAMs, 1968 DSPs, 4GB DDR4) over PCIe Gen3 x4. No CXL hardware. Kernel version not captured.
papers.evalSetup: Storage-offloaded training of GPT-2 variants (4.0B, 8.4B, 16.6B, 33.0B), BERT-345M, BLOOM, ViT with batch size 4, mixed precision, on a single server with 1-10 SmartSSDs; fine-tuning accuracy case studies on GLUE tasks (MNLI, QQP, SST-2, QNLI); scaling studies over number of CSDs and GPU type.
papers.baselines: DeepSpeed ZeRO-Infinity with software RAID0 across the same SSDs (state-of-the-art storage-offloaded training framework).
papers.keyFindings: SmartUpdate alone gives 1.18x-1.24x speedup with 6 SSDs and 1.54x-1.60x with 10 SSDs over ZeRO-Infinity+RAID0; adding the transfer optimization reaches 1.60x-1.66x; the full system (SmartUpdate + optimization + gradient compression) reaches 1.85x-1.98x, and up to 2.11x with an A100 GPU. Fine-tuning accuracy is preserved on GLUE despite gradient compression. Speedups grow with the number of CSDs because host storage-bandwidth pressure is removed.
papers.limitations: Authors admit a slight slowdown with a single CSD (benefits need >=4 CSDs), SmartSSD cost (~6x a plain SSD) hurting cost-efficiency at low device counts, and reduced speedup in multi-GPU settings due to PCIe congestion; extending compression to quantization/pruning/low-rank is left as future work. Methodologically: single-node only, FPGA-based CSDs (product-grade but niche hardware), no CXL or memory-tiering component at all, no multi-tenant or interference study.
papers.openQuestions: Integration of quantization/pruning/low-rank compression into CSD-side update (explicitly deferred); scaling to multi-node distributed training; interaction with faster interconnects (PCIe Gen4/5 or CXL-attached memory) which could change where the bottleneck sits.
evidenceQuotes: "We use at most 10 SAMSUNG SmartSSD devices. Each SmartSSD has a 4TB NVMe SSD which directly communicates with Kintex UltraScale+ KU15P FPGA through a PCIe Gen3.0 x4 bus. The attached FPGA has approximately 522K LUTs, 984 BRAMs, 1968 DSPs, and DDR4 4GB DRAM."
Testbed table (Table II): "GPU: NVIDIA A5000, A100 (40GB), A4000; CPU: Xeon(R) Gold 6342, 2x48C 96T; Memory: 32x32GB DDR4-3200; SSD: SAMSUNG SmartSSD, 4TB"

No CXL devices, no memory tiering/placement, no NUMA aspects.

papers.title: FaTRQ: Tiered Residual Quantization for LLM Vector Search in Far-Memory-Aware ANNS Systems
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.LG, cs.AR, cs.IR)
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (one hypothetical CXL Type-2 device simulated via Ramulator extension; no physical CXL hardware)
papers.mainProblem: In ANNS for RAG, the second-pass refinement stage that fetches full-precision vectors from SSD dominates query latency for modern high-dimensional text/multimodal embeddings; storing full vectors in fast memory is too costly.
papers.mainIdea: FaTRQ replaces SSD full-vector refinement with a progressive distance estimator over compact ternary-encoded residuals ("tiered residual quantization") streamed from CXL far memory, with early termination once a candidate is provably outside top-k; a custom accelerator inside a CXL Type-2 device performs the refinement locally (near-memory), so only 4-byte coarse distances cross the link from the GPU.
papers.hardwareEnv: Host for software experiments/baselines: 40-thread Intel Xeon Gold 6230 CPU, 128 GB DRAM, 1 TB SSD, NVIDIA A10 GPU (24 GB). CXL device: NOT real — Ramulator extended to simulate far-memory access of a CXL Type-2 device (8Gb x16 DDR5-4800, timings 34-34-34; assumed CXL latency/throughput 271 ns / 22 GB/s; SSD 45 us / 1200K IOPS). Accelerator synthesized in Verilog at 1 GHz in ASAP7 (0.729 mm^2). No kernel version relevant; no physical CXL device.
papers.evalSetup: Datasets: Wiki (88M SBERT 768-D embeddings, 251 GB) and LAION (100M CLIP embeddings, 286 GB). Two variants evaluated: FaTRQ-SW (residual codes in CXL memory, filtering on CPU) and FaTRQ-HW (filtering offloaded to simulated CXL Type-2 accelerator). GPU does coarse index traversal; refinement latency modeled with the Ramulator-based CXL simulation; accelerator area/power via ASAP7 synthesis. Metrics: throughput vs recall, distance-estimation MSE, storage efficiency.
papers.baselines: IVF-FAISS (CPU), CAGRA-cuVS (GPU graph ANNS); scalar-quantization residual schemes for accuracy comparison.
papers.keyFindings: FaTRQ-HW delivers 3.1x-9.4x speedup over IVF-FAISS and 2.6x-4.9x over CAGRA-cuVS; 2.4x storage efficiency improvement over prior refinement schemes; distance-estimation MSE 0.0159 vs 0.258 for scalar quantization; accelerator costs 0.729 mm^2 in ASAP7 at 1 GHz. Speedup narrows at 95% recall as coarse traversal begins to dominate.
papers.limitations: The CXL Type-2 device and its accelerator are entirely simulated (Ramulator extension + ASAP7 synthesis) — no real CXL silicon or FPGA prototype, so link contention, real .mem protocol behavior, and host-device coherence costs are not validated. Single hypothetical device; no multi-device, multi-tenant, or interference experiments. Fixed assumed CXL parameters (271 ns, 22 GB/s). Authors admit speedup narrows at high (95%) recall; no other explicit limitations section.
papers.openQuestions: Behavior on real CXL Type-2/Type-3 hardware (real latency ~277 ns matches their assumption, but real per-device bandwidth ceilings and co-runner interference are untested); scaling across multiple CXL devices; integration with OS tiering; index update/insertion path; multi-tenant sharing of the CXL accelerator; end-to-end RAG pipeline impact.
evidenceQuotes: We extend Ramulator to simulate far-memory access patterns of a CXL Type-2 device, with DRAM parameters listed in Table I
A custom accelerator is deployed in a CXL Type-2 device to perform low-latency refinement locally
Hardware overhead is assessed by synthesizing our accelerator in Verilog at 1 GHz using the ASAP7
40-thread Intel Xeon Gold 6230 CPU with 128 GB DRAM and a 1 TB SSD

papers.title: TRACE: Unlocking Effective CXL Bandwidth via Lossless Compression and Precision Scaling
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2509.03377)
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no physical CXL device; one hypothetical CXL Type-3 device is modeled analytically)
papers.mainProblem: LLM inference with weights/KV cache offloaded to CXL memory is bottlenecked by CXL link and device-side DDR bandwidth; raw CXL bandwidth is far below what long-context decoding and large-model weight streaming need.
papers.mainIdea: TRACE puts transparent lossless compression inside the CXL Type-3 device controller, behind an unmodified CXL.mem interface. It stores tensors in a channel-major, disaggregated bit-plane layout (so low-entropy exponent/sign bit-planes compress well and precision can be scaled by reading fewer bit-planes), applies a KV-specific transform before compression, and uses an inline generic codec on 4 KB blocks staged in device SRAM — amplifying effective link and DDR bandwidth without host software or protocol changes.
papers.hardwareEnv: No physical testbed. Analytical/first-order bandwidth model in Python of a "single-GPU + CXL Type-3 system with a 512 GB/s per-direction CXL link and 256 GB/s device DDR bandwidth" (PCIe 7.0 x16-class link; DDR5-6400 / DDR6-12800 device channels; 76 GB usable HBM modeled on GPU side). Controller logic implemented in SystemVerilog and synthesized in ASAP7 7 nm at 2 GHz / 0.7 V; DRAM energy via DRAMSim3. No CPU model, kernel, or real CXL device — none exists in the evaluation.
papers.evalSetup: Trace-driven/analytical evaluation: real tensor data from LLaMA 3.1 8B/70B, Gemma 2 2B, Mistral 7B, OPT 13B/30B, Mixtral 8x7B, GPT-OSS-120B-MXFP4 over WikiText, BookSum (LongBench), C4, UltraChat, contexts 4K–256K tokens. Compression ratios measured on real weights/KV tensors; decoding throughput computed by first-order bandwidth accounting (per-token bytes over CXL link and device DDR channels, bottleneck taken); hardware cost/energy via 7nm synthesis and DRAMSim3.
papers.baselines: CXL-Plain (word-major layout, no compression) and CXL-GComp (word-major layout + inline generic lossless compression); comparisons across link/DDR bandwidth settings.
papers.keyFindings: Bit-plane layout + KV transform enables 25.2% lossless footprint reduction for BF16 weights and 46.9% for BF16 KV cache (per-layer peaks 2.69x). Modeled decode throughput up to 4.24x for GPT-OSS-120B-MXFP4 at 128k tokens (16.28 -> 68.99 tok/s). Up to 40.3% lower DRAM access energy (DRAMSim3, per-head/neuron granularity on OPT-30B), 29.9% at per-expert granularity; model load latency reduced up to 30.0%. 7 nm SystemVerilog implementation sustains 256 GB/s device bandwidth.
papers.limitations: Entirely simulated/modeled: no real CXL silicon, no FPGA prototype, no end-to-end system run — throughput numbers come from first-order bandwidth-ceiling accounting, ignoring latency effects, queuing, interference, and host software stack. Assumes futuristic link speeds (512 GB/s per-direction, PCIe 7.0-class) far beyond shipping CXL 2.0 devices. Single hypothetical device, single GPU, single tenant; no multi-device or contention study. Authors acknowledge combined policies with lossy techniques (quantization, KV eviction) are unevaluated future work.
papers.openQuestions: How the design behaves on real CXL hardware at realistic (tens of GB/s) bandwidth and ~250-300ns latency; interaction with OS-level page placement and multi-tenant contention; a physical FPGA/ASIC prototype behind an actual CXL.mem endpoint; combining device-internal lossless compression with lossy quantization/eviction policies (explicitly punted); variable-size compressed block management and address indirection overheads at scale.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Low direct relevance to the requester's 4x CZ120 testbed: TRACE is a device-architecture proposal evaluated purely in simulation at hypothetical 512 GB/s links, whereas the requester's measured per-region bandwidth is ~35.5 GiB/s on real CXL 2.0 silicon — nothing in TRACE can be reproduced or deployed on CZ120s. It is useful as related work for the "effective bandwidth is the scarce resource" motivation and as a contrast point: TRACE amplifies bandwidth inside one device, while the requester's candidate direction (per-device placement, cross-device interference, tail-aware QoS) manages bandwidth across devices in software. If pursuing the multi-device direction, cite TRACE as an orthogonal hardware-side approach that a placement runtime like ObjPlace could sit above.

For each setting, we compute per-token traffic on the CXL link and on the device-side DDR channels, then convert each to a tok/s ceiling by dividing the corresponding bandwidth by bytes-per-token and taking the bottleneck.

papers.title: Scalable Processing-Near-Memory for 1M-Token LLM Inference: CXL-Enabled KV-Cache Management Beyond GPU Limits
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.AR, cs.AI), arXiv:2511.00321
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 physical (simulated: up to 8 CXL-PNM devices per DGX node, and 1-4 standalone PNM nodes in rack-scale configs)
papers.mainProblem: Multi-million-token LLM context windows blow past GPU HBM capacity; existing CXL non-eviction KV-cache offloading frameworks still pay costly recall transfers moving non-resident KV tokens back over CXL/PCIe into limited GPU memory, throttling long-context decode throughput.
papers.mainIdea: Put a processing-near-memory (PNM) accelerator inside the CXL memory device so KV-cache token-page selection and attention over offloaded KV pages execute near the LPDDR5X CXL memory instead of recalling data to the GPU. papers.hardwareEnv: Fully simulated: cycle-level simulator parameterized by synthesized 7nm timing/power models. Modeled system: NVIDIA DGX with up to 8x A100-80GB GPUs (2 TB/s HBM2E), Intel 4th-gen Xeon host; CXL-PNM devices with LPDDR5X-based CXL memory, 512 GB and 1.1 TB/s per module, connected through a CXL 3.0 switch (PCIe 6.0 PHY), x8 lanes per device, x16 host-to-switch. Configurations sweep GPU count x PNM device count (e.g., 1GPU+8PNM, 2GPU+8PNM) and rack-scale 2x GPU nodes with 1-4 PNM nodes.
papers.baselines: (i) CXL-memory-expanded DGX baseline (no PNM), (ii) PNM-KV (CXL-PNM-attached DGX offloading KV-cache), (iii) PnG-KV (PNM-KV plus hybrid GPU+PNM steady mode); plus pure GPU scaling and eviction-based StreamingLLM vs non-eviction ArkVale for accuracy.
papers.keyFindings: Up to 21.9x throughput improvement and up to 60x lower energy per token vs the CXL-expanded DGX baseline (Llama3.1-70B, 2GPU+8PNM PnG-KV); average 2.7x throughput and 4.9x lower energy for that config; up to 7.3x higher cost efficiency (1GPU+8PNM vs 8-GPU baseline, Llama3.1-8B). papers.title: Context-Aware Mixture-of-Experts Inference on CXL-Enabled GPU-NDP Systems
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.LG, cs.AR)
papers.numCXLDevices: 1 (simulated: 1x DDR-based CXL-NDP device, 512 GB, alongside 1x H100 GPU)
papers.mainProblem: MoE LLMs (Mixtral-8x7B/8x22B) have expert weights far exceeding GPU HBM capacity; conventional offloading moves cold expert parameters over PCIe on every activation, making decoding latency dominated by parameter transfer, while CXL-NDP devices have too little compute to run experts at full precision.
papers.mainIdea: Execute cold experts in place on a CXL-attached near-data-processing (NDP) memory device — moving small activations instead of large parameters — and use prefill-stage expert-activation statistics (which correlate strongly with decoding-stage routing, cosine similarity ~0.89 for Mixtral-8x7B) to drive per-sequence context-aware expert placement (hot experts on GPU HBM, cold on NDP) plus per-expert mixed-precision quantization (1-4 bit) so the compute-limited NDP can keep up.
papers.hardwareEnv: Fully simulated GPU-NDP system, no physical CXL hardware. NDP side simulated on Ramulator following MoNDE's methodology; GPU modeled as NVIDIA H100 (80 GB HBM3, 132 SMs, 989.4 TFLOP/s peak). System composition: 1x H100 GPU + 1x DDR-based NDP (512 GB capacity, 512 GB/s internal bandwidth, 64x 4x4 systolic arrays at 1 GHz), interconnect PCIe Gen4 x16. No real CXL device model, no CPU/kernel details (not applicable — simulation).
papers.evalSetup: Simulation of MoE inference with Mixtral-8x7B (45.1B expert params) and Mixtral-8x22B (135.5B expert params). Accuracy evaluated on MMLU (5-shot), MathQA, HellaSwag, ARC-Easy/Challenge, BoolQ, WinoGrande, PIQA (zero-shot). Performance (decoding throughput, end-to-end speedup) measured in the Ramulator-based GPU-NDP simulator using the same configuration as MoNDE for fair comparison.
papers.baselines: MoNDE (prior GPU-NDP MoE offloading system, primary baseline), HOBBIT (GPU-only mixed-precision expert offloading), and original full-precision models as accuracy reference.
papers.keyFindings: Executing cold experts in place on the CXL-NDP with context-aware placement and mixed-precision quantization yields 6.6-8.7x end-to-end speedup over MoNDE (Mixtral-8x7B, 3-bit), 8.7x decoding throughput at 3-bit (11.2x at 2-bit), up to 18x over GPU-only offloading, with only ~0.13% average accuracy drop at 3-bit. papers.limitations: Entirely simulation-based (Ramulator NDP simulator, no real CXL silicon or FPGA); the NDP device with 64 systolic arrays is hypothetical hardware that does not exist as a product. Interconnect is modeled as PCIe Gen4 x16 rather than an actual measured CXL link, so real CXL latency/contention effects are not captured. Authors state no explicit limitations or future-work section in the conclusion. Batch/serving-level dynamics (continuous batching, real inference server) untested.

papers.title: CXL-CCL: Inter-Node Collective GPU-Communication Using a CXL Shared Memory Pool (v1 title: CCCL: Node-Spanning GPU Collectives with CXL Memory Pooling)
papers.venue: ICS '26 (40th ACM International Conference on Supercomputing); arXiv:2602.22457 (v1 2026-02-25, v3 2026-05-06)
papers.numCXLDevices: 6 (six Micron CZ120 128GB cards behind a TITAN-II CXL switch, shared by 3 host nodes); scalability beyond 3 nodes via an analytical bandwidth-sharing emulator
papers.mainProblem: Cross-node GPU collective communication (AllReduce, AllGather, Broadcast, etc.) today requires expensive RDMA NICs/switches (InfiniBand); the paper asks whether a switch-attached CXL shared-memory pool can replace RDMA for inter-node collectives, despite CXL 2.0's lack of cross-host hardware cache coherence, higher latency, and per-device bandwidth limits.
papers.mainIdea: CXL-CCL, an NCCL-compatible collective library that stages data through a multi-host CXL 2.0 shared memory pool: (1) doorbell/semaphore synchronization built on explicit cache-line flush + re-read to get read-after-write visibility across hosts without hardware coherence; (2) software round-robin interleaving of data blocks across the six individual CXL devices (with exclusive per-rank device ranges for N-to-N collectives) to aggregate per-device x8 bandwidth and avoid contention; (3) parallelized CPU-GPU DMA pipelines (DAX mmap + cudaHostRegister + cudaMemcpyAsync) to overlap GPU-CXL transfers.
papers.hardwareEnv: Three nodes, each: Intel Xeon 6960P (72 physical cores), 256 GB DRAM, 1x NVIDIA H100 80GB on PCIe Gen5 x16; nodes attach via PCIe/CXL Gen5 x16 to an XConn TITAN-II CXL switch; behind the switch a memory box with six Micron CZ120 CXL Type-3 cards, 128 GB each (PCIe/CXL Gen5 x8), 768 GB total pool; Linux 6.2.6, CUDA 12.8. Pool exposed as devdax, sequentially stacked address space (device i at [i*128GB,(i+1)*128GB)), mmap'ed by all hosts.
papers.evalSetup: Microbenchmarks of 8 collectives (AllReduce, Broadcast, Reduce, AllGather, Gather, ReduceScatter, Scatter, AllToAll) with message sizes 1MB-4GB across the 3 real nodes; pool characterization (latency/bandwidth vs DRAM); LLM training case study: Llama-3-8B on Wikipedia with PyTorch FSDP; scalability study 3-12 nodes via an emulator that assumes concurrent requests share device bandwidth uniformly.
papers.baselines: NCCL 2.28.3 over 200 Gb/s InfiniBand (RDMA). No Gloo/MPI baselines.
papers.keyFindings: On real 3-node CXL-pool hardware, CXL-CCL beats NCCL-over-200Gbps-IB by 1.34x (AllGather), 1.84x (Broadcast), 1.94x (Gather); Llama-3-8B FSDP training gets 1.11x speedup while cutting interconnect hardware cost 2.75x. Characterization: CXL pool load latency 658ns vs 214ns local DRAM (3.1x); GPU-to-CXL transfer bandwidth ~20 GB/s (bounded by per-device Gen5 x8 and one GPU DMA engine per direction). Software per-device interleaving is essential: without it concurrent accesses converge on one device and serialize; emulated scaling holds to ~12 nodes before device contention degrades performance.
papers.limitations: Only 3 real nodes; all scaling beyond that is an analytical emulator with a uniform bandwidth-sharing assumption (no queuing/tail effects). Single baseline (NCCL/IB at 200 Gbps; no 400G NDR comparison). Small messages are software-overhead dominated. CXL 2.0 pool has no hardware cross-host coherence, so correctness rests on flush/re-read discipline; pool exposed only via devdax (no NUMA integration). Latency 3.1x DRAM. Authors note large multi-host CXL pool platforms 'remain difficult to access commercially' and that CXL-CCL is research-only, not in ByteDance production. No multi-tenant or interference experiments; one GPU per node only.
papers.openQuestions: No explicit future-work section. Untested: >3 real nodes, multiple GPUs per node, contention between collective traffic and other tenants sharing the pool, tail latency/QoS under mixed workloads, comparison against 400Gbps+ RDMA, CXL 3.x hardware coherence replacing the software doorbell scheme, and per-device scheduling policies beyond static round-robin interleaving.

papers.title: ITME: Inference Tiered Memory Expansion with Disaggregated CXL-Hybrid Memories
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2606.12556)
papers.numCXLDevices: performance testbed: 1 SK hynix CMM (CXL DRAM+NAND hybrid, 32 GB used as DRAM cache) plus 2 KIOXIA PCIe Gen5 NVMe SSDs; functional testbed: 1 Intel Agilex 7 FPGA CXL prototype (32 GB DDR4 cache) plus 2 SK hynix Platinum P51 Gen5 SSDs
papers.mainProblem: Agentic and long-context LLM inference produces TB-scale context state (model weights + prefix/KV caches) that exceeds GPU HBM and host DRAM; conventional disaggregated NVMe-oF storage tiers impose block-I/O software overheads and stall inference, while pure DRAM expansion is too costly at TB scale.
papers.mainIdea: ITME builds a remote "shared context tier" (T3.5) out of CXL-hybrid memory devices — NAND flash fronted by a hardware-managed CXL-DRAM cache — exposed as a CPU-less NUMA node on a memory server and reached by GPU servers as byte-addressable memory over standard RDMA. Because weights and prefix caches have deterministic access patterns, a user-level prefetch API (chm_prefetch / chm_prefetch_object / chm_prefetch_size) lets the inference framework proactively stage data from NAND into the CXL-DRAM cache, driving a pipelined multi-tier DMA path (remote CXL-hybrid -> host memory -> GPU). Integrated into vLLM v0.17.0.
papers.hardwareEnv: GPU/host server: dual Intel Xeon 6730, 256 GB DDR5 (128 GB/socket, tier T2), NVIDIA A100 80 GB HBM (T1); servers interconnected via dual Mellanox ConnectX-6 100 Gbps NICs (RDMA). Remote memory server: production-grade platform with one SK hynix CMM (32 GB of its capacity used as DRAM cache, exposed as CPU-less NUMA node over PCIe/CXL) + two KIOXIA PCIe Gen5 NVMe SSDs (8 PCIe lanes total, ~22 GB/s peak read; CMM host path ~18 GB/s, 4-channel DRAM / 2-channel SSD config). Separate functional prototype: Intel Agilex 7 I-Series FPGA with 32 GB DDR4 hardware-managed cache + two SK hynix Platinum P51 Gen5 NVMe SSDs. Kernel version not stated in what I read.
papers.evalSetup: Multi-turn LLM inference in a modified vLLM v0.17.0 with Llama-3.1 8B and 70B; ShareGPT and Mooncake datasets; e.g. 128 concurrent conversations up to 5 turns with >=2000 tokens, extended 35-turn / 256-conversation benchmarks. Performance runs on the SK hynix CMM empirical platform; the FPGA prototype validates hardware control logic and the software prefetcher functionally.
papers.baselines: GPU-memory-only with recomputation (T1); CPU-offload baseline (128 GB host memory, T2); recompute-only; local NVMe-oF disaggregated-storage baseline (local to eliminate network overhead); ideal 80 GB GPU-memory configuration.
papers.keyFindings: Up to 35.7% throughput improvement over the CPU-offload baseline in extended multi-turn runs; 1.81x speedup over recomputation by turn 5; 1.80x throughput improvement over the NVMe-oF disaggregated-storage baseline; internal hardware prefetcher + user-level prefetch API hides NAND latency behind the CXL-DRAM cache for deterministic weight/prefix-cache streams.
papers.limitations: Authors admit the FPGA prototype's bandwidth collapses below 1 GB/s on cache misses (theoretical max 23.3 GB/s, still being optimized) and that ITME shows performance fluctuations from unpredictable I/O stalls under intense contention. Methodological weaknesses: single CMM device and single memory server — no multi-device or scale-out evaluation; performance results come from the CMM platform while the actual ITME hardware logic is only functionally validated on the FPGA (performance and function are validated on different platforms); no multi-tenant runs; no CXL-vs-DRAM interference study; industry preprint (SK hynix Memory Systems Research), not peer-reviewed.
papers.openQuestions: Scaling to multiple CXL-hybrid devices or multiple memory servers (pooling, cross-device scheduling) is not addressed; write-heavy KV-cache paths and cache-miss behavior at full bandwidth remain open; multi-tenant sharing of the "shared context tier" and QoS/isolation are untested; interaction of the internal hardware prefetcher with irregular (non-deterministic) access patterns is unexplored.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: ITME is single-CXL-device and remote/RDMA-disaggregated: one SK hynix CMM (DRAM-cache-over-NAND hybrid) on a memory server, not multiple locally-attached expanders like the requester's 4x CZ120. It offers no evidence on per-device placement, CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference, or multi-tenant isolation — the requester's candidate direction remains unclaimed by this work. Its useful overlap is the exploitation of deterministic LLM access patterns (weights, prefix caches) via an explicit application-level prefetch API, which is conceptually adjacent to ObjPlace's phase/skew-driven object placement; ITME's 35.7%/1.80x numbers also confirm that byte-addressable CXL-backed tiers beat block-I/O NVMe-oF for KV-cache overflow. Its admitted single-device, no-contention-handling gaps strengthen the motivation for treating each CXL device as an independently schedulable resource.
evidenceQuotes: we developed a production-grade empirical platform integrating an SK Hynix CMM (SK hynix, [2024]) and two KIOXIA PCIe Gen5 NVMe SSDs (KIOXIA, [2024]). To maintain architectural consistency with the FPGA prototype, we utilized 32 GB of the CMM capacity as the DRAM cache.

A functional prototype, implemented on an Intel Agilex 7 I-Series FPGA (Altera, [2026]), validates the hardware-level control logic and the software prefetcher. This platform integrates 32 GB of DDR4 DRAM as a hardware-managed cache for two SK Hynix Platinum P51 PCIe Gen5 NVMe SSDs.

By operating over the PCIe physical layer and exposing itself to the host operating system as a CPU-less NUMA node, the device successfully bypasses the physical pin-count limitations of traditional DDR channels.
The remote region functions as a massive, byte-addressable memory, providing GPU servers with a scalable extension of their physical memory via standard RDMA protocols.
The host features dual Intel Xeon 6730 CPUs and 256 GB of DDR5 DRAM (128 GB per socket), representing the host memory tier (T2). It is equipped with an NVIDIA A100 (80 GB HBM) GPU (T1).

Overall, ITME enhances conventional CPU-offloading by providing additional remote memory expansion to accommodate large KV cache footprints beyond host memory limits, achieving up to a 35.7% throughput improvement.
The current FPGA implementation's bandwidth degrades below 1 GB/s upon cache misses. We are actively optimizing the hardware logic to close this gap and reach the theoretical maximum of 23.3 GB/s.

papers.title: Demystifying CXL Memory Bandwidth Expansion for Analytical Workloads
papers.venue: ADMS'25 workshop @ VLDB 2025 (16th Intl. Workshop on Accelerating Analytics and Data Management Systems)
papers.mainProblem: Whether transparent DRAM+CXL interleaving actually delivers memory bandwidth expansion for in-memory analytical (OLAP) workloads. Prior work (Huang et al., ADMS'24) claimed a single static interleaving configuration suffices across workloads; this paper re-evaluates that claim across multiple hardware configurations (SNC modes, prefetching on/off, many interleave ratios).
papers.mainIdea: Systematic measurement study (not a system): run SSB SF100 on the Proteus JIT-compiled analytical engine plus four operator-level microbenchmarks (sequential scan/write, hash join build/probe, filtering with varying selectivity, radix partitioning with varying fanout) across DRAM:CXL weighted-interleave ratios (Linux MPOL_WEIGHTED_INTERLEAVE, 2 MiB huge pages), three SNC configurations (full socket / SNC-2 / SNC-4), and hardware prefetching enabled/disabled; profile with VTune top-down and PCM to attribute stalls. Distills three design principles: hardware-consciousness, workload-adaptive (per-operator) interleaving, and maximizing memory-level parallelism (SIMD, coroutine software prefetching, hyper-threading when bandwidth is underutilized).
papers.hardwareEnv: Dual-socket 48-core Intel Xeon Platinum 8468 Sapphire Rapids (CXL 1.1 host), 210 MB LLC, 8 DDR5 channels x 32 GB RDIMM per socket; only one socket (48 physical cores) used, HT disabled except scaling experiments. One SMART Modular CXA-4F1W CXL 2.0 Type 3 memory expander populated with 4x64 GB DDR5 RDIMMs (256 GB), attached via x16 PCIe 5.0 (32 GT/s/lane), operating under CXL 1.1. Linux kernel 6.9.0 with weighted memory interleaving. Measured: DRAM peak 268.6 GB/s (MLC, full socket, prefetch on) vs CXL 43.0 GB/s; idle latency DRAM 111 ns vs CXL 229 ns (full socket).
papers.evalSetup: Star Schema Benchmark SF100 (SF1000 spot-checked) on Proteus, a pipelined parallel in-memory JIT (LLVM) query engine, cache-resident hash joins; plus microbenchmarks: 32 GB sequential read/write, 16 GB hash-table build + probe, filtering across power-of-2 selectivities, radix partitioning across power-of-2 fanouts. Variables: DRAM:CXL weighted-interleave ratio (9:1 through CXL-only), SNC off/SNC-2/SNC-4 (8/4/2 DRAM channels), hardware prefetching on/off, scalar vs AVX-512 reads, core-count scaling, hyper-threading. Profiling via Intel MLC, sysbench, PCM, VTune top-down (memory-bound slots, bandwidth-/latency-bound stalls).
papers.baselines: DRAM-only placement (primary baseline for all normalized speedups); CXL-only placement; range of static DRAM:CXL weighted-interleave configurations. Positioned against Huang et al. ADMS'24 ("Bandwidth Expansion via CXL"), whose single-config claim it refutes. No tiering systems (TPP/Memtis etc.) are run as baselines.
papers.keyFindings: (1) Transparent DRAM:CXL interleaving degrades SSB average performance by 20% on full-socket and SNC-2 with prefetching enabled, even at the lightest 9:1 ratio; disabling hardware prefetching cuts degradation to at most 7%, showing prefetchers misbehave on heterogeneous interleaved memory. (2) Only SNC-4 (2 DRAM channels, DRAM bandwidth comparable to CXL) with prefetching sees gains: 2% average, 10% best single query (Q3.1) at 8:2. (3) No single interleave ratio is optimal: optimal ratios shift up to 88% with workload parameters (e.g., partitioning fanout: 9:1 to 5:5; filter selectivity: 6:4 to 4:6); microbenchmark upsides are large where DRAM is scarce (up to 72-90% speedups in SNC-4). (4) Loaded CXL latency inflates up to 5x under load with prefetching (DRAM up to 2x); loaded DRAM latency can exceed idle CXL latency. (5) Bandwidth expansion helps only when DRAM bandwidth is actually saturated; scalar reads cannot saturate full-socket DRAM (underutilization costs up to 60% of potential gains), AVX-512 SIMD or hyper-threading recovers this; SNC is not required for bandwidth expansion benefits.
papers.limitations: Single CXL device (one SMART CXA-4F1W expander behind one x16 link, ~43 GB/s) — no multi-device, no per-device management, no CXL-to-CXL interference. Single CPU platform (Intel SPR, CXL 1.1 host); no AMD results despite AMD trends motivating the paper. Measurement/insights paper only: the proposed adaptive per-operator interleaving system is described as implementation strategies but never built or evaluated. Single-workload-at-a-time runs; no multi-tenant or co-runner interference experiments. SSB only for full queries (SF100; SF1000 only spot-checked on full socket); hash tables cache-resident in SSB runs. Static weighted-interleave page allocation only; no migration or dynamic policies tested. No tail-latency analysis (throughput/runtime only).
papers.openQuestions: Authors explicitly punt on building the workload-adaptive runtime they advocate (per-operator interleave selection, predictive data migration between hash-join build/probe phases, hysteresis against thrashing, counter-driven prefetch toggling) — all left as "implementation strategies." Untested: behavior with multiple CXL devices or higher aggregate CXL bandwidth; AMD hosts; CXL 2.0/3.x hosts and back-invalidate; concurrent queries / multi-tenant contention on the CXL link; why exactly hardware prefetchers interact pathologically with interleaved memory (mechanism not root-caused); OS/buffer-pool integration of placement hints.
evidenceQuotes: For CXL memory expansion, we use a SMART® CXA-4F1W device [42], which is a CXL 2.0 Type 3 memory expander, populated with 4x64 GB DDR5 RDIMMs. This device connects to the utilized CPU socket via a 16-lane (x16) PCIe 5.0 interface. Consequently, the CXL link operates under the CXL 1.1 protocol, utilizing the PCIe 5.0 physical layer's data rate of 32 GT/s per lane.

We conduct our experiments on a server running Linux kernel version 6.9.0 with support for weighted memory interleaving [7]. The server has a dual-socket 48-core Intel® Xeon® Platinum 8468 Sapphire Rapids CPU supporting the CXL 1.1 protocol with 2 hyperthreads per physical core, a 210 MB last-level cache (LLC), and 8 DDR5 DRAM channels with 1x32 GB DDR5 RDIMMs per channel.
We find that interleaving DRAM and CXL memory transparently to a state-of-the-art query execution engine Proteus, when running the SSB workload, degrades its average performance by 20%.
However, disabling hardware prefetching dramatically reduces this penalty, limiting performance degradation to at most 7% for the lightest interleaving configurations (9:1, 8:2).
No single memory interleaving configuration achieves optimal performance across workload variations, with optimal ratios varying by up to 88% based on workload parameters
But even before the memory bandwidth is fully utilized, the loaded CXL latency increases up to 5x times when hardware prefetching is enabled.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Strong methodological neighbor but orthogonal to the 4-device direction: it uses exactly one CXL expander behind one x16 link, so it says nothing about per-device scheduling or CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference — the requester's testbed (4x CZ120, 2 already interleaved into node 1) can directly extend its questions. Its core findings independently corroborate the requester's own measurements: modest CXL bandwidth (~43 GB/s per link vs their ~35.5 GiB/s per region), severe loaded-latency inflation on CXL (up to 5x, matching their 2.0-2.13x co-runner victim slowdown), and that naive/transparent interleaving hurts unless DRAM bandwidth is saturated. Its explicitly unbuilt future work — per-operator, phase-aware, counter-driven adaptive placement with hysteresis — is essentially what ObjPlace already implements at object granularity, making this a citable motivation paper and a claim ObjPlace can be positioned against; the per-device/multi-tenant extension remains entirely open for the requester.

papers.title: Enabling Efficient Large Recommendation Model Training with Near CXL Memory Processing (ReCXL)
papers.venue: ISCA 2024 (51st ACM/IEEE Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture), pp. 382-395
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 physical CXL devices. Naive-CXL baseline: remote NUMA socket of a real dual-socket Xeon server emulating one CXL memory pool (1 DDR5 channel on socket 1). Proposed ReCXL: simulated only — default config is one ReCXL device with 4 channels x 2 DIMMs (1 TB, 16 ranks); scalability study sweeps up to 128 ranks / multiple simulated devices.
papers.mainProblem: DLRM training embedding layers need 100s of GB-TBs of capacity and huge irregular memory bandwidth; placing them in CXL memory scales capacity but the CXL link (PCIe 5.0 x8, 32 GB/s — slower than one DDR5-4800 channel at 38.4 GB/s) causes 1.8-3.1x per-iteration slowdown vs local DRAM, making naive CXL memory impractical for training.
papers.mainIdea: ReCXL: a CXL Type-2 near-memory-processing memory-pool device that executes the ENTIRE embedding training (forward + backward + optimizer update) inside CXL memory using rank-level NMP PUs in the DIMM data buffers plus an 8-core device processor, so only indices/gradients cross the bandwidth-limited CXL link. Software-hardware co-optimizations: dependency-free prefetching (resolves RAW dependencies between gradient updates and next-batch lookups) and fine-grained update scheduling, plus embedding-table placement that splits long vectors across ranks.
papers.hardwareEnv: No real CXL silicon. (1) Real dual-socket server for the naive-CXL baseline: 2x Intel Xeon Gold 6430 32-core @2.1 GHz, 4 ranks x 4x 128GB DDR5-4800 DIMMs; socket 0 = 4 channels local memory, socket 1 = 1 channel "emulated as CXL memory". (2) ReCXL itself: cycle-accurate simulator built from modified Ramulator ("Romulator") + ZSim; simulated device = 4 channels x 2 DIMMs DDR5-4800, 1 TB total, 1x 128-bit SIMD PE per rank-level PU, 8-core @2.4 GHz device processor; CXL latency modeled at 70 ns; DNN-layer times taken from a real A100 GPU and replayed. Synopsys DC 28nm for PU area/power, Micron DDR4 power calculator + CACTI-IO for energy. No kernel version relevant.
papers.evalSetup: DLRM open-source model with 4 configurations RM1-RM4 (RM1-3 from Gupta et al., RM4 an extreme case: 80 tables, 1M rows, dim 128, 160 lookups), training batch sizes 1024-8192 (sensitivity up to 64K), embedding dims 16-256, lookups 10-160. End-to-end training time simulated by offloading embedding ops from ZSim to Ramulator and replaying A100 cycles for MLP layers. Scalability swept 16-128 ranks.
papers.baselines: (1) Hybrid CPU-GPU baseline (embeddings in host DRAM, CPU processes them; GPU does MLPs); (2) NaiveCXL (embeddings in CXL memory, CPU processing); (3) RecNMP (inference-only rank-level NMP, forward pass only); (4) ReCXL-D (device processor only, no rank-level NMP); (5) ReCXL-I (idealized infinite CXL bandwidth, zero latency).
papers.keyFindings: ReCXL outperforms the CPU-GPU baseline by 7.1-10.6x (9.4x avg) and naive CXL memory by 12.7-31.3x (22.6x avg); beats RecNMP by 6.4-8.1x and ReCXL-D by 4.3-7.9x (6.5x avg). NaiveCXL is 1.8-2.9x SLOWER than the CPU-GPU baseline, quantifying the CXL-bandwidth penalty for bandwidth-bound workloads. ReCXL-I (infinite CXL bandwidth) gains only marginally over ReCXL, showing NMP fully hides the link bottleneck. Performance scales with rank count until internal bandwidth exceeds ~20-80x the CXL link bandwidth (r<1 saturation); RM4 still scales at 128 ranks, RM3 saturates at 32. Also reports energy reductions vs all baselines (Fig 16).
papers.limitations: Entirely simulation-based for the proposed system (custom Ramulator+ZSim integration, not silicon-validated); the "CXL memory" in all real-machine measurements is a remote NUMA socket, and CXL link latency is an optimistic fixed 70 ns model. No real CXL device (no ASIC/FPGA) anywhere in the evaluation. Requires custom NMP hardware in DIMM data buffers plus a device processor and PyTorch/driver stack changes — nothing deployable on commodity CXL expanders. Single-workload class (DLRM embedding training); no multi-tenant runs, no interference or QoS study, no tail-latency analysis. Multiple ReCXL devices are treated as one flat pooled address space; cross-device contention is never measured. Energy uses a DDR4 power calculator despite modeling DDR5.
papers.openQuestions: How ReCXL behaves with real CXL controller latencies/variability rather than a fixed 70 ns; sharing the ReCXL pool among multiple training jobs or tenants (isolation, scheduling across devices); CXL 2.0/3.0 switch-fabric effects when "up to 4K nodes" are claimed but never simulated at scale beyond 128 ranks; coherence cost of the Type-2 design; applicability to inference serving or other sparse workloads; interaction with host-side tiering when embedding tables are mixed across host DRAM and ReCXL (mentioned as possible but not evaluated in depth).
sourceUrls: https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/stampPDF/getPDF.jsp?tp=&arnumber=10609725 (full PDF read via NCSU library subscription)
evidenceQuotes: To thoroughly evaluate the performance of our ReCXL architecture, we employ both real machines and simulators. As prior research indicates [10], [45], [61], the performance metrics (bandwidth and latency) of CXL memory closely resemble those of a remote NUMA node in a dual-socket system. Hence, we simulate the naïve CXL memory using a real dual-socket system by allocating memory in the remote NUMA node, with detailed configurations provided in Table I.

While for ReCXL, we developed a cycle-accurate simulator by integrating the DRAM simulator Romulator [34] and the host simulator ZSim [57] to evaluate its performance and effectiveness. Romulator is modified to simulate the NMP-featured ReCXL memory pool by adding the rank-level PU and the ReCXL device processor

Table I (System Configurations): Host CPU: 2×Intel Xeon Gold 6430 32-core @2.1GHz; DIMM: 4 Ranks ×4 128GB DDR5-4800 DIMM; Memory: socket 0: 4 channels (local memory), socket 1: 1 channel (emulated as CXL memory) — Configuration of ReCXL: NMP-DIMM 4 Ranks ×4 128GB DDR5-4800 DIMM; Device Memory: 4 channels, 2 DIMMs per channel, 1TB in total; NMP PU: 1×128 bit-width SIMD PE per PU, 1 PU per Rank; Device Processor: 8-core @2.4GHz
The CXL memory access latency we modeled aligns with a latency of 70 ns as per [60], which adheres to the recommended latency targets in the CXL Specification [5].
the ReCXL device can connect to the CXL switch via its PCIe slot. Multiple ReCXL devices can compose a highly scalable CXL memory pool where embedding tables are stored.
Evaluation results show that ReCXL outperforms the CPU-GPU baseline and the naïve CXL memory by 7.1× ∼ 10.6× (9.4× on average) and 12.7× ∼ 31.3× (22.6× on average), respectively.
the transmission bandwidth of CXL, particularly over PCIe 5.0 ×8, is only 32GB/s, slower than even a single channel of DDR5-4800 memory, which offers 38.4GB/s
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Low direct methodological relevance: ReCXL is a simulated custom NMP hardware proposal with zero real CXL devices, so it offers no techniques deployable on the requester's 4x CZ120 testbed. Its main value is as motivation and related-work positioning: it independently confirms (via NUMA emulation) that bandwidth-bound ML workloads degrade 1.8-3.1x on CXL because link bandwidth (~32 GB/s PCIe5 x8) trails even one DDR5 channel — closely matching the requester's measured ~35.5 GiB/s per-region saturation and 2.0-2.13x co-runner slowdown. Notably, ReCXL treats multiple devices as one flat pooled address space and never studies per-device scheduling, cross-device interference, or multi-tenant QoS, so it leaves open exactly the per-device independent-resource direction the requester is considering; cite it as the NDP/accelerator end of the design space that ObjPlace-style software placement contrasts with.

papers.title: No Atomics, No Problem. Developing a RAG Pipeline for Shared CXL Memory
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Computers, vol. 75, issue 4, pp. 1291-1308 (CXL special issue); DOI 10.1109/TC.2026.3667821
papers.numCXLDevices: unknown (full text paywalled; abstract confirms shared fabric-attached memory behind an H3 Falcon C5022 CXL switch and famfs page-level interleaving, which implies >=2 memory devices, but the exact device count and model are never visible in any text I could access)
papers.mainProblem: How to actually build and run a commercial RAG pipeline (vector search + database) on real multi-host SHARED CXL memory today, given that hosts sharing CXL fabric-attached memory form two disjoint cache-coherency domains and current x86 CPUs cannot use atomic operations correctly on shared CXL memory — so standard shared-memory synchronization is unavailable.
papers.mainIdea: Experience paper: run unmodified DuckDB and Faiss over shared CXL memory via famfs (Fabric-Attached Memory File System), using famfs producer-consumer queues to get synchronization patterns that need no atomics; use famfs page-level interleaving to scale multi-host read throughput from one shared Faiss index; orchestrate shared-memory allocations with Kubernetes in a full vertical RAG deployment.
papers.hardwareEnv: H3 Falcon C5022 CXL 2.0 switch chassis with fabric-attached CXL memory shared by multiple hosts (single- and multi-host experiments; a second host serves queries from the same Faiss index). NVMe SSD used as the demand-paging comparison tier. Host CPU models, DRAM config, CXL memory device model/capacity/count, link widths, and kernel version are in the paywalled full text — could not verify. Authors span Scalemem AS (Oslo), Micron (famfs author John Groves), H3 Platform, and PNNL.
papers.evalSetup: Commercial RAG pipeline over all of English Wikipedia split into 46 million text passages embedded into a high-dimensional embedding space; Faiss vector index + DuckDB passage store placed in shared CXL memory via famfs; subjected to heavy load in single-host and multi-host experiments with both real query workloads and synthetic workloads; multi-host scaling test with a second host serving queries from the same shared Faiss index; Kubernetes-orchestrated full vertical RAG deployment.
papers.baselines: Same queries run with demand paging from NVMe (mmap/page-cache over NVMe SSD) as the primary baseline; presumably local-DRAM numbers also appear in the full text but I could not verify that.
papers.keyFindings: (1) Unmodified DuckDB and Faiss get up to 12x query-latency reduction on real workloads and 40x on synthetic workloads when data lives in shared CXL memory vs demand paging from NVMe. (2) famfs producer-consumer queues provide correct synchronization across the two disjoint coherency domains without any atomic operations on current x86. (3) famfs page-level interleaving gives near-linear throughput scaling when a second host serves queries from the same shared Faiss index. (4) Shared-memory allocations can be orchestrated by Kubernetes in a full vertical RAG deployment.
papers.limitations: Authors' own admission (abstract): high-performance atomics and locking in shared CXL memory remain open challenges — their solution sidesteps rather than solves synchronization, restricting the model to read-mostly sharing plus lock-free producer-consumer queues. Methodology weaknesses visible from accessible text: baseline is NVMe demand paging (an easy target), not DRAM, so the 12x/40x numbers say CXL beats storage, not how close it gets to memory; multi-host scaling shown only up to a second host; single switch testbed; experience-paper style with no interference/QoS/tail-latency analysis and no per-device measurements evident. Full evaluation details unverifiable (paywalled).
papers.openQuestions: Explicitly punted: high-performance atomics and locking mechanisms for shared CXL memory across coherency domains (they discuss it as an open challenge). Obviously untested from what is visible: scaling beyond two hosts, write-heavy shared workloads, multi-tenant isolation and cross-host/cross-device interference on the shared fabric, tail-latency behavior under contention, and comparison against DRAM-resident serving rather than only NVMe paging.
evidenceQuotes: We share early experiments with software development for shared CXL memory on the H3 Falcon C5022 CXL switch.
we measure up to 12x latency reduction with real workloads and 40x reduction with synthetic workloads on CXL, compared to the same queries run with demand paging on NVMe

Lastly we show how famfs page-level interleaving enables near-linear throughput scaling when a second host serves queries from the same Faiss index on shared fabric-attached memory and how shared memory allocations can be orchestrated by Kubernetes in a full vertical RAG deployment.

We explain the current challenges of working with two disjoint cache coherency domains and explain how the Fabric-Attached Memory File System (famfs) and famfs producer-consumer queues provide synchronization patterns without atomic operations on current x86 CPUs.

Author affiliations (CSDL metadata): Alfred Bratterud / Gisle Dankel / Amin Farajianzadeh — Scalemem AS, Oslo, Norway; John Groves — Micron Technology, Inc., Boise, ID, USA; Chengyi Juan — H3 Platform, Inc., New Taipei City, Taiwan; Joshua Suetterlein — Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, WA, USA
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Directly relevant tooling overlap: the requester already runs famfs on 2 of their 4 CZ120 devices, and this paper is the flagship application study of famfs (co-authored by famfs creator John Groves), including famfs page-level cross-device interleaving — the switch-attached analogue of the requester's root-decoder 2-way interleaved region. However, its setting is multi-HOST sharing through an H3 Falcon C5022 switch, not single-host multi-device management: devices are fused into one shared pool, the baseline is NVMe paging rather than DRAM, and there is no per-device treatment, interference, or QoS analysis. For the candidate direction (per-device placement, CXL-to-CXL interference, tail-aware QoS), this paper is complementary motivation — it demonstrates real RAG/vector-search demand for pooled CXL and near-linear multi-consumer scaling under interleaving — while leaving cross-device contention and independent per-device scheduling completely unexamined, which supports the novelty claim of ObjPlace's next step. It also flags no-atomics synchronization as an open problem, orthogonal to the requester's single-host coherent setup.

papers.title: Analysis and Optimized CXL-Attached Memory Allocation for Long-Context LLM Fine-Tuning
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.DC), no conference venue indicated
papers.numCXLDevices: Config A: 1 (CXA-8F2W 512GB AIC); Config B: 2 (CXA-4F1W 256GB AICs) — SMART Modular CMM CXL 2.0 add-in cards
papers.mainProblem: Long-context LLM fine-tuning with optimizer/parameter offloading exhausts host DRAM; CXL AIC memory could extend capacity but PyTorch lacks per-tensor NUMA allocation control and naive placement of latency-critical optimizer data on higher-latency CXL memory severely degrades training throughput.
papers.mainIdea: Characterize CXL AIC memory for fine-tuning offload workloads, then build (1) a PyTorch extension enabling tensor-level system-memory/NUMA placement control and (2) a CXL-aware memory allocator (latency-first greedy algorithm producing an allocation table with per-data-item placement policy and interleave ratio) that pins latency-critical tensors (optimizer states used in the CPU optimizer STEP) in local DRAM while interleaving latency-tolerant, bandwidth-consuming data across one or more CXL devices.
papers.hardwareEnv: 1x Intel Xeon 6780E (Sierra Forest E-core), 512 GB DDR5-6400 (4x128GB) local DRAM, 2x NVIDIA H100 80GB PCIe GPUs, PCIe 5.0 x16 for GPUs and AICs; CXL: Config A = 1x SMART Modular CXA-8F2W 512GB CXL 2.0 AIC, Config B = 2x CXA-4F1W 256GB CXL 2.0 AICs; CXL exposed as CPU-less NUMA nodes; Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, Linux kernel v6.9; PyTorch 2.5.1, DeepSpeed ZeRO-Offload, Flash-Attention, Liger-Kernel.
papers.evalSetup: Causal-LM fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-7B and Mistral NeMo 12B with 4K-32K context lengths, batch sizes 1-48, bf16 mixed precision with fp32 master params/optimizer states offloaded to CPU memory via DeepSpeed ZeRO-Offload; activation checkpointing; single- and dual-GPU runs; measured end-to-end training throughput and per-phase (e.g., optimizer STEP) latency under DRAM-only vs naive CXL interleaving vs proposed allocator, on single-AIC and dual-AIC configs.
papers.baselines: DRAM-only (all offload data in local DRAM); naive CXL placement via numactl --interleave=all; comparison discussion vs OS-level tiering systems TPP and NOMAD (argued suboptimal, workload-agnostic).
papers.keyFindings: Naive interleaving across DRAM+CXL yields 76-94% (7B) and 72-93% (12B) of DRAM-only throughput; the CXL-aware allocator recovers 97-99% (7B, up to +21% over naive) and 88-96% (12B, up to +16%) with a single AIC, and 100-101% of DRAM-only with dual AICs. Naive CXL placement inflates CPU optimizer STEP latency to ~4x baseline for >20M-element tensors, motivating DRAM pinning of optimizer data. GPU<->host transfer bandwidth from CXL is comparable to DRAM over PCIe; latency differences are negligible for asynchronous transfers. PyTorch lacks tensor-level NUMA control, requiring their extension.
papers.limitations: Authors admit limited CXL device availability constrains testbed scope (claiming observations are "representative and transferable"); single-AIC with 12B or dual-GPU setups shows residual bandwidth contention that only dual AICs fully resolve. Methodological weaknesses: max 2 CXL devices; single workload class (offload-based fine-tuning, one framework stack); no multi-tenant or co-runner interference experiments; E-core Xeon 6780E host may not generalize to P-core/AMD platforms; allocation table appears offline/profile-driven for a predictable workload, not dynamic; no comparison against actual runs of TPP/NOMAD kernels (discussed, not measured as far as reported).
papers.openQuestions: Scaling beyond 2 AICs and cross-device interference when multiple independently managed CXL devices serve different tenants/streams; dynamic/online placement for less predictable workloads; interaction with OS tiering (TPP/NOMAD) rather than replacing it; multi-GPU larger-model training; QoS between latency-critical and bandwidth-hungry tenants sharing the same AIC. Authors explicitly leave "future exploration of advanced memory management strategies in heterogeneous systems" enabled by their PyTorch extension.
