papers.title: Space-Control: Process-Level Isolation for Sharing CXL-based Disaggregated Memory
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2603.06951)
papers.numCXLDevices: 1 (simulated shared disaggregated-memory device modeled in SST, shared by 8 simulated gem5 hosts)
papers.mainProblem: CXL 3.0 shared/pooled memory only enforces host-level access control: once a host is authorized for a shared region, every process on that host can access it, violating least privilege. Process-level isolation is left to each host's OS, so a compromised or malicious OS/kernel on any sharing host can read/corrupt other tenants' data in shared disaggregated memory (SDM). The paper asks: "How can we ensure isolation in shared disaggregated memory that enforces the principle of least privilege and operates independently of the OS with minimal overhead?"
papers.mainIdea: Space-Control, a HW/SW co-design that adds a cross-host process identity primitive and moves authorization out of the OS. Three components: (1) SPACE (Secure Process Attribute Context Engine), a hardware-rooted validation engine that registers/authenticates a process's address space and mints an immutable ContextID; (2) a Permission Table mapping PA ranges of shared memory to authorized ContextIDs across hosts, with keys/permissions managed via the CXL fabric manager; (3) a Permission Checker, an on-chip enforcer after the LLC / before the CXL downstream port that validates every LD/ST to shared memory, with a small permission cache to amortize lookups. Supports up to 127 concurrent processes across 255 hosts.
papers.hardwareEnv: No real hardware. Simulation: CXL-ClusterSim = gem5 (host fidelity) + SST (shared disaggregated memory, parallelized simulation). Simulated config (Table 2): 8-core TimingSimpleCPU @ 4 GHz, 32 KiB L1 I+D/core, 1 MiB L2/core, 16 MiB shared L3; local memory 16 GB DDR4-2400, 2 channels (38.4 GiB/s); remote (SDM) memory 16 GiB, 4 channels, 76.8 GiB/s; Ubuntu 22.04.4, kernel 6.9.9. Eight simulated hosts; fabric-manager communication modeled over shared CXL.mem instead of CXL.io.
papers.evalSetup: GAPBS graph kernels (pr, bfs, bc, tc; ordered regular-to-random access), modified so a graph is shared across hosts in the SDM region; number of hosts accessing the same SDM region scaled 1 to 8 in powers of two; first 4 billion cycles of the region of interest simulated per workload per host. Sensitivity studies on permission-cache size and permission-table structure/fragmentation.
papers.baselines: Baseline CXL 3.0 system with no per-access permission checks ("cxl"); an ideal flat permission-table structure similar to Border-Control (Olson et al. 2015); "deact-like" (Kommareddy et al. 2021); "mondrian-ext" (Mondrian memory protection, Witchel et al. 2002).
papers.keyFindings: With a modest 16 KiB permission cache, Space-Control incurs ~3.3% average performance overhead vs. the unchecked CXL 3.0 baseline. Single-entry best case is 7.3% average overhead at 1 host, growing to 12.1% at 8 hosts; worst-case fragmentation (tc with relabeling skipped) reaches 3.8x vs cxl. A 2 KiB permission cache already reaches 99.9% hit rate and improves CPI overhead 2.3x over uncached. Storage overhead of permission metadata is 1.56% for 255 hosts sharing 4 KiB pages across 127 processes.
papers.limitations: Authors' own: revocation cannot stop in-flight instructions from committing — a tiny window of at most two BISnp exists where an attacker can violate isolation; they trust CXL hardware to function correctly and provide availability; physical attacks and side channels are out of scope. Methodological: entirely simulated (gem5+SST CXL-ClusterSim) — no real CXL silicon, no FPGA prototype; only one shared memory device modeled; simplified fabric-manager modeling (CXL.mem instead of CXL.io); small simulated system (8-core TimingSimpleCPU hosts, 16 GiB SDM, 4B-cycle windows); only GAPBS graph kernels — no databases, LLM, or general multi-tenant cloud workloads; the SPACE engine and Permission Checker require new hardware in CPUs/devices that does not exist in any shipping product.
papers.openQuestions: How the design performs on real CXL 3.x hardware or at datacenter scale; interaction with CXL TSP/IDE and confidential-computing (TEE) stacks; multi-device pooled memory and cross-device permission management; performance under bandwidth-saturating or latency-sensitive (tail) workloads rather than graph kernels; revocation-window closure; key-management scalability beyond 127 processes / 255 hosts; integration with dynamic capacity (DCD) and memory tiering/placement runtimes.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Low direct relevance to the requester's testbed work: Space-Control targets CXL 3.0 multi-host shared/pooled memory security and is evaluated purely in gem5+SST simulation, whereas the requester has a single-host CXL 2.0 memory-expansion box (4x CZ120) with no cross-host sharing and no hardware hooks for SPACE/Permission Checker. It offers no data on per-device bandwidth, cross-device interference, or tail latency. It is useful mainly as related work for the multi-tenant-isolation framing: it shows the security/permission side of CXL multi-tenancy is being addressed architecturally, letting the requester position per-device performance isolation and QoS (which Space-Control explicitly does not address) as a complementary, hardware-measurable gap.
evidenceQuotes: We have used CXL-ClusterSim (Goswami et al., [2026]) for evaluating Space-Control. CXL-Clustersim uses gem5 (Lowe-Power et al., [2020]) to model the hosts for fidelity and SST (Rodrigues et al., [2011]) to model the shared disaggregated memory and parallelize the simulation.
Number of devices: 1
There are eight hosts. For simplicity, instead of modeling CXL.io for FM, we use shared CXL.mem for host and FM communication.

We run GAPBS kernels while scaling the number of hosts accessing the same SDM region from 1 to 8 in powers of two. We use four representative kernels: pr, bfs, bc, tc; ordered from more regular to more random access patterns.
Space-Control incurs a minimal 3.3% performance penalty with a modest 16 KiB cache

Current CXL-based sharing mechanisms provide coarse-grained, host-level access control: once a host is authorized, all processes on that host can access the shared region. This violates the principle of least privilege.
One limitation of permission revocation is that it fails to prevent on-flight instructions getting committed. There exists a tiny window of at most two BISnp where an attacker can violate isolation.

papers.title: PIPM: Partial and Incremental Page Migration for Multi-host CXL Disaggregated Shared Memory
papers.venue: ASPLOS 2026 (Vol. 2), Session 6D Disaggregated Memory Systems; DOI 10.1145/3779212.3790203
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 physical (fully simulated; models 1 shared CXL-DSM memory node of 128GB serving 4 hosts in ChampSim)
papers.mainProblem: Existing page-migration schemes (Nomad, Memtis, HeMem), designed for single-host tiered memory, are inefficient in multi-host CXL 3.x cache-coherent disaggregated shared memory (CXL-DSM): (1) "local gain, global pain" — promoting a hot shared page into one host's DRAM makes other hosts' accesses non-cacheable inter-host accesses that are slower than CXL memory access; (2) kernel-based whole-page (4KB) migration overheads (page-table updates, TLB shootdowns, bulk copies) are amplified across hosts.
papers.mainIdea: Hardware-based partial + incremental migration co-designed with the CXL multi-host coherence protocol. Partial migration: migrate only the cache blocks exclusively/majority-accessed by one host (majority-vote policy with per-page access counters), keeping the rest in CXL memory. Incremental migration: data moves via ordinary cache-fill/eviction traffic — no extra bulk transfers, no kernel involvement. Architectural support: a two-level hardware remapping table (16KB global remapping cache on the CXL device + 1MB local remapping cache per host RC) and a PIPM coherence protocol (verified with Murphi model checking on MSI) enabling coherent inter-host access to blocks resident in another host's local DRAM.
papers.hardwareEnv: No physical testbed — cycle-level, trace-based timing simulation using ChampSim ("the Championship simulator"), 8x scaled-down config (Table 2): 4 hosts, each 1 single-socket CPU with 4 OoO cores @4GHz (6-wide, 224-entry ROB), 32KB L1, 2MB/core LLC; per-host local DRAM 1x DDR5-4800 channel 32GB; shared CXL-DSM 2x DDR5-4800 channels 128GB; CXL link 50ns latency / 5GB/s per direction (100ns switch case in sensitivity); CXL directory 2048-set 16-way x16 slices. Traces collected with Intel Pintool on real hardware, replayed with 1B-instruction checkpoints, 10B instructions per core.
papers.evalSetup: 13 memory-intensive workloads (Table 1): GAPBS graph kernels SSSP/BFS/PR/CC/BC/TC on Kron (48GB each), XSBench (42GB), PARSEC streamcluster/fluidanimate/canneal/bodytrack (8-18GB), Silo TPC-C (24GB) and YCSB R:W 4:1 (15GB). Heap data shared across the 4 simulated hosts and initially placed in CXL-DSM; code/page tables/stacks private local. Migration baselines assume 20us per-4KB kernel migration cost, 10ms interval, batched TLB shootdowns. Sensitivity: CXL link latency (50 vs 100ns), bandwidth (x8/x16/x32 lanes), remapping-cache sizes, migration threshold (4-16 similar).
papers.baselines: (1) Native CXL-DSM (no migration); (2) Nomad (recency-based, async kernel migration); (3) Memtis (frequency-based); (4) HeMem (frequency-based); ablations: (5) OS-skew (PIPM policy + kernel migration mechanism), (6) HW-static (PIPM incremental mechanism + static mapping, Intel Flat Mode-like); (7) Local-only / Ideal upper bound (single socket, all-DRAM).
papers.keyFindings: PIPM achieves 1.86x average (up to 2.54x) speedup over Native CXL-DSM and reaches 0.73x of the all-DRAM Ideal; graph analytics gain 142-151%, databases (TPC-C/YCSB) 36-53%. Single-host schemes Nomad/Memtis/HeMem give only marginal gains and degrade performance by up to 18% in five workloads. PIPM beats ablations OS-skew and HW-static by 41.7% and 61.1% avg. Local memory hit rate 56.1% avg vs Nomad 26.5%/Memtis 31.0%/HeMem 28.1%; inter-host access stalls drop to 1.5% of execution time. Memory frugal: 7.3% of footprint remapped at page level, only 5.5% actually moved at line level (vs 25% fixed for HW-static). With 100ns switch latency PIPM gains an extra 55.7% avg. Hardware cost: 16KB global + 1MB per-host remapping caches; coherence protocol verified deadlock-free/SC with Murphi.
papers.limitations: Entirely simulation-based (ChampSim trace-driven, 8x scaled-down: 4 cores/host, 5GB/s CXL links) — no real CXL silicon, no FPGA prototype, and requires new hardware in both the CXL device and each host's root complex plus a modified coherence protocol, so it is not deployable on any existing platform. Only 4 hosts simulated; scalability to more hosts is argued qualitatively in the Discussion (majority-vote "continues to suppress performance-degrading migrations") but not measured. Single shared CXL memory node modeled — no multi-device CXL pool, no device-level interference or QoS. Assumes CXL 3.x multi-host hardware coherence, which has no shipping hardware. No tail-latency or multi-tenant isolation evaluation; migration baselines' kernel costs are assumed constants (20us/4KB) rather than measured on the simulated system.
papers.openQuestions: Behavior at larger host counts and with CXL switches/fabrics beyond a latency knob; interaction with multiple CXL devices or pooled/interleaved regions; software interfaces for application-directed line-level migration (mentioned as future possibility in Related Work); how PIPM composes with capacity pressure in local DRAM (eviction policy under contention is lightly treated); real-hardware validation once CXL 3.x coherent multi-host devices exist; multi-tenant/QoS effects of hardware migration.
evidenceQuotes: We model the multi-host CXL-DSM architecture using a cycle-level, trace-based timing simulator [1, 24]. The simulator configuration is detailed in Table 2.
using the Championship simulator [1, 24] configured as a four-host CXL-DSM

Table 2. Scaled-down System Configuration. Architecture: 4 hosts, 1 single-socket CPU each host ... DRAM: 2x DDR5-4800 channels 128GB CXL-DSM; 1x DDR5-4800 channel 32GB DRAM per host ... CXL link latency: 50ns, bandwidth: 5GB/s (per direction)
We use an 8x scaled-down setting as the default configuration (32 cores => 4 cores per host, 64 GB/s (40 GB/s effective [15]) => 8 GB/s (5 GB/s) over x16 CXL lanes).
(1) We first execute the target multi-threaded workloads on real hardware and use Intel Pintool [8] to collect instruction and memory traces for each thread.
PIPM outperforms the other schemes across all workloads, achieving an average performance of 1.86x and 0.73x (up to 2.54x and 0.94x) compared to Native CXL-DSM and Ideal, respectively

papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Useful to cite as the migration-granularity counterpoint to page-level placement: PIPM's core evidence that whole-4KB migration is wasteful and that cache-block/incremental movement plus a placement policy aware of cross-host sharing wins (1.86x avg) supports ObjPlace's argument that placement granularity and access-pattern awareness matter more than hotness alone. However, it is pure ChampSim simulation of a hypothetical CXL 3.x coherent multi-host system with new hardware in the device and root complex — nothing runs on real silicon like the requester's CZ120 testbed, and it models one shared CXL memory node, not multiple independently schedulable devices. For the per-device direction, PIPM is orthogonal prior art (multi-host sharing vs single-host multi-device); its 'local gain, global pain' framing has a loose analog in cross-device interference but the paper offers no data on device-level bandwidth contention, QoS, or tail latency. Cite it in related work on migration granularity and hardware tiering (alongside Intel Flat Mode, Nomad, Memtis), not as a competing evaluation.

papers.title: A Programming Model for Disaggregated Memory over CXL (CXL0)
papers.numCXLDevices: 1 (one FPGA configured as a CXL 1.1 Type 2 device attached to one x86 host, plus a Teledyne LeCroy T516 protocol analyzer on the link)
papers.mainProblem: CXL promises cache-coherent shared/disaggregated memory pools, but there is no formal programming model for concurrent programs over CXL, so one cannot reason about correctness, data management, or crash consistency (including partial crashes where one machine fails while the pool survives) of systems built on it.
papers.mainIdea: CXL0, the first formal programming model for concurrent programs over CXL: an abstract machine of compute/memory nodes each with cache+memory, a small set of memory-access primitives (Read, LStore/RStore/MStore, LFlush/RFlush, RMWs) with formal operational semantics covering partial-system crashes; a mapping (via protocol-analyzer observation) from real CXL.mem/CXL.cache transactions to CXL0 primitives; and a general FliT-based transformation that makes any linearizable concurrent object durably linearizable under CXL0 in the distributed partial-crash setting.
papers.hardwareEnv: One x86 CPU host (model not stated) + one FPGA device using "a proprietary CXL IP by Intel" configured as a CXL 1.1 Type 2 device, with custom logic between FPGA memory and the CXL IP; a Teledyne LeCroy T516 Protocol Analyzer (PCIe 5.0/CXL) on the link. CPU accesses FPGA memory (HDM) via CXL.mem; FPGA accesses host memory via CXL.cache; both coherent. CPU model, DRAM config, link width, FPGA board model, and kernel version are not stated in the text. Latency measured with LATTester (CPU side) and custom AXI-cycle counting (FPGA side).
papers.evalSetup: Two-part evaluation: (1) use the protocol analyzer to observe which concrete CXL.mem/CXL.cache transactions are generated for every CXL0 primitive under all MESI state pairs (Table 1), showing a many-to-one mapping and that some primitives (host RStore, LFlush from either side) cannot be generated at all; (2) microbenchmark latency of individual CXL0 primitives in isolation for five access types (host->HM, host->HDM, device->HM, device->HDM host-bias, device->HDM device-bias), median of 1000 sequential accesses, invalid initial cache state for loads, full-cache-line stores. No application workloads, no end-to-end system, no throughput/bandwidth or multi-tenant experiments.
papers.baselines: No system baselines; results are cross-checked against prior latency characterizations ("consistent with previous findings [25, 51]"). The durability transformation adapts FliT [Wei et al.] and is compared conceptually (not empirically) to Izraelevitz et al., NVTraverse, Mirror, Montage.
papers.keyFindings: Local loads/stores are ~2x faster than remote for Read and MStore: 2.34x faster on the CPU, 1.94x on the FPGA device. Host and device accesses to their respective remote memory show the same latency despite different sub-protocols. For device writes to host-attached memory, MStore is 1.45x slower than RStore, which is 2.08x slower than LStore. RFlush is the only flush both sides can invoke; its latency is nearly identical to MStore. Current hardware/spec cannot generate host-side RStore or LFlush from either side, restricting programmer control, so the authors advocate extending the CXL spec with precise ISA-level primitives. Theoretically, the adapted FliT transformation gives durable linearizability under CXL0 with address-based automatic instrumentation.
papers.limitations: Authors admit: "given that CXL 3.0 hardware is not currently available, we cannot test our model against actual implementations. Thus, our evaluation is confined to version 1.1 of the CXL standard"; also no CPU/pool device implements CXL 3.0 back-invalidation, so cache-coherent shared pools are only modeled, not measured; CXL0 does not apply to today's non-coherent pools; the durability transformation still needs manual flush tuning; they omit modeling hardware write-back-responsibility policies. Evident from methodology: single FPGA prototype device, no production CXL ASIC, no memory-expander (Type 3) latency/bandwidth characterization, only isolated-primitive latency microbenchmarks (no applications, bandwidth, contention, or multi-device experiments), hardware model details (CPU, FPGA board, kernel) unreported, transformation never implemented/measured on hardware.
papers.openQuestions: How to compensate in software for missing hardware coherence in realistic (non-coherent or partially coherent) CXL 3.0 memory pools — explicitly called "an interesting open research question"; whether/when the CXL spec will expose the missing primitives (RStore from host, LFlush) as ISA-level controls; performance of the FliT-based durability transformation on real disaggregated hardware; behavior under real multi-host, multi-device pool configurations, which are only modeled abstractly.
evidenceQuotes: Our setup consists of an x86 CPU (host) and an FPGA (device), both running CXL 1.1, with a protocol analyzer connected between them. The CPU accesses FPGA memory via CXL.mem, and the FPGA accesses CPU memory via CXL.cache.
On the FPGA side, we use a proprietary CXL IP by Intel to configure it as a CXL Type 2 device.
The analyzer is a Teledyne LeCroy's T516 Protocol Analyzer for PCIe 5.0 and CXL, which supports all CXL sub-protocols and device types.
We observe that loads and stores to local memory are twice as fast as those to remote memory for Read and MStore primitives. For the CPU, it is 2.34x faster, and for the device, it is 1.94x faster
When a device writes to Host-attached Memory (green bars), MStore is 1.45x slower than RStore, which is, in turn, 2.08x slower than LStore.
However, given that CXL 3.0 hardware is not currently available, we cannot test our model against actual implementations. Thus, our evaluation is confined to version 1.1 of the CXL standard (see §5).
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Low direct relevance to the requester's 4x CZ120 Type 3 memory-expansion testbed: this paper's hardware is a single CXL 1.1 Type 2 FPGA (CXL.cache + CXL.mem coherent sharing), and its contribution is a formal semantics/durability model, not placement, bandwidth, interference, or QoS. It contains no multi-device, multi-tenant, or bandwidth-contention experiments, so it neither supports nor competes with per-device scheduling or CXL-to-CXL interference work. Useful mainly as related-work framing: its "partitioned disaggregated memory pool" configuration formally models exactly the requester's setting (N disjoint memory nodes per host), and its finding that primitive choice changes latency ~2x echoes the requester's 1.53x load-to-use measurement. Cite it if the paper discusses crash consistency or future coherent pools; otherwise it is orthogonal to ObjPlace-style placement/isolation.

papers.title: MEGALON: Efficient Data Sharing for Partly Coherent CXL Memory
papers.venue: OSDI (20th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation, OSDI '26)
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no physical CXL devices; CXL memory emulated as one NUMA socket of a 4-socket server)
papers.mainProblem: CXL 3.x lets multiple hosts share memory, but hardware cache coherence is expected to cover only a small coherent region (SCR, a few hundred MB) while total CXL memory spans TBs (the large non-coherent region, LNR). Existing software-coherence schemes (HCMeta, as in Tigon) put per-object coherence records AND the index in SCR; for large datasets the metadata does not fit, causing repeated unshare/reshare "churn" that degrades throughput by up to ~10x.
papers.mainIdea: Split the sharing metadata: the big but infrequently-updated index is logically shared by replicating it in each host's local DRAM and keeping replicas consistent via a CXL shared log (Node-Replication-style, with only the log tail pointer required to be in the SCR); only tiny, heavily-updated per-object coherence records (a lock bit + counter) live in the hardware-coherent SCR, and they are allocated dynamically only for read-write-shared objects. The shared log additionally enables cheap churn, local-DRAM partitions, local read-only data copies, and shrinkable coherence records.
papers.hardwareEnv: 4-socket server with Intel Xeon Gold 6418H CPUs. NUMA node 0 designated as emulated CXL memory (uncore frequency throttled to approximate CXL latency, following prior work); NUMA nodes 1-3 act as 3 emulated hosts, each with 24 physical cores (hyperthreading disabled) and 64 GB local DRAM. SCR is 200 MB by default (matching Tigon). No real CXL device, no link parameters; kernel version not stated; achieved emulated latency values not reported.
papers.evalSetup: Two applications built on MEGALON: a linearizable KV store (1KB objects, up to 24M keys) and a user-level shared file-system page cache (48GB dataset of 4KB pages). Microbenchmarks: Zipfian (0.99 and 0.7) read-only and read-write (5%/50% write) workloads while varying dataset size, SCR size (32MB-1GB+), key size (10-90B), coherence-record size (8-32 bits), and shared ratio; plus YCSB A/B/C/D/F macrobenchmark on 18M objects. Threads distributed equally across the 3 emulated hosts.
papers.baselines: HCMeta (authors' reimplementation of Tigon-style hardware-coherent metadata-based sharing in their KV store), HCMeta-Local (data in host-local DRAM, shared objects moved to CXL), HCMeta-Unlimited (idealized unlimited SCR); Tigon artifact measured directly for churn overhead (~55 us); MEGALON self-variants AllLog (all metadata via shared log) and Megalon-Data-Copy (local object replicas).
papers.keyFindings: With a 200MB SCR, MEGALON supports up to 12x larger datasets without churn than HCMeta (coherence records for up to 50M objects), improving throughput 4x-10x (10.11x at 5% writes / 24M keys, 4.22x at 50% writes); even when MEGALON itself churns it is 2.5x-14.9x faster (e.g., 11.16x at 64MB SCR) and each churn is ~8x cheaper. Read-only: 15x over HCMeta and even beats HCMeta-Unlimited thanks to local index replicas. YCSB speedups 3.18x-14.18x; page cache 1.88x-5.68x. Cost: only 7.6% more memory (27.71GB vs 25.76GB at 24M objects) for 15.25x higher throughput (14.19x more MOps/s per GB). MEGALON sustains high throughput down to 128MB SCR, 8x smaller than HCMeta needs.
papers.limitations: Entirely emulation-based: "CXL 3.0 hardware is not commercially available," so both the CXL memory and the SCR are emulated via a NUMA socket with uncore throttling on one 4-socket box — no real CXL latency/bandwidth asymmetries, no real multi-host fabric, no CXL.mem back-invalidation hardware. Only 3 emulated hosts evaluated; authors state MEGALON targets 8-16 nodes because local-memory footprint (index replicas) grows linearly with node count. Fail-stop model: failure of any host or CXL memory fails the whole system; KV store has no checkpointing. Coherence-record size is fixed at 32 bits (no dynamic sizing). Inter-host RPC path "barely optimized". No multi-tenant or interference experiments; no real bandwidth-contention study.
papers.openQuestions: Scaling beyond 8-16 hosts (partial metadata views, sharding across multiple shared logs) is explicitly left open. Dynamically choosing optimal coherence-record size per workload is unimplemented. Moving MPMC queue entries to LNR / using the shared log for RPC left as future work. Behavior on real CXL 3.x hardware with actual back-invalidate coherence, real link bandwidth limits, and cross-host contention is untested. Fault tolerance beyond fail-stop (host crash recovery via the shared log) is not addressed.
evidenceQuotes: Setup. CXL 3.0 hardware is not commercially available, so we emulate CXL and hosts on a 4-socket server with Intel Xeon Gold 6418H processors. We designate NUMA node 0 as CXL memory and nodes 1-3 as hosts. Each emulated host has 24 physical cores with hyperthreading disabled and 64GB local DRAM. To approximate CXL latencies, we throttle the uncore frequency of node 0, as in prior work [3].
We compare against three baselines: HCMeta, HCMeta-local, and HCMeta-Unlimited
All experiments by default runs on the KV Store application with 1KB objects. Unless stated otherwise, we use 200MB for the SCR (like in Tigon [26]).
Currently, M EGALON is targeted to a system with 8–16 nodes as M EGALON’s local memory footprint grows linearly with the number of nodes.
In fact, with a 200MB SCR, M EGALON can hold coherence records for up to 50M objects, which is 12× more than what HCMeta can support without churn.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Low direct relevance to the requester's testbed and direction. MEGALON is about multi-host CXL 3.x shared memory with a small hardware-coherent region — the requester's single-host EPYC 9745 + 4x CZ120 CXL 2.0 memory-expansion setup has no multi-host sharing, no SCR, and MEGALON's evaluation is pure NUMA emulation with zero physical CXL devices (so it offers no data on per-device behavior, cross-device interference, or bandwidth contention relevant to ObjPlace). Two indirect connections: (1) its metadata-splitting logic (put small hot state in the scarce fast/coherent tier, replicate large cold state) is a placement-policy pattern conceptually adjacent to ObjPlace's object-granularity DRAM/CXL split; (2) if the requester ever uses the famfs-hosted devices for cross-process shared state, MEGALON's shared-log/replicated-index design is the closest software-coherence prior art to cite. It is a useful related-work citation, not a competing baseline.

papers.title: Blowfish: Elastic Virtual Machine Memory for Disaggregated Memory
papers.venue: OSDI 2026 (USENIX)
papers.mainProblem: Memory overcommitment across VMs is bottlenecked by cold-memory rebalancing: page-access tracking under Transparent Huge Pages (THP) and frequent guest/IO page-table remapping make reclamation and restoration of cold (and free) VM memory slow, causing throughput and latency problems for existing mechanisms (ballooning, virtio-mem, HyperAlloc-style approaches).
papers.mainIdea: Blowfish is a paravirtualization-based memory overcommitment framework built on disaggregated memory that performs cold/free memory reclamation and restoration at microsecond scale: a lightweight guest-level THP-aware hotness tracker identifies cold pages using guest program semantics, and the hypervisor directly reclaims and reallocates host physical memory across VMs via a dedicated cross-layer path for cold memory that bypasses guest page-table and I/O page-table modifications.
papers.hardwareEnv: Unknown — full text not available before the conference. The abstract says the framework is "built on disaggregated memory" but does not name CXL, RDMA, or any hardware; no testbed details (CPU, DRAM, device model, kernel) could be read.
papers.evalSetup: Unknown in detail. From the abstract, evaluation compares reclamation/restoration speed and reclamation ratios against HyperAlloc under a bounded (5%) performance-degradation budget; specific workloads and how VMs were run are not stated in the abstract.
papers.baselines: HyperAlloc (explicitly named as state-of-the-art baseline). Likely also virtio-balloon/virtio-mem given the topic, but that is not verified from the paper text.
papers.keyFindings: Per the abstract: Blowfish performs cold/free memory reclamation and restoration at microsecond scale; page reclamation 2.48x faster and restoration 2.14x faster than HyperAlloc; improves memory reclamation ratios by 1.6x-6.1x while staying within 5% performance degradation.
papers.limitations: Cannot assess methodology weaknesses — the full text (methodology/evaluation sections) is not publicly available as of 2026-07-07 (OSDI '26 proceedings PDF not yet posted, no arXiv preprint found). From the abstract alone: the mechanism requires paravirtualized guests (guest-level hotness tracker), so it does not apply to unmodified/opaque guest VMs; the abstract never specifies the disaggregated-memory substrate, so whether results hold on real CXL hardware vs RDMA vs emulation is unverifiable.
papers.openQuestions: Whether the disaggregated-memory substrate is real CXL (and how many devices), RDMA, or emulation; multi-tenant interference behavior; applicability to unmodified guests. Unresolvable until the full paper is released at OSDI '26.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Blowfish operates at the hypervisor/VM layer (cross-VM cold-memory reclamation via paravirtualization), which is orthogonal to the requester's ObjPlace object-granularity DRAM/CXL placement and to the candidate per-device scheduling direction — it manages capacity elasticity, not device-level bandwidth/interference. It is relevant as related work if the requester pursues multi-tenant CXL memory elasticity or QoS: Blowfish's us-scale reclaim/restore path is the kind of mechanism a per-device, tail-aware placement system could sit under or compete with. However, since the abstract never names CXL and the testbed is unknown, it currently provides no evidence about real multi-device CXL behavior on hardware like the 4x CZ120 setup. Watch for the full text at OSDI '26 (July 2026) to check whether its "disaggregated memory" is CXL-based.
evidenceQuotes: In this paper, we propose Blowfish, a memory overcommitment framework built on disaggregated memory, performing cold (and free) memory reclamation and restoration at μs-scale.

Based on paravirtualization, Blowfish leverages a lightweight guest-level THP-aware hotness tracker to monitor page access and let the hypervisor directly reclaim and reallocate host physical memory across VMs with a dedicated cross-layer path for cold memory, bypassing the modifications of guest page table and modifications of I/O page table while benefiting from the rich program semantics of guest VM when recognizing the cold memory.

As a result, Blowfish significantly speeds up the page reclamation and restoration, 2.48× and 2.14× faster than the state-of-the-art solution, HyperAlloc, respectively, and improves memory reclamation ratios by 1.6×-6.1× within 5% performance degradation.

papers.title: MDK: Rethinking the Data Center Memory Reclamation Problem
papers.venue: OSDI '26 (USENIX), session "Memory Tiering and CXL"
papers.numCXLDevices: unknown
papers.mainProblem: Traditional memory-management tooling (OPT/Belady, Miss Ratio Curves, efficient MRC generation) optimizes application performance under a fixed memory budget. Data centers face the inverted problem: maximize the number of co-located jobs per server without violating performance SLOs by proactively reclaiming memory from running jobs; the traditional tools do not apply to this flipped optimization problem.
papers.mainIdea: MDK (Memory Designer's Kit): a framework for designing and evaluating data-center memory reclamation policies, comprising (1) an offline provably optimal reclamation policy (a bound analogous to OPT), (2) Memory Performance Curves (MPCs) that show how memory savings vary when constrained by a performance target (the dual of MRCs), and (3) an efficient MPC-generation technique up to 208x faster than simulation. Used to design three new data-center reclamation policies.
papers.hardwareEnv: Not verifiable — full paper embargoed until OSDI '26 (July 13-15, 2026). Abstract gives no testbed; the "208x faster than simulation" phrasing suggests a largely trace-/simulation-driven methodology, but this is inference, not verified fact. No CXL hardware is mentioned anywhere in the abstract.
papers.evalSetup: Not verifiable from available sources. Abstract states only that they "demonstrate MDK's utility by developing three data center policies" evaluated for average memory savings against a state-of-the-art policy; workloads, traces, and infrastructure are not disclosed in the abstract.
papers.baselines: Abstract mentions comparison against "a state-of-the-art policy" (unnamed in abstract; plausibly Google's proactive-reclamation/zswap lineage given the author list, but unverified) and against simulation for MPC-generation speed.
papers.keyFindings: From abstract only: MDK's MPC-generation technique is up to 208x faster than simulation; the three MDK-designed policies improve average memory savings by up to 10% relative to a state-of-the-art policy; the offline policy is provably optimal for the data-center reclamation objective (maximize savings subject to SLO), establishing an upper bound analogous to OPT/Belady in the traditional setting.
papers.limitations: Full text unreadable, so authors' own admissions unknown. From what is visible: the abstract never mentions CXL, tiered hardware, or any physical testbed, so this appears to be a policy/modeling framework paper (analytic + trace/simulation) rather than a CXL hardware evaluation; whether policies were validated on real machines, with real far-memory backends (zswap/CXL), or under multi-tenant interference cannot be determined.
papers.openQuestions: Unknown from abstract: whether MPCs and the optimal policy account for reclamation-target heterogeneity (compressed RAM vs disk vs CXL tier), for bandwidth interference between co-located jobs, or for tail-latency SLOs vs average performance; whether the framework extends to placement (promotion/demotion) rather than pure reclamation; online applicability of the offline optimal policy.
evidenceQuotes: MDK: Rethinking the Data Center Memory Reclamation Problem. Shaurya Patel, Google and University of British Columbia; Suli Yang and Yawen Wang, Google; Kan Wu, xAI; Alexandra (Sasha) Fedorova, University of British Columbia and MongoDB; Margo Seltzer, University of British Columbia; Kimberly Keeton, Google

Since a key constraint for placing additional jobs is memory, data center systems proactively reclaim memory from running jobs to create space for new jobs. This difference fundamentally flips the optimization problem that memory management policies need to address.

We present the Memory Designer's Kit, MDK, a framework for designing and evaluating data center memory management policies. MDK includes an offline provably optimal policy; Memory Performance Curves (MPCs), which show how memory savings vary when constrained by performance; and an efficient technique that is up to 208× faster than simulation for producing MPCs. We demonstrate MDK's utility by developing three data center policies that improve average memory savings by up to 10% relative to a state-of-the-art policy.

NOTE: the word 'CXL' does not appear anywhere in the paper's official abstract; the session title 'Memory Tiering and CXL' is the only CXL association. No testbed, device count, or hardware description is available before the embargo lifts.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Conceptually relevant, not hardware-relevant: MDK gives no evidence of touching real CXL devices, so it says nothing about the requester's 4x CZ120 per-device questions. Its useful import is methodological — Memory Performance Curves (memory savings as a function of a performance constraint) and a provably optimal offline bound are exactly the kind of tooling ObjPlace lacks for justifying placement decisions; an analogous 'DRAM-savings vs slowdown' curve per object class, or an offline-optimal placement bound, would strengthen an ObjPlace-successor paper's evaluation. It also signals that OSDI reviewers value flipped-objective formulations (maximize consolidation subject to SLO), which maps directly onto the candidate multi-tenant per-CXL-device QoS direction. Re-check the full PDF after July 13, 2026 to confirm whether reclamation targets include a CXL/far tier.

papers.title: Break On Through to the Other Side: Pooling Memory Elastically with RamRyder
papers.venue: OSDI '26 (20th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation)
papers.numCXLDevices: unknown
papers.mainProblem: Cloud vendors allocate VM memory capacity in a fixed ratio to vCPUs and offer no mechanism at all for allocating memory bandwidth; when an application's capacity vs. bandwidth demands diverge or change over time, both resources are underutilized.
papers.mainIdea: RamRyder is a software-defined elastic memory system for cloud VMs that decouples memory bandwidth from capacity allocation: it controls the mapping between guest-OS memory pages and the underlying physical memory channels, giving per-VM performance isolation and allowing bandwidth and capacity to be re-allocated dynamically and (mostly) independently.
papers.hardwareEnv: Unknown — full paper is locked on USENIX (open-access PDF not yet posted as of 2026-07-07) and no preprint exists. The abstract does not name any CPU, DRAM, or CXL hardware. papers.evalSetup: Unknown beyond abstract: cluster-scale evaluation with cloud-VM workloads measuring capacity utilization, bandwidth utilization, and performance vs. exclusive access. Workloads, VM counts, and traces not readable.
papers.baselines: Unknown; abstract only compares against "the best case with exclusive access" (static exclusive allocation). Named baseline systems not readable.
papers.keyFindings: RamRyder improves average capacity utilization by 28.6% and average bandwidth utilization by 43.2% across the cluster, while delivering performance comparable to the best case in which each VM has exclusive access to its memory.
papers.limitations: Cannot assess from full text. From the abstract alone: bandwidth and capacity are only "(mostly) independently" allocatable, i.e., the decoupling is admittedly partial. papers.title: Duhu: Shared Disaggregated Memory for Distributed Data Processing Frameworks
papers.venue: OSDI '26 (USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation)
papers.numCXLDevices: unknown
papers.mainProblem: Distributed data processing frameworks (DDFs) like Ray/Spark incur large memory and network-transfer overheads because every node must copy objects into local memory before processing; shared disaggregated memory (SDM) clusters could avoid these copies, but current SDMs provide weak coherence guarantees and coherence poses scalability/complexity challenges, so DDFs would otherwise need invasive logic changes and software coordination to adopt SDM.
papers.mainIdea: Duhu is an SDM-based object store that sits between DDFs and the shared disaggregated memory, handling coherence/coordination so that DDFs can use SDM without modifying their processing logic. It is integrated with Ray as the object store, letting Ray tasks on different nodes access shared objects in a CXL-attached memory pool instead of copying them over the network.
papers.hardwareEnv: Not verifiable from public sources as of 2026-07-07. Abstract states only: an "SDM cluster with a prototype CXL-attached memory pool" (SK hynix co-authors suggest an SK hynix pooled-memory prototype, but this is inference, not verified). No CPU, DRAM, CXL device model/count, link width, or kernel version available.
papers.evalSetup: From abstract only: system integrated with Ray and evaluated on an SDM cluster with a prototype CXL-attached memory pool; workloads include at least a shuffle workload where JCT is measured. Full workload list, cluster size, and configuration unverifiable pre-publication.
papers.baselines: Not verifiable from abstract; presumably vanilla Ray (Plasma object store with network object transfer), but the paper text naming the baselines could not be read.
papers.keyFindings: Duhu improves job completion time by up to 3.39x on a shuffle workload versus the baseline (per abstract). No other numbers publicly available yet.
papers.limitations: Cannot assess from full text (not yet released). From the abstract alone: evaluation is on a single "prototype" CXL-attached memory pool, i.e., pre-production pooling hardware not commercially available (unlike memory-expansion ASICs such as CZ120); the headline 3.39x number is for shuffle, a best-case copy-heavy workload; nothing in the abstract indicates multi-tenant or interference-aware evaluation, and coherence is explicitly worked around (weak-coherence SDM) rather than solved in hardware.
papers.openQuestions: Whether the approach generalizes beyond Ray to other DDFs; behavior under multi-tenant sharing/contention on the pool; scalability of the software-coordination layer as node count grows; performance on non-shuffle workloads; portability to commodity (non-prototype) CXL 2.0/3.x pooling hardware. All are inferred gaps — the paper text could not be read to check what the authors themselves punt on.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Adjacent rather than directly comparable: Duhu targets multi-host shared CXL memory pooling (SDM) with a prototype pool, while the requester's testbed is single-host memory expansion with 4x CZ120 behind one EPYC 9745 — no cross-host sharing or hardware pooling is possible there. Duhu's object-store-level placement of DDF objects into CXL overlaps conceptually with ObjPlace's object-granularity DRAM/CXL placement, so it is a must-cite for positioning and for the argument that object granularity is the right interface for CXL memory. It does not appear to address per-device scheduling, CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference, or tail-aware QoS, so the requester's candidate direction (treating each of the 4 devices as an independently schedulable resource) remains unclaimed by this paper as far as the abstract shows — but this must be rechecked when the full OSDI '26 PDF drops on ~2026-07-13.
evidenceQuotes: We have integrated Duhu with Ray, and evaluated our system on an SDM cluster with a prototype CXL-attached memory pool. We show that Duhu can improve job completion time (JCT) by up to 3.39× on a shuffle workload.

Emerging shared disaggregated memory (SDM) clusters enable an alternate approach because they allow nodes to access data in a shared memory. However, using SDMs for DDFs is challenging: current SDM clusters provide weak coherence guarantees, and even for emerging SDMs coherence poses a scalability and complexity challenge.
In this paper, we describe Duhu, an SDM-based object store that is designed to allow DDFs to use SDMs without these changes, simplifying their adoption.
