papers.title: Building A CSFQ-Inspired Transport for Switched CXL Memory Pooling
papers.venue: NSDI
papers.numCXLDevices: unknown (memory chassis "holds up to 12 vendor-agnostic CXL DIMMs" [Micron/SMART Modular referenced]; populated count never stated; rDIMM-to-rDIMM experiments imply >=2; plus 1 XConn B2 Apollo CXL switch ASIC and ASIC host/endpoint adapters)
papers.mainProblem: In switched CXL memory pooling, the host-core-to-remote-DIMM data path (cache hierarchy, host adapter, CXL switch, endpoint adapter, rDIMM) is shared by concurrent intra- and inter-host memory streams with no explicit performance control, causing severe, unpredictable interference. Characterization identifies three issues: (1) intra-host contention (FlexBus/M2PCIe queueing up to 13.4x latency increase, 50.1ns to 669.4ns; host adapter's best-effort VL FLIT scheduling cuts a victim stream's bandwidth 82.6% and inflates latency 230.2ns to 1624.2ns); (2) in-fabric congestion (credit-based hop-by-hop flow control causes HoL blocking; a 64B request interleaved with 4KB requests sees 6.9x/3.8x read/write slowdown; a 4KB stream grabs 97.8% of bandwidth vs a 64B stream); (3) unmanaged host-rDIMM interaction from hardware prefetching that transparently over-subscribes the endpoint link.
papers.mainIdea: MemChannel: a transport layer over the CXL.mem fabric with an "mchannel" abstraction — a managed memory channel between a host core Ci and a specific remote CXL DIMM rDIMMj with performance attributes. A Sender-Driven Fabric-Informed protocol inspired by Core-Stateless Fair Queueing (CSFQ) admits just enough CXL loads/stores per mchannel based on estimated Core<->rDIMM bandwidth availability: time-based rate control via POSIX-timer suspension of application execution, host-side admission control, cross-host bookkeeping through shared CXL memory, fluid-model rate estimation from performance counters (OCR events, CHA occupancy, rdpmc), device-internal load as a congestion signal, and delay-based link-capacity probing. Extensions cover weighted fairness and multi-layer switching. Fair-share calculation runs once per 100us scheduling window.
papers.hardwareEnv: Real switched CXL pool: XConn Titan evaluation platform — ASIC host and endpoint adapters; XConn B2 Apollo CXL switch (XC50256 crossbar) with 14 upstream/downstream ports, 2 CEM slots, 128 CXL 2.0 lanes (x2/x4/x8 bifurcation); MCIO/EDSFF memory chassis holding up to 12 vendor-agnostic CXL DIMMs (E1.S/E3.S/E3.L; Micron and SMART Modular CXL modules cited); MX8 fabric-manager board. Hosts: 2U Intel Emerald Rapids servers, each 2x Xeon Gold 6530 (32 cores @2.1GHz, 160MB LLC), 1536GB DDR5, one CXL host adapter with two x8 CXL ports, Ubuntu 24.04. MLC baseline to the pool: 220.5ns latency, 47.2GB/s per server. Each rDIMM is exposed via driver as HDM / a CPUless NUMA node. DIMM capacity, vendor model, populated count, and host count not stated.
papers.baselines: (1) Same testbed without MemChannel (w/o MC) throughout; (2) TPP (Linux tiered-memory page promotion/demotion) under varying background traffic with local:remote capacity ratio 8:1. No comparison to other QoS/isolation systems (e.g., no Memstrata, no CXL-QoS hardware knobs).
papers.keyFindings: Characterization: switched-pool access 220.5ns/47.2GB/s per server; FlexBus congestion inflates CXL latency up to 13.4x (50.1 to 669.4ns); LLC/CHA contention up to 2.9x; host-adapter VL scheduling cuts victim bandwidth 82.6% (230.2 to 1624.2ns) at ~30% load; 64B vs 4KB interleaving gives 6.9x/3.8x slowdowns and 97.8% bandwidth capture by the large stream; prefetch-driven strided access oversubscribes the endpoint (read bandwidth 21.9 to 12.8GB/s at stride 8). MemChannel results: applications gain 2-3.5x; Silo avg CXL latency reduced 28.6-38.4% and tail 5.8-29.3% across YCSB; 225.3 MOPS / 41.0GB/s with two adapters at 64 threads; inter-host slowdown cut from 7.2x/4.2x to 3.1x/2.1x (BC/PR) at 100% contending load with 97.2% bandwidth utilization; fairness gap between co-located apps shrinks (8.9 to 1.3GB/s Bwaves+Silo, 11.5 to 1.8GB/s Bwaves+MICA, 3.1 to 0.1GB/s MICA+Silo); vs TPP: TPP 1.2x better uncontended, MemChannel 1.5x throughput and 43% latency win under heavy contention; overhead 1.7% (POSIX-timer interrupts, 100us window).
papers.limitations: Authors' own (Section 5.7 Discussion): evaluated only at rack scale on a single switch, not cluster-scale scale-out fabrics with PBR; relies on device-internal load + end-to-end delay rather than explicit in-fabric congestion notification; does not yet handle CXL bundled ports. Evident from methodology: the testbed table omits the populated CXL DIMM count, DIMM vendor/model/capacity, and the number of host servers used — key reproducibility gaps; rate control throttles applications by suspending execution via POSIX timers (coarse, CPU-time-costing mechanism); only TPP as an external baseline (no comparison to other bandwidth/QoS isolation systems); hosts are Intel-only (EMR counter-based estimation, CHA/OCR events, may not port to AMD like the requester's EPYC Turin); characterization single-switch, ASIC adapters proprietary (root causes established partly "by discussing with the device vendor"); no LLM/ML workloads.
papers.openQuestions: Multi-tier/PBR cluster-scale CXL fabrics; explicit congestion notification support in switches; CXL bundled ports; portability of the counter-based rate estimation to non-Intel CPUs; interaction with tiering/placement systems beyond the TPP comparison (they explicitly position mchannels as complementary to tiered/object memory systems); direct-attached (non-switched) multi-device contention is out of scope; how weights map to SLO-level tail-latency guarantees.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Highly relevant to the requester's candidate direction: MemChannel's core abstraction is a per-(core, individual rDIMM) channel with per-device load signals and admission control — i.e., NSDI'26-level validation that treating each CXL device as an independently schedulable resource pays off. Its Issue #1 (intra-host contention: adapter/port FLIT scheduling agnostic to request streams, victim bandwidth -82.6%) and Issue #3 (prefetch-induced oversubscription) occur before any switch and plausibly transfer to the requester's direct-attached 4x CZ120 box, echoing their measured 2.0-2.13x CXL co-runner slowdown; the in-fabric switch congestion findings do not apply. Differentiation room for the requester: no switch needed, AMD EPYC instead of Intel EMR (their CHA/OCR-counter rate estimation is Intel-specific), object-granularity placement (ObjPlace) + per-device scheduling rather than execution-throttling admission control, and LLM workloads which MemChannel never touches. MemChannel is now the closest related work for any 'CXL bandwidth QoS/fair sharing' claim and must be cited and contrasted (transport/throttling vs placement).
evidenceQuotes: We take the recent Titan platform [18] from the XConn Tech as the evaluation target (Figure 1-b). It consists of (1) ASIC-based host and endpoint adapters; (2) an XConn B2 Apollo CXL switch with 14 upstream and downstream ports, 2 CEM [1] slots, and 128 CXL2.0 lanes, supporting ×2, ×4, and ×8 bifurcations; (3) a memory chassis using an MCIO/EDSFF backplane that holds up to 12 vendor-agnostic CXL DIMMs [8, 12] under the compact EDSFF E1.S, E3.S, and E3.L form factors [7]; and (4) an MX8 board operating as the management host and fabric manager.

Experimental Methodology. We use 2U Intel Emerald Rapids servers as hosts, where each contains two Xeon Gold 6530 CPUs, 1536GB DDR5 memory, and two Samsung 9MA3 960GB NVMe drives. Each processor has 32 cores running at 2.1GHz and 160MB LLC. All the hosts run Ubuntu 24.04. Each server is equipped with one CXL host adapter enclosing two ×8 CXL ports. Using Intel MLC [5], we observe that the server achieves 220.5ns and 47.2GB/s when accessing the switched CXL memory pool.
a device driver that makes remote memory as host-managed device memory (HDM) and exposes it as a CPUless NUMA node. The host OS fabricates an attached CXL DIMM as a memory node
A mchannel, established between a host core (Ci ) and a CXL DIMM (rDIMM j ), is associated
We intermix small and large memory requests and deploy memory streams in two directions: host→rDIMM and rDIMM→rDIMM.
When the adapter is nearly saturated, we observe that in the Read(T1)-Read(T2) case, the victim stream’s bandwidth is reduced by 82.6%, with latencies increased from 230.2ns to 1624.2ns.
Second, MemChannel is evaluated at rack scale rather than at cluster scale. It will be interesting to explore how MemChannel operates in a scale-out CXL fabric with PBR.
couldNotVerify: Exact number of CXL DIMMs populated in the chassis during evaluation (only 'holds up to 12' is stated; rDIMM-to-rDIMM experiments imply at least 2)
CXL DIMM vendor model and per-DIMM capacity (only generic Micron/SMART Modular product-page citations)
Exact number of host servers used in the multi-host experiments
Linux kernel version (only Ubuntu 24.04 stated)

papers.title: CXL-DMSim: A Full-System CXL Disaggregated Memory Simulator With Comprehensive Silicon Validation
papers.venue: IEEE TCAD (per arXiv comments); arXiv 2411.02282 (v7, 2026-01-11)
papers.numCXLDevices: 2 physical devices on the validation testbed: 1x Intel Agilex I-Series FPGA CXL 1.1 device (16GB DDR4) + 1x in-house CXL ASIC device with two CXL memory controllers (128GB DDR5, exposed as two CPU-less NUMA nodes). The simulator itself models arbitrary configurations including switch-attached pools.
papers.mainProblem: Researchers lack accessible, accurate tools to study CXL disaggregated memory: real CXL silicon is scarce, NUMA-based emulation misrepresents CXL latency/bandwidth behavior, and existing simulators lack full-system CXL protocol support (drivers, kernel-managed vs app-managed modes) and silicon validation.
papers.mainIdea: Build a gem5-based open-source full-system simulator (CXL-DMSim) with CXL.mem/CXL.io protocol modeling, CXL device drivers, both app-managed (devdax-style) and kernel-managed (NUMA) modes, and switch-attached topologies; then comprehensively validate it against a real dual-Xeon testbed hosting both an FPGA CXL prototype and an in-house CXL ASIC device, achieving ~3.4% average simulation error.
papers.hardwareEnv: Validation testbed: dual-socket Intel Xeon Platinum 8468V (4 iMCs / 8 channels each; one 32GB DDR5-4800 DIMM populated per NUMA node), Linux kernel v6.5.0. CXL devices (both on Socket1): (a) Intel Agilex I-Series FPGA Dev Kit with hard CXL 1.1 IP, 16GB DDR4-3200, exposed as CPU-less NUMA4; (b) in-house CXL ASIC with two CXL memory controllers each driving two DDR5 DIMMs, 128GB total, exposed as two CPU-less NUMA nodes (NUMA2, NUMA3). Remote-NUMA DDR used as an emulation baseline. Simulator: gem5-based; also models switch-attached ASIC (CXL-DMSimS).
papers.evalSetup: Microbenchmarks: LMbench lat_mem_rd (2048 MB array, 64 B stride) for latency; STREAM Copy/Scale/Add/Triad (1024 MB) for bandwidth — run on real local DDR, remote NUMA DDR, CXL-FPGA, CXL-ASIC, and in CXL-DMSim for cross-validation. Applications: Redis 5.0.5 with YCSB A/B (800 MB working set, single thread), Viper hybrid PMEM-DRAM KV store, Meta DLRM inference (bandwidth-sensitive); memory-constrained scenarios with CXL as capacity expansion, and 50:50 DDR:CXL interleaving for bandwidth expansion.
papers.baselines: Real hardware baselines: local DDR, remote NUMA DDR (emulation), CXL-FPGA, CXL-ASIC (direct and switch-attached). Simulator baselines: vanilla gem5 (speed overhead comparison); simulated variants CXL-DMSimA (app-managed) / kernel-managed / CXL-DMSimS (switched) validated against corresponding real configurations.
papers.keyFindings: (1) Simulator fidelity: average simulation error 3.4% vs real silicon (STREAM ~4.3% avg); simulation speed comparable to gem5 (CXL-DMSimA ~16% slower). (2) Characterization: CXL-ASIC load latency 284 ns = 2.18x local DDR (130 ns); CXL-FPGA 375 ns = 2.88x; switch-attached ASIC 487 ns = 3.75x. Bandwidth: CXL-FPGA 45-69% of local DDR, CXL-ASIC 82-83%, remote NUMA DDR 68-74% — NUMA emulation mimics neither latency nor bandwidth of real CXL. (3) Apps: Viper up to 25x/23x faster with CXL capacity expansion in memory-constrained settings; DLRM +39%/+60% with 50:50 DDR-CXL interleaving.
papers.limitations: Authors admit: gem5 cache model causes high latency error in the LLC-transition region (96-384 MB working sets); simulation ~16% slower than gem5 with inherently slow speed, high modeling complexity for new features, and limited system scale. Methodology weaknesses: real-device characterization treats each CXL device independently — no measurement of cross-device interference or multi-tenant contention on real silicon; switch-attached topology exists only in simulation; app validation is single-thread/small working sets (Redis 800 MB); the ASIC is an in-house device, not a commercial product like CZ120, limiting comparability.
papers.openQuestions: Cross-device CXL-to-CXL interference and QoS on real multi-device systems (their two devices are characterized separately, never contended); validation of switch/pooling models against real switch silicon; CXL 2.0/3.x features (hot-plug, sharing, back-invalidation); large-scale multi-tenant workloads; more accurate LLC modeling in gem5.
evidenceQuotes: Intel Agilex I-Series FPGA Development Kit with an integrated hard CXL IP ... 16GB 3200MT/s DDR4 memory, connected to the CPU via a CXL 1.1 interface ... recognized as a separate CPU-less NUMA node (denoted as NUMA4)

In-house CXL-ASIC device has two CXL memory controllers, each of which is composed of a CXL protocol controller plus a DDR5 controller driving two DIMMs ... 128GB ... appearing in the OS as two separate NUMA nodes without CPUs (denoted as NUMA2 and NUMA3 respectively)

Dual-socket Intel Xeon Platinum 8468V processors, each of which has 4 integrated memory controllers with 8 memory channels ... a single memory channel (i.e., a 32GB DDR5 4800MT/s DIMM) for each NUMA node ... Linux kernel v6.5.0
average simulation error of 3.4%
CXL-ASIC: 2.18 times higher than local DDR (284 ns vs. 130 ns) ... CXL-FPGA: 2.88 times (375 ns)
Remote NUMA memory lacks realism and accuracy in mimicking CXL memory
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Directly useful as a validated simulation companion to the requester's real 4x CZ120 testbed: CXL-DMSim could model per-device and switch-attached topologies (including CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference scenarios) that the 4-device box cannot easily reconfigure, and its silicon-validated error (~3.4%) lends credibility to simulated extensions of ObjPlace experiments. Its characterization corroborates the requester's numbers (ASIC latency 2.18x DRAM vs their 1.53x; NUMA emulation shown inadequate — a citation supporting the value of real-hardware work). Notably, the paper never contends two real CXL devices against each other, so the requester's per-device interference/QoS direction remains unclaimed; the simulator could serve as a scaling/sensitivity tool for that direction (e.g., >4 devices, switches).
couldNotVerify: Verbatim quotes were extracted from the arXiv v7 HTML via the fetch pipeline's summarizer; exact wording could differ slightly from the PDF.
Whether the two real CXL devices were ever interleaved together on the testbed (evidence indicates they were characterized independently).
Final IEEE TCAD publication details (volume/pages) — venue taken from arXiv comments field.

papers.title: DPC: A Distributed Page Cache over CXL
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2604.19494)
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no physical CXL devices; QEMU-emulated CXL devices backed by shared host DRAM across NUMA nodes on one ARM server)
papers.mainProblem: Distributed file systems use uncoordinated per-node page caches that replicate hot data locally on every node, wasting aggregate cluster DRAM through redundancy and incurring heavy coherence/consistency overhead when data is shared across nodes.
papers.mainIdea: An OS-level distributed page cache built on CXL 3.0 shared-memory semantics that treats the whole cluster's DRAM as one cache budget and enforces a single-copy invariant at page granularity: each file page has exactly one owner node holding the sole resident DRAM copy; all other nodes map that page remotely over CXL (via a dpc_dax driver) instead of replicating it, eliminating redundancy and coherence traffic. Offers both a relaxed-consistency mode (DPC) and a strong-consistency mode (DPC_SC).
papers.hardwareEnv: Dual-socket 64-bit ARMv8.2 server (model withheld for anonymization; affiliation suggests Huawei Kunpeng-class), 2 compute dies per socket, 32 cores @2.6 GHz per die = 128 physical cores; 256 GiB DDR4-2933 spread across 4 NUMA nodes; 2 TB RAID-0 of 4x480 GB SAS SSDs. Cluster of 4 QEMU VMs (16 vCPUs, 32 GB RAM each); each VM's memory is a host memory-backend file, and other VMs' backend files are attached as emulated CXL devices behind QEMU CXL root ports, all coherent because they reside in shared host DRAM. No real CXL silicon or FPGA; kernel version not captured.
papers.evalSetup: 4-VM emulated CXL 3.0 cluster on one ARM NUMA server. Microbenchmarks with fio (libaio and mmap engines, read/write, cache-hit/cache-miss cases). Application workloads: RocksDB (60 GB KV store), DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat LLM inference (30 GB mmapped weights), DiskANN (40 GB ANN index), Filebench Webserver (32 GB) and Fileserver (32 GB).
papers.baselines: virtiofs (unmodified), NFSv4.1, JuiceFS v1.3; plus DPC's own strong-consistency variant DPC_SC vs. relaxed DPC.
papers.keyFindings: On data-sharing workloads DPC achieves up to 12.4x speedup with a 5.6x cross-workload geomean over baselines; microbenchmarks show up to 72.8x read-IOPS improvement on cache-hit reads and 2.6x read-latency reduction vs virtiofs; Webserver/Fileserver see up to ~16.2x/15.2x. Single-copy ownership removes replica redundancy so aggregate DRAM caches more distinct data. Cost side: synchronous single-page invalidation takes 99.7 us under DPC vs 11 us for virtiofs, and DPC_SC pays per-write overhead for stronger consistency.
papers.limitations: Authors admit production CXL 3.0 multi-host shared-memory hardware does not exist, so the entire evaluation is QEMU + intra-server NUMA coherence emulation — remote-CXL latency/bandwidth is whatever cross-NUMA access on one ARM box gives (no evidence of injected fabric latency), likely optimistic vs a real CXL 3.0 fabric. Zero physical CXL devices; no real multi-host coherence, no fabric contention or bandwidth ceilings. Fault tolerance is weak: owner-node failure can lose dirty pages. Reclamation/invalidation coordination is ~9x slower than local. Only 4 nodes, single physical machine; no multi-tenant or interference study.
papers.openQuestions: Behavior on real CXL 3.0 fabrics with back-invalidation/HDM-DB coherence, realistic ~250-400ns+ latencies and shared-link bandwidth contention; scalability beyond 4 nodes; robust fault tolerance for dirty single-copy pages; interaction with memory tiering/placement policies on the owner node; write-heavy and strongly-consistent workloads at scale.
evidenceQuotes: Because production CXL 3.0 hardware is not yet available, our evaluation platform cannot rely on real CXL fabrics. Instead, we emulate CXL in QEMU and use NUMA nodes with the hardware cache-coherence protocol of the underlying system to provide a realistic model of coherent, byte-addressable shared memory.

We evaluate DPC on a dual-socket 64-bit ARMv8.2 server (model not specified for anonymization). Each socket integrates two compute dies, with each incorporating 32 cores at 2.6 GHz, for a total of 128 physical cores. The system has 256 GiB of DDR4-2933 memory, evenly distributed across the four NUMA nodes that correspond to the compute dies.

For every VM, we attach the memory-backend files of the other VMs as CXL devices behind CXL root ports in QEMU, where they are handled by the dpc_dax driver. As all CXL-backed regions ultimately reside in shared host DRAM, loads and stores from different VMs observe a coherent view of these regions.
Across these workloads within a multi-node setup, DPC achieves speedups of up to 12.4×, with a cross-workload geomean speedup of 5.6×.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Low direct relevance to the requester's 4x CZ120 CXL 2.0 memory-expansion testbed: DPC targets hypothetical CXL 3.0 multi-host shared-memory fabrics and is evaluated entirely on QEMU/NUMA emulation with zero physical CXL devices, so its numbers say nothing about real per-device latency (277ns), ~35.5 GiB/s per-region bandwidth ceilings, or CXL-to-CXL co-runner interference the requester measured. CXL 2.0 expanders like CZ120 cannot provide the cross-host coherent sharing DPC requires. Useful mostly as related work for positioning (single-copy ownership and page-granularity remote mapping ideas could inform ObjPlace-style placement, e.g., famfs-backed shared pages), and as an example of the emulation-only evaluation gap the requester's real-hardware, per-device-scheduling direction can attack.
couldNotVerify: Kernel/OS and QEMU versions in the testbed
Whether any extra latency was injected to model CXL fabric latency (no such sentence found; cross-NUMA latency appears to be used as-is)
Exact per-workload speedup breakdown beyond the headline numbers

papers.title: Cohet: A CXL-Driven Coherent Heterogeneous Computing Framework with Hardware-Calibrated Full-System Simulation (SimCXL)
papers.venue: HPCA 2026 (arXiv 2511.23011, "Accepted by HPCA 2026")
papers.numCXLDevices: real calibration testbed: 2 (1x Intel Agilex I-Series FPGA dev kit as CXL type-1/2 device + 1x Samsung CMM-D 512 GB memory expander as type-3); main application evaluations (RAO, RPC) run entirely in the SimCXL simulator
papers.mainProblem: Conventional heterogeneous (CPU+accelerator) computing built on PCIe suffers from inefficient fine-grained host-device interactions (DMA at cacheline granularity is slow) and complex programming models; there is also no full-system, cycle-level simulation infrastructure covering all three CXL protocols and all device types to explore CXL-coherent heterogeneous architectures.
papers.mainIdea: Cohet: a CXL-driven coherent heterogeneous computing framework that "decouples the compute and memory resources to form unbiased CPU and XPU pools which share a single unified and coherent memory pool," programmable via standard malloc/mmap. To study it, the authors build SimCXL, a cycle-level full-system simulator (gem5-based, X86O3CPU, modified Linux v6.12) whose modular CXL controller models CXL.io/.cache/.mem and type-1/2/3 devices, calibrated against a real FPGA+expander testbed to ~3% mean absolute percentage error.
papers.hardwareEnv: Real calibration testbed: Intel 4th-gen Xeon Platinum 8468V (48 cores, 97.5 MB LLC), 1 TB DDR5-4800; CXL devices: Intel Agilex I-Series FPGA Development Kit at 400 MHz on PCIe5.0 x16 (type-1/2, 128 KB 4-way host-managed cache) and Samsung CMM-D 512 GB expander on PCIe5.0 x8 to Socket1, exposed as a CPU-less NUMA node; Linux v6.5.0. SimCXL config: 48-core X86O3CPU, 32 GB DDR5-4400, modified kernel v6.12.
papers.evalSetup: Calibration: custom load/store-unit microbenchmarks measuring CXL.cache and DMA latency/bandwidth on the real FPGA, using CLDEMOTE/CLFLUSH to control cacheline placement (HMC hit / LLC hit / memory hit). Application evaluation runs in SimCXL: six remote-atomic-operation (RAO) access patterns from the CircusTent benchmark (CENTRAL, STRIDE1, SCATTER, GATHER, SG, RAND) and six RPC (de)serialization benches from HyperProtoBench (Google Protobuf).
papers.baselines: PCIe-NIC (conventional DMA-based design), CXL-NIC (coherent design, with and without prefetching), and an RpcNIC reference design for RPC offloading.
papers.keyFindings: CXL.cache reduces latency by 68% vs DMA for a memory hit at 64B granularity and delivers 14.4x DMA bandwidth for fine-grained transfers. SimCXL achieves a mean absolute percentage error of 3% vs the real FPGA testbed. In simulation, CXL-NIC RAO speedups over PCIe-NIC range from 5.5x (RAND) to 40.2x (CENTRAL), 22.4x for STRIDE1; RPC deserialization 1.33-2.05x, serialization with CXL.mem 2.0-4.06x, average 1.86x for (de)serialization.
papers.limitations: Authors admit ATS-based address translation overhead "remains unexplored due to the lack of ATS support on current CXL FPGA platforms," and CXL.mem H2D access measurement is deferred ("will be presented in another paper"). Methodological: only one type-3 memory expander (Samsung CMM-D) and one FPGA on the real testbed despite the abstract's "various memory expanders" phrasing; all killer-app results (RAO, RPC) come from simulation, not hardware; no multi-expander, multi-tenant, or interference experiments; simulated memory config (32 GB) is far smaller than the real testbed.
papers.openQuestions: ATS translation overhead; CXL.mem host-to-device performance characterization (explicitly deferred); behavior with multiple type-3 devices / pooled memory and CXL 3.x fabrics; contention/QoS between coherent accelerators and memory-expansion traffic; validation of simulator accuracy for type-3-heavy (memory-tiering) workloads rather than type-1/2 accelerator traffic.
evidenceQuotes: SimCXL has been rigorously calibrated against a real CXL-supported testbed with Intel FPGA accelerators and various memory expanders, achieving an average simulation error of 3%.
The CXL devices on the testbed include an Intel Agilex I-Series FPGA Development Kit and a Samsung 512 GB memory expander.
The Samsung expander, connected to Socket1 via PCIe5.0 ×8, is exposed to the system as a CPU-less NUMA node.
We evaluated six RAO access patterns from the CircusTent benchmark on both PCIe-NIC and CXL-NIC in SimCXL.
The modular CXL controller in SimCXL can model CXL type-1/2/3 devices.
After all calibration tests, our simulator achieves a mean absolute percentage error of 3%.
Cohet decouples the compute and memory resources to form unbiased CPU and XPU pools which share a single unified and coherent memory pool.
The overhead of ATS-based address translation remains unexplored due to the lack of ATS support on current CXL FPGA platforms.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Low direct relevance to the requester's 4x Micron CZ120 type-3 testbed: Cohet is about CXL.cache-coherent accelerators (type-1/2 FPGA NICs) and its real testbed has only ONE type-3 expander (Samsung CMM-D, exposed as one CPU-less NUMA node), with all application results in simulation — it offers no data on per-device placement, CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference, or multi-tenant QoS. Its main value to the requester is SimCXL itself (open source, TianheMICALab/SimCXL): a hardware-calibrated cycle-level simulator that models multiple type-3 devices could be used to explore per-device scheduling / interference scenarios beyond what the 4-device box allows, or to sanity-check ObjPlace policies at scale. Also useful as a citation that fine-grained coherent access beats DMA, but that is orthogonal to memory-expansion tiering.
couldNotVerify: Whether the calibration table includes additional memory expander models beyond the Samsung CMM-D (abstract says 'various memory expanders' but only Samsung 512 GB + Agilex FPGA are named in the testbed section)
Exact CXL.mem latency numbers for the Samsung expander (paper defers H2D CXL.mem measurement to another paper)

papers.title: Cxlalloc: Safe and Efficient Memory Allocation for a CXL Pod
papers.venue: ASPLOS 2026 (31st ACM ASPLOS, Vol. 2, March 22-26, 2026, Pittsburgh)
papers.numCXLDevices: testbed A (Chameleon Ice Lake, scalability runs): 0 CXL devices (DRAM shared-memory file); testbed B: 1 (one Intel Agilex 7 CXL Type-2 device)
papers.mainProblem: Memory allocation for a "CXL pod" (8-16 hosts sharing one multi-headed CXL memory device at cacheline granularity) faces three challenges existing allocators fail on: (1) CXL devices may not support inter-host hardware cache coherence (HWcc), so CPU CAS is unsafe across hosts; (2) the heap is concurrently accessed by different processes with independent virtual address spaces, breaking pointer consistency when heaps grow or huge allocations change memory mappings; (3) partial failures (one thread/process crashing mid-allocation) become more likely with more hosts and must not block or leak.
papers.mainIdea: Cxlalloc, a user-space lock-free allocator that: separates metadata into a small contiguous HWcc region vs. a software-cache-coherent (SWcc) region so it works under full/limited/no HWcc; provides spatial+temporal pointer consistency via offset pointers, consistent-offset layout, signal-handler-based asynchronous mmap installation, and a hazard-pointer protocol for mapping reclamation (first allocator supporting cross-process huge, e.g. 1 GiB, allocations with heap extension); tolerates partial failure via an 8-byte atomically-updated per-operation redo state enabling idempotent non-blocking recovery; and for no-HWcc devices contributes a memory-based CAS (mCAS) primitive implemented in near-memory-processing logic on an FPGA.
papers.hardwareEnv: Two machines. (A) Scalability/KV-store runs: Chameleon compute_icelake_r650, Ubuntu 22.04.5, Linux 5.15, 2x Intel Xeon Platinum 8380 @2.30GHz (40 cores, 120 MiB LLC, 128 GiB DDR4-3200 per socket), no CXL device — allocators backed by a 64 GiB shared-memory file bound to NUMA node 0. (B) CXL runs: Ubuntu 24.04.2, Linux 6.8, Intel Xeon 8568 (Emerald Rapids) @2.0GHz, 48 cores, 300MB LLC, 8-channel DDR5-4800; one Intel Agilex 7 CXL Type-2 device over PCIe 5.0 x16 (ASIC memory controller + ASIC-based CXL IPs, FPGA used only for the NMP mCAS logic; device supports CXL 2.0 but CPU only CXL 1.1). Measured: CXL read latency 357ns vs 112ns DRAM; CXL bandwidth 19.9 GB/s (2 channels) vs 114 GB/s local (4 channels).
papers.evalSetup: Ported YCSB (Load/A/D) into an in-memory KV store plus 4 production Twitter memcached cluster traces (MC-12/15/31/37); allocator microbenchmarks threadtest and xmalloc (small objects, and a 1 GiB-object huge-allocation variant, 9.6M ops); Memento recoverable queue/hashmap with 0/1/2 injected thread crashes; CAS latency microbenchmark (sw_cas vs sw_flush_cas vs hw_cas mCAS) on the CXL device up to 16 threads. Cross-process runs use 10 processes, 1-8 threads/proc; 10 trials, cores pinned, turbo/HT/NUMA-balancing/KSM disabled. All sharing is among processes on ONE host; no actual multi-host pod is run.
papers.baselines: mimalloc (single-process performance ceiling), Boost.Interprocess, Lightning's internal cross-process allocator, ralloc (lock-free recoverable PM allocator), cxl-shm (partial-fault-tolerant CXL memory management, SOSP'23).
papers.keyFindings: On YCSB/memcached traces cxlalloc is among the best in throughput and PSS memory (cxl-shm crashes on MC-12/MC-37 due to its 1 KiB allocation-size limit). On threadtest cxlalloc gets 47% of mimalloc's throughput; on xmalloc 81%. HWcc-metadata footprint is 0.02% of total memory on average (7.1% of ralloc's HWcc usage). Partial-failure support costs only 0.3% vs a non-recoverable variant on average (94.7% threadtest, 88.4% xmalloc); recovers from thread crashes without blocking or leaking, unlike ralloc's GC-or-leak choice. Only allocator to complete the 1 GiB huge-allocation benchmark (all baselines crash or exceed 30 min). On real CXL with mCAS (no HWcc): cxlalloc-mcas reaches 80% of cxlalloc-hwcc on threadtest and 10-99x ralloc-mcas; on xmalloc it drops to 1% of hwcc (every remote free needs an mCAS) but is 9.9x ralloc-mcas at 24 threads. FPGA hw_cas: 17.4% lower p50 / 20% lower p99 than sw_flush_cas at 16 threads, but slow at 1 thread (p50 2.3us).
papers.limitations: Despite targeting a multi-host "pod", every experiment runs on a single host — inter-host sharing is modeled by multiple processes on one machine; no multi-headed CXL device or second host is used. Only one CXL device (Agilex 7 FPGA card, CXL 1.1 host mode), not production memory-expander ASICs; main KV-store/scalability results are on a DRAM shared-memory file with no CXL at all. Authors admit: mCAS FPGA prototype has high uncontended latency (2.3us p50, expect ASIC to close gap); xmalloc-mcas drops to 1% of HWcc throughput; split HWcc/SWcc metadata can increase total memory usage; processes are assumed correct and trusted (no memory protection); NUMA-awareness not addressed. No bandwidth-interference, tiering, or tail-latency-under-contention evaluation.
papers.openQuestions: Actual multi-host pod deployment on multi-headed CXL 3.x hardware (they note it is "unclear if HWcc will become widely supported"); ASIC implementation of mCAS; adapting Tigon (which used an early cxlalloc) to mCAS is explicitly called "interesting future work"; extending the design with MPK-style heap protection; NUMA/device-aware placement of the heap; behavior under memory-bandwidth contention or with multiple CXL devices is untested.
evidenceQuotes: We evaluate on two machines: a Chameleon [39] instance that does not have a CXL device, but does have 80 cores to better compare scalability, and another machine with a CXL Type-2 device, 32 cores, and our mCAS prototype to measure the effect of HWcc.

Our test machine runs Ubuntu 24.04.2 LTS, Linux kernel version 6.8. It has an Intel Xeon 8568 CPU running at 2.0GHz, with 48 cores and 300MB LLC. The machine is equipped with 8-channel DDR5 4800 DRAM. We use a commercially available CXL Type-2 device, the Intel Agilex 7 [21], connected to the CPU via a PCIe 5.0 x16 link. It integrates an FPGA with ASIC-based CXL IPs. The memory controller is an ASIC, the FPGA is only for implementing near memory processing logic (NMP). While the device supports CXL 2.0, our Intel Emerald Rapids CPU only supports 1.1 [37, 58].
CXL read latency is 357ns, compared with 112ns for local memory. Its bandwidth is 19.9 GB/s (using two channels), compared with 114 GB/s for local memory (using four channels).
It has two Intel Xeon Platinum 8380 CPUs running at 2.30GHz, with 40 cores, 120 MiB LLC, and 128GiB DDR4 3200 DRAM per socket. We bind all memory to NUMA node 0
Using a commercial CXL device, we demonstrate that cxlalloc can achieve up to 80% of its maximum allocation throughput with no HWcc (using mCAS).
Each memory allocator is backed by a 64 GiB shared memory file.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Adjacent but orthogonal to the requester's direction: cxlalloc manages allocation on a single shared CXL device for multi-host/multi-process pods (coherence, pointer consistency, crash recovery), not DRAM/CXL placement, bandwidth interference, or per-device scheduling — so it does not overlap with ObjPlace's placement policy contribution, but it IS the closest published claim to "allocator-level CXL memory management," so ObjPlace's positioning should cite it and stress that placement/interference across 4 independent CZ120 devices is a different problem. Its evaluation is single-host, single FPGA device with no multi-device or interference experiments, leaving the requester's per-device independent-resource direction untouched. Useful methodological reference points: their MLC-measured 357ns/19.9 GB/s Agilex numbers (vs the requester's 277ns/35.5 GiB/s CZ120 region) and their process-on-one-host emulation of pod sharing.
couldNotVerify: Exact CXL device memory capacity on the Agilex 7 card (text cut off in extraction; capacity not stated in the testbed paragraph I read)
Whether the CXL testbed CPU has 32 or 48 cores (paper states both in different sentences)

papers.title: Cylon: Fast and Accurate Full-System Emulation of CXL-SSDs
papers.venue: USENIX FAST '26 (24th USENIX Conference on File and Storage Technologies)
papers.numCXLDevices: validation testbed: 1 (Samsung CMM-H FPGA prototype, 1TB); emulation testbed: 0 real CXL devices (Cylon emulates one CXL-SSD in software on a dual-socket Xeon)
papers.mainProblem: CXL-SSD research lacks a usable evaluation platform: commercial prototypes like Samsung CMM-H are black boxes; trace-driven and gem5-based simulators are too slow and cannot run full software stacks; vanilla QEMU CXL emulation inflates every access to ~15us via MMIO/VM-exits.
papers.mainIdea: Cylon is a FEMU-based full-system CXL-SSD emulator with a hybrid access path: Dynamic EPT Remapping (DER) lets DRAM-cache hits complete as direct cacheline-granular load/stores with no VM-exit (~remote-NUMA latency), while cache misses trap into FEMU's validated NAND timing engine (channel/die/plane parallelism, GC interference); Shared EPT Memory between KVM and userspace QEMU/FEMU cuts miss-path syscall overhead (23.04us -> 16.27us). On top it provides a configurable caching framework (FIFO/LIFO/CLOCK/S3FIFO eviction, next-N prefetching) and an application-level hint interface for HW-SW co-design. Upstreamed to FEMU (github.com/MoatLab/FEMU); ~implementation spans QEMU, KVM module, on Linux v6.4.6.
papers.hardwareEnv: Two testbeds. (1) Emulation host: dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6242, 384GB DDR4 (192GB/socket), local/remote DRAM latency 90ns/150ns (MLC), Ubuntu 20.04, modified Linux kernel v6.4.6; guest VM Ubuntu 22.04, vanilla kernel v6.4.6, 8 vCPUs, 96GB DRAM; emulated CXL-SSD = 96GB DAX device with 4.8GB DRAM cache, NAND timing 40us read / 200us write / 2000us erase; guest vCPUs pinned to node 0, backend memory reserved on NUMA node 1 so emulated hits incur remote-NUMA latency. (2) Hardware validation: dual-socket Intel Xeon 6710E, 512GB DDR5 (256GB/socket), one Samsung CMM-H CXL-SSD prototype (48GB DRAM cache with 4KB cachelines + 1TB NVMe SSD backend, Intel Agilex FPGA controller, PCIe Gen5) exposed as a CPU-less NUMA node with 1TB capacity, Ubuntu 24.04, kernel v6.13.0. CloudLab infrastructure acknowledged.
papers.evalSetup: Microbenchmarks: Intel MLC (latency/bandwidth) and MIO pointer chasing (sequential/random/stride patterns), sweeping working-set size (WSS) normalized to each device's DRAM-cache capacity for apples-to-apples Cylon-vs-CMM-H comparison. Macrobenchmarks: Redis with YCSB workload C (100% reads, 1KB records, Zipfian, 8 threads) at 0.33x/1.06x/2.10x normalized WSS; GAPBS Betweenness Centrality on kron graphs (10.2/20.4/40.8GB footprints, Cylon cache matched to CMM-H's). Policy studies: 4 eviction policies (FIFO/LIFO/CLOCK/S3FIFO) and next-N prefetching (N=0..8) across access patterns.
papers.baselines: Real Samsung CMM-H hardware (ground truth for validation) and QEMU-CXL (upstream QEMU CXL Type-3 emulation) as software baseline; internal variants Cylon-I (ioctl-based EPT remap) vs Cylon-S (shared EPT memory). Other platforms (MQSim-CXL, ESF, CXL-SSD-Sim, CXL-DMSim, OpenCXD) discussed but not directly compared (trace-driven, gem5-speed, or FPGA-gated).
papers.keyFindings: (1) At 100% hit rate Cylon matches remote-NUMA latency (0.16us) vs QEMU-CXL's 14.74us (>2 orders of magnitude inflation); miss-path emulation overhead is 16.27us (Cylon-S) vs 23.04us (Cylon-I). (2) Cylon reproduces the bimodal latency distribution of real CXL-SSDs: avg 977ns hits + tens-of-us misses, while QEMU collapses everything to ~14.6us. (3) Bandwidth: Cylon sustains remote-NUMA bandwidth (32GB/s) until its 4.8GB cache saturates, then converges to NAND-bound throughput like CMM-H; CMM-H degrades earlier due to opaque controller overheads and has higher hit latency (~800ns from FPGA controller). (4) Redis and GAPBS trends track CMM-H closely across cache-resident to NAND-dominated regimes. (5) Policy exploration: S3FIFO improves hit rates over FIFO/CLOCK on sequential/stride patterns; LIFO surprisingly best for Zipfian Redis; next-8 prefetching lifts Stride-4096 hit rate 18%->86%; random access collapses all policies to ~24% hits.
papers.limitations: Authors' own: CMM-H is a first-generation FPGA prototype with evolving firmware, so Cylon models "intended architectural behavior" rather than reproducing prototype-specific artifacts — absolute latencies/bandwidth diverge (Cylon faster on hits, slower on some misses); the earlier CMM-H bandwidth drop cannot be explained because the device is a black box; direct capacity comparison required WSS normalization since Cylon's emulated cache (4.8GB) is 10x smaller than CMM-H's (48GB). Methodological: only ONE CXL device (one CMM-H) ever used — no multi-device, no interleaving, no CXL memory expanders; emulation-only for all policy studies; no multi-tenant or interference experiments; miss-path still carries 16us software overhead (hidden only when NAND latency dominates); validation and emulation hosts are different machines (Xeon 6710E vs Gold 6242), so hit-latency comparisons conflate platform differences.
papers.openQuestions: How severe end-to-end stalls from tens-of-us misses are across real full stacks, and which cache/prefetch policies best mitigate them — Cylon is the vehicle, but the paper only scratches these with FIFO-family policies and next-N prefetching. Untested: multiple CXL-SSDs or mixed CXL memory + CXL-SSD tiers, multi-tenant sharing/QoS of the device DRAM cache, CXL 3.x pooling/sharing semantics, write-heavy workloads and GC-induced tails at application level, and emulation of next-gen designs beyond CMM-H (NVMe-oC, SkyByte-style) which they claim Cylon supports but do not deeply evaluate.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Low direct relevance to the requester's 4x CZ120 memory-expander testbed: Cylon targets CXL-SSDs (DRAM cache + NAND behind CXL.mem, tens-of-us misses), a very different latency regime from the requester's 277ns CZ120 loads, and its evaluation is single-device with no interference or multi-tenant study. It is useful as (a) a tool if the requester ever wants to prototype per-device placement or QoS policies against a hypothetical CXL device with configurable internals without hardware access, and (b) methodological precedent that FAST accepts emulator/validation papers — reinforcing that the requester's real-4-device cross-device-interference angle is largely unoccupied. Notably, this is the same VT group (Liu/Noh/Li, authors of the ASPLOS'25 Melody/MIO CXL characterization and Pond), so they are active adjacent competitors in CXL systems.
evidenceQuotes: Validation Testbed. For hardware validation, we use a dual-socket Intel Xeon 6710E server with 512GB DDR5 DRAM (256GB per socket). A commercial CXL-SSD prototype, Samsung's CMM-H, is attached and recognized by the host as a CPU-less NUMA node with 1TB capacity [1]. The system runs Ubuntu 24.04 with Linux kernel v6.13.0.

Host Platform. Experiments run on a dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6242 server with 384GB DDR4 DRAM (192GB per socket). Local and remote DRAM latencies, measured with Intel MLC [38], are 90ns and 150ns, respectively. The host runs Ubuntu 20.04 with a modified Linux kernel v6.4.6.
CMM-H is a hybrid CXL memory prototype that integrates a 48GB DRAM cache (4KB cacheline) with a 1TB NVMe SSD backend, coordinated by an Intel Agilex FPGA controller over PCIe Gen5 [8].

Cylon exposes a 96GB CXL DAX device to the guest, emulating a CXL-SSD with a 4.8GB DRAM cache and 96GB NAND flash. NAND timing parameters are fixed to realistic values (40 µs read, 200 µs write, and 2,000 µs erase)

With a 100% cache-hit rate, Cylon matches remote-NUMA latency (0.16µs), because cached pages are served via direct load/store instructions with no VM-exit. By contrast, QEMU's MMIO-based design inflates access latency to 14.74µs

CMM-H is a first-generation FPGA prototype with evolving firmware and opaque controller behavior. Internal overheads (e.g., metadata management, controller-level prefetching) lead to higher cache-hit latency (∼800ns) and lower bandwidth even before cache saturation on our platform
couldNotVerify: Exact CMM-H CXL link width (paper says PCIe Gen5 but not xN lanes)
Whether the emulation host has any CXL hardware at all (none mentioned; NUMA node 1 is the second socket's DRAM)

papers.title: Octopus: Enhancing CXL Memory Pods via Sparse Topology
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.AR), arXiv:2501.09020; authors from Columbia, Microsoft Azure, UW-Madison, UW (incl. D. Berger, M. Hill)
papers.numCXLDevices: 3 (three pre-production multi-ported pooling devices/MPDs, each with two x8 CXL 2.0 ports, shared across three servers); scaled-up results with 25/64/96 servers and 4-port MPDs are simulation only
papers.mainProblem: Existing CXL memory-pooling pod designs either fully connect a small number of servers to multi-port devices (limiting pod size and pooling benefit) or route through CXL switches (adding ~220 ns per hop and enough CapEx that switch cost can outweigh pooling savings). Pods must also serve two conflicting goals: memory pooling (wants broad reachability) and low-latency pairwise communication (wants overlap on the same device).
papers.mainIdea: Octopus builds switchless, sparsely connected CXL pods from low-port-count (e.g., 4-port) multi-ported devices (MPDs): each MPD connects a carefully chosen subset of servers. Servers are grouped into "islands" with high overlap for low-latency intra-island shared-memory communication/RPC, while cross-island links are laid out to maximize pooling reachability. Firmware interleaving across MPDs is disabled and each CXL port is exposed as a distinct NUMA node so software can target specific MPDs for capacity balancing and sharing.
papers.hardwareEnv: Prototype: three servers, each AMD EPYC 9825 (Turin), local DDR5-5600, 100 Gbit Mellanox CX5 NIC, Arista 7060X 100G switch, Ubuntu 24.04. Three pre-production MPDs each with two x8 CXL 2.0 ports (N=2); custom soldered risers route CXL control signals; only 16 of 64 CXL lanes per CPU used (two x8), forming a simplified island X=N=2 where each server pair shares one MPD. Measured MPD: 267 ns read latency (vs 233 ns CXL expansion device, ~115 ns local DRAM), 24.7 GiB/s read / 22.5 GiB/s write per x8 link (mixed R/W only 28.8 GiB/s due to MPD firmware issue). MPD vendor and capacity not stated; ASIC vs FPGA not explicitly stated (pre-production silicon implied; commercial 2-port MPDs cited from AsteraLabs, Marvell, xFusion).
papers.evalSetup: Four parts: (1) three-server hardware prototype (§6.2): RPC latency/bandwidth over shared CXL memory, all-gather bandwidth, and application slowdown on cloud workloads — Ruby YJIT (web), YCSB on Redis and Memcached, TPC-C on Silo, TPC-H on PostgreSQL; (2) scaled-up simulations (§6.3) of 25/64/96-server pods with 2-8-port MPDs (focus N=4), replaying Azure VM memory-demand traces collected over two weeks in Dec 2024 from thousands of cloud VMs; (3) physical layout/cabling validation under 1.5 m copper-cable constraints (§6.4); (4) cost modeling (§6.5).
papers.baselines: In-rack RDMA (100G, ToR), CXL switch topologies (e.g., XConn XC50256 class), fully-connected MPD pods (256B firmware interleaving), other sparse MPD/expander topologies (Jellyfish-style), and CXL expansion devices as latency reference.
papers.keyFindings: On real hardware, Octopus RPCs are 3.2x faster than in-rack RDMA and 2.4x faster than CXL switches (median ~1.2 us), and 4.5x lower latency than other sparse MPD topologies with good pooling savings. MPD adds only 267 ns vs 233 ns for an expansion device, so application slowdowns closely match plain CXL expansion, whereas a CXL switch would increase the slowdown of 25% of applications by 3x. Assuming 10% tolerable slowdown, 65% of memory can be pooled via MPDs vs 35% via switches. Per-server bandwidth saturates at 22.1 GiB/s with both sharers active. In simulation (up to 96 servers, 4-port MPDs), pooling savings pay for device costs: 5.4% overall server cost reduction with existing CXL expansion, 3.0% without; CXL switches always net a cost increase. Open source at github.com/yuhong-zhong/Octopus-CXL-Pod.
papers.limitations: Authors' own (§7): cross-island communication traverses two MPD hops (higher latency/lower bandwidth); broadcast-style collectives favor full connectivity and need multi-hop reads or replication in Octopus; suboptimal pooling under extremely skewed demand (per-server reachability bounded by MPDs it connects to); irregular cabling harder to manage; topologies are specific to X/N and re-optimization for other port counts is left to future work. Methodological: hardware prototype is only 3 servers with N=2 MPDs (the target N=4, X=8 design is never built); all pooling-savings and cost numbers come from trace-driven simulation and a cost model with assumed device prices; MPD vendor/capacity undisclosed and pre-production firmware limits bidirectional bandwidth; mixed R/W bandwidth artifact attributed to firmware bug; no multi-tenant isolation or QoS experiments.
papers.openQuestions: Re-optimizing island/cross-island port splits for other X,N configurations (explicitly left to future work); combining MPD islands with a small switch fabric for global reachability; optical CXL links; security of shared MPDs; memory-allocation policy on distinct per-port NUMA nodes; multi-socket servers; behavior at production scale (8 ports, 400 Gbit NICs) beyond the 4x-scaled-down prototype; contention/interference between the two servers sharing an MPD is only touched via bandwidth saturation, not tail latency or QoS.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Highly relevant precedent for the requester's candidate direction: Octopus explicitly disables cross-device interleaving and exposes each CXL port as a distinct NUMA node so software can target individual devices — the same per-device-independence stance the requester is considering for their 4x CZ120 box (where 2 devices are currently interleaved into one node). Octopus is a topology/cost paper, not a placement/QoS paper: it does not study CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference, tail latency under co-runners, or multi-tenant isolation on a device, leaving exactly the gap the requester's interference measurements (2.0-2.13x victim slowdown) and ObjPlace could fill at the single-host level. Its measured MPD numbers (267 ns, ~24.7 GiB/s per x8 port saturating quickly) corroborate the requester's CZ120 observations that per-device bandwidth is the scarce, contended resource. Also useful as motivation/citation that industry pods will present many small independently addressable CXL devices per host, making per-device scheduling a forward-looking abstraction.
evidenceQuotes: We have access to three pre-production MPDs with two ×8 CXL 2.0 ports (i.e., N=2). To connect them, we soldered custom risers to route CXL control signals to all ports. We use three servers each with an AMD EPYC 9825 Processor, local DDR5-5600 memory, and a 100 Gbit Mellanox CX5 NIC.
Each server has 64 CXL lanes, but we connect only 16 lanes (two ×8 lanes) per CPU to form a simplified Octopus island (X=N=2): each pair of servers shares one MPD.

Octopus disables this interleaving in firmware and exposes each CXL port as a distinct NUMA node (Figure 9(b)). This lets software target a specific MPD for capacity balancing and for sharing with peer servers that connect to the same MPD.
On our lab system, our N=2 MPD offers 267 ns read latency and 28 GiB/s read bandwidth per port.

Given that MPDs have higher latency than expansion devices (267 ns vs. 233 ns, measured with our hardware), we evaluate slowdown across a broad set of cloud workloads: web (Ruby YJIT), key-value stores (YCSB on Redis and Memcached), and databases (TPC-C on Silo, and TPC-H ...

On hardware, Octopus RPCs are 3.2× faster than in-rack RDMA and 2.4× faster than CXL switches. In simulation, Octopus achieves net server cost savings of 3–5.4% whereas CXL switches result in a net cost increase.
We simulate scaled-up Octopus topologies of 25, 64, and 96 servers based on 4-port MPDs.
couldNotVerify: Whether the pre-production MPDs are ASIC or FPGA-based is not explicitly stated (classified real-asic based on 'pre-production' silicon description and 267 ns latency; vendor undisclosed)
MPD memory capacity per device is not stated
Exact kernel version (only 'an updated Ubuntu 24.04' given)

papers.title: CXL Is Dead In The AI Era
papers.venue: SemiAnalysis (industry newsletter blog post) — NOT HotInfra 2024; the HotInfra'24 program (verified) contains no paper by this title
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no evaluation testbed of any kind; pure market/architecture analysis from published specs)
papers.mainProblem: Whether CXL will become the dominant interconnect/memory fabric of the AI datacenter era, as CXL proponents claimed circa 2023-2024.
papers.mainIdea: Position/analysis piece arguing CXL is a dead end for AI systems: (1) GPU vendors don't support it (Nvidia GPUs lack CXL; AMD MI300X doesn't expose it properly); (2) PCIe-based SerDes are ~3x less bandwidth-dense per mm2 of chip shoreline/beachfront than Ethernet-style 112G/224G SerDes, and that scarce die-edge area goes to NVLink/HBM instead; (3) PCIe x16 (~64 GB/s/direction) is dwarfed by NVLink (450 GB/s). Hence hyperscalers quietly shelved CXL projects; CXL is at best relegated to legacy memory-pooling/expansion niches on CPUs.
papers.hardwareEnv: None. No testbed, no CPU/DRAM/CXL device specified. Analysis is based on architecture comparisons and published specifications (PCIe 5/6, NVLink, 112G/224G Ethernet SerDes, BER specs).
papers.evalSetup: No experiments. Qualitative + back-of-envelope quantitative analysis of SerDes bandwidth density, BER requirements (PCIe 6 < 1e-12 vs Ethernet 1e-4), and GPU product support status. Substantial portion (memory pooling/expansion use-cases, hyperscaler custom silicon) is behind a paywall and was not readable.
papers.baselines: None (no systems compared experimentally). Rhetorical comparisons: NVLink, Infinity Fabric, Ethernet-style SerDes vs PCIe/CXL.
papers.keyFindings: Claims (not measurements): PCIe x16 = 64 GB/s per direction vs NVLink 450 GB/s; Ethernet-style SerDes have ~3x more bandwidth per unit of chip shoreline area than PCIe-style SerDes (persisting at 224G vs PCIe 6.0); PCIe 6 requires BER < 1e-12 vs 1e-4 for Ethernet, making PCIe SerDes heavier per bit; Nvidia GPUs don't support CXL at all, so CXL cannot participate in the GPU-centric AI memory hierarchy; many hyperscaler CXL projects were reportedly quietly shelved by 2023-2024.
papers.limitations: Not peer-reviewed; no measurements or testbed whatsoever; key sections (memory pooling/expansion verdict) paywalled; argument is scoped to CXL as a GPU-attached AI interconnect and does not (in the free portion) refute CPU-side memory expansion/tiering, which is exactly what the requester's testbed does; product-support claims are a 2024 snapshot and partially contested (e.g., subsequent Micron/MemVerge demos of CXL improving LLM GPU utilization, and later work like CXLAimPod arXiv:2508.15980 arguing the opposite).
papers.openQuestions: Whether CXL memory expansion/pooling on CPU hosts remains economically viable for AI serving (paywalled/unresolved); whether future GPUs ever expose CXL; quantitative evaluation of CXL-attached memory for LLM inference (KV-cache offload) is entirely absent — the piece never tests any CXL device.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: This is an industry op-ed, not an academic paper, and it contains zero CXL measurements — cite it (if at all) only as motivation/counterpoint framing, e.g., "despite industry skepticism about CXL as a GPU interconnect, host-side CXL memory expansion for LLM serving is real and measurable." Its argument targets CXL as a GPU-to-GPU/scale-up fabric (shoreline area, NVLink comparison), which is orthogonal to the requester's setup: 4x CZ120 CPU-attached expanders behind an EPYC 9745 used for capacity/tiering. It says nothing about multi-device scheduling, cross-device interference, or QoS, so it neither anticipates nor conflicts with the per-device-independent direction; ObjPlace-style results (1.53x latency, 35.5 GiB/s/region, 2x co-runner slowdown) are exactly the evidence-based counterweight to this piece's evidence-free framing.
evidenceQuotes: The simple answer is no - the people pushing CXL for AI are dead wrong.
Currently, CXL availability is the main issue, as Nvidia GPUs don't support it
we estimate that per mm² across a large variety of SOCs, Ethernet-style SerDes...have 3x more bandwidth per unit of shoreline area.
PCIe 6 requires a BER of < 1e-12 while Ethernet requires 1e-4

PCIe 16-lane provides "64GB/s of bandwidth in each direction" versus Nvidia NVLink's "450 GB/s bandwidth" (paraphrase confirmed against page; no testbed or measurement of any CXL device appears anywhere in the readable text)
couldNotVerify: Paywalled subscriber section (memory pooling / memory expansion verdict, hyperscaler custom-silicon discussion) could not be read
Authorship note: search metadata lists Dylan Patel and Jeremie Eliahou Ontiveros; some 2024 coverage attributes it to Dylan Patel and Myron Xie - byline on the current page reflects the former
Confirmed absence from HotInfra 2024 program via the official site; did not additionally check HotInfra 2023/2025 programs for a similarly titled academic response paper
papers.excludeReason: Not excluded, but flagged: this is NOT an academic/HotInfra 2024 paper — it is a SemiAnalysis newsletter position article (2024-03-16) with no evaluation, no testbed, and no CXL hardware. papers.title: Aquifer: Hierarchical Memory Pooling with CXL and RDMA for MicroVM Snapshots
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2606.24079)
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no physical CXL device; CXL pool emulated via the remote NUMA node of a dual-socket CloudLab r6525; RDMA tier uses a real ConnectX-6 Dx NIC)
papers.mainProblem: Memory stranding wastes 25-35% of installed DRAM in production cloud clusters; MicroVM snapshot restore latency dominates serverless cold starts, and neither CXL (pod-limited) nor RDMA (high-latency, per-access software overhead) alone is an adequate pooling substrate.
papers.mainIdea: Serve MicroVM snapshots from a two-tier hierarchical memory pool: characterization shows most snapshot pages are zero or cold, so a hotness-based snapshot format drops zero pages, places the hot working set in a pod-local CXL multi-headed-device (MHD) pool and cold pages in a cluster-wide RDMA pool. An ownership-based coherence protocol built on cross-host atomics (plus clflushopt on every "borrow") gives correctness on CXL 2.0 MHDs that lack hardware inter-host coherence. Restore pre-installs hot pages from CXL via uffd.copy/zeropage before resume and demand-pages cold pages asynchronously over RDMA; a pre-provisioned MicroVM skeleton pool removes control-plane latency.
papers.hardwareEnv: CloudLab Clemson r6525 node (single dual-socket machine): 2x AMD EPYC Milan 7543 @2.8 GHz, 32 cores; DRAM 2x 8x 16 GiB ECC DDR4-3200; 480 GiB Samsung PM883 SATA + 1.6 TiB Samsung PM1733 NVMe; control NIC 25 Gb/s ConnectX-5 MT27800; experiment NIC 100 Gb/s Mellanox ConnectX-6 Dx MT28924 (SR-IOV VFs via eSwitch, DOCA driver 2.9.3, FW 22.47.1088). No CXL hardware: the remote NUMA node's DRAM emulates the shared CXL MHD pool; two VMs (orchestrator + pool master, 16 pcores / 64 GiB each, pinned to one NUMA node) both map the region via virtio-pmem/DAX and use clflushopt to mimic non-coherence. Ubuntu 24.04, stock Linux 6.8.0, Firecracker v1.15 unmodified; Aquifer orchestrator + pool master in 5,953 LoC Rust.
papers.evalSetup: 9 serverless function workloads from FunctionBench and SeBS (chameleon, compression, json, ffmpeg, image, matmul, pagerank, pyaes, recognition) restored as Firecracker MicroVMs via userfaultfd; ablation of invocation-time stages on chameleon (32 concurrent restores); scalability sweep restoring n = 1..32 concurrent MicroVMs (recognition only to 16); end-to-end invocation time median+IQR.
papers.baselines: All adapted to run over the same RDMA pool: (1) Firecracker demand paging (every fault -> RDMA read + uffd.copy); (2) REAP (record-and-prefetch, adapted to RDMA); (3) FaaSnap (prefetch non-zero working set, adapted to RDMA); (4) FcTiered (Firecracker + Aquifer's hotness format and two-tier serving, no prefetch).
papers.keyFindings: Geometric-mean end-to-end invocation speedup of 2.2x over Firecracker, 1.3x over FaaSnap, 1.1x over REAP across 9 workloads; per-workload speedups over FaaSnap 1.00x (pyaes) to 1.57x (json), over REAP up to 1.35x (image). Ablation (chameleon, 32 concurrent): 2.12x lower total invocation time than Firecracker, 1.19x than FaaSnap; setup 1.45x/1.67x faster than FaaSnap/REAP; demand-paging baselines pay 187x higher page-installation cost. Fastest in 8 of 9 workloads; loses to REAP only on ffmpeg (many zero pages in working set that Aquifer skips prefetching). CXL-based page pre-installation is currently serialized and slower than parallel RDMA prefetch.
papers.limitations: Authors' own (Sec 3.6): coherence protocol assumes cross-host CXL atomics, which prior empirical work supports but the CXL 2.0 spec does not formally guarantee; assumes CXL pool capacity always fits all hot data (eviction only sketched); offline-profiled hot sets can go stale under input shift; single pool master is a single point of failure (Raft failover only proposed); snapshot deduplication not implemented. Methodology weaknesses: entirely NUMA-emulated CXL on ONE physical machine — two VMs on one dual-socket box stand in for two hosts sharing an MHD, so real MHD latency, coherence, and link-bandwidth behavior are untested; no real CXL device of any kind; remote-NUMA "latency characteristic" emulation, no bandwidth throttling described; RDMA "cluster" is SR-IOV VFs looped through one NIC's eSwitch; concurrency capped at 32 MicroVMs by the benchmarking harness; no multi-pod or true multi-node experiments; no interference or multi-tenant isolation study.
papers.openQuestions: Behavior on real CXL 2.0 MHD silicon (atomics support, actual cross-head latency/bandwidth contention); CXL pool eviction policy under capacity pressure; online hot-set refresh; automated pool-master failover; deduplication's cache-flush interference across MicroVMs sharing a host; parallelizing the currently serialized CXL page pre-install; scaling beyond 32 concurrent restores and beyond a single emulated pod.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Low direct hardware relevance: Aquifer has zero real CXL devices (remote-NUMA emulation of a multi-headed pool on one CloudLab box), so it says nothing empirical about per-device bandwidth, cross-device interference, or real CZ120 behavior — it actually strengthens the gap your 4x-CZ120 testbed can fill, since even a 2026 pooling paper still emulates. Conceptually adjacent to ObjPlace: its hotness-based hot/cold partition across a fast CXL tier and a slow far tier is page/snapshot-granularity tiering, and its finding that serialized CXL page pre-install underperforms parallel RDMA prefetch is a placement-runtime data point. Its ownership/clflushopt coherence protocol targets multi-headed cross-host sharing, which your single-host memory-expander devices do not exhibit; the closest tie to your "per-device independent resource" direction is that Aquifer treats the whole CXL pool as one flat region and never considers per-device scheduling or CXL-to-CXL interference — an explicit non-goal you could contrast against.
evidenceQuotes: Because CloudLab does not currently offer machines with CXL-attached memory devices, we emulate CXL memory using a remote NUMA node, following prior work [35]. We use a dual-socket r6525 node from the CloudLab Clemson cluster
CPU 2× AMD EPYC Milan 7543 @2.8 GHz, 32 cores / DRAM 2× 8× 16 GiB ECC DDR4-3200 / ... Experiment NIC 100 Gb/s Mellanox ConnectX-6 Dx MT28924 (Table 1: Hardware configuration of CloudLab r6525 nodes)

To emulate a shared CXL memory pool on a single dual-socket machine, we run two VMs on one NUMA node, one acting as the orchestrator and the other as the pool master, each pinned to 16 dedicated physical cores with 64 GiB of memory. The memory attached to the remote NUMA node serves as the CXL pool media, while emulating the access latency characteristic.

Although the two VMs share the same physical machine and thus have implicit cache coherence over the backing memory, we still treat the region as non-cache-coherent and require clflushopt on every borrow, emulating a CXL 2.0 MHD where no inter-host coherence is provided.
Overall, Aquifer achieves a geometric-mean speedup of 2.2× over Firecracker and 1.3 × over FaaSnap, with per-workload speedups over FaaSnap ranging from 1.00× under pyaes to 1.57× under json.

Aquifer's coherence protocol (§3.3) relies on atomic operations across hosts sharing a CXL MHD, an assumption supported by prior empirical findings [49] but not formally guaranteed by the CXL 2.0 specification [1].

papers.title: Xerxes: Extensive Exploration of Scalable Hardware Systems with CXL-Based Simulation Framework
papers.venue: FAST (USENIX Conference on File and Storage Technologies), 24th
papers.numCXLDevices: validation testbed: 1 physical CXL memory expander (Montage MXC M88MX5891 controller, 4x DDR5-4800 DIMMs, 128 GB, CXL 2.0 / PCIe 5.0 x16); all design-space experiments are simulated (1 to 64 simulated devices/endpoints)
papers.mainProblem: No hardware exists for the newest CXL 3.x features (port-based routing/PBR for non-tree fabrics, device-managed coherence/DMC via back-invalidate, PCIe 6.0 full-duplex), and existing tools cannot model them: NUMA-based emulation is physically limited to socket counts and tree topologies; gem5-style computation-centric simulators lack PCIe/CXL fabric detail; behavioral simulators (MESS, CXLMemSim) need ground-truth latency-bandwidth curves and miss cross-layer effects.
papers.mainIdea: Xerxes, a from-scratch simulation framework with two collaborating layers: a graph-based interconnect layer (topology graphs + shortest-path routing enabling arbitrary non-tree fabrics and peer-to-peer paths) and a device layer (requesters, buses with full-duplex bandwidth allocation, PBR switches with routing tables, device-side snoop filters implementing DMC with pluggable victim policies). Integrates with gem5 (full-system), DRAMsim3, and SimpleSSD; open-sourced at github.com/ChaseLab-PKU/Xerxes.
papers.hardwareEnv: Validation platform: dual-socket server, each socket an Intel Xeon Gold 6416H with 8x DDR5-4800 DIMMs (76.8 GB/s peak, 512 GB total main memory). One socket attaches one CXL memory expander using a Montage Technology MXC controller (M88MX5891), CXL 2.0 / PCIe 5.0 x16, containing 4x DDR5-4800 DIMMs = 128 GB CXL HDM-H memory; expander splits lanes (MCIO cable to remote socket) so each socket effectively gets PCIe 5.0 x8 (~24 GB/s practical). Kernel version not stated. All other experiments run inside the Xerxes simulator (DRAMsim3 endpoints; gem5 for full-system, cache hierarchy matched to hardware: 1.7 MB L1D, 72 MB L2, 96 MB L3).
papers.evalSetup: Three-stage validation: (1) MLC-driven idle latency, peak bandwidth at varying R:W ratios, and loaded latency measured on local DRAM / NUMA remote / real CXL expander vs. Xerxes synthetic requesters; (2) CXL 3.1 features (PBR, DMC) validated against theoretical performance models since no CXL 3.1 hardware exists; (3) end-to-end workload validation (execution-time overhead of CXL memory, SPEC-style workloads via gem5-Xerxes and trace-driven Xerxes-standalone) plus application traces (BTree, liblinear, redis, silo, XSBench). Design-space case studies simulate topologies (chain/tree/ring/spine-leaf/fully-connected) up to system scale 64, DMC snoop-filter policies (FIFO/LRU/LFI/LIFO/MRU), InvBlk lengths, and full-duplex PCIe with varying R:W mix and header overheads.
papers.baselines: Real CXL hardware (Montage MXC expander), NUMA-based emulation (remote socket, DIMM count matched to 4), behavioral simulators MESS and CXLMemSim (fed ground-truth hardware curves), and gem5-garnet as detailed architectural simulator.
papers.keyFindings: Accuracy vs. real CXL hardware: bandwidth errors 0.1-10%; loaded-latency curves average error 4.3%; end-to-end CXL-overhead errors as low as 0.7%, while MESS and CXLMemSim (even with ground-truth inputs) err up to 28.3% and 16.5% (avg 9.3%/16.6% on loaded latency), NUMA emulation up to 9.2%, gem5-garnet up to 9.0%. Speed: only ~2% simulation-time overhead over vanilla gem5 vs. 22.5% for garnet; large-scale simulations stay under 90 s up to scale 64. Case studies: tree/chain topologies bottleneck at 1x port bandwidth while spine-leaf/fully-connected scale (fully-connected gives up to 3.63x throughput and 0.28x latency vs. chain on real traces); scaling 1 to 16 endpoints behind switches raises average latency ~9x from port contention; LIFO snoop-filter victim policy improves bandwidth ~5% and latency ~15% over FIFO, LFI cuts invalidations ~15%; InvBlk length 2 helps but longer lengths do not; each +0.1 in read-write mix degree yields ~9% bandwidth gain on full-duplex links, but high header-to-payload ratios can negate the full-duplex benefit.
papers.limitations: Authors' own: no CXL 3.1 hardware exists, so PBR/DMC are validated only against theoretical models, not silicon ("Since hardware is unavailable for validation of CXL 3.1 features..."); end-to-end validation measures only CXL-induced execution-time overhead because exact CPU micro-architecture cannot be simulated. Methodological: the real testbed has just one CXL 2.0 device on an Intel (not AMD) platform, so all multi-device, multi-switch, and coherence results are purely simulated; latency parameters partly calibrated from prior-work empirical numbers; no real multi-tenant or OS-level (tiering, kernel) experiments; largest simulated scale is 64 devices, and DRAM-endpoint-only workload traces (no accelerators exercised in validation).
papers.openQuestions: Extending Xerxes to other coherent interconnects (Huawei UB, UB-Mesh topologies) is explicitly left as future work. Untested: validation of PBR/DMC against any real CXL 3.x silicon or FPGA once available; interaction with OS memory management / tiering policies; multi-tenant contention and QoS on shared fabrics; energy/power modeling; behavior at true rack scale beyond 64 devices.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Xerxes is a simulator, not a systems mechanism, so it does not compete with ObjPlace; its real testbed (1 Montage CXL 2.0 expander on Intel) is smaller than the requester's 4x CZ120 box. Its value here is as a what-if tool for the candidate per-device direction: it can simulate multiple independent CXL endpoints, switch port contention, and topologies, and its finding that latency rises ~9x when scaling from 1 to 16 endpoints behind switches (port contention) supports the thesis that cross-device interference and per-device scheduling matter. Its validation data (MLC loaded-latency curves on real hardware, ~24 GB/s practical per-socket CXL bandwidth) is a useful comparison point to the requester's 35.5 GiB/s 2-way-interleaved region. Conversely, Xerxes contains no data on real multi-device interference on one host, which leaves the requester's 4-device, CXL-to-CXL co-runner measurements unoccupied territory.
evidenceQuotes: Each socket is equipped with an Intel Xeon Gold 6416H CPU [11] and eight DDR5-4800 DRAM DIMMs, offering a peak bandwidth of 76.8 GB/s and providing 512 GB of main memory. One of the sockets is attached by a CXL memory expander with a CXL memory expander controller (MXC) from Montage Technology [9], supporting up to CXL 2.0 and PCIe 5.0 × 16 interconnections.
The memory expander consists of four DDR5-4800 DRAM DIMMs, providing 128 GB of CXL HDM-H memory.

Since hardware is unavailable for validation of CXL 3.1 features (e.g., PBR and DMC), we verify Xerxes’ correctness by comparing its simulation results against established theoretical performance models.
To simulate the CXL system, we construct an example system in Xerxes, which includes a requester, an interconnect bus, and four memory endpoints.
The validation experiment proves the accuracy of Xerxes with errors ranging from 0.1% to 10%.
The codes of Xerxes are open-sourced and available at https://github.com/ChaseLab-PKU/Xerxes.

papers.title: ReScue: Reliable and Secure CXL Memory
papers.venue: HPCA 2026 (IEEE International Symposium on High-Performance Computer Architecture)
papers.numCXLDevices: 1 (one Intel Agilex 7 I-series FPGA acting as a CXL Type-3 device)
papers.mainProblem: Hyperscalers want to recycle past-generation (e.g., DDR4) DRAM modules behind CXL memory expanders, but such recycled modules (i) contain many uncorrectable/unrepairable faulty words after years of strenuous hyperscale use, and (ii) are more vulnerable to modern attacks such as Row Hammer (and to timing side channels that reverse-engineer physical-to-DRAM address mappings) because their defenses were designed for older attack models. Additionally, host/controller AXI interface limitations under delayed CXL responses can cause full system hangs.
papers.mainIdea: A suite of in-CXL-controller hardware mechanisms that exploit two CXL-unique properties: variable-latency out-of-order responses and near-memory processing. ReScue-R stores the remap pointer to a fault-free block inside the faulty 64B block itself; on access to a faulty block it follows the pointer (with a Bloom filter to identify faulty blocks cheaply) and returns data without blocking subsequent accesses. ReScue-S shapes (equalizes/randomizes) memory-access latency at the device to defeat timing side channels used to reconstruct DRAM address mappings for Row Hammer. They also identify an AXI in-flight-command limitation that hangs the system under delayed CXL memory and validate a makeshift fix that caps in-flight commands. All implemented in RTL on a real Intel Agilex CXL platform.
papers.hardwareEnv: Host: "Intel Xeon scalable server with CXL support" (exact CPU model not stated in accessible sources). CXL device: one Intel Agilex 7 I-series FPGA (revision RBES) configured with Intel Agilex FPGA Hard IP for CXL as a CXL Type-3 memory device; link width/speed and attached DRAM module details not stated in accessible sources. OS: Linux kernel 6.5.5. FPGA tooling: Intel Quartus Prime Programmer.
papers.evalSetup: Four artifact experiment sets on the FPGA testbed: (1) system-hang reproduction with a delayed-CXL bitstream and a custom multithreaded microbenchmark sweeping RD:WR ratios and thread counts, plus validation of the in-flight-command-limiting makeshift (Fig. 4); (2) latency-distribution measurements of baseline CXL vs ReScue-S equalizer vs ReScue-S randomizer using a DRAMA-based latency harness (Figs. 11-12); (3) ReScue-S execution-time overhead on SPEC CPU2017 (Fig. 13); (4) ReScue-R overhead with/without a Bloom filter (e.g., 512Kb) (Fig. 10). GAPBS graph benchmarks also listed as performance workloads. Each configuration is a different FPGA bitstream programmed via Quartus followed by a host power cycle.
papers.baselines: Standard SECDED ECC (fault-tolerance comparison for ReScue-R); baseline (unmodified) CXL Type-3 FPGA design with no repair / no latency shaping; ReScue-R without Bloom filter; ReScue-S pure latency equalizer vs latency randomizer variants.
papers.keyFindings: ReScue-R achieves fault tolerance 9.6x10^4 times higher than standard SECDED ECC with only 0.2% performance degradation. ReScue-S prevents timing-based side-channel attacks (e.g., reconstructing physical-address-to-DRAM-address mapping functions for Row Hammer) at 1.1% performance degradation, merging the two CXL latency groups into one; the randomizer gives slightly lower average latency than pure equalization. They also demonstrate that high write intensity + high thread count triggers system hangs on an AXI-based CXL memory controller under delayed responses, and that limiting in-flight commands removes the hangs.
papers.limitations: Single FPGA CXL device only — no multi-device, no interleaving, no pooling, no multi-tenant experiments visible in the artifact. FPGA prototype latencies/bandwidth differ from production ASIC expanders (e.g., CZ120), so the 0.2%/1.1% overhead numbers may not transfer directly. The recycled-DDR4 fault model is central to the motivation, but the artifact documentation does not show evaluation on actually degraded recycled modules (fault injection/Bloom-filter configs suggest modeled faults). Full paper text is paywalled, so authors' own stated limitations could not be read; workload coverage in the artifact is limited to SPEC CPU2017, GAPBS, DRAMA, and custom microbenchmarks — no datacenter/LLM/multi-tenant workloads.
papers.openQuestions: Behavior with multiple CXL devices or interleaved regions (does per-device latency shaping interact badly with host interleaving?); interaction of ReScue-S latency randomization with host-side tiering/placement policies that assume stable CXL latency; scalability of the block-remap scheme as fault density grows over module lifetime; whether the AXI in-flight-command hang and makeshift generalize to production ASIC controllers; security analysis against adaptive attackers who average over randomized latencies.
evidenceQuotes: All experiments are evaluated on an Intel Agilex FPGA–based CXL Type-3 device connected to an Intel Xeon system.
Device: **Intel Agilex 7 I-series FPGA (revision version RBES)** (CXL Type-3 device) configured with Intel Agilex FPGA Hard IP for CXL.
Host: Intel Xeon scalable server with **CXL support**.
OS: Linux with **kernel 6.5.5** (or compatible) configured and selected as default.

ReScue-R stores the remapping addresses to fault-free blocks in faulty 64-byte blocks... accomplishing fault tolerance 9.6 × 10^4 times higher than standard SECDED ECC with only 0.2% performance degradation. (HPCA program page abstract)

ReScue-S shapes the latency of memory accesses to prevent timing-based side-channel attacks, such as reconstructing physical-address-to-DRAM-address mapping functions for Row Hammer attacks, with 1.1% performance degradation. (HPCA program page abstract)
Compare latency distributions of Baseline CXL design, eScue-S latency equalizer and ReScue-S latency randomizer.
Evaluate performance impact of ReScue-R under: Baseline (no repair) and ReScue-R with Bloom filter (e.g., 512Kb)
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Low direct relevance to the requester's direction: ReScue is a device-controller (RTL) paper on a single FPGA CXL Type-3 prototype, not host-side placement or multi-device scheduling on ASIC expanders like the CZ120s. Two useful touchpoints: (1) it documents that CXL devices legitimately return variable-latency out-of-order responses and can even hang AXI-based controllers under high write intensity — a device-side source of tail-latency variance the requester's per-device QoS/interference story could cite; (2) ReScue-S deliberately reshapes/randomizes per-device latency, which would confound any host-side placement runtime (like ObjPlace) that profiles per-device latency — an interesting adversarial consideration but not a baseline. Nothing here addresses multi-device interleaving, cross-device interference, or multi-tenant isolation.
