papers.title: Where are the Joules? Energy Demand Analysis of Heterogeneous Memory Technologies
papers.venue: HCDS 2025 (4th Workshop on Heterogeneous Composable and Disaggregated Systems, co-located with EuroSys/ASPLOS, Rotterdam) — lightning talk, ACM, DOI 10.1145/3723851.3723857
papers.numCXLDevices: 0 (no CXL device in the presented measurements; CXL-equipped systems are explicitly listed as future work in the author slides)
papers.mainProblem: System provisioners lack conclusive, comparable energy-consumption data for emerging heterogeneous memory technologies (DRAM, NVRAM/persistent memory, CXL): existing data is "too minimal or too specific" to guide energy-optimized memory selection.
papers.mainIdea: meBench, a memory-agnostic configurable workload generator that sweeps read/write ratio, access pattern (sequential/random), access granularity, parallelism, NUMA placement, and cache optimizations (normal / non-temporal / clflush), and measures energy per data volume (J/GiB) using Intel RAPL and an external power meter, to systematically characterize the energy demand of different memory technologies.
papers.hardwareEnv: Not fully verifiable from the slides. Measured technologies: DRAM vs NVRAM (persistent memory; vendor/model not stated in slides — keywords per search results mention Optane), on a multi-socket NUMA machine (near vs far memory experiments). Slide-stated run configs: "2 cores, 32 threads, ... 80 s duration". CPU model, DRAM config, kernel version not given in the slides; no CXL device present in any measurement.
papers.evalSetup: Synthetic microbenchmarks generated by meBench: read-only / mixed / write-only workloads, sequential vs random access, with cache-optimization variants (normal stores, non-temporal stores, clflush), and NUMA near vs far placement; energy measured via Intel RAPL plus an external power meter; results reported as J/GiB (2 cores, 32 threads, 80 s per run).
papers.baselines: No system baselines — it is a characterization/benchmark-tool paper comparing memory technologies (DRAM vs NVRAM) against each other; authors position it as improving on prior "theoretic carbon analysis" work.
papers.keyFindings: From the slide charts (J/GiB): reads are cheap on both (DRAM ~0.1, NVRAM ~0.6-1.9); writes are where NVRAM's energy cost explodes: sequential/random NVRAM writes ~20.1-20.6 J/GiB vs DRAM ~0.7-1.6 J/GiB (~13-25x). Cache-optimization choice dominates NVRAM write energy: non-temporal stores ~14.9-21.6 J/GiB, clflush pushes NVRAM to 36.5-43.0 J/GiB vs DRAM 1.6-3.4. NUMA distance barely matters for energy-per-GiB: DRAM near 0.8 vs far 0.8; NVRAM near 20.6 vs far 21.2 J/GiB.
papers.limitations: CXL is in the title framing/keywords but is NOT measured — the slides explicitly defer "more in-depth measurements ... of CXL-equipped systems" to future work; only DRAM and NVRAM are characterized. Synthetic microbenchmarks only (no application workloads); short workshop/lightning-talk scope; energy attribution relies on RAPL plus one external meter (whole-system attribution deferred as future work); testbed details (CPU, DIMM models) not visible in the material I could access.
papers.openQuestions: Authors explicitly punt on: extending meBench to more access patterns and architectures; in-depth measurements of the entire system's energy (not just memory-domain RAPL); and, most relevantly, energy measurements of CXL-equipped systems. Untested: any CXL device energy, multi-device or multi-tenant scenarios, real application workloads, energy-aware placement policies built on the data.
papers.relevanceTo4Dev: Low direct relevance: despite CXL in its keywords, the paper measures only DRAM vs NVRAM energy and defers CXL to future work, so it offers no data on CZ120-class devices, multi-device setups, or interference. Its indirect value is methodological: the meBench J/GiB methodology (RAPL + external meter, per-technology and near/far NUMA sweeps) could be replicated on the requester's 4x CZ120 box to add an energy dimension (per-device energy under placement/interference) to ObjPlace or a per-device-scheduling paper — an angle this workshop paper shows is still open for CXL. It provides no guidance on treating CXL devices as independently schedulable resources.

corrections.to: 0 CXL devices. The slow tier is 4x 128GB Intel persistent memory modules (512GB PM) on one socket; fast tier is 4x 16GB DDR4 (64GB DRAM).

corrections.paper: ArtMem: Adaptive Migration in Reinforcement Learning-Enabled Tiered Memory
corrections.to: Two-tier DRAM + Optane-style persistent memory: kernel distinguishes tiers by hardcoded physical address ranges (DRAM below 0x2080000000, PM above), samples accesses via Intel PEBS (MEM_LOAD_L3_MISS_RETIRED.LOCAL_DRAM etc.), and enforces per-NUMA-node capacity via cgroup 'memory.max_at_node${NODE_ID}'. Not CXL devices, not CXL-interleaving; single-socket 64GB DRAM / 512GB PM evaluation.
